paras.en: Lastly, in these words, by kings, judges and princes are to be understood the heads of both jurisdictions [Latin *utriusque juris*, "of both laws", that is, of the Church and of the civil power], namely rulers spiritual as well as secular; indeed the spiritual above all, whose dignity is far greater and who are bound to a greater perfection. These two jurisdictions are the two swords [the "two swords" of Luke 22:38, long read as the spiritual and the temporal power], the two eyes, and the two great lights in the very body of the Church; but as the sun is greater and brighter than the moon, so the spiritual power is more excellent and more luminous than the secular. And as the sun lights the moon, so the spiritual power has to teach and direct the secular, as the soul does the body.

paras.t: Itaque, o præsidentes, advertite ista, Quoniam data est a Domino potestas vobis prælatica, præsidentialis auctoritas, et temporale dominium, et virtus punitiva et correctiva reorum, ab Altissimo : quia non est potestas nisi a Deo, teste Apostolo, imo et Christo, qui dixit Pilato : Non haberes adversus me potestatem ullam, nisi datum tibi esset desuper. Hinc sæculares quoque principes, secundum Apostolum, ministri atque vicarii Dei sunt. Nec obstat quod Dominus loquitur per Osee, de vitiosis principibus : de quibus agitur et hic, quia paulo post subditur, Quum essetis ministri regni illius, non recte judicastis : non, inquam, obstat quod per Osee locutus est Dominus : Ipsi regnaverunt, et non ex me ; principes exstiterunt, et non cognovi. Ex quibus verbis sequi videtur, quod non acceperunt suam a Domino potestatem. Et respondendum, quod potestas ipsa a Deo est, non autem potestatis abusus, ob quem dicuntur non regnasse ex Deo, nisi permissive : secundum quod apud eumdem Prophetam protestatur, Dabo tibi regem in furore meo. De quo etiam in libro Job asseritur : Qui regnare facit hominem hypocritam, propter peccata populi.
paras.en: Therefore, O you who preside, mark these things: [[6:4|For power is given you by the Lord|Quoniam data est a Domino potestas vobis]], prelatical power, the authority to preside, and temporal dominion, [[6:4|and strength|et virtus]] to punish and correct the guilty, [[6:4|by the most High|ab Altissimo]]: for [[Rom 13:1|there is no power but from God|non est potestas nisi a Deo]], as the Apostle witnesses, and indeed Christ too, who said to Pilate: [[John 19:11|Thou shouldst not have any power against me, unless it were given thee from above|Non haberes adversus me potestatem ullam, nisi datum tibi esset desuper]]. Hence secular princes too, according to the Apostle, are ministers and vicars of God[[Rom 13:4||]][[Rom 13:6||]]. Nor is it against this that the Lord speaks through Osee of vicious princes (and such are spoken of here too, for shortly after it is added: [[6:5|being ministers of his kingdom, you have not judged rightly|Quum essetis ministri regni illius, non recte judicastis]]); it is not, I say, against this that the Lord spoke through Osee: [[Osee 8:4|They have reigned, but not by me: they have been princes, and I knew not|Ipsi regnaverunt, et non ex me ; principes exstiterunt, et non cognovi]]. From these words it seems to follow that they did not receive their power from the Lord. And the answer is that the power itself is from God, but not the abuse of the power, on account of which they are said not to have reigned from God, except by His permission; as He declares in the same Prophet: [[Osee 13:11|I will give thee a king in my wrath|Dabo tibi regem in furore meo]] [the margin gives Osee xiii without a verse; the words are in 13:11]. Of which it is also asserted in the book of Job: [[Job 34:30|Who maketh a man that is a hypocrite to reign for the sins of the people.|Qui regnare facit hominem hypocritam, propter peccata populi]]

paras.t: Qui interrogabit opera vestra, id est, examinabit vos de actibus vestris, imo et de omissionibus agendorum ; et cogitationes scrutabitur, id est, non solum opera vestra exteriora, sed et actus vestros interiores, videlicet cogitationes et affectiones, discutiet, dijudicabit, discernet.
paras.en: [[6:4|who will examine your works|Qui interrogabit opera vestra]], that is, He will examine you on your deeds, and indeed on your omissions of what was to be done; [[6:4|and search out your thoughts|et cogitationes scrutabitur]]: that is, not only your outward works but your inward acts too, namely your thoughts and affections, He will sift, judge and discern.

paras.t: Quoniam quum essetis ministri regni illius, id est servi et vicarii Dei in regimine populi ejus. Quocirca inquiritur, qualiter vitiosi præsidentes, etiam infideles, dicantur servi Dei atque ministri. Respondetur, quod servi sunt Dei, non servitute caritatis ac obedientiæ salutaris, sed ratione generalis subjectionis, et quantum ad id quod bene agunt, loquendo de bene agere in genere. Sic enim subserviunt Deo, etiam ignorantes, juxta illud : Dei minister est, in iram ei qui male agit. Nam et per eos Deus providentiæ suæ effectus prosequitur, prout ibidem rursus asserit Paulus : Dei ministri sunt, in hoc ipsum servientes. Non recte judicastis subditos vestros, imo nec vosmetipsos : si enim vos ipsos dijudicaretis, vitam vestram corrigeretis ; nec custodistis legem justitiæ, id est legem naturalem : cujus renovatio atque suppletio fuit lex scripta; utramque vero evangelica lex perfecit. Unde potest per legem justitiæ, Decalogus accipi, cujus præcepta sunt de operibus justitiæ. Neque secundum voluntatem Dei ambulastis, servando præcepta, et exemplariter coram subditis conversando ac sine personarum acceptione proferendo sententiam, et castigando peccantes. Nempe, ut ait Ambrosius : Maximum crimen in præsidentibus est, quod attendunt personas, non causas.
paras.en: [[6:5|Because being ministers of his kingdom|Quoniam quum essetis ministri regni illius]], that is, servants and vicars of God in the governing of His people. Here it is asked how vicious rulers, even unbelievers, are called servants and ministers of God. The answer is that they are God's servants not by the service of charity and of saving obedience, but by reason of a general subjection, and as regards what they do well, speaking of doing well in its kind [that is, of an act good in its outward kind, not of one done in charity]. For in this way they serve God even without knowing it, according to that saying: He is [[Rom 13:4|God's minister: an avenger to execute wrath upon him that doth evil|Dei minister est, in iram ei qui male agit]]. For through them too God carries out the effects of His providence, as Paul again asserts in the same place: [[Rom 13:6|they are the ministers of God, serving unto this purpose|Dei ministri sunt, in hoc ipsum servientes]]. [[6:5|you have not judged rightly|Non recte judicastis]] your subjects, nor indeed yourselves: for if you judged yourselves, you would amend your life; [[6:5|nor kept the law of justice|nec custodistis legem justitiæ]], that is, the natural law, whose renewal and supplement was the written law, while the law of the Gospel perfected both. Hence by the law of justice the Decalogue may be understood, whose precepts concern works of justice. [[6:5|nor walked according to the will of God|Neque secundum voluntatem Dei ambulastis]], by keeping the commandments, by living as an example before your subjects, by passing sentence without respect of persons, and by chastising those who sin. For, as Ambrose says: The greatest crime in those who preside is that they look to persons, not to causes.

paras.t: Horrende et cito apparebit vobis, id est, terribiliter ac celeriter judicabit vos, et per justitiæ suæ effectum, per præfatam discussionem ac reprobationem vobis apparebit, non solum in generali judicio, sed et in hora mortis vestræ per particulare judicium, mox ut anima fuerit separata a corpore, dicente Apostolo ad Hebræos : Statutum est hominibus semel mori, post hoc autem judicium. Unde legitur apud Jacobum : Ecce Judex ante januam adsistit.
paras.en: [[6:6|Horribly and speedily will he appear to you|Horrende et cito apparebit vobis]]: that is, He will judge you terribly and swiftly, and will appear to you by the effect of His justice, through the sifting and rejection spoken of above, not only at the general judgment but also at the hour of your death, in the particular judgment, as soon as the soul is parted from the body; as the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 9:27|it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment|Statutum est hominibus semel mori, post hoc autem judicium]]. Hence we read in James: [[Jas 5:9|Behold the judge standeth before the door|Ecce Judex ante januam adsistit]].

paras.t: Quoniam judicium durissimum in his qui præsunt, fiet : id est, ipsos præsidentes Judex cœlestis districtissime judicabit atque acerrime puniet, si præfato modo habuerint se. Eorum enim peccata, ceteris paribus, sunt graviora : quia quo gradus et dignitas altior, eo lapsus major et gravior; et quo dignioris sunt officii, eo virtuosiores esse tenentur. Eorum quoque peccata plurimos scandalizant, et maximum damnum inferunt Deo : quia suis scandalositatibus, negligentiis, et perversitatibus plures trahunt ad damnationem. Sunt etiam maxime infideles ingratique Deo, cujus vices gerunt, nec implent. Insuper, quum de suis dignitatibus atque officiis consequantur a subditis suis commoda et honores, nec tamen condigna suorum exsecutione officiorum hæc mereantur; nec subjectis impendant quod eis tenentur, sed eos potius scandalizent, gravent, ac perdant : nonne justissimum est, ut durissimum seu rigorosissimum eis fiat judicium? Hinc Jacobus in sua scribit Canonica : Nolite plures magistri fieri, fratres mei, scientes quia gravius judicium accipitis. Itaque, quo plus evadunt humana judicia, eo horribilius incidunt in divina; et qui nunc per præsidentes punit vitia subditorum, paulo post per se ipsum puniet præsidentium scelera. Qui, ut in Job habetur, dicit regi, Apostata; qui vocat duces, impios; qui non accipit personas principum, nec cognovit tyrannum.
paras.en: [[6:6|for a most severe judgment shall be for them that bear rule|Quoniam judicium durissimum in his qui præsunt, fiet]]: that is, the heavenly Judge will judge those who preside most strictly and punish them most sharply, if they have behaved in the way described. For their sins, other things being equal, are graver: because the higher the rank and dignity, the greater and graver the fall; and the worthier their office, the more virtuous they are bound to be. Their sins also scandalize a great many and do God the greatest harm, since by their scandals, negligences and perversities they draw many to damnation. They are also most unfaithful and ungrateful to God, whose place they hold and do not fill. Moreover, since from their dignities and offices they obtain advantages and honours from their subjects, and yet do not earn them by a worthy discharge of their offices, nor render to those beneath them what they owe them, but rather scandalize, burden and ruin them: is it not most just that a most severe, or most rigorous, judgment should be passed on them? Hence James writes in his Epistle [Latin *Canonica*, his "canonical epistle"]: [[Jas 3:1|Be ye not many masters, my brethren, knowing that you receive the greater judgment|Nolite plures magistri fieri, fratres mei, scientes quia gravius judicium accipitis]]. And so, the more they escape human judgments, the more dreadfully they fall into the divine; and He who now through those who preside punishes the vices of subjects will shortly punish by Himself the crimes of those who preside: He who, as we have it in Job, [[Job 34:18|saith to the king: Thou art an apostate: who calleth rulers ungodly|dicit regi, Apostata; qui vocat duces, impios]]; [[Job 34:19|Who accepteth not the persons of princes: nor hath regarded the tyrant|qui non accipit personas principum, nec cognovit tyrannum]].

paras.t: Exiguo enim conceditur misericordia, id est, hominibus egenis et parvi status, facilius Deus ignoscit, et mitius judicat eos : quia et, ceteris paribus, minora sunt eorum peccata, id est, in hac vita plura habent adversa, et a majoribus corripiuntur. Ideo loquitur Isaias : Pauperum suorum miserebitur. Tales quoque communiter ex infirmitate vel ignorantia peccant. Potentes autem potenter, id est intense et acriter, tormenta patientur. Non de omnibus potentibus dictum est hoc, quum scriptum sit, Deus potentes non abjicit, quum et ipse sit potens; sed de potentibus violentis, superbis, concessa sibi potentia abutentibus : de quibus gloriosissima Virgo, Deposuit, inquit, potentes de sede.
paras.en: [[6:7|For to him that is little, mercy is granted|Exiguo enim conceditur misericordia]]: that is, God pardons more readily men who are needy and of low estate, and judges them more mildly: because, other things being equal, their sins are lesser; and [the Latin has *id est*, "that is", where the sense asks for "and also"] in this life they have more adversities, and are corrected by their betters. Therefore Isaias says: He [[Is 49:13|will have mercy on his poor ones|Pauperum suorum miserebitur]]. Such men also commonly sin out of weakness or ignorance. [[6:7|but the mighty|Potentes autem]] shall be [[6:7|mightily|potenter]], that is, intensely and sharply, [[6:7|tormented|tormenta patientur]]. This is not said of all the mighty, since it is written: [[Job 36:5|God doth not cast away the mighty, whereas he himself also is mighty.|Deus potentes non abjicit, quum et ipse sit potens]] It is said of the mighty who are violent and proud and abuse the power granted them, of whom the most glorious Virgin says: [[Luke 1:52|He hath put down|Deposuit]] (she says) [[Luke 1:52|the mighty from their seat|potentes de sede]].

paras.t: Non enim subtrahet personam cujusquam Deus, qui est omnium dominator : id est, nullum quantumlibet parvum, a sua providentia et judicio eximit aut excludit, nec ab eo, quod meruit, demit aut removet in hora judicii ejus; nec verebitur magnitudinem cujusquam, quum ipse sit omnibus infinite potentior. Qui ait per Jeremiam : Quis similis mei? aut quis sustinebit me? aut quis est iste pastor, qui resistat vultui meo? Quoniam pusillum et magnum ipse fecit : nulla autem est comparatio creaturæ ad Creatorem, sicut nec finiti ad infinitum; et æqualiter est illi cura de omnibus hominibus, scilicet pusillis et magnis. Porro cura in Deo, non est aliqua inquieta sollicitudo, sed tranquillissima providentia ejus, quæ in ipso omnium invariabili provisore, una ac simplex est : et loquendo de hominibus, ut homines sunt, sic æqualiter est ei cura de omnibus, et omnes vult fieri salvos, nec est apud eum personarum acceptio. Verumtamen, loquendo in speciali, secundum quod aliqui sunt electi, aliqui reprobi; et hoc, in multiplici differentia, quoniam quidam sunt magis aut minus electi et justi, aliqui vero magis aut minus injusti ac reprobi : secundum hoc habet omnipotens Deus de aliquibus curam et providentiam magis aut minus specialem.
paras.en: [[6:8|For God will not except any man's person|Non enim subtrahet personam cujusquam Deus]], He who is the Lord of all [these words, *qui est omnium dominator*, stand in Denis's text of the verse but not in the Clementine Vulgate]: that is, He exempts or shuts out no one, however small, from His providence and judgment, nor takes away or removes from anyone what he has deserved, in the hour of His judgment; [[6:8|neither will he stand in awe of any man's greatness|nec verebitur magnitudinem cujusquam]], since He is infinitely mightier than all. He it is who says through Jeremias: [[Jer 49:19|who is like to me? and who shall abide me? and who is that shepherd that can withstand my countenance?|Quis similis mei? aut quis sustinebit me? aut quis est iste pastor, qui resistat vultui meo?]][[Jer 50:44||]] [[6:8|for he made the little and the great|Quoniam pusillum et magnum ipse fecit]]: and there is no comparison between creature and Creator, as there is none between finite and infinite; [[6:8|and he hath equally care of all|et æqualiter est illi cura de omnibus]] men, that is, of the little and the great. Now care in God is not some restless anxiety, but His most tranquil providence, which in Him, the unchanging provider of all things, is one and simple: and speaking of men as men, He has thus an equal care of all, and [[1 Tim 2:4|will have all men to be saved|omnes vult fieri salvos]], and [[Eph 6:9|there is no respect of persons with him|est apud eum personarum acceptio]][[2 Par 19:7||]][[Rom 2:11||]][[Col 3:25||]][[1 Pet 1:17||]]. Yet, speaking in particular, according as some are elect and some reprobate, and this with manifold difference, since some are more or less elect and just, others more or less unjust and reprobate: in this respect almighty God has a care and providence for some that is more or less special.

paras.t: Fortioribus autem fortitudine sua detestabiliter abutentibus, fortior instat cruciatio.
paras.en: But [[6:9|for the more mighty|Fortioribus]], who detestably abuse their might, [[6:9|a greater punishment is ready|fortior instat cruciatio]].

paras.t: Ad vos ergo, reges, id est præsidentes in ecclesiastico aut civili regimine, sunt hi sermones mei : quia vos specialiter cupio informare, tamen ad subditorum profectum, quibus valde prodest bona majorum instructio ; ut discatis sapientiam, et non excidatis, id est, non deficiatis a tenore justitiæ et veritatis agnitione.
paras.en: [[6:10|To you, therefore, O kings|Ad vos ergo, reges]], that is, you who preside in Church or civil government, [[6:10|are these my words|sunt hi sermones mei]]: for it is you especially that I wish to instruct, yet for the profit of your subjects, to whom good instruction from their superiors is of great benefit; [[6:10|that you may learn wisdom, and not fall from it|ut discatis sapientiam, et non excidatis]]: that is, that you may not fall away from the course of justice and from the knowledge of the truth.

paras.t: Qui enim custodierint justitiam, id est, in veritate et observatione justitiæ usque in finem permanserint, prout sanctus Job fatetur : Donec deficiam, non recedam ab innocentia mea ; justificationem quam cœpi tenere, non deseram ; juste judicabuntur. Certum est quod etiam impii juste judicabuntur : ideo istud intelligendum est de judicio approbationis et beatæ remunerationis, de quo ait Propheta, Judica me, Domine, secundum justitiam meam, et secundum innocentiam meam super me. Et qui didicerint justa, id est divina præcepta et jura, ac sacræ Scripturæ sapientialia documenta, ita ut faciant ea, invenient quid respondeant, id est, in judicio pro se rationem reddere poterunt. Proponentibus quoque sibi dubia, dabunt veram solutionem ; et inquirentibus rationem et expositionem eorum quæ fidei sunt, promptum dabunt responsum. Unde admonet princeps Apostolorum : Parati semper ad satisfactionem omni petenti vos rationem de ea, quæ in vobis est, fide et spe. Unde et Paulus de institutione episcopi loquens, ait : Potens sit exhortari in doctrina sana, et eis qui contradicunt, resistere.
paras.en: [[6:11|For they that have kept|Qui enim custodierint]] justice [Denis reads *custodierint justitiam … juste judicabuntur*, "have kept justice … shall be judged justly"; the Vulgate has *custodierint justa juste, justificabuntur*, "have kept just things justly, shall be justified"], that is, have persevered to the end in the truth and observance of justice, as holy Job declares: [[Job 27:5|till I die I will not depart from my innocence|Donec deficiam, non recedam ab innocentia mea]]; [[Job 27:6|My justification, which I have begun to hold, I will not forsake|justificationem quam cœpi tenere, non deseram]]; they shall be judged [[6:11|justly|juste]]. It is certain that the wicked too will be judged justly; so this is to be understood of the judgment of approval and of blessed reward, of which the Prophet says: [[Ps 7:9|Judge me, O Lord, according to my justice, and according to my innocence in me|Judica me, Domine, secundum justitiam meam, et secundum innocentiam meam super me]]. [[6:11|and they that have learned|Et qui didicerint]] just things [Denis reads *justa*, "just things", where the Vulgate has *ista*, "these things"], that is, the divine commandments and laws and the wise teachings of Holy Scripture, so as to do them, [[6:11|shall find what to answer|invenient quid respondeant]]: that is, they will be able to give an account for themselves at the judgment. To those also who put doubts to them they will give the true solution; and to those who ask the reason and explanation of the things of faith they will give a ready answer. Hence the prince of the Apostles admonishes: [[1 Pet 3:15|being ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you|Parati semper ad satisfactionem omni petenti vos rationem de ea, quæ in vobis est, fide et spe]] [Denis reads *fide et spe*, "of that faith and hope"; the Vulgate has *spe*, "hope", alone]. Hence Paul too, speaking of the appointing of a bishop, says: that he [[Tit 1:9|may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and to convince the gainsayers|Potens sit exhortari in doctrina sana, et eis qui contradicunt, resistere]] [Denis reads *eis qui contradicunt resistere*, "to resist the gainsayers"; the margin gives the Vulgate's readings *eos* and *arguere*, "to convince"].

paras.t: Concupiscite ergo concupiscentia intellectuali : de qua in Psalmo, Concupiscit et defecit anima mea in atria Domini; sermones meos, et diligite illos, et habebitis disciplinam, id est scientiam a magistris acceptam ; correptionem quoque libenter accipietis.
paras.en: [[6:12|Covet ye, therefore,|Concupiscite ergo]] with an intellectual desire [Latin *concupiscentia*, the noun of the verb "covet"], of which it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 83:3|my soul longeth and fainteth for the courts of the Lord|Concupiscit et defecit anima mea in atria Domini]] [*Concupiscit*, "longeth", is the same verb again]; [[6:12|my words|sermones meos]], [[6:12|and love them|et diligite illos]], [[6:12|and you shall have instruction|et habebitis disciplinam]], that is, knowledge received from masters; you will also accept correction willingly [*disciplina* means both "instruction" and "correction"].

paras.t: Denique quæ sequuntur, de increata Sapientia accipi possunt, de sapientia quoque quæ est donum præcipuum Spiritus.
paras.en: Further, what follows can be taken of the uncreated Wisdom, and also of the wisdom that is the chief gift of the Spirit.

paras.t: Clara est, et quæ numquam marcescit, sapientia. Increata etenim Sapientia, est lux puritatis immensæ, et veritas superpulcherrima omnino invariabilis, ut infra magis patebit. Et facile videtur ab his qui diligunt eam : quia per fidem formatam ac donum sapientiæ eam contemplantur; et invenitur ab his qui quærunt illam. Ipsa enim hortatur ac protestatur : Quærite, et invenietis; pulsate, et aperietur vobis. Omnis enim qui petit, accipit; et qui quærit, invenit.
paras.en: [[6:13|Wisdom is glorious, and never fadeth away|Clara est, et quæ numquam marcescit, sapientia]]. For the uncreated Wisdom is the light of boundless purity, and truth surpassingly beautiful and wholly unchangeable, as will appear more fully below. [[6:13|and is easily seen by them that love her|Et facile videtur ab his qui diligunt eam]]: for they contemplate her by formed faith [that is, faith given life by charity] and by the gift of wisdom; [[6:13|and is found by them that seek her|et invenitur ab his qui quærunt illam]]. For she herself exhorts and declares: [[Matt 7:7|seek, and you shall find: knock, and it shall be opened to you|Quærite, et invenietis; pulsate, et aperietur vobis]]. [[Matt 7:8|For every one that asketh, receiveth: and he that seeketh, findeth|Omnis enim qui petit, accipit; et qui quærit, invenit]].

paras.t: Præoccupat qui se concupiscunt, id est, gratiose prævenit eos, et frequenter eos illuminat et accendit, antequam rogent, sicut ait vir sanctus : Misericordia ejus prævenient me; ut illis se prior ostendat per illuminationem internam : tamen in hac vita communiter per speculum in ænigmate. Nam et ipsa inquit : Ego sto ad ostium, et pulso; atque in Canticis, Aperi mihi, soror mea, sponsa.
paras.en: [[6:14|She preventeth them that covet her|Præoccupat qui se concupiscunt]] [*prevent* in its old sense, "go before"], that is, she graciously goes before them, and often enlightens and kindles them before they ask, as the holy man says: [[Ps 58:11|his mercy shall prevent me|Misericordia ejus prævenient me]]; [[6:14|so that she first sheweth herself unto them|ut illis se prior ostendat]] by inward enlightening: yet in this life commonly [[1 Cor 13:12|through a glass in a dark manner|per speculum in ænigmate]]. For she herself says: [[Apoc 3:20|I stand at the gate and knock|Ego sto ad ostium, et pulso]]; and in the Canticles: [[Cant 5:2|Open to me, my sister|Aperi mihi, soror mea]], my spouse [Denis has *sponsa*, "spouse", where this verse reads *amica mea*, "my love"; "my sister, my spouse" is the phrase of Cant 4:9–12].

paras.t: Qui de luce vigilaverit ad illam, id est, cito ac mane, et statim in exordio illustrationis internæ, diligenter et fervide applicuerit ac disposuerit se ad eam, non laborabit, id est, non indigebit multum fatigari pro ejus adeptione, infusione seu incremento. Quum enim fecerit homo quod suum est, Deus gratiam mox apponit aut perficit. Ideo subditur : assidentem enim illam foribus suis inveniet, id est prompte et ultro se offerentem, ac per exteriorum sensuum objecta se ingerentem ac præsentantem : quia in illis, tanquam in effectibus suis, relucet.
paras.en: [[6:15|He that awaketh early to seek her|Qui de luce vigilaverit ad illam]] [Latin *de luce*, "at daybreak"], that is, he who quickly and in the morning, at once at the very beginning of the inward enlightening, applies and disposes himself to her diligently and fervently, [[6:15|shall not labour|non laborabit]]: that is, he will not need to toil much for her attainment, her infusion or her increase. For when a man has done what is his to do, God soon adds or perfects His grace. Therefore it is added: [[6:15|for he shall find her sitting at his door|assidentem enim illam foribus suis inveniet]], that is, offering herself readily and of her own accord, and pressing in upon him and presenting herself through the objects of the outward senses: for she shines in them, as in her effects.

paras.t: Cogitare ergo de illa, sensus est consummatus : id est, perfectio intellectus consistit in consideratione et contemplatione Sapientiæ hujus : secundum quod ait ad Patrem, Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum, et quem misisti Jesum Christum; et per Jeremiam, In hoc glorietur, qui gloriatur, scire et nosse me. Et qui vigilaverit propter illam, id est, continuando vigilias oraverit, et per alia exercitia studuerit pro ejus infusione et incremento, cito securus erit : id est, in ea et per eam in tantum proficiet, quod vanum et inordinatum timorem excludet, et confidens ac constans erit in Domino, et tanquam leo confidens, absque terrore quiescet. Sicque conveniet sibi, et experietur quod scriptum est : Secura mens quasi juge convivium. Omnia bona hæc confert sapientia. Propter quod in Proverbiis dictum est : Vir sapiens fortis est, et vir doctus robustus. Contemplatur etenim Omnipotentem ubique præsentem, atque sperantes in se protegentem, sine cujus permissione nil potest pars adversa inferre. Ideo dixit vir sanctus : Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea : quem timebo?
paras.en: [[6:16|To think, therefore, upon her, is perfect understanding|Cogitare ergo de illa, sensus est consummatus]]: that is, the perfection of the intellect consists in the consideration and contemplation of this Wisdom; as He says to the Father: [[John 17:3|this is eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent|Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum, et quem misisti Jesum Christum]]; and through Jeremias: [[Jer 9:24|let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me|In hoc glorietur, qui gloriatur, scire et nosse me]]. [[6:16|and he that watcheth for her|Et qui vigilaverit propter illam]], that is, he who has prayed in continued vigils and striven by other exercises for her infusion and increase, [[6:16|shall quickly be secure|cito securus erit]]: that is, he will so far advance in her and through her that he will shut out vain and disordered fear, and will be confident and steadfast in the Lord, and, [[Prov 28:1|bold as a lion|leo confidens]], will rest [[Prov 28:1|without dread|absque terrore]]. And so there will befit him, and he will experience, what is written: [[Prov 15:15|a secure mind is like a continual feast|Secura mens quasi juge convivium]]. All these good things wisdom bestows. Wherefore it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 24:5|A wise man is strong: and a knowing man, stout|Vir sapiens fortis est, et vir doctus robustus]]. For he contemplates the Almighty, present everywhere and protecting those who hope in Him, without whose permission the adversary can inflict nothing. Therefore the holy man said: [[Ps 26:1|The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?|Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea : quem timebo?]]

paras.t: Quoniam dignos se ipsa circuit, id est, undique protegit et custodit, quærens ut quæratur, id est, instigans ad se inquirendam, et in viis suis ostendens se illis hilariter, id est, in actibus sibi placentibus, scilicet exsecutionibus præceptorum, præsertim in adimpletione præceptorum caritatis Dei ac proximi, gratiose manifestans se illis. In virtuosis equidem actibus adest. Ideo in Ecclesiastico dicitur : Diligite Dominum, et illuminabuntur corda vestra. Et in Evangelio apertissime protestatur : Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et Pater meus diliget eum; et ad eum veniemus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus. Et in omni prudentia occurret illis, id est, in omni actu quo prudenter, discrete, et rationabiliter occupant se, præbet eis subsidium. Ipsa quoque in omni, id est cum perfecta et summa prudentia, facit hoc.
paras.en: [[6:17|For she goeth about seeking such as are worthy of her|Quoniam dignos se ipsa circuit]], that is, she protects and guards them on every side, [[6:17|seeking|quærens]] to be sought [Denis reads *quærens ut quæratur*, "seeking that she may be sought"], that is, stirring them to seek her out; [[6:17|and she sheweth herself to them cheerfully|ostendens se illis hilariter]] [[6:17|in the ways|et in viis suis]] [Denis reads *in viis suis*, "in her ways"], that is, in the acts pleasing to her, namely in the carrying out of the commandments, above all in fulfilling the commandments of the love of God and of neighbour, she graciously shows herself to them. For she is present in virtuous acts. Therefore it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 2:10|love him, and your hearts shall be enlightened|Diligite Dominum, et illuminabuntur corda vestra]]. And in the Gospel it is most plainly declared: [[John 14:23|If any one love me, he will keep my word. And my Father will love him and we will come to him and will make our abode with him|Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et Pater meus diliget eum; et ad eum veniemus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus]]. And in all prudence [Denis reads *prudentia*, "prudence"; the margin gives *providentia*, the Vulgate's reading, which the Douay-Rheims follows] she [[6:17|meeteth them|occurret illis]]: that is, in every act in which they busy themselves prudently, discreetly and reasonably, she gives them help. She herself also does this [[6:17|with all|in omni]], that is, with perfect and highest prudence.

paras.t: Initium enim illius, verissima est disciplinæ concupiscentia : id est, sincerum desiderium instructionis, est initium acquirendi sapientiam istam. Hoc enim desiderium, facit hominem docilem et intentum ad illuminationem divinam, angelicam ac humanam, et ad lectionem Scripturæ. Docilitas vero ponitur prima pars prudentiæ, ac sapientiæ infusæ seu acquisitæ.
paras.en: [[6:18|For the beginning of her is the most true desire of discipline|Initium enim illius, verissima est disciplinæ concupiscentia]]: that is, a sincere desire for instruction is the beginning of acquiring this wisdom. For this desire makes a man teachable and attentive to enlightening, divine, angelic and human, and to the reading of Scripture. And teachableness is reckoned the first part of prudence, and of wisdom, whether infused or acquired.

paras.t: Cura ergo disciplinæ, id est sollicitudo seu diligentia acquirendi disciplinam, seu proficiendi in ea, dilectio est, id est signum et effectus dilectionis sapientiæ; et dilectio, custodia legum illius est, id est, dilectio spiritualis, causa est observationis præceptorum sapientiæ. Ideo in prima sua Canonica ait Joannes : Hæc est caritas, ut præcepta ejus custodiamus. Custoditio autem legum, id est observantia præceptorum seu adimpletio legis naturalis et divinæ ac positivæ, consummatio incorruptionis est, id est perfecta integritas, reformatio, sanitas mentis; ad beatam quoque immortalitatem et inviolabilem integritatem æternæ salutis perducens. Hæc nempe integritas, est immunitas a peccato, quod mentem lædit, corrumpit, occidit. Unde ait Apostolus : Integer spiritus vester et anima servetur. De peccatoribus autem fertur in Psalmo : Corrupti sunt, et abominabiles facti sunt in iniquitatibus; et alibi, Divisum est cor eorum.
paras.en: [[6:19|And the care of discipline|Cura ergo disciplinæ]], that is, solicitude or diligence in acquiring discipline or in advancing in it, [[6:19|is love|dilectio est]], that is, a sign and effect of the love of wisdom; [[6:19|and love is the keeping of her laws|et dilectio, custodia legum illius est]], that is, spiritual love is the cause of the keeping of wisdom's commandments. Therefore John says in his first Epistle: [[1 John 5:3|this is the charity of God: That we keep his commandments|Hæc est caritas, ut præcepta ejus custodiamus]]. [[6:19|and the keeping of her laws|Custoditio autem legum]], that is, the observance of the commandments, or the fulfilling of the natural, divine and positive law, [[6:19|is the firm foundation of incorruption|consummatio incorruptionis est]] [Latin *consummatio*, "the perfecting"], that is, the perfect integrity, renewal and health of the mind, which leads also to blessed immortality and to the inviolable integrity of eternal salvation. For this integrity is freedom from sin, which wounds, corrupts and kills the mind. Hence the Apostle says: [[1 Thess 5:23|your whole spirit and soul|Integer spiritus vester et anima]] [[1 Thess 5:23|may be preserved|servetur]]. But of sinners it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 52:2|They are corrupted, and become abominable in iniquities|Corrupti sunt, et abominabiles facti sunt in iniquitatibus]]; and elsewhere: [[Osee 10:2|Their heart is divided|Divisum est cor eorum]].

paras.t: Incorruptio autem facit esse proximum Deo : quia a Deo nil separat nos, nisi peccatum, Isaia dicente : Iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter Deum vestrum et vos. Propter quod iterum dicit : Iste est omnis fructus, ut auferatur iniquitas. Denique incorruptio ista proxime mentem disponit ad dona gloriæ ac salutem, quæ est immediata et proxima unio mentis cum Deo.
paras.en: [[6:20|And incorruption bringeth near to God|Incorruptio autem facit esse proximum Deo]]: for nothing separates us from God but sin, as Isaias says: [[Is 59:2|your iniquities have divided between you and your God|Iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter Deum vestrum et vos]]. For which reason he says again: [[Is 27:9|this is all the fruit, that the sin thereof should be taken away|Iste est omnis fructus, ut auferatur iniquitas]] [Denis reads *iniquitas*, "iniquity", for the Vulgate's *peccatum ejus*, "the sin thereof"]. Lastly, this incorruption disposes the mind most nearly to the gifts of glory and to salvation, which is the immediate and closest union of the mind with God.

paras.t: Ex his concludit : Concupiscentia itaque sapientiæ, deducet ad regnum perpetuum, id est ad beatificam Deitatis fruitionem, per profectum intermedium ascendentem gradatim atque paulatim, sicut jam tactum est : quia paulatim proficitur, nec subito fit quis summus.
paras.en: From this he concludes: [[6:21|Therefore the desire of wisdom bringeth to the everlasting kingdom|Concupiscentia itaque sapientiæ, deducet ad regnum perpetuum]], that is, to the beatific enjoyment of the Godhead, through a progress in between that climbs by degrees and little by little, as has already been touched on: for one advances little by little, and no one becomes the highest all at once.

paras.t: Insuper præinducta possunt exponi de sapientia creata infusa, quæ est donum, cum profectu et illuminatione sibi annexis. Nam et hæc sapientia clara est, id est splendidissimus habitus mentis, non marcescens, quantum in se est, et manens in patria. Quæ facile videtur et invenitur : quia quicumque habet caritatem, habet et sapientiam istam, quæ per actus suos probabiliter potest cognosci. Præoccupat quoque eos qui se concupiscunt, id est, cito et gratiose infunditur illis, cum præventione benigna, et ita in ea proficiunt; et si quis eam non habet, quam cito veram habet contritionem, suscipit ipsam, quia simul cum caritate infunditur. Et quia tam necessaria est ad salutem, et primum ac nobilissimum donum Spiritus Sancti; ideo cogitare de ea, qualiter scilicet obtineatur, conservetur, perficiatur, sensus est consummatus, id est perfecta actio interioris sensus, utpote intellectus. Et sicut increata Sapientia facit hominem cito securum efficienter, sic ista formaliter : quæ et in actibus bonis facit hominem delectari in Deo, ad cujus intuitum elevat mentem.
paras.en: Moreover, the foregoing can be expounded of created, infused wisdom, which is a gift, with the progress and enlightening joined to it. For this wisdom too [[6:13|is glorious|clara est]], that is, a most splendid habit of the mind, and [[6:13|never fadeth away|non marcescens]], so far as lies in itself, and remains in the homeland [that is, in heaven]. It [[6:13|is easily seen|facile videtur]] [[6:13|and is found|et invenitur]]: for whoever has charity has this wisdom too, which can be known with probability through its acts. It also [[6:14|preventeth them that covet her|Præoccupat quoque eos qui se concupiscunt]], that is, it is infused into them quickly and graciously, with a kindly prevenience, and so they advance in it; and if anyone has it not, as soon as he has true contrition he receives it, for it is infused together with charity. And because it is so necessary to salvation, and is the first and noblest gift of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]]: [[6:16|To think, therefore, upon her|cogitare de ea]], that is, upon how it is obtained, preserved and perfected, [[6:16|is perfect understanding|sensus est consummatus]], that is, the perfect act of the inward sense, namely the intellect. And as the uncreated Wisdom makes a man [[6:16|quickly be secure|cito securum]] as his efficient cause, so this wisdom does as his formal cause [that is, uncreated Wisdom brings his security about, while created wisdom is itself the quality by which he is secure]; and in good works it makes a man delight in God, to the sight of whom it lifts the mind.

paras.t: Si ergo delectamini sedibus, vel, ut aliqui habent, stemmatibus, id est dignitatibus prælaturæ, et sceptris, o reges populi, id est regia potestate aut regnis : in quibus delectari, in se vanum, intimoratum, et ambitiosum censetur, ut dictum est super illud, Et placetis vobis in turbis nationum. Ideo sensus est : Si delectamini, id est, si ordinate delectari vultis, sedibus et regnis, puta in Domino, et in fructuosa exsecutione officiorum vestrorum, diligite sapientiam increatam, tanquam principale caritatis objectum: sapientiam quoque infusam et acquisitam, tanquam medium pertingendi ad felicitatem : ut in perpetuum regnetis, id est, in vita ista tam virtuose ac meritorie præsideatis, ut de præsenti regno atque regimine transferamini ad regnum cœleste : in quo omnes sunt gloriose coronati, juxta id quod dictum est supra. Ideo accipient regnum decoris, et diadema speciei.
paras.en: [[6:22|If then your delight be in thrones|Si ergo delectamini sedibus]], or, as some copies have it, in garlands [Latin *stemmatibus*, "wreaths, crowns"], that is, in the dignities of prelacy, [[6:22|and sceptres, O ye kings of the people|et sceptris, o reges populi]], that is, in royal power or in kingdoms: to delight in which is in itself judged vain, void of the fear of God [Latin *intimoratum*, "without fear"] and ambitious, as was said on the words: [[6:3|and that please yourselves in multitudes of nations|Et placetis vobis in turbis nationum]]. So the sense is: [[6:22|If then your delight be|Si delectamini]], that is, if you wish to delight in an orderly way in thrones and kingdoms, namely in the Lord and in the fruitful discharge of your offices, [[6:22|love wisdom|diligite sapientiam]]: uncreated wisdom, as the chief object of charity; and infused and acquired wisdom too, as the means of reaching happiness; [[6:22|that you may reign for ever|ut in perpetuum regnetis]], that is, that you may preside in this life so virtuously and meritoriously that from your present kingdom and rule you may be taken over to the heavenly kingdom, in which all are gloriously crowned, according to what was said above: [[Wis 5:17|Therefore shall they receive a kingdom of glory, and a crown of beauty|Ideo accipient regnum decoris, et diadema speciei]].

paras.t: Diligite lumen sapientiæ, id est sapientiam luminosam, mentis illuminativam, et lumen illud æternum a quo omnis sapientia profluit : de quo Joannes ait, Erat lux vera quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum; omnes qui præestis populis, ut subditos possitis purgare, illuminare, dirigere, imo vos ipsos in primis irreprehensibiles exhibere. Cæcus enim si cæco ducatum præbeat, ambo in foveam cadunt. Et rex seu prælatus illitteratus, est quasi asinus coronatus.
paras.en: [[6:23|Love the light of wisdom|Diligite lumen sapientiæ]], that is, luminous wisdom that enlightens the mind, and that eternal light from which all wisdom flows, of which John says: [[John 1:9|That was the true light, which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world|Erat lux vera quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum]]; [[6:23|all ye that bear rule over peoples|omnes qui præestis populis]], so that you may be able to purify, enlighten and direct your subjects, and indeed first of all to show yourselves blameless. For [[Matt 15:14|if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit|Cæcus enim si cæco ducatum præbeat, ambo in foveam cadunt]]. And an unlettered king or prelate is like a crowned ass.

paras.t: Quid est autem sapientia, et quemadmodum facta sit, id est a Deo infusa, vel per lectionis studium, propriam perscrutationem, aut aliorum informationem acquisita, referam; et non abscondam a vobis sacramenta, id est sacra mysteria, et occulta beneficia, ac magnifica et mystica opera, Dei, sed ab initio nativitatis investigabo, id est, de ipsa sapientia disseram ab exordio suæ productionis, qualiter scilicet nata sit aut infusa, aut in me seu aliis inceperit esse. Et hoc sequenti capitulo ac deinceps agit hic auctor. Vel, Investigabo de me ipso, ab ipso nativitatis meæ exordio, tractando de mea conceptione ac nativitate : ut sequenti patet capitulo. Et ponam in lucem, id est, evidenter manifestabo, scientiam illius, id est veram sapientiæ cognitionem : nam de sapientia, tanquam de objecto, est quædam scientia, quemadmodum de fide et caritate: et non præteribo veritatem necessariam aut utilem sciri de ista materia.
paras.en: [[6:24|Now what wisdom is, and what was her origin|Quid est autem sapientia, et quemadmodum facta sit]] [literally "how she was made"], that is, infused by God, or acquired by the study of reading, by one's own searching, or by the teaching of others, [[6:24|I will declare|referam]]: [[6:24|and I will not hide from you the mysteries|et non abscondam a vobis sacramenta]], that is, the sacred mysteries, the hidden benefits, and the great and mystical works, [[6:24|of God|Dei]]; [[6:24|but will seek her out from the beginning of her birth|sed ab initio nativitatis investigabo]], that is, I will discourse of wisdom herself from the start of her bringing forth, namely how she was born or infused, or began to be in me or in others. And this the author does in the following chapter and onwards. Or [[6:24|will seek her out|Investigabo]] may mean: I will search into myself from the very start of my birth, treating of my conception and birth, as appears in the following chapter. [[6:24|and bring|Et ponam]] [[6:24|to light|in lucem]], that is, I will make plainly manifest, [[6:24|the knowledge of her|scientiam illius]], that is, the true knowledge of wisdom: for there is a certain knowledge [Latin *scientia*, "science"] of wisdom as of its object, as there is of faith and charity; [[6:24|and will not pass over the truth|et non præteribo veritatem]] that is necessary or useful to know on this matter.

paras.t: Neque cum invidia tabescente iter habebo : id est, invidis de aliorum bono tristantibus, nec bona sibi concessa communicantibus proximis, non assimilabor; imo caritative ac liberaliter communicabo vobis spiritualia bona mihi collata; quoniam talis homo, scilicet invidus, non erit particeps sapientiæ quæ est donum : nisi de invidia sua pœnitens, obtineat caritatem, sine qua donum sapientiæ non habetur. Sapientia tamen scholastica acquisita (aut etiam infusa, quæ est donum gratiæ gratis datæ) potest cum mortali peccato haberi.
paras.en: [[6:25|Neither will I go with consuming envy|Neque cum invidia tabescente iter habebo]]: that is, I will not be like the envious, who are saddened at the good of others and do not share with their neighbours the good things granted them; rather I will share with you, in charity and freely, the spiritual goods bestowed on me; [[6:25|for such a man|quoniam talis homo]], namely the envious, [[6:25|shall not be partaker of wisdom|non erit particeps sapientiæ]] that is a gift, unless, repenting of his envy, he obtains charity, without which the gift of wisdom is not had. Acquired, scholastic wisdom, however (or infused wisdom too, the kind that is a gift of grace freely given [*gratia gratis data*, a grace given for the good of others, not one that makes its bearer holy]), can be had together with mortal sin.

paras.t: Multitudo autem sapientium sanitas est orbis terrarum, id est causa spiritualis curationis hominum commorantium in hoc mundum. Sapientes etenim verbo et exemplo ædificant alios, corripiunt, purgant, illustrantque proximos, potissime sibi commissos. Et sicut per sanitatem corpus est aptum ad exercendum opera sibi convenientia, sic genus humanum per sapientiam redditur aptum ad actus suæ salutis. Ideo Salomon loquitur : Pretiosi spiritus vir eruditus; et rursus, Labia sapientiæ erudiunt plurimos. Et rex sapiens populi stabilimentum est : quia stabilit eos in vita honesta, et in conversatione pacifica, sicque merentur suis hostibus prævalere. Ideo beata est respublica, quæ a sapientibus gubernatur, et regem habet prudentem, cui innititur. Nam qualis est rector civitatis, tales et inhabitantes in ea. Maxime autem Christus rex noster, stabilimentum est suorum fidelium sibi obedientium : quos stabiles atque immobiles facit in bono, et protegit ab adversis.
paras.en: [[6:26|Now the multitude of the wise is the welfare of the whole world|Multitudo autem sapientium sanitas est orbis terrarum]] [Latin *sanitas*, "health"], that is, the cause of the spiritual healing of men dwelling in this world. For the wise, by word and example, edify others, and correct, cleanse and enlighten their neighbours, above all those entrusted to them. And as by health the body is fit to perform the works proper to it, so by wisdom the human race is made fit for the acts of its salvation. Therefore Solomon says: [[Prov 17:27|the man of understanding is of a precious spirit|Pretiosi spiritus vir eruditus]]; and again: [[Prov 10:21|The lips of the just teach many|Labia sapientiæ erudiunt plurimos]] [Denis reads *Labia sapientiæ*, "the lips of wisdom"; the margin gives *justi*, the Vulgate's reading]. [[6:26|and a wise king is the upholding of the people|Et rex sapiens populi stabilimentum est]]: for he establishes them in an upright life and in peaceable living, and so they deserve to prevail over their enemies. Therefore blessed is the commonwealth that is governed by the wise, and has a prudent king on whom it leans. For [[Ecclus 10:2|what manner of man the ruler of a city is, such also are they that dwell therein|qualis est rector civitatis, tales et inhabitantes in ea]]. But above all Christ our King is the upholding of His faithful who obey Him: He makes them steadfast and immovable in good, and protects them from adversity.

paras.t: Ergo accipite disciplinam, id est moralem et salubrem informationem, per sermones meos, et proderit vobis ad salutem : ignorantia quippe est periculosissimum vitium. Oportet enim in primis scire quid fieri debeat, quid vitari. Ideo, teste Apostolo, Qui ignorat, ignorabit. Et asserit Dominus apud Osee : Conticuit populus meus, eo quod non habuerit scientiam Dei : quia tu scientiam repulisti, repellam te ego, ne sacerdotio fungaris mihi.
paras.en: [[6:27|Receive, therefore, instruction|Ergo accipite disciplinam]], that is, moral and wholesome teaching, [[6:27|by my words|per sermones meos]], [[6:27|and it shall be profitable to you|et proderit vobis]] for salvation: for ignorance is a most dangerous vice. For one must first of all know what ought to be done and what avoided. Hence, as the Apostle witnesses: [[1 Cor 14:38|if any man know not|Qui ignorat]], [[1 Cor 14:38|he shall not be known|ignorabit]] [Denis has *Qui ignorat, ignorabit*, "he that is ignorant shall be ignorant"; the Vulgate reads *ignorabitur*, "he shall not be known"]. And the Lord declares in Osee: [[Osee 4:6|My people have been silent, because they had no knowledge|Conticuit populus meus, eo quod non habuerit scientiam]] of God: [[Osee 4:6|because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will reject thee, that thou shalt not do the office of priesthood to me|quia tu scientiam repulisti, repellam te ego, ne sacerdotio fungaris mihi]].

7.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI SEPTIMI : SUM QUIDEM ET EGO MORTALIS HOMO.
7.title_en: Exposition of the seventh chapter: I myself am a mortal man

paras.t: Ostensurus auctor hic quid sit sapientia, et multa sublimia locuturus, propriam conditionem et defectuositatis suæ originem reduci ad memoriam, ad declarandum quid conveniat sibi ex sua natura, et quid ex gratia, et ne videatur excedere suam mensuram.
paras.en: The author, being about to show here what wisdom is, and about to say many lofty things, calls to mind his own condition and the origin of his defectiveness, in order to make plain what belongs to him by his nature and what by grace, and lest he should seem to go beyond his measure.

paras.t: Sum quidem et ego mortalis homo, similis omnibus, id est ceteris in natura specifica, et ex genere terreno, id est carnali propagine, illius qui prior factus, id est formatus est, scilicet Adæ protoplasti parentis : de quo legitur, Formavit Deus hominem de limo terræ ; et in ventre matris figuratus sum caro : id est, caro mea in matrice ex semine est formata, et organizata atque aptata ad animæ susceptionem. Totum autem a parte frequenter denominationem sortitur.
paras.en: [[7:1|I myself am a mortal man, like all others|Sum quidem et ego mortalis homo, similis omnibus]], that is, like the rest in the nature of the species, [[7:1|and of the race|et ex genere terreno]] [Denis reads *terreno*, "of the earthly race", where the Vulgate has *terreni*, "of the earthly one", which the Douay-Rheims renders "made of the earth"], that is, by fleshly descent, [[7:1|of him, that was first made|illius qui prior factus]], that is, formed, namely of Adam, our first-formed parent, of whom we read: [[Gen 2:7|the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth|Formavit Deus hominem de limo terræ]]; [[7:1|and in the womb of my mother I was fashioned to be flesh|et in ventre matris figuratus sum caro]]: that is, my flesh was formed from seed in the womb, and organized and fitted to receive the soul. For the whole frequently takes its name from a part [that is, the whole man is here called "flesh" from his body].

paras.t: Decem mensium tempore coagulatus sum in sanguine, id est, tanto tempore fui in utero, et ad corpusculi soliditatem redactus sum ex sanguinolento semine matris meæ et ex semine patris. Unde subjungitur : ex semine hominis. Vir enim est perfectior in naturalibus, et semen ejus in formatione habet se per modum agentis : quia in eo est vis formativa, formans semen ministratum a matre in corpusculum fetus, concurrente influxu cœlesti, juxta illud : Homo generat hominem et sol. Et juxta physicos, semen viri magis est candidum, semen feminæ sanguinolentum. Et delectamento somni conveniente : quia in ipsa conceptione fuit delectatio magna et naturalis, rationem absorbens, ita quod ratio fuit quasi sopita et dormiens, id est ab usu et actu proprio cessans.
paras.en: [[7:2|In the time of ten months I was compacted in blood|Decem mensium tempore coagulatus sum in sanguine]], that is, I was so long a time in the womb, and was brought to the solidity of a little body from the blood-like seed of my mother and from the seed of my father. Hence is added: [[7:2|of the seed of man|ex semine hominis]]. For the man is the more perfect in natural things, and his seed behaves in the forming after the manner of an agent: for in it is the formative power, which forms the seed supplied by the mother into the little body of the fetus, with the concurrence of the heavenly influence [that is, the influence of the heavenly bodies], according to the saying: Man begets man, and the sun also [Aristotle, *Physics* II, 2]. And according to the natural philosophers, the man's seed is whiter, the woman's blood-like. [[7:2|and the pleasure of sleep concurring|Et delectamento somni conveniente]]: because in conception itself there was a great and natural delight, absorbing the reason, so that the reason was as it were lulled and asleep, that is, ceasing from its proper use and act.

paras.t: Denique, quamvis dicatur hic, Decem mensium tempore, etc., non est tamen putandum quod omnes fetus humani tam diu in utero sint : imo communiter dicuntur novem mensibus esse in utero. Aliqui vero pertingunt usque ad decimum mensem : qui magis vitales esse feruntur. Nonnulli autem septimo mense, quidam octavo nascuntur.
paras.en: Lastly, although it is said here, [[7:2|In the time of ten months|Decem mensium tempore]], etc., it is not however to be thought that all human offspring are so long in the womb: on the contrary, they are commonly said to be nine months in the womb. Some, however, reach as far as the tenth month, and these are reported to be the more vigorous. But some are born in the seventh month, some in the eighth.

paras.t: Circa hæc ait Glossa ex Rabano : Cœlestis Adam sine virili semine natus de Virgine, proprium nativitatis habet modum : qui et mortis suæ ordinavit occasum. Decimo mense post conceptionem, nativitas ejus celebratur a Christianis ; et ab octavo calendas Aprilis, quo conceptus creditur, usque octavum calendas Januarii, quando natus traditur, ducenti septuaginta sex dies numerantur, id est novem menses, et sex dies.
paras.en: On these things the Gloss says, from Rabanus: The heavenly Adam, born of the Virgin without the seed of man, has his own manner of birth, he who also ordained the setting of his own death. His nativity is celebrated by Christians in the tenth month after his conception; and from the eighth day before the calends of April [25 March], on which he is believed to have been conceived, to the eighth day before the calends of January [25 December], when he is held to have been born, two hundred and seventy-six days are counted, that is, nine months and six days.

paras.t: Et ego natus accepi communem aerem, id est, mox ut natus sum, cœpi per respirationem aeris vivere, seu actus vitales ostendere, sicut et ceteri; et in similiter factam decidi terram : id est, egrediendo ex utero, in terrenum sustentaculum descendens, receptus sum ab obstetrice, aut alia adsistente; et primam vocem similem omnibus emisi plorans : id est, instar aliorum infantulorum, in vocem lamentationis erupi statim ut ventrem exivi, quasi ipso ploratu contestans, me in vallem lacrimarum, exsiliumque venisse. Atque, ut dicitur, masculus nascens, cum gemitu dicit, A ; femina, E ; veluti conquerentes de primorum transgressione parentum, ob quam nascuntur proles iræ atque miseriæ. Verumtamen Augustinus in libro de Civitate Dei recitat Zoroastrem magicarum artium inventorem, mox ut natus fuit, risisse : quem risum Augustinus monstruosum appellat, tanquam diabolici festi præludium. Aliqui quoque dicunt, Moysen natum mox suæ matri arrisisse.
paras.en: [[7:3|And being born, I drew in the common air|Et ego natus accepi communem aerem]], that is, as soon as I was born I began to live by breathing the air, or to show the acts of life, as the rest do too; [[7:3|and fell upon the earth, that is made alike|et in similiter factam decidi terram]]: that is, coming forth from the womb and coming down onto an earthly support, I was received by the midwife or by some other woman attending; [[7:3|and the first voice which I uttered was crying, as all others do|et primam vocem similem omnibus emisi plorans]]: that is, like other little infants, I broke out into a cry of lamentation as soon as I came out of the womb, as though by that very wailing bearing witness that I had come into a vale of tears and into exile. And, as it is said, a male at birth says with a groan, A; a female, E [the old saying took these for the first letters of Adam and Eve], as though complaining of the transgression of our first parents, on account of which offspring are born children of wrath[[Eph 2:3||]] and of misery. Augustine, however, in the book of the City of God, relates that Zoroaster, the inventor of the magic arts, laughed as soon as he was born [*City of God* XXI, 14]: a laugh which Augustine calls monstrous, as being the prelude to a feast of the devil. Some also say that Moses, as soon as he was born, smiled at his mother.

paras.t: In involumentis, id est panniculorum involutionibus, nutritus sum, et curis magnis. Infantuli namque pannis involvuntur, et ob suam teneritudinem atque mollitiem, ac rationis defectum, diu et sollicite custodiuntur et educantur.
paras.en: [[7:4|in swaddling clothes|In involumentis]], that is, in the wrappings of little cloths, [[7:4|I was nursed|nutritus sum]], [[7:4|and with great cares|et curis magnis]]. For little infants are wrapped in cloths, and on account of their tenderness and softness, and their want of reason, they are long and carefully guarded and brought up.

paras.t: Nemo enim ex regibus aliud habuit nativitatis initium : ideo non est mirum, quod inferiores ita prodeunt in hanc lucem.
paras.en: [[7:5|For none of the kings had any other beginning of birth|Nemo enim ex regibus aliud habuit nativitatis initium]]: therefore it is no wonder that those of lower rank come forth into this light in the same way.

paras.t: Unus ergo in specie introitus est omnibus hominibus ad vitam naturæ, et similis exitus, utpote mors. Et quamvis diversi diversimode suam finiant vitam, quidam morte naturali, aliqui violenta (quam aliqui inferunt sibimetipsis, alii patiuntur ab aliis) : tamen quantum ad hoc, est omnibus similis exitus, quod per separationem animæ a corpore, seu per corporalis harmoniæ corruptionem, exeunt de hoc mundo; et item, quod per magnam angustiam et omnium terrenorum derelictionem.
paras.en: [[7:6|For all men have one entrance|Unus ergo in specie introitus est omnibus hominibus]] (one, that is, in kind) [[7:6|into life|ad vitam naturæ]] (the life of nature), [[7:6|and the like going out|et similis exitus]], namely death. And though different men end their life in different ways, some by a natural death, others by a violent one (which some inflict on themselves, while others suffer it from others), yet in this respect the going out is alike for all: that it is by the separation of the soul from the body, or by the breaking down of the body's harmony, that they go out of this world; and also, that it is through great anguish and the leaving behind of all earthly things.

paras.t: Propter hoc optavi. Quasi dicat : Quum tanta fuerit defectuositas originis meæ, constat quod sapientiæ meæ excellentiam et gratiæ affluentiam, a me ipso non habui, sicut nec ceteri; imo, quia in ignorantia natus sum, optavi sapientiam obtinere.
paras.en: [[7:7|Wherefore I wished|Propter hoc optavi]]. As if to say: Since the defectiveness of my origin was so great, it is plain that I did not have the excellence of my wisdom and the abundance of grace from myself, any more than the rest do; rather, because I was born in ignorance, I wished to obtain wisdom.

paras.t: Præterea, ut multi dicunt expositores, auctor hujus voluminis in isto capitulo, sicut et in quibusdam sequentibus, in persona loquitur Salomonis : quod et infra ex textu manifeste ostenditur. Salomon autem, data sibi desuper optione, sapientiam præelegit, prout tertio Regum et secundo Paralipomenon recitatur. Nihilo minus quæ hic dicuntur, de quocumque homine studioso, desiderio sapientiæ inflammato, pro maxima parte exponi.
paras.en: Moreover, as many expositors say, the author of this volume speaks in this chapter, as also in some of those that follow, in the person of Solomon: which is also plainly shown from the text below[[7:17||]]. Now Solomon, when the choice was given him from above, chose wisdom before all else, as is related in the third book of Kings[[3 Kings 3:5||]][[3 Kings 3:9||]] and in the second of Paralipomenon[[2 Par 1:7||]][[2 Par 1:10||]]. Nonetheless, what is said here may for the most part be expounded of any studious man inflamed with the desire of wisdom.

paras.t: Et datus est mihi sensus, id est intellectus illuminatus, seu habitus sapientiæ. Fuit autem Salomoni infusa, non solum sapientia quæ est donum, sed et illa quæ pertinet ad munera gratiæ gratis datæ, per quam scit quis ea quæ fidei sunt, persuadere, declarare, defendere. Sapientia etiam naturalis, quæ studio humano naturalique ratione potest acquiri, fuit supernaturaliter ei infusa. Et invocavi, id est, ex intimo cordis Dominum exoravi pro sapientiæ infusione, incremento, perfectione; et venit in me spiritus sapientiæ, id est ipsum sapientiæ donum : quod nomine spiritus designatur, quia spiritus denotat quamdam impulsionem seu motionem. Unde frequenter pro vento accipitur. Porro septem dona faciunt hominem prompte mobilem ac dirigibilem a Spiritu Sancto. Propter quod Isaias loquens de eis, singula exprimit cum adjectione hujus nominis, Spiritus : Requiesceret, inquiens, super eum spiritus Domini, spiritus sapientiæ et intellectus, spiritus consilii et fortitudinis, etc.
paras.en: [[7:7|and understanding was given me|Et datus est mihi sensus]], that is, an enlightened intellect, or the habit of wisdom. Now there was infused into Solomon not only the wisdom which is a gift [that is, one of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost], but also that which belongs to the graces *gratis datæ* [graces "freely given", granted for the good of others rather than for the holiness of the one who receives them], by which a man knows how to persuade, explain and defend the things that are of faith. Natural wisdom too, which can be acquired by human study and natural reason, was infused into him supernaturally. [[7:7|and I called upon God|Et invocavi]], that is, from the depth of my heart I besought the Lord for the infusion, increase and perfection of wisdom; [[7:7|and the spirit of wisdom came upon me|et venit in me spiritus sapientiæ]], that is, the gift of wisdom itself, which is designated by the name of spirit because spirit denotes a certain impulse or motion. Hence it is frequently taken for wind. Further, the seven gifts make a man readily moved and directed by the Holy Ghost. For which reason Isaias, speaking of them, expresses each one with the addition of this name, Spirit, saying: [[Is 11:2|And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom, and of understanding, the spirit of counsel, and of fortitude|Requiesceret, inquiens, super eum spiritus Domini, spiritus sapientiæ et intellectus, spiritus consilii et fortitudinis]], etc.

paras.t: Vel, Spiritus sapientiæ, id est Spiritus Sanctus, auctor, doctor et dator sapientiæ salutaris : qui dicitur Spiritus sapientiæ, sicut et Spiritus veritatis. De quo ait Salvator : Quum venerit ille Spiritus veritatis, docebit vos omnem veritatem. Qui venit in hominem, non locum mutando, nec mutationem in se aliquam sustinendo, sed sua munera influendo, gratiosque intus agendo.
paras.en: Or, [[7:7|the spirit of wisdom|Spiritus sapientiæ]], that is, the Holy Ghost, the author, teacher and giver of saving wisdom, who is called the Spirit of wisdom as he is also called the Spirit of truth. Of whom the Saviour says: [[John 16:13|when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will teach you all truth|Quum venerit ille Spiritus veritatis, docebit vos omnem veritatem]]. He comes into a man not by changing place, nor by undergoing any change in himself, but by pouring in his gifts and making men gracious within.

paras.t: Et præposui illam regnis et sedibus, id est auctoritatibus judicialibus; et divitias corporales nihil esse dixi in comparatione illius : quia incomparabiliter melior illis est. Juxta quem modum ait Apostolus : Qui se dicit aliquid esse, quum nihil sit.
paras.en: [[7:8|And I preferred her before kingdoms and thrones|Et præposui illam regnis et sedibus]], that is, judicial authorities; [[7:8|and esteemed riches|et divitias]], bodily riches, [[7:8|nothing in comparison of her|nihil esse dixi in comparatione illius]]: because she is incomparably better than they. In the same way the Apostle speaks of him who claims himself [[Gal 6:3|to be some thing, whereas he is nothing|aliquid esse, quum nihil sit]] [the Vulgate has *existimat*, "thinks", where Denis has *dicit*, "says"].

paras.t: Nec comparavi illi in dignitate lapidem pretiosum : quoniam omne aurum in comparatione illius, arena est exigua, et tanquam lutum æstimabitur argentum in conspectu illius, id est modicæ reputationis et res vilis sicut arena. Super salutem, id est plus quam corporalem sanitatem, aut temporalem prosperitatem, et speciem, id est pulchritudinem, dilexi illam. Hiis consonat illud Proverbiorum : Beatus homo qui invenit sapientiam, et affluit prudentia; melior est acquisitio ejus negotiatione auri et argenti. Pretiosior est sapientia cunctis opibus; et omnia quæ desiderantur, huic non valent comparari. Illud quoque Job : Nescit homo pretium ejus; non dabitur aurum obrizum pro ea, nec conferetur tinctis Indiæ coloribus, nec lapidi sardonycho pretiosissimo, vel sapphiro. Hinc et Apostolus protestatur : Existimo omnia detrimentum esse propter eminentem scientiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi, propter quam omnia arbitror ut stercora. Cetera quoque dona gratiæ ac virtutum, ac spiritualia charismata, sunt exterioribus et corporalibus rebus præstantiora.
paras.en: [[7:9|Neither did I compare unto her|Nec comparavi illi]] in worth [[7:9|any precious stone|lapidem pretiosum]]: [[7:9|for all gold, in comparison of her, is as a little sand; and silver, in respect to her, shall be counted as clay|quoniam omne aurum in comparatione illius, arena est exigua, et tanquam lutum æstimabitur argentum in conspectu illius]], that is, of small account, and a worthless thing like sand. [[7:10|above health|Super salutem]], that is, more than bodily health or temporal prosperity, [[7:10|and beauty|et speciem]], that is, comeliness, [[7:10|I loved her|dilexi illam]]. With these agrees that saying of Proverbs: [[Prov 3:13|Blessed is the man that findeth wisdom, and is rich in prudence|Beatus homo qui invenit sapientiam, et affluit prudentia]]; [[Prov 3:14|The purchasing thereof is better than the merchandise|melior est acquisitio ejus negotiatione]] of gold and silver. [[Prov 3:15|She is more precious than all riches: and all the things that are desired, are not to be compared to her|Pretiosior est sapientia cunctis opibus; et omnia quæ desiderantur, huic non valent comparari]]. And that of Job too: [[Job 28:13|Man knoweth not the price thereof|Nescit homo pretium ejus]]; [[Job 28:15|The finest gold shall not purchase it|non dabitur aurum obrizum pro ea]], [[Job 28:16|It shall not be compared with the dyed colours of India, or with the most precious stone sardonyx, or the sapphire|nec conferetur tinctis Indiæ coloribus, nec lapidi sardonycho pretiosissimo, vel sapphiro]]. Hence the Apostle too declares: [[Phil 3:8|I count all things to be but loss for the excellent knowledge of Jesus Christ, my Lord|Existimo omnia detrimentum esse propter eminentem scientiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi]], for the sake of which I [[Phil 3:8|count them but as dung|omnia arbitror ut stercora]]. The other gifts of grace and of the virtues, and the spiritual charisms, are likewise more excellent than outward and bodily things.

paras.t: Et proposui pro luce habere illam, id est pro splendida ductrice ac directrice mea in omnibus. Quemadmodum enim lux exterior dirigit foris, sic sapientia intus et in cunctis agendis. Quoniam inextinguibile est lumen illius. Lumen sapientiæ, est ipsamet sapientia lucens ac fulgida : quæ non est exstinguibilis aut corruptibilis directe aut ex sua natura; sed quantum in se est, manet in mente etiam in patria, et ita non excidit, sicut nec caritas. Indiget tamen indesinenter conservatione divina, sicut et quælibet res creata. Ideo, sicut mortaliter peccans caritatem amittit, quam Deus in eo conservare desistit; sic perdit et sapientiam quæ est donum.
paras.en: [[7:10|and chose to have her instead of light|Et proposui pro luce habere illam]], that is, as my shining leader and guide in all things. For as the outward light guides us outwardly, so wisdom guides us inwardly and in all that is to be done. [[7:10|for her light cannot be put out|Quoniam inextinguibile est lumen illius]]. The light of wisdom is wisdom itself, shining and resplendent, which cannot be put out or corrupted directly or of its own nature; but, so far as lies in it, it remains in the mind even in our heavenly fatherland, and so it does not fall away, any more than charity does[[1 Cor 13:8||]]. Yet it needs God's preserving without ceasing, as does every created thing. Therefore, as one who sins mortally loses charity, which God ceases to preserve in him, so too he loses the wisdom which is a gift.

paras.t: Venerunt autem mihi omnia bona pariter cum illa, scilicet fama, gloria, honor, opulentia. Unde et tertio Regum legitur Deus Salomoni dixisse : Quoniam petisti sapientiam, hæc quoque quæ non postulasti, dedi tibi. Et innumerabilis honestas, id est virtuositas, modestia, probitas, per manus, id est virtutem et actiones, illius. Sapientiæ etenim quæ est donum, connexa sunt alia dona, et virtutes infusæ ac meritoria opera. Sapientia quoque ordinatum efficit hominem, probatum, constantem, facetum. Sic et Christus disseruit : Quærite primum regnum Dei et justitiam ejus, et hæc omnia adjicientur vobis.
paras.en: [[7:11|Now all good things came to me together with her|Venerunt autem mihi omnia bona pariter cum illa]], namely fame, glory, honour, wealth. Hence too we read in the third book of Kings that God said to Solomon: [[3 Kings 3:11|Because thou hast asked|Quoniam petisti]] wisdom, [[3 Kings 3:13|the things also which thou didst not ask, I have given thee|hæc quoque quæ non postulasti, dedi tibi]]. [[7:11|and innumerable riches|Et innumerabilis honestas]] [*honestas*, "honourableness", which Denis takes as moral worth], that is, virtue, modesty, uprightness, [[7:11|through her hands|per manus]], that is, through her power and actions. For with the wisdom which is a gift are joined the other gifts, and the infused virtues and meritorious works. Wisdom also makes a man well ordered, tried, steadfast and gracious in manner. So too Christ taught: [[Matt 6:33|Seek ye|Quærite]] [[Matt 6:33|first the kingdom of God, and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you|primum regnum Dei et justitiam ejus, et hæc omnia adjicientur vobis]].

paras.t: Et lætatus sum in omnibus gaudio spirituali, quoniam antecedebat me ista sapientia, id est, actiones meas prævenit, ostendens mihi intus quid et qualiter operari deberem forinsecus, tanquam optima ductrix, perfundens et irradians mentem. Qui autem in omnibus ordinate procedit, pacem habet, et delectabiliter operatur, nec perturbatur. Animus vero inordinatus, sibi ipsi pœnalis ac gravis est. Et ignorabam quoniam horum omnium mater est : id est, tunc, quando sapientiam hanc nondum sortitus fui, non putavi quod tot ac tanta bona eam consequerentur, et orirentur ex ea, quemadmodum filiæ ex matre; sed de hac re experientia docuit me.
paras.en: [[7:12|And I rejoiced in all these|Et lætatus sum in omnibus]] with spiritual joy, [[7:12|for this wisdom went before me|quoniam antecedebat me ista sapientia]], that is, went before my actions, showing me within what I ought to do outwardly and how, as the best of guides, flooding and enlightening the mind. Now he who goes forward in an orderly way in all things has peace, and works with delight, and is not troubled. But a disordered mind is a punishment and a burden to itself. [[7:12|and I knew not that she was the mother of them all|Et ignorabam quoniam horum omnium mater est]]: that is, at that time, when I had not yet obtained this wisdom, I did not think that so many and such great good things would follow upon her and spring from her, as daughters from a mother; but experience taught me this.

paras.t: Quam sapientiam sine fictione didici ex revelatione divina, aut aliis modis, ut dictum est, et sine invidia communico proximis, docendo, exhortando, dirigendoque alios: prout beatissimus Petrus hortatur, Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrando; et honestatem illius non abscondo, id est, proprietates sapientiæ hujus cunctis aperio per verba et scripta, videlicet dignitatem, claritatem, inextinguibilitatem, efficaciam, modestiam, et salubritatem ipsius. Unde apud Jacobum legitur : Quæ desursum est sapientia, primum quidem pudica est, deinde pacifica, modesta, suasibilis, bonis consentiens, plena misericordia et fructibus bonis. Hæc autem docendo, alios ad sapientiæ hujus amorem et amplexum allicio et accendo.
paras.en: [[7:13|Which I have learned without guile|Quam sapientiam sine fictione didici]], by divine revelation or in other ways, as has been said, [[7:13|and communicate without envy|et sine invidia communico]] to my neighbours, by teaching, exhorting and directing others, as the most blessed Peter exhorts: [[1 Pet 4:10|As every man hath received grace, ministering the same one to another|Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrando]]; [[7:13|and her riches I hide not|et honestatem illius non abscondo]] [*honestas* again], that is, I lay open to all, by word and by writing, the properties of this wisdom, namely its dignity, brightness, unquenchableness, efficacy, modesty and wholesomeness. Hence we read in James: [[Jas 3:17|the wisdom that is from above, first indeed is chaste, then peaceable, modest, easy to be persuaded, consenting to the good, full of mercy and good fruits|Quæ desursum est sapientia, primum quidem pudica est, deinde pacifica, modesta, suasibilis, bonis consentiens, plena misericordia et fructibus bonis]]. By teaching these things I draw and kindle others to the love and embrace of this wisdom.

paras.t: Infinitus enim thesaurus est, id est, opulentia valde magna, et impretiabile bonum est sapientia ista, hominibus eam habentibus. Infinitum quippe vocatur interdum aliquid insolito modo magnum. Sicque libro Josue leguntur filii Ruben et Gad, fecisse altare infinitæ magnitudinis. Quo qui usi sunt, participes facti sunt amicitiæ Dei : id est, sapientes utendo dono sapientiæ per contemplationem divinorum, et conversationem honestam ac ordinatam, facti sunt amici Dei, utpote Deo præcipue cari, uniti, placentes, et conformati : quoniam sicut vita superbeatissimi Dei, est suæ æternæ veritatis, infinitæque bonitatis contemplatio atque dilectio; sic et tales, ipsius Dei veritatem et bonitatem pro modulo suo assidue contemplantur ac diligunt, sicque divinorum secretorum agnitionem merentur. Unde Christus loquitur talibus : Vos autem dixi amicos, quia omnia quæcumque audivi a Patre meo, nota feci vobis. Propter disciplinæ dona commendati, id est commendabiles atque laudabiles facti per opera ac merita disciplinæ, quam receperunt.
paras.en: [[7:14|For she is an infinite treasure|Infinitus enim thesaurus est]], that is, this wisdom is very great wealth and a priceless good, [[7:14|to men|hominibus]] who have her. For something is sometimes called infinite when it is great in an unusual degree. Thus in the book of Josue we read that the sons of Ruben and Gad made [[Jos 22:10|an altar immensely great|altare infinitæ magnitudinis]] [literally "of infinite size"]. [[7:14|which they that use, become the friends of God|Quo qui usi sunt, participes facti sunt amicitiæ Dei]] [literally "were made partakers of the friendship of God"]: that is, the wise, using the gift of wisdom by the contemplation of divine things and by an upright and orderly way of life, have become friends of God, as being especially dear to God, united to him, pleasing and conformed to him: for as the life of the supremely blessed God is the contemplation and love of his own eternal truth and infinite goodness, so such men too, in their small measure, constantly contemplate and love the truth and goodness of God himself, and so merit the knowledge of the divine secrets. Hence Christ says to such: [[John 15:15|But I have called you friends. because all things, whatsoever I have heard of my Father, I have made known to you|Vos autem dixi amicos, quia omnia quæcumque audivi a Patre meo, nota feci vobis]]. [[7:14|being commended for the gifts of discipline|Propter disciplinæ dona commendati]], that is, made commendable and praiseworthy through the works and merits of the discipline which they received.

paras.t: Mihi autem dedit Deus dicere ex sententia, id est, sententialiter loqui, seu ex certitudine, gustu interno et experientia, proferre quæ doceo; et præsumere digna horum quæ mihi dantur, id est moderate attentare talia, qualia decet me attentare, juxta mensuram gratiæ ac sapientiæ mihi collatæ. Itaque non sum præsumptuosus, in altiora tendendo, aut aggrediendo ea quæ vires gratiæ mihi concessæ excedunt; nec pusillanimis sum, non audendo me ad ea extendere, sed in his potius discrete me habeo.
paras.en: [[7:15|And God hath given to me to speak as I would|Mihi autem dedit Deus dicere ex sententia]] [Latin *ex sententia*, which Denis takes as "with settled judgement"], that is, to speak with weight, or to bring forth what I teach from certainty, from inward taste and from experience; [[7:15|and to conceive thoughts worthy of those things that are given me|et præsumere digna horum quæ mihi dantur]] [*præsumere*, "to take upon oneself", "to undertake"], that is, to undertake with moderation such things as it befits me to undertake, according to the measure of the grace and wisdom bestowed on me.
