And so I am not presumptuous, reaching after higher things or setting about what exceeds the strength of the grace granted me; nor am I faint-hearted, not daring to reach out to them; but rather I bear myself with discretion in these things.

paras.t: Quoniam ipse sapientiæ dux est : id est, sicut Deus est auctor sapientiæ, eam infundendo, ita ducit ac dirigit hominem in usu seu actu sapientiæ, ne immoderate aut indiscrete se habeat utendo sapientiæ habitu : ne scilicet aliquid extranei, utpote vana gloria, elatio, præsumptio, pusillanimitas, indiscretio, negligentia, ingratitudo, aut tale quid, ei se misceat. Quamvis enim ipsis donis atque virtutibus nemo male utatur directe, ita quod elicitive non nisi actio bona procedit ex eis; tamen nisi adsit auxilium Dei, et custodia cordis, multa se vitia ipsis admiscent, quæ eorum maculant puritatem, et tandem omnino ea corrumpunt. Denique Deus Pater, seu Trinitas Deus, ductor in omnibus fuit Christi hominis, qui est sapientia Patris, a cujus Spiritu ductus est in desertum. Et per Isaiam testatur : Spiritus Domini super me; ad evangelizandum mansuetis misit me.
paras.en: [[7:15|because he is the guide of wisdom|Quoniam ipse sapientiæ dux est]]: that is, as God is the author of wisdom by infusing it, so he leads and directs a man in the use or exercise of wisdom, so that he may not behave immoderately or indiscreetly in using the habit of wisdom: so, namely, that nothing foreign may mingle itself with it, such as vainglory, pride, presumption, faint-heartedness, indiscretion, negligence, ingratitude or the like. For although no one makes bad use of the gifts and virtues themselves directly, so that no action but a good one proceeds from them as its source [*elicitive*: as acts "elicited" by them]; yet unless God's help and the guarding of the heart are there, many vices mingle themselves with them, which stain their purity and in the end corrupt them altogether. Lastly, God the Father, or God the Trinity, was the leader in all things of Christ as man, who is the wisdom of the Father[[1 Cor 1:24||]], by whose Spirit he was led into the desert[[Matt 4:1||]]. And through Isaias he testifies: [[Is 61:1|The spirit of the Lord is upon me|Spiritus Domini super me]]; [[Is 61:1|he hath sent me to preach to the meek|ad evangelizandum mansuetis misit me]].

paras.t: Et sapientium emendator. Nam quia sapientes ac justi quotidie venialiter peccant, indigent disciplina. Ideo Deus eos emendat per adversa, et per vicariorum suorum correptiones ac correctiones, per compunctionem quoque internam, quam ingerit eis. Unde fatetur : Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo. Hinc Psalmista de Moyse, Aaron, et Samuele loquitur Deo : Deus, tu propitius fuisti eis, et ulciscens in omnes adinventiones eorum. Est quoque Deus sapientium emendator, id est meliorator, perficiendo in eis sua charismata, ac perducendo eos ad meliora et viciniora salutis. Propter quod oravit vir sanctus : Perfice gressus meos in semitis tuis.
paras.en: [[7:15|and the director of the wise|Et sapientium emendator]] [*emendator*, literally "corrector", "amender"]. For since the wise and just sin venially every day, they stand in need of discipline. Therefore God amends them by adversities, and by the reproofs and corrections of his vicars, and also by the inward compunction which he sends into them. Hence he declares: [[Apoc 3:19|Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise|Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo]]. Hence the Psalmist, speaking of Moses, Aaron and Samuel, says to God: [[Ps 98:8|thou wast a merciful God to them, and taking vengeance on all their inventions|Deus, tu propitius fuisti eis, et ulciscens in omnes adinventiones eorum]]. God is also the *emendator* of the wise, that is, the one who makes them better, by perfecting his charisms in them and leading them on to better things and nearer to salvation[[Heb 6:9||]]. For which reason a holy man prayed: [[Ps 16:5|Perfect thou my goings in thy paths|Perfice gressus meos in semitis tuis]].

paras.t: In manu enim illius et nos, et sermones nostri, id est, nos ipsi, et verba nostra ac documenta, constituti sumus in potestate Omnipotentis : quia in esse naturæ ac gratiæ indigemus indesinenter conservari, nec possumus aliquid meritorie cogitare, appetere, loqui aut operari, sine auxilio gratiæ, actualique motione ipsius, sicut testatur Apostolus : Fiduciam talem habemus ad Deum : non quod simus sufficientes cogitare aliquid a nobis, quasi ex nobis; sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est. Hinc etiam alio loco scriptum est : Domine, rex omnipotens, in ditione tua cuncta sunt posita. Simili modo in manu ejus est et omnis sapientia mentium creatarum, quæ nec ad momentum possunt in data sibi sapientia permanere, nec ea salubriter uti, sine conservatione et adjutorio Dei : quod qui rite perpendit, non superbit; et operum scientiæ disciplina, id est moralis doctrina operum scientiæ ethicæ ac practicæ, ex qua opera bona reformationesque passionum procedunt : et per scientiam potest hic specialiter prudentia designari.
paras.en: [[7:16|For in his hand are both we, and our words|In manu enim illius et nos, et sermones nostri]], that is, we ourselves, and our words and teachings, are set in the power of the Almighty: for in our being, both of nature and of grace, we need to be preserved without ceasing, and we cannot meritoriously think, desire, speak or do anything without the help of grace and his actual moving of us, as the Apostle testifies: [[2 Cor 3:4|And such confidence we have|Fiduciam talem habemus]] [[2 Cor 3:4|towards God|ad Deum]]: [[2 Cor 3:5|Not that we are sufficient to think any thing of ourselves, as of ourselves: but our sufficiency is from God|non quod simus sufficientes cogitare aliquid a nobis, quasi ex nobis; sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est]]. Hence too it is written in another place: O Lord, [[Esth 13:9|almighty king|rex omnipotens]], [[Esth 13:9|all things are in thy power|in ditione tua cuncta sunt posita]]. In like manner in his hand is [[7:16|all wisdom|omnis sapientia]] of created minds, which cannot remain even for a moment in the wisdom given them, nor use it to their salvation, without God's preserving and help: and he who duly weighs this is not proud; [[7:16|and the knowledge and skill of works|et operum scientiæ disciplina]] [Denis reads *operum scientiæ disciplina*, "the discipline of the knowledge of works", where the Vulgate has *operum scientia, et disciplina*], that is, the moral teaching of the works of ethical and practical knowledge, from which good works and the reforming of the passions proceed: and by knowledge [*scientia*] prudence can here be specially designated.

paras.t: Deinde auctor libri istius, in persona Salomonis loquitur evidenter. Ipse enim dedit mihi horum quæ sunt, id est rerum creaturarum exsistentium in natura, scientiam veram. Scientia namque infusa non habet falsitatem admixtam, sicut scientia acquisita et philosophica sæpius habet. Istud autem intelligitur de scientia naturalium quæ est donum gratiæ gratis datæ. Nam sequitur : ut sciam dispositionem orbis terrarum, id est, qualiter elementum terræ situetur et gubernetur a Deo, et qualiter ad alias mundi partes se habeat, quarum centrum vocatur; et virtutes elementorum, id est aliorum trium elementorum qualitates, ac vires activas atque passivas, et quæ ex eis possint produci, juxta illud : Producant aquæ reptile animæ viventis.
paras.en: Next, the author of this book plainly speaks in the person of Solomon. [[7:17|For he hath given me|Ipse enim dedit mihi]] [[7:17|of the things that are|horum quæ sunt]], that is, of the created things existing in nature, [[7:17|the true knowledge|scientiam veram]]. For infused knowledge has no falsehood mixed in it, as acquired and philosophical knowledge quite often has. Now this is understood of the knowledge of natural things, which is a gift of grace freely given [*gratia gratis data*: a grace given for the good of others, not to make the one who receives it holy]. For there follows: [[7:17|to know the disposition of the whole world|ut sciam dispositionem orbis terrarum]] [*orbis terrarum*, literally 'the circle of the lands', which Denis takes of the earth], that is, how the element of earth is placed and governed by God, and how it stands toward the other parts of the world, of which it is called the centre; [[7:17|and the virtues of the elements|et virtutes elementorum]], that is, the qualities of the other three elements, and their active and passive powers, and what can be produced from them, according to that saying: [[Gen 1:20|let the waters bring forth the creeping creature having life|Producant aquæ reptile animæ viventis]].

paras.t: Initium et consummationem et medietatem temporum. Qualiter tempus simul cum cœlo et motu ipsius incepit, et tandem cessante motu cœli deficiet, et jam interim currat, Salomon novit : similiter, qualiter quælibet temporis particula dividatur in principium, medium, et finem, sicut et cetera continua, de quorum numero tempus est. Verumtamen, quando motus cœli cessabit, tempusque finietur, nescivit, quum dicat Salvator : De die illo et hora nemo scit; et item, Non est vestrum nosse tempora vel momenta, quæ Pater posuit in sua potestate. Vicissitudinum permutationes, id est variationes mutationum quæ fiunt secundum temporum cursum, in quibus quandoque prædominatur frigus, aliquando calor; et consummationes temporum, id est complementa certarum periodorum generabilibus ac corruptibilibus præfixarum : quia unicuique earum ex sua natura competit certa mensura durationis : quæ tamen in diversis individuis ex certis causis, ac principiis intrinsecis aut extrinsecis, et ex divinæ providentiæ moderatione multipliciter variantur. Unde de hominis periodo legitur in Job : Constituisti terminos ejus, qui præteriri non poterunt. Morum mutationes, id est, qualiter juxta complexionum diversitates diversi sint hominum mores : qui tamen possunt mutari de malo in bonum, et e converso, et de bono in melius; et divisiones temporum in dies, hebdomadas, menses, et annos, secundum illud : Fiant luminaria in firmamento cœli, et dividant diem ac noctem, et sint in signa et tempora, et dies et annos.
paras.en: [[7:18|The beginning, and ending, and midst of the times|Initium et consummationem et medietatem temporum]]. How time began together with the heaven and its motion, and will at last fail when the motion of the heaven ceases, and meanwhile runs on: this Solomon knew; and likewise how any small part of time is divided into beginning, middle and end, as are the other continuous things, of whose number time is [that is, continuous quantities, such as lines and motions]. Yet when the motion of the heaven will cease and time be ended, he did not know, since the Saviour says: [[Matt 24:36|of that day and hour no one knoweth|De die illo et hora nemo scit]]; and again: [[Acts 1:7|It is not for you to know the time or moments, which the Father hath put in his own power|Non est vestrum nosse tempora vel momenta, quæ Pater posuit in sua potestate]]. [[7:18|the alterations of their courses|Vicissitudinum permutationes]], that is, the variations of the changes that come about with the course of the seasons, in which sometimes cold prevails, sometimes heat; [[7:18|and the changes of seasons|et consummationes temporum]] [Denis reads *consummationes*, 'completions', where the Clementine Vulgate has *commutationes*, 'changes'], that is, the completions of the fixed periods appointed for things that are generated and corrupted: for to each of them a certain measure of duration belongs by its nature, which nevertheless varies in many ways in different individuals, from certain causes, from intrinsic or extrinsic principles, and from the governance of divine providence. Hence it is read in Job of the period of man: [[Job 14:5|thou hast appointed his bounds which cannot be passed|Constituisti terminos ejus, qui præteriri non poterunt]]. 'The changes of manners' [these words, and 'the divisions of the times' below, stand in Denis's text of the verse but not in the Clementine Vulgate or the Douay-Rheims], that is, how the manners of men differ according to the differences of their complexions [that is, their bodily temperaments]; and yet these can be changed from bad to good, and the reverse, and from good to better; 'and the divisions of the times' into days, weeks, months and years, according to that saying: [[Gen 1:14|Let there be lights made in the firmament of heaven, to divide the day and the night, and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years|Fiant luminaria in firmamento cœli, et dividant diem ac noctem, et sint in signa et tempora, et dies et annos]].

paras.t: Anni cursus, id est, qualiter annus duret et defluat per quatuor partes suas : quæ sunt, ver, æstas, autumnus, et hiems; et stellarum dispositiones, quantum ad situm et motum ac influentiam. Hæc scivit Salomon saltem in generali, et quædam in speciali. Verumtamen non scivit omnia hæc perfecte et in speciali, quum a quodam dicatur : Qui stellas numeras, quarum tu nomina solus, Signa, potestates, loca, cursus, tempora nosti.
paras.en: [[7:19|The revolutions of the year|Anni cursus]], that is, how the year lasts and runs its course through its four parts, which are spring, summer, autumn and winter; [[7:19|and the dispositions of the stars|et stellarum dispositiones]], as to their position, motion and influence. These things Solomon knew, at least in general, and some of them in particular. Yet he did not know all these things perfectly and in particular, since a certain writer says [in two lines of verse addressed to God]: Thou who numberest the stars, of which thou alone knowest the names, signs, powers, places, courses and times.

paras.t: Naturas, id est proprietates, vires, efficacias, animalium : de quibus et philosophi, Aristoteles, Theophrastus, et alii multi scripserunt; et iras bestiarum : quarum multæ sunt feroces et iracundæ; vim ventorum : aliqui enim venti sunt calidi, aliqui frigidi; aliqui tempestuosi, alii vero sereni et quieti; et cogitationes hominum : quas in se ipsis intra cordis secretum cognoscere, Deo est proprium, nec sine ejus revelatione noscuntur in via; possunt tamen conjecturaliter sciri per exteriora quædam indicia et gestus ac apparatus, juxta illud Proverbiorum : Quomodo in aquis resplendent vultus prospicientium, sic corda hominum manifesta sunt prudentibus. Et Ecclesiasticus ait : Ex visu cognoscitur vir, et ab occursu faciei cognoscitur sensatus. Differentias virgultorum : quæ distinguuntur ab invicem per differentias essentiales et accidentales, variasque virtutes et operationes; et virtutes radicum : quæ habent diversas vires medicinales, miras, perutiles.
paras.en: [[7:20|The natures|Naturas]], that is, the properties, powers and efficacies, [[7:20|of living creatures|animalium]], about which the philosophers too, Aristotle, Theophrastus and many others, have written; [[7:20|and rage of wild beasts|et iras bestiarum]], many of which are fierce and wrathful; [[7:20|the force of winds|vim ventorum]]: for some winds are hot, some cold; some stormy, others clear and calm; [[7:20|and reasonings of men|et cogitationes hominum]]: to know these as they are in themselves, within the secret of the heart, belongs to God alone, nor are they known without his revelation in this life [literally 'on the way', *in via*, that is, in this present life as opposed to the homeland of glory]; yet they can be known by conjecture through certain outward signs, gestures and bearing, according to that saying of the Proverbs: [[Prov 27:19|As the faces of them that look therein, shine in the water, so the hearts of men are laid open to the wise|Quomodo in aquis resplendent vultus prospicientium, sic corda hominum manifesta sunt prudentibus]]. And Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 19:26|A man is known by his look, and a wise man, when thou meetest him, is known by his countenance|Ex visu cognoscitur vir, et ab occursu faciei cognoscitur sensatus]]. [[7:20|the diversities of plants|Differentias virgultorum]], which are distinguished from one another by essential and accidental differences, and by various virtues and operations; [[7:20|and the virtues of roots|et virtutes radicum]], which have diverse medicinal powers, wonderful and most useful.

paras.t: Et quæcumque sunt absconsa, id est hominibus incognita, et improvisa, tanquam subito et impræmeditate evenientia, didici ex revelatione et infusione divina. Omnium enim artifex docuit me sapientia, id est Sapientia increata, quæ est ars omnium productiva, exemplaribus et idealibus rerum rationibus plena, juxta illud : Quod factum est in ipso vita erat. Hinc alibi scriptum est : Dedit Dominus sapientiam Salomoni, et prudentiam multam nimis : et disputavit super lignis, a cedro quæ est in Libano, usque ad hyssopum quæ egreditur de pariete; et disseruit de jumentis, et volucribus, et reptilibus, et piscibus. Porro, quod increata Sapientia potuit eum ita docere, declarat subdendo :
paras.en: [[7:21|And all such things as are hid|Et quæcumque sunt absconsa]], that is, unknown to men, [[7:21|and not foreseen|et improvisa]], as happening suddenly and without forethought, [[7:21|I have learned|didici]] by divine revelation and infusion. [[7:21|for wisdom, which is the worker of all things, taught me|Omnium enim artifex docuit me sapientia]], that is, uncreated Wisdom, which is the art that produces all things, full of the exemplar and ideal reasons of things [that is, the patterns of all things as they are in the divine mind], according to that saying: [[John 1:3|that was made|Quod factum est]], [[John 1:4|In him was life|in ipso vita erat]] [Denis reads the words together, as many of the Fathers did: 'What was made, in him was life']. Hence it is written elsewhere: [[3 Kings 4:29|And God gave to Solomon wisdom, and understanding exceeding much|Dedit Dominus sapientiam Salomoni, et prudentiam multam nimis]]: [[3 Kings 4:33|And he treated about trees, from the cedar that is in Libanus, unto the hyssop that cometh out of the wall: and he discoursed of beasts, and of fowls, and of creeping things, and of fishes.|et disputavit super lignis, a cedro quæ est in Libano, usque ad hyssopum quæ egreditur de pariete; et disseruit de jumentis, et volucribus, et reptilibus, et piscibus]] Further, that uncreated Wisdom could teach him so, he declares by adding:

paras.t: Est enim in illa spiritus intelligentiæ sanctus. Per spiritum intelligentiæ sanctum, potest intelligi Spiritus Sanctus : de quo dictum est supra, Benignus est enim spiritus sapientiæ. Qui est in Christo, secundum naturam assumptam, secundum illud in Isaia : Requiescet super eum spiritus Domini, spiritus sapientiæ et intellectus. Est quoque in Christo secundum quod Deus, quia procedit a Patre et Filio, et manet in utroque. Insuper unaquæque divina et increata Persona est spiritus, et tota simul Trinitas adoranda est unus spiritus, sicut et unus Deus, quum dicatur, Spiritus est Deus. Sicque in Sapientia increata est spiritus sapientiæ sanctus, id est mens seu animus intellectualis, qui est ipsamet Sapientia increata : sicut in ea est divina essentia et beatitudo, ac pulchritudo immensa.
paras.en: [[7:22|For in her is the spirit of understanding; holy|Est enim in illa spiritus intelligentiæ sanctus]]. By the holy spirit of understanding can be understood the Holy Ghost, of whom it was said above: [[Wis 1:6|For the spirit of wisdom is benevolent|Benignus est enim spiritus sapientiæ]]. He is in Christ according to the nature he assumed, according to that saying in Isaias: [[Is 11:2|And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom, and of understanding|Requiescet super eum spiritus Domini, spiritus sapientiæ et intellectus]]. He is also in Christ according as he is God, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son, and abides in both. Moreover, each divine and uncreated Person is spirit, and the whole Trinity together, to be adored, is one spirit, as it is also one God, since it is said: [[John 4:24|God is a spirit|Spiritus est Deus]]. And so in uncreated Wisdom there is the holy spirit of wisdom, that is, the intellectual mind or soul, which is uncreated Wisdom itself: just as in her is the divine essence and beatitude, and immense beauty.

paras.t: Est igitur utroque modo in ea spiritus sapientiæ sanctus, id est essentialiter purus, unicus in natura, et maxime simplex, multiplex in effectu, id est multiplices gratias præstans. Quorum utrumque insinuans Paulus : Alii, inquit, per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ, alii gratia sanitatum, alii operatio virtutum, etc., et addit, Hæc omnia operatur unus atque idem Spiritus, dividens singulis prout vult. Subtilis, id est omnia acutissime ac profundissime scrutans ac intuens, dicente Apostolo : Spiritus omnia scrutatur, etiam profunda Dei; et rursus, Quæ sunt Dei, nullus novit nisi Spiritus ejus; itemque, Vivus est sermo Dei et efficax, et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti. Ab ipso quoque est omnis ingeniorum subtilitas. Disertus, id est eloquens, efficaciamque loquendi concedens : qui et omnium linguarum notitiam in primitiva frequenter dedit Ecclesia; et, ut infra habetur, Linguas infantium fecit disertas. Mobilis, id est maxime agilis, et omnia cetera movens, atque ad electorum corda se dirigens, et illis progressum in spirituali profectu distribuens. Unde ait Vas electionis : Quicumque Spiritu Dei aguntur, hi filii sunt Dei. Juxta hunc modum loquendi divinus Dionysius asserit, divinas ad nos illuminationes, Patre moto, descendere. Et Plato perhibuit, primum motorem mobilem esse.
paras.en: In both ways, then, there is in her the holy spirit of wisdom: [[7:22|holy|sanctus]], that is, essentially pure; [[7:22|one|unicus]] in nature, and supremely simple; [[7:22|manifold|multiplex]] in effect, that is, bestowing manifold graces. Hinting at both of these, Paul says: [[1 Cor 12:8|To one indeed|Alii]], he says, [[1 Cor 12:8|by the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom: and to another, the word of knowledge|per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ]], [[1 Cor 12:9|to another, the grace of healing|alii gratia sanitatum]], [[1 Cor 12:10|To another the working of miracles|alii operatio virtutum]], etc.; and he adds: [[1 Cor 12:11|But all these things, one and the same Spirit worketh, dividing to every one according as he will|Hæc omnia operatur unus atque idem Spiritus, dividens singulis prout vult]]. [[7:22|subtile|Subtilis]], that is, searching and beholding all things most keenly and most deeply, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 2:10|For the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God|Spiritus omnia scrutatur, etiam profunda Dei]]; and again: [[1 Cor 2:11|the things also that are of God, no man knoweth, but the Spirit of God|Quæ sunt Dei, nullus novit nisi Spiritus ejus]] [the margin gives only 1 Cor. ii]; and likewise: [[Heb 4:12|the word of God is living and effectual and more piercing than any two edged sword|Vivus est sermo Dei et efficax, et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti]]. From him too comes all subtlety of mind. [[7:22|eloquent|Disertus]], that is, well-spoken, and granting power in speaking: who in the primitive Church often gave the knowledge of all tongues as well; and, as is found below, [[Wis 10:21|made the tongues of infants eloquent|Linguas infantium fecit disertas]]. [[7:22|active|Mobilis]] [*mobilis*, literally 'movable', 'quick-moving'], that is, supremely agile, and moving all other things, and directing himself to the hearts of the elect, and dispensing to them progress in spiritual advancement. Hence the Vessel of election [that is, Paul, so called in the Acts of the Apostles] says: [[Rom 8:14|For whosoever are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God|Quicumque Spiritu Dei aguntur, hi filii sunt Dei]]. In this manner of speaking the divine Dionysius asserts that the divine illuminations come down to us, the Father being moved [Dionysius, Celestial Hierarchy, ch. 1]. And Plato held that the first mover is movable.

paras.t: Incoinquinatus : quia mundissimus, et incontaminabilis, et inquinata emundans; certus : quoniam cuncta infallibiliter novit, et certitudinem in verorum notitia donans; suavis : est enim naturaliter dulcis, et summe conveniens ac consolatorius : quo adspirante, jugum Dei videtur suave; amans bonum, acutus : quoniam unumquodque in tantum diligit naturali amore, quantum habet de bonitate : maxime tamen amat bonum gloriæ, deinde bonum gratiæ, et tertio loco bonum naturæ. Nam et similitudo ratio est amoris : unumquodque autem quantum habet de bonitate, tantum assimilatur Spiritui Sancto. Ideo amat omne bonum, secundum quod tale, et sic conservat illud in esse, saltem ad tempus. Qui nihil vetat benefacere : imo ad omne bonum instigat, et quæ justa sunt, fieri jubet. Sed obviare videtur, quod in Actibus Apostolorum leguntur Paulus et Silas vetati a Spiritu Sancto loqui verbum Dei in Asia. Et respondendum, quod bona agenda sunt tempore opportuno, ac desuper præstituto. Ideo, quod Spiritus tunc prohibuit Paulo, post fieri jussit. Sic et Christus ante passionem suam prohibuit discipulis prædicare gentilibus, ad quos postea misit eos.
paras.en: [[7:22|undefiled|Incoinquinatus]], because most pure, and incapable of being stained, and cleansing what is defiled; [[7:22|sure|certus]], since he knows all things infallibly, and bestows certainty in the knowledge of what is true; [[7:22|sweet|suavis]], for he is by nature gentle, and supremely fitting and consoling: when he breathes upon us, the yoke of God seems sweet; [[7:22|loving that which is good|amans bonum]], [[7:22|quick|acutus]], since he loves each thing with natural love in so far as it has goodness: yet he loves most the good of glory, next the good of grace, and in the third place the good of nature. For likeness is the ground of love; and each thing, so far as it has goodness, is so far made like the Holy Ghost. Therefore he loves every good as such, and so keeps it in being, at least for a time. [[7:22|which nothing hindereth, beneficent|Qui nihil vetat benefacere]] [Denis reads *qui nihil vetat benefacere*, 'who forbids nothing to do good', that is, who forbids no good work; the Clementine Vulgate has *quem nihil vetat, benefaciens*, 'whom nothing hinders, beneficent']: nay, he urges on to every good, and commands that what is just be done. But against this seems to stand what we read in the Acts of the Apostles, that Paul and Silas were [[Acts 16:6|forbidden by the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia|vetati a Spiritu Sancto loqui verbum Dei in Asia]]. And the answer must be that good things are to be done at the fitting time, appointed from above. Therefore what the Spirit then forbade to Paul, he afterwards bade him do[[Acts 18:6||]][[Acts 18:19||]][[Acts 19:10||]] [the margin gives Acts xviii, 6, 18–23; xix, 9, 10]. So too Christ before his passion forbade the disciples to preach to the gentiles[[Matt 10:5||]], to whom he afterwards sent them[[Matt 28:19||]][[Mark 16:15||]][[Luke 24:47||]].

paras.t: Humanus, id est communicativus et compassivus, non per veritatem affectus, sed per similitudinem operis; benignus : quia naturaliter pius; stabilis, id est invariabilis, et nos in virtutibus sanctis stabiliens; certus, securus : quia scit nil sibi posse resistere, de sua beatitudine infinita æternaliter tutus; omnem habens virtutem, id est potestatem perfectam, tanquam omnipotens : in quo universæ virtutes superexcellentissime ac simplicissime continentur, et sunt ipsa ejus essentia, qui substantialiter virtuosus ac sanctus est; omnia prospiciens : omnia namque nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus; et qui capiat omnes spiritus intelligibiles, id est omnium intellectualium creaturarum et a materia abstractarum contentivus : quia illos conservat in esse, et comprehendit in se; et quidquid perfectionis in illis est divisim ac imperfecte, in ipso est simplicissime cum infinita perfectione; mundus, subtilis : sicut expositum est. Aliqui tamen habent, Mundos, subtiles : quia intellectuales creaturæ, præsertim a materia separatæ, sunt in sua natura puræ, quamvis quædam sint voluntatis perversæ; sunt quoque acutæ ingenio.
paras.en: [[7:23|Gentle|Humanus]] [*humanus*, literally 'humane'], that is, communicative and compassionate, not by true feeling but by likeness of working [that is, he does not suffer with us, but acts as one who suffers with us would]; [[7:23|kind|benignus]], because by nature loving; [[7:23|steadfast|stabilis]], that is, unchangeable, and making us steadfast in holy virtues; [[7:23|assured, secure|certus, securus]], because he knows that nothing can resist him, safe for ever in his infinite beatitude; [[7:23|having all power|omnem habens virtutem]], that is, perfect power, as being almighty: in whom all virtues are contained most supereminently and most simply, and are his very essence, who is substantially virtuous and holy [*virtus* means both 'power' and 'virtue']; [[7:23|overseeing all things|omnia prospiciens]], for [[Heb 4:13|all things are naked and open to his eyes|omnia namque nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus]]; [[7:23|and containing all spirits: intelligible|et qui capiat omnes spiritus intelligibiles]] [Denis reads *intelligibiles*, so that the word goes with 'spirits': 'all intelligible spirits'], that is, containing all intellectual creatures and those abstracted from matter: because he keeps them in being and comprehends them in himself; and whatever perfection is in them divided and imperfectly is in him most simply, with infinite perfection; [[7:23|pure, subtile|mundus, subtilis]], as has been explained. Some, however, read *Mundos, subtiles* [in the plural, so that the words go with 'spirits']: because intellectual creatures, above all those separate from matter, are pure in their nature, though some are of perverse will; and they are also keen of mind.

paras.t: Omnibus enim mobilibus mobilior est sapientia. Sapientia increata eo sensu fertur mobilis, et cunctis mobilior, quo jam dictum est de spiritu sapientiæ, quod sit mobilis. Sapientia igitur cunctis mobilibus est mobilior, id est agilior, quia velocissime procedit per effectum ad universa quæ vult, imo instantanee, quum sit potentiæ infinitæ, cui competit agere in instanti : in qua vivimus, movemur, et sumus, quoniam procedit ad universa per suam providentiam, gubernationem, rerumque conservationem. Hinc subditur : Attingit autem ubique, quum sit incircumscripta et omnibus influxiva, portans omnia verbo suæ virtutis, propter suam munditiam, id est puritatem et simplicitatem immensam : in qua non est materia limitans, nec differentia contrahens, nec potentialitas ulla coarctans : ideo purus actus vocatur, et incircumscriptibile lumen.
paras.en: [[7:24|For wisdom is more active than all active things|Omnibus enim mobilibus mobilior est sapientia]]. Uncreated Wisdom is called active, and more active than all things, in the sense in which it was said just now of the spirit of wisdom that he is active. Wisdom, then, is more active than all active things, that is, more agile, because she goes forth most swiftly by her working to all things she wills, nay, instantly, since she is of infinite power, to which it belongs to act in an instant: in whom [[Acts 17:28|we live and move and are|vivimus, movemur, et sumus]], since she goes forth to all things by her providence, her governance and her keeping of things in being. Hence it is added: [[7:24|and reacheth everywhere|Attingit autem ubique]], since she is uncircumscribed and flows into all things, [[Heb 1:3|upholding all things by the word of his power|portans omnia verbo suæ virtutis]], [[7:24|by reason of her purity|propter suam munditiam]], that is, her immense purity and simplicity, in which there is no matter to limit her, no difference to contract her [that is, no specific difference narrowing her to one kind of being], no potentiality to confine her: therefore she is called pure act, and light that cannot be circumscribed.

paras.t: Vapor est enim virtutis Dei, id est ab omnipotente Patre procedens, sicut vapor ab aqua elevatus virtute solis. Itaque Sapientia dicitur vapor Dei similitudinarie. Et emanatio quædam est claritatis omnipotentis Dei sincera, id est res et persona æternaliter profluens et nascens ex Deo Patre : qui intuendo ac intelligendo se ipsum, id quod in se et de se intelligitur ac noscit, hoc intra se profert ac gignit; et quod sic gignitur generatione intellectuali supermundissima et immanente, est Verbum Dei Patris æternum, et unicus Filius ejus, in quo quidquid Patris est, naturaliter atque plenarie splendet ac repræsentatur. Et ideo nihil inquinatum in illam incurrit, id est, nihil imperfectionis, tenebrositatis, aut maculæ invenitur aut est in ea, quum sit verus Deus incommutabilis et perfectus. De quo S. Joannes ait : Deus lux est, et tenebræ non sunt in eo ullæ.
paras.en: [[7:25|For she is a vapour of the power of God|Vapor est enim virtutis Dei]], that is, proceeding from the almighty Father, as vapour is raised from water by the power of the sun. So Wisdom is called the vapour of God by way of likeness. [[7:25|and a certain pure emmanation of the glory of the Almighty God|Et emanatio quædam est claritatis omnipotentis Dei sincera]], that is, a reality and a person flowing forth and born eternally from God the Father, who, beholding and understanding himself, brings forth and begets within himself that which is understood and known in himself and of himself; and what is thus begotten, by an intellectual generation supremely pure and immanent [that is, remaining within the one who begets], is the eternal Word of God the Father and his only Son, in whom whatever is the Father's shines and is shown forth, by nature and in fullness. [[7:25|and therefore no defiled thing cometh into her|Et ideo nihil inquinatum in illam incurrit]], that is, nothing of imperfection, darkness or stain is found or is in her, since she is true God, unchangeable and perfect. Of whom St. John says: [[1 John 1:5|God is light and in him there is no darkness|Deus lux est, et tenebræ non sunt in eo ullæ]].

paras.t: Candor est enim lucis æternæ, id est splendidissima lux procedens a Patre, et splendor pulcherrimus in quo Pater plene relucet ac cernitur, prout ait : Qui videt me, videt et Patrem; et speculum sine macula Dei majestatis, id est immaculatissimum speculum majestatis paternæ, in quo et infinita excellentia Patris resplendet, et cuncta creata clarissime idealiterque relucent. Quemadmodum enim Pater unico actu se ipsum et universa creata intelligit, sic unica generatione genuit Filium, in quo ipse perfecte resplendet, et universa relucent creata. Hinc subditur : et imago bonitatis illius, id est ipsius superboni Dei Patris : cujus infinita bonitas manifestatur in hoc, quod bonitatem suam tam plene et infinite communicat Filio suo, nil proprium et singulare sibi reservans. Bonum namque est sui diffusivum. Est itaque Sapientia increata ac genita, seu Unigenitus Patris, naturalis et perfecta imago ipsius, ipsum plenissime repræsentans. Intellectualis autem creatura, vocatur imago Dei imitativa, vel potius ad Dei imaginem condita. Denique de ratione filii est, quod sit similis genitori. His concordat illud Apostoli, loquentis de Christo : Qui quum sit splendor gloriæ, et figura substantiæ ejus, portansque omnia verbo virtutis suæ; et alibi, Qui est imago Dei invisibilis, primogenitus omnis creaturæ.
paras.en: [[7:26|For she is the brightness of eternal light|Candor est enim lucis æternæ]], that is, the most splendid light proceeding from the Father, and the most beautiful splendour in which the Father shines back in full and is seen, as he says: [[John 14:9|he that seeth me seeth the Father also|Qui videt me, videt et Patrem]]; [[7:26|and the unspotted mirror of God's majesty|et speculum sine macula Dei majestatis]], that is, the most spotless mirror of the Father's majesty, in which both the infinite excellence of the Father shines, and all created things shine back most clearly and ideally [that is, in their ideas, the patterns of them in the divine mind]. For as the Father understands himself and all created things by a single act, so by a single generation he has begotten the Son, in whom he himself shines perfectly and all created things shine back. Hence it is added: [[7:26|and the image of his goodness|et imago bonitatis illius]], that is, of the supremely good God the Father himself, whose infinite goodness is shown in this, that he communicates his goodness so fully and infinitely to his Son, keeping back nothing as his own and peculiar to himself. For the good is diffusive of itself. So uncreated and begotten Wisdom, or the Only-begotten of the Father, is his natural and perfect image, representing him most fully; whereas the intellectual creature is called the image of God by imitation, or rather, made to the image of God[[Gen 1:27||]][[Wis 2:23||]]. Lastly, it belongs to the very notion of a son that he be like his begetter. With these things agrees that saying of the Apostle, speaking of Christ: [[Heb 1:3|Who being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance and upholding all things by the word of his power|Qui quum sit splendor gloriæ, et figura substantiæ ejus, portansque omnia verbo virtutis suæ]]; and elsewhere: [[Col 1:15|Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature|Qui est imago Dei invisibilis, primogenitus omnis creaturæ]].

paras.t: Et quum sit una, id est simplex ac indivisa in sua essentia ac persona, omnia potest, quia omnipotens, sicut et Pater : imo utriusque est una potestas; et in se permanens, id est invariabiliter impermixtibiliterque consistens, quia nil ei potest misceri, omnia innovat, id est, regendo immutat, et per generationum successionem restaurat hæc mixta, et elementum terræ in vere, autumno, hieme, et æstate; animas quoque rationales, per gratiæ infusionem seu augmentationem, et spiritualem profectum. Unde dicitur in Psalmo : Emittes Spiritum tuum, et creabuntur, et renovabis faciem terræ; atque in Apocalypsi : Dixit qui sedebat in throno, Ecce nova facio omnia. Et per nationes, id est in diversis nationibus absque personarum acceptione, et per generationum successiones, in animas sanctas se transfert, multiplicando in eis divina charismata, et tam gratiæ gratum facientis, quam gratiæ gratis datæ dona. Nam animæ sanctæ capaciores sunt ceteris divinæ illuminationis et inhabitationis supernæ : imo jugiter stant quasi in contactu Solis æterni, a quo radios sapientiæ, inflammationes caritatis divinæ, stillicidia gratiæ frequenter ac liberaliter sortiuntur. Amicos Dei et Prophetas constituit : id est, eos quos sapientia caritateque replet, et de futuris illuminat, facit Dei amicos atque Prophetas.
paras.en: [[7:27|And being but one|Et quum sit una]], that is, simple and undivided in her essence and person, [[7:27|she can do all things|omnia potest]], because she is almighty, as is the Father too: nay, the power of both is one; [[7:27|and remaining in herself the same|et in se permanens]], that is, abiding without change and without mixture, since nothing can be mixed with her, [[7:27|she reneweth all things|omnia innovat]], that is, by ruling them she changes, and by the succession of generations restores, these mixed bodies [that is, bodies compounded of the elements], and the element of earth in spring, autumn, winter and summer; and rational souls too, by the infusion or increase of grace, and by spiritual progress. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 103:30|Thou shalt send forth thy spirit, and they shall be created: and thou shalt renew the face of the earth|Emittes Spiritum tuum, et creabuntur, et renovabis faciem terræ]]; and in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 21:5|And he that sat on the throne, said: Behold, I make all things new|Dixit qui sedebat in throno, Ecce nova facio omnia]]. [[7:27|and through nations|Et per nationes]], that is, in diverse nations without respect of persons, and through the succession of generations, [[7:27|conveyeth herself into holy souls|in animas sanctas se transfert]], multiplying in them the divine gifts, the gifts both of grace that makes pleasing and of grace freely given [*gratia gratum faciens*, sanctifying grace, which makes the soul pleasing to God; *gratia gratis data*, given for the good of others]. For holy souls are more capable than others of divine illumination and of the indwelling from on high: nay, they stand continually as it were in touch with the eternal Sun, from whom they receive, often and liberally, rays of wisdom, the burnings of divine charity and the droppings of grace. [[7:27|she maketh the friends of God and prophets|Amicos Dei et Prophetas constituit]]: that is, those whom she fills with wisdom and charity and enlightens about things to come, she makes friends of God and prophets.

paras.t: Neminem enim diligit Deus, nisi eum qui cum sapientia inhabitat, id est, nisi eos qui per caritatem uniuntur Sapientiæ increatæ, et manent in ea per adhæsionem fidelem; vel qui ipsum sapientiæ infusæ donum intra se habent ac servant. Tales etenim diligit Deus dilectione prædestinationis æternæ, dummodo finaliter perseverent; vel secundum præsentem justitiam, quamdiu sunt tales. Nam sapientiæ donum a caritate non separatur. Quicumque autem hoc dono caret, habet in se vitium puerilitatis dono illi contrarium, quod vocatur stultitia : quod cunctis inest iniquis, de quibus in Ecclesiaste habetur : Stultorum infinitus est numerus. Præterea in lege naturæ, et postea tempore legis scriptæ, multi gentiles facti sunt tales, et non tantum Hebræi.
paras.en: [[7:28|For God loveth none but him that dwelleth with wisdom|Neminem enim diligit Deus, nisi eum qui cum sapientia inhabitat]], that is, none but those who are united by charity to uncreated Wisdom and abide in her by faithful adherence; or who have and keep within them the very gift of infused wisdom. For such God loves with the love of eternal predestination, provided they persevere to the end; or according to their present justice, as long as they are such. For the gift of wisdom is not separated from charity. But whoever lacks this gift has in himself the vice of childishness opposed to that gift, which is called folly; and it is in all the wicked, of whom it is said in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 1:15|the number of fools is infinite|Stultorum infinitus est numerus]] [the margin gives Eccles. i, 13; the words are in v. 15]. Moreover, under the law of nature, and afterwards in the time of the written law, many gentiles became such, and not only Hebrews.

paras.t: Est enim luce speciosior sole : quo utique increata Sapientia infinite est pulchrior. Sapientia quoque infusa, quum sit spirituali pollens decore, et præclarissima inter dona, speciosior est omni corporea venustate. Et super omnem dispositionem stellarum luci comparata, id est corporali claritati astrorum, seu luci stellis superfusæ assimilata, prior invenitur : quoniam Sapientia increata prior est illa luce, non solum infinita dignitate, sed et causalitate atque æternitate. Sapientia quoque infusa prior est dignitate : imo in angelis prior fuit illa luce etiam duratione.
paras.en: [[7:29|For she is more beautiful than the sun|Est enim luce speciosior sole]] [Denis's text reads *luce speciosior sole*, 'more beautiful in light than the sun'], than which uncreated Wisdom is indeed infinitely fairer. Infused wisdom too, since it is rich in spiritual beauty and the most glorious among the gifts, is more beautiful than all bodily comeliness. [[7:29|and above all the order of the stars|Et super omnem dispositionem stellarum]] [[7:29|being compared with the light|luci comparata]] [Denis takes these words together: 'compared with the light that is over the whole array of the stars'], that is, likened to the bodily brightness of the stars, or to the light poured over the stars, [[7:29|she is found before it|prior invenitur]]: for uncreated Wisdom is before that light not only in infinite dignity, but also in causality and eternity. Infused wisdom too is before it in dignity; nay, in the angels it was before that light even in time.

paras.t: Illi enim succedit nox, id est, lucem claritatis diurnæ nox sequitur; sapientiam autem non vincit malitia : imo, per donum sapientiæ resistit homo tentationi, et vincit in bono malum, servans patientiam in adversis, et sua probitate aliorum superans ac confundens improbitatem. Quod si sapientia vinci dicatur a malitia aut insipientia, hoc est ex fragilitate et libertate sui subjecti, quod sponte consentit iniquitati. Verumtamen istud de increata Sapientia dictum censetur, quia mox subditur : Attingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter, etc. Certum est enim, quod increatam Sapientiam nulla queat malitia superare; nec diabolus potuit suis tentationibus vincere Christum.
paras.en: [[7:30|For after this cometh night|Illi enim succedit nox]], that is, night follows the light of the brightness of day; [[7:30|but no evil can overcome wisdom|sapientiam autem non vincit malitia]]: nay, by the gift of wisdom a man resists temptation and does [[Rom 12:21|overcome evil by good|vincit in bono malum]], keeping patience in adversity, and by his own uprightness overcoming and confounding the wickedness of others. And if wisdom is said to be overcome by malice or by folly, this comes from the frailty and the freedom of the one in whom it is, who of his own accord consents to iniquity. Yet this is judged to be said of uncreated Wisdom, because there follows straight after: [[Wis 8:1|She reacheth, therefore, from end to end mightily|Attingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter]], etc. [the next verse, which opens chapter 8 in the Vulgate]. For it is certain that no malice can overcome uncreated Wisdom; nor could the devil overcome Christ by his temptations.

8.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI OCTAVI : ATTINGIT ERGO A FINE USQUE AD FINEM FORTITER.
8.title_en: Explanation of the eighth chapter: She reacheth therefore from end to end mightily

paras.t: Adhuc de excellentia et effectibus increatæ Sapientiæ, et qualiter se ad eam habuerit, et quid fructus ex ea sit consecutus, prosequitur auctor in isto capitulo.
paras.en: In this chapter the author continues on the excellence and the effects of the uncreated Wisdom, and on how he stood towards her, and what fruit he obtained from her.

paras.t: Attingit ergo a fine usque ad finem fortiter. Hæc etenim Sapientia quum sit incircumscriptibilis, ubique est præsens, et omnia penetrat, ipsisque essentiis rerum illabitur. Idcirco ab uno fine universi usque ad alium ejus finem, seu de uno extremo mundi ad aliud ejus extremum, attingit, nec infra hos limites terminatur. Hinc in Ecclesiastico protestatur: Gyrum cœli circuivi sola, et profundum abyssi penetravi. Insuper, quum Sapientia ista sit vere æterna, attingit a fine, id est a termino in quo mundus incepit, usque ad terminum in quo mundus sensibilis iste deficiet. Propter quod in Proverbiis fatetur: Quando præparabat cœlos, aderam; quando certa lege et gyro vallabat abyssos. Rursus, Attingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter: quia sicut per eam omnia facta sunt potenter, sic per eam gubernantur omnia sapienter. Unde subjungitur: et disponit omnia suaviter, id est, cuncta regit et ordinat convenienter, secundum naturam uniuscujusque eorum, per media apta ad finem congruum sibi, ad quem unicuique inclinationem indidit naturalem. Nam etsi hominem ad supernaturalem condidit finem, nihilo minus impressit ei naturalem inclinationem ad felicitatem: et supernaturalis illa beatitudo, est homini incomparabiliter melior ac delectabilior quam naturalis felicitas. Hinc et in Job asseritur: Universorum finem considerat, et omnia quæ sub cælo sunt, respicit. Istud Christus sapientia Patris in Evangelio compendiosissime docet, prohibens sollicitudinem temporalium immoderatam, volens nos in Deo tanquam in providissimo, piissimo ac fidelissimo patre confidere, et declarans etiam irrationalia et inanimata a divina providentia procurari: Respicite, inquiens, volatilia cœli, quoniam non seminant neque metunt; et Pater vester cœlestis pascit ea.
paras.en: [[8:1|She reacheth, therefore, from end to end mightily|Attingit ergo a fine usque ad finem fortiter]]. For since this Wisdom is uncircumscribable [that is, not contained within any bounds of place], she is present everywhere, and penetrates all things, and flows into the very essences of things. Therefore she reaches from one end of the universe to its other end, or from one extremity of the world to its other extremity, and is not bounded within these limits. Hence she declares in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 24:8|I alone have compassed the circuit of heaven, and have penetrated into the bottom of the deep|Gyrum cœli circuivi sola, et profundum abyssi penetravi]]. Moreover, since this Wisdom is truly eternal, she reaches from the end, that is, from the term at which the world began, to the term at which this sensible world shall fail. For this reason she confesses in Proverbs: [[Prov 8:27|When he prepared the heavens, I was present: when with a certain law, and compass, he enclosed the depths|Quando præparabat cœlos, aderam; quando certa lege et gyro vallabat abyssos]]. Again, [[8:1|She reacheth, therefore, from end to end mightily|Attingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter]]: because as all things were made mightily through her, so all things are governed wisely through her. Hence it is added: [[8:1|and ordereth all things sweetly|et disponit omnia suaviter]], that is, she rules and orders all things fittingly, according to the nature of each of them, by means suited to the end proper to it, towards which she has given each a natural inclination. For although she created man for a supernatural end, she nonetheless impressed on him a natural inclination to happiness; and that supernatural beatitude is incomparably better and more delightful for man than natural happiness. Hence it is also said in Job: [[Job 28:3|the end of all things he considereth|Universorum finem considerat]], [[Job 28:24|and looketh on all things that are under heaven|et omnia quæ sub cælo sunt, respicit]]. Christ, the wisdom of the Father, teaches this most concisely in the Gospel, forbidding immoderate anxiety about temporal things, wishing us to trust in God as in a most provident, most loving and most faithful father, and declaring that even irrational and inanimate things are cared for by divine providence: [[Matt 6:26|Behold|Respicite]], he says, [[Matt 6:26|the birds of the air, for they neither sow, nor do they reap|volatilia cœli, quoniam non seminant neque metunt]]; [[Matt 6:26|and your heavenly Father feedeth them|et Pater vester cœlestis pascit ea]].

paras.t: Denique subtiliores ac meliores philosophi, ex consideratione decentissimi ordinis rerum, et propria uniuscujusque adornatione, proprietate, eventu, dixerunt hæc omnia sub divina providentia cadere. Unde decimo de Civitate Dei loquitur Augustinus: Plotinus Platonicus de Providentia disputans, eam a summo Deo usque ad hæc terrena et ima pertingere, flosculorum ac foliorum pulchritudine comprobat: quæ omnia quasi abjecta ac velocissime pereuntia, decentissimos formarum suarum numeros habere non posse affirmat, nisi inde formentur, ubi forma intelligibilis et incommutabilis simul habens omnia, perseverat. Propter hoc, quinto de Civitate Dei rursus disseruit Augustinus: Deus nec exigui et contemptibilis animantis viscera, nec herbæ flosculum, nec arboris folium sine suarum convenientia partium et quadam veluti pace reliquit. Idcirco et in libro de Causis pulchre probatur, quod causa prima regit res omnes per finem decoris, id est cum summo decore. Siquidem inferiora regit per superiora, irrationalia per intellectualia, homines per angelos, sed et per se ipsam aliqua agit in rebus. Et quamvis in se et per se universa disponit, providentiam tamen per causas secundas in multis exsequitur.
paras.en: Finally, the subtler and better philosophers, from considering the most seemly order of things, and the proper adornment, property and outcome of each, said that all these things fall under divine providence. Hence Augustine says in the tenth book of the City of God: Plotinus the Platonist, disputing on Providence, proves from the beauty of little flowers and leaves that it reaches from the highest God down to these earthly and lowest things: all of which, being as it were cast off and perishing very swiftly, he affirms could not have the most seemly proportions [Latin *numeros*, "numbers", that is, measured harmonies] of their forms unless they were formed from that place where the intelligible and unchangeable form, having all things together, abides. For this reason Augustine again discoursed in the fifth book of the City of God: God has left neither the entrails of a small and contemptible animal, nor the little flower of a herb, nor the leaf of a tree, without the agreement of its parts and a kind of peace. Therefore it is also finely proved in the Book of Causes that the first cause rules all things through the end of comeliness, that is, with the highest comeliness. For it rules lower things through higher, irrational things through intellectual ones, men through angels; but it also does some things in creatures by itself. And although in itself and by itself it disposes all things, yet in many things it carries out its providence through secondary causes.

paras.t: Præterea, quamvis in rerum regimine multa videantur indecentia et injusta, ut quod justi ab impiis opprimuntur, ac consimilia; tamen in ordine ad providentiam Dei cuncta congruentissime disponuntur. Et frequenter quod esse videtur pœna, est medicina; et quod reputatur injuria, est corona. Sed in talibus occulta sunt et latent nos divina judicia.
paras.en: Moreover, although in the governing of things many things seem unseemly and unjust, as that the just are oppressed by the wicked, and the like, yet in relation to the providence of God all things are most fittingly ordered. And often what seems to be a punishment is a medicine, and what is reckoned an injury is a crown. But in such matters the divine judgements are hidden and concealed from us.

paras.t: Hanc, scilicet increatam Sapientiam, et etiam infusam sapientiam quæ est donum, amavi, et exquisivi, id est, obtinere multipliciter laboravi, a juventute mea, in qua non concupiscentiæ, sed sapientiæ studui: quoniam ipsa locuta est: Ego diligentes me diligo; et qui mane vigilaverit ad me, inveniet me. Unde rursus Sapiens exhortatur: Fili, a juventute tua excipe doctrinam, et usque ad canos invenies sapientiam. Et quæsivi sponsam eam mihi assumere: id est, studui ei amorose ac familiariter adhærere, eamque brachiis caritatis amplecti, atque ex unione cum ea fructum actuum virtuosorum producere: quod totum tam de Sapientia increata, quam de sapientia infusa, suo potest modo intelligi. Porro in Canticis canticorum Sapientia ista increata ac genita, non sponsa, ut hic, sed sub nomine fratris et regis ac dilecti, sponsus vocatur. Cujus triplex, ut ibi expositum fuit, est sponsa: videlicet generalis, quæ est universalis Ecclesia, et etiam sponsa particularis, videlicet anima justi, sponsaque singularis, quæ est beatissima et incomparabilis Virgo Maria. Ipsa etenim sapientia dicitur sponsa, propter rationes jam tactas. Unde et in Proverbiis legitur: Dic sapientiæ, Soror mea es; et prudentiam voca amicam. Est itaque sponsa, quia amator sincerus, homo justus, seu spiritus rationalis mundus et sanctus, suscipit eam, et brachiis eam stringit amoris, et conjungit se ei, atque ex unione cum ea parit fructum virtutum. Est quoque sponsus, quoniam mentem creatam applicat sibi, et sancta succendit dilectione, spiritualiterque fecundat, atque ex ea et per eam producit opera bona, juxta illud in Isaia: Omnia opera nostra operatus es in nobis. Unde dixit Apostolus: Deus est qui operatur in nobis velle et perficere.
paras.en: [[8:2|Her|Hanc]], namely the uncreated Wisdom, and also the infused wisdom which is a gift, [[8:2|have I loved, and have sought her out|amavi, et exquisivi]], that is, I laboured in many ways to obtain her, [[8:2|from my youth|a juventute mea]], in which I applied myself not to concupiscence but to wisdom: for she herself has said: [[Prov 8:17|I love them that love me: and they that in the morning early watch for me, shall find me|Ego diligentes me diligo; et qui mane vigilaverit ad me, inveniet me]]. Hence the Wise Man exhorts again: [[Ecclus 6:18|My son, from thy youth up receive instruction, and even to thy grey hairs thou shalt find wisdom|Fili, a juventute tua excipe doctrinam, et usque ad canos invenies sapientiam]]. [[8:2|and have desired to take for my spouse|Et quæsivi sponsam eam mihi assumere]]: that is, I strove to cleave to her lovingly and familiarly, and to embrace her with the arms of charity, and from union with her to bring forth the fruit of virtuous acts: all of which can be understood in its own way both of the uncreated Wisdom and of infused wisdom. Further, in the Canticle of Canticles this uncreated and begotten Wisdom is called not the bride, as here, but the Bridegroom, under the name of brother[[Cant 8:1||]] and king[[Cant 1:3||]][[Cant 1:11||]] and beloved[[Cant 2:8||]] [the margin gives Cant. viii, 1; i, 3, 11; ii, v–viii: *beloved* recurs throughout chapters 2 and 5–8]. His bride, as was explained there, is threefold: namely the general bride, which is the universal Church; and also the particular bride, namely the soul of the just man; and the singular bride, who is the most blessed and incomparable Virgin Mary. For wisdom herself is called a bride, for the reasons already touched on. Hence we read in Proverbs too: [[Prov 7:4|Say to wisdom: Thou art my sister: and call prudence thy friend|Dic sapientiæ, Soror mea es; et prudentiam voca amicam]]. She is therefore a bride because the sincere lover, the just man, or the pure and holy rational spirit, receives her, and clasps her in the arms of love, and joins himself to her, and from union with her brings forth the fruit of the virtues. She is also the Bridegroom, because she draws the created mind to herself, and kindles it with holy love, and makes it spiritually fruitful, and from it and through it brings forth good works, according to that saying in Isaias: [[Is 26:12|thou hast wrought all our works for us|Omnia opera nostra operatus es in nobis]]. Hence the Apostle said: [[Phil 2:13|it is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish|Deus est qui operatur in nobis velle et perficere]].

paras.t: Et amator factus sum formæ illius, id est pulchritudinis Sapientiæ increatæ, imo et sapientiæ infusæ, quæ est pulcherrimus mentis ornatus, increatæ menti ac Sapientiæ ejus æternæ eam conformans. At vero, quamvis pulchritudo toti supergloriosissimæ conveniat Trinitati, attamen Sapientiæ genitæ seu Verbo æterno appropriatur. Verbum namque est emanatio intellectus, ad quod pertinet repræsentare intelligentis conceptum. Ideo quidquid Patris est, repræsentatur ac plene refulget in Filio: quod ad pulchritudinis pertinet rationem. Ideo subtilissime dixit Hilarius: Æternitas est in Patre, species in imagine, id est pulchritudo in Filio, usus in munere, id est communio in Spiritu Sancto, qui est donum Patris ac Filii.
paras.en: [[8:2|and I became a lover of her beauty|Et amator factus sum formæ illius]], that is, of the beauty of the uncreated Wisdom, nay, and of infused wisdom, which is the most beautiful adornment of the mind, conforming it to the uncreated Mind and to his eternal Wisdom. But although beauty belongs to the whole most supremely glorious Trinity, yet it is appropriated [that is, attributed especially to one Person, though common to all three] to the begotten Wisdom, or the eternal Word. For a word is an emanation of the intellect, to which it belongs to represent the concept of the one who understands. Therefore whatever is the Father's is represented and shines forth fully in the Son: which belongs to the notion of beauty. Therefore Hilary said most subtly: Eternity is in the Father, form [Latin *species*, "form" or "beauty"] in the Image, that is, beauty in the Son; use in the Gift, that is, communion in the Holy Ghost, who is the gift of the Father and the Son.

paras.t: Generositatem illius, id est nobilitatem et excellentiam Sapientiæ increatæ, imo et doni sapientiæ, glorificat, id est, præclaram et summam esse manifestat, contubernium habens Dei, id est quicumque illuminatus a Deo, et per caritatem sapientiamque infusam, societatem quamdam habens cum eo, ac Creatori cohabitans per charismata gratiæ. Talis quippe sic desuper illustratus per fidem rationibus credendorum ornatam, et infusæ sapientiæ gustum, ac contemplationis acumen, novit, confitetur, magnificat Sapientiam increatam, ejusque donum ac radium, sapientiam infusam. Et talis fuit Salomon, saltem ad tempus, qui de deitate, eminentia, ac generatione æterna increatæ ac genitæ Sapientiæ, evidenter locutus est in Proverbiis; alii quoque sancti Prophetæ, et præsertim Apostoli. Potissime autem Christus secundum quod homo, plenissime adimpletus omni supero charismate suæ perfectioni non derogante, contubernalisque Patri, sicut in Apocalypsi testatur, Sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus; declaravit nobis suam deitatem, sapientiam, excellentiamque immensam, juxta illud: Deum nemo vidit unquam; unigenitus Filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse enarravit.
paras.en: [[8:3|her nobility|Generositatem illius]], that is, the nobility and excellence of the uncreated Wisdom, nay, and of the gift of wisdom, [[8:3|She glorifieth|glorificat]], that is, shows it to be most glorious and supreme, [[8:3|by being conversant with God|contubernium habens Dei]] [Latin *contubernium*, "sharing a dwelling", "companionship"]: that is, whoever is enlightened by God and, through charity and infused wisdom, has a certain fellowship with him, and dwells with the Creator through the gifts of grace. For such a man, thus enlightened from above by a faith furnished with reasons for the things to be believed, and by the taste of infused wisdom and keenness of contemplation, knows, confesses and magnifies the uncreated Wisdom, and her gift and ray, infused wisdom. And such was Solomon, at least for a time, who spoke plainly in Proverbs of the deity, eminence and eternal generation of the uncreated and begotten Wisdom[[Prov 8:22||]] [the margin gives Prov. viii, 22–31]; and so did the other holy Prophets, and especially the Apostles. But above all Christ as man, most fully filled with every heavenly gift that does not detract from his perfection, and companion of the Father, as he testifies in the Apocalypse, [[Apoc 3:21|am set down with my Father in his throne|Sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus]], has declared to us his deity, wisdom and boundless excellence, according to that saying: [[John 1:18|No man hath seen God at any time: the only begotten Son who is in the Bosom of the Father, he hath declared him|Deum nemo vidit unquam; unigenitus Filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse enarravit]].

paras.t: Sed et omnium Dominus dilexit illam, id est, Deus Pater dilexit ac diligit Sapientiam istam æternam, utpote Verbum suum æternum et unicum Filium, sicut in ejus baptizatione ac transfiguratione locutus est: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacui. Diligit, inquam, cum dilectione intensive immensa, videlicet tanta, quanta se ipsum. Christum vero secundum naturam assumptam, diligit plus quam totum pariter universum, quia majus bonum voluit communicavitque ei, hoc est increatum et hypostaticum esse Verbi æterni, ad quod assumpta est humanitas Christi.
paras.en: [[8:3|yea, and the Lord of all things hath loved her|Sed et omnium Dominus dilexit illam]], that is, God the Father has loved and loves this eternal Wisdom, as being his eternal Word and only Son, as he spoke at his baptism[[Matt 3:17||]] and transfiguration: [[Matt 17:5|This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased|Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacui]]. He loves him, I say, with a love intensively boundless [that is, infinite in its strength, not merely in its extent], namely as great as that with which he loves himself. But Christ according to the nature assumed he loves more than the whole universe together, because he willed and communicated to him a greater good, that is, the uncreated and hypostatic being of the eternal Word, to which the humanity of Christ was assumed.

paras.t: Doctrix est enim disciplinæ Dei, id est moralis scientiæ, per quam homines fiunt Deo placentes. Quam disciplinam Christus in Evangelio docuit copiose, dicendo: Beati pauperes spiritu, etc. Nam de plenitudine ejus accepimus omnes. Et quamvis doctrina ista non sit causa a priori, ob quam Pater diligit Christum modis jam tactis, est tamen causa a posteriori, seu signum quod diligit ipsum. Juxta quem modum Filius in Evangelio ait: Pater non reliquit me solum: quia ego quæ placita sunt ei, facio semper. Et electrix operum illius, id est, opera veraciter virtuosa ac placita Deo, approbat et eligi facit, vitiosaque reprobat, dicens: Attendite vobis a falsis prophetis, etc.; a fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos.
paras.en: [[8:4|For it is she that teacheth the knowledge of God|Doctrix est enim disciplinæ Dei]] [Latin *disciplinæ*, "discipline", "teaching"], that is, of the moral science through which men become pleasing to God. This discipline Christ taught abundantly in the Gospel, saying: [[Matt 5:3|Blessed are the poor in spirit|Beati pauperes spiritu]], etc. For [[John 1:16|of his fulness we all have received|de plenitudine ejus accepimus omnes]]. And although this teaching is not a cause a priori, for which the Father loves Christ in the ways already touched on, yet it is a cause a posteriori, or a sign that he loves him. In which way the Son says in the Gospel: The Father [[John 8:29|hath not left me alone. For I do always the things that please him|non reliquit me solum: quia ego quæ placita sunt ei, facio semper]]. [[8:4|and is the chooser of his works|Et electrix operum illius]], that is, she approves works truly virtuous and pleasing to God and causes them to be chosen, and condemns vicious ones, saying: [[Matt 7:15|Beware of false prophets|Attendite vobis a falsis prophetis]], etc.; [[Matt 7:16|By their fruits you shall know them|a fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos]].

paras.t: Et si divitiæ appetuntur in terra, quid sapientia locupletius? quasi dicat: Quicumque cupit et amat divitias temporales, merito debet sapientiam istam appetere et amare: quia in ea est omnium bonorum, omniumque pulchrorum ac desiderabilium plenitudo immensa. Quæ in Proverbiis contestatur: Mecum sunt divitiæ et gloria. Et iterum Salomon loquitur: Quid prodest stulto habere divitias, quum sapientiam emere non possit? quia in sapientia consistit opulentia vera. Nam et vita æterna est in actu sapientiæ, qui est primæ et summæ contemplatio veritatis. Unde locutus est Isaias: Divitiæ salutis sapientia et scientia. Quæ omnia operatur. Increata namque Sapientia, omnium est creatrix, juxta quod in Evangelio legitur: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Et cuncta quotidie moderatur ac administrat et regit, quemadmodum testatur: Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Quum igitur omnia operetur, constat quod omnium perfectiones in ea consistant, et ipsa universis sit ditior.
paras.en: [[8:5|And if riches be desired in life|Et si divitiæ appetuntur in terra]] [Denis's text reads *in terra*, "on earth"; a marginal note gives the reading *in vita*, "in life", which is the Vulgate's], [[8:5|what is richer than wisdom|quid sapientia locupletius]]? as if to say: Whoever desires and loves temporal riches ought by rights to desire and love this wisdom: because in her is the boundless fullness of all goods and of all things beautiful and desirable. She declares in Proverbs: [[Prov 8:18|With me are riches and glory|Mecum sunt divitiæ et gloria]]. And again Solomon says: [[Prov 17:16|What doth it avail a fool to have riches, seeing he cannot buy wisdom?|Quid prodest stulto habere divitias, quum sapientiam emere non possit?]]? because true wealth consists in wisdom. For eternal life too lies in the act of wisdom, which is the contemplation of the first and highest truth. Hence Isaias said: [[Is 33:6|riches of salvation, wisdom and knowledge|Divitiæ salutis sapientia et scientia]]. [[8:5|which maketh all things|Quæ omnia operatur]]. For the uncreated Wisdom is the creatress of all things, according to what we read in the Gospel: [[John 1:3|All things were made by him|Omnia per ipsum facta sunt]]. And daily she moderates, administers and rules all things, as he testifies: [[John 5:17|My Father worketh until now; and I work|Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor]]. Since therefore she works all things, it is clear that the perfections of all things are found in her, and that she is richer than all.

paras.t: Si autem sensus operatur, id est, si intellectus creatus, seu humana notitia, est activa diversorum effectuum, quis horum quæ sunt, magis quam illa, est artifex? tanquam dicat: Utique nullus, quoniam Sapientia increata est universorum exemplaris effectivaque causa, a qua cuncta procedunt, sicut artificiata a suo artifice. Ex quo sequitur, quod nihil potentius sapientia: ideoque, si quæratur potestas, ipsa vere omnipotens, summe est expetenda.
paras.en: [[8:6|And if sense do work|Si autem sensus operatur]], that is, if the created intellect, or human knowledge, brings about various effects, [[8:6|who is a more artful worker than she of those things that are?|quis horum quæ sunt, magis quam illa, est artifex?]]? as if to say: Surely none, since the uncreated Wisdom is the exemplar and efficient cause of all things, from which all things proceed as works of art from their craftsman. From which it follows that nothing is more powerful than wisdom; and therefore, if power is sought, she, being truly almighty, is to be sought above all.

paras.t: Et si justitiam quis diligit, id est, si quis appetit esse virtuosus. Justitia enim uno modo dicitur esse omnis seu quælibet virtus, quoniam per unamquamque virtutem homo se habet ut decet ac debet, debitumque impendit Deo obsequium: quod etiam de misericordia clarum est, quia per eam proximis subvenitur, quod a Deo præcipitur. Labores hujus magnas habent virtutes: id est, actus quibus pro sapientia obtinenda ac possidenda laboratur, annexas habent ac promerentur virtutes præcipuas, seu earum opera bona, sive profectuum incrementa, quemadmodum dictum est supra: Bonorum laborum gloriosus est fructus. Ipsa etiam increata Sapientia taliter laborantibus infundit virtutes, aut spirituales profectus. Propterea subditur: Sobrietatem enim, id est temperantiam, et sapientiam, id est prudentiam, docet: quia eas largitur, et qualiter utendum sit eis, inspirat; et justitiam quæ est virtus specialis, et virtutem, id est fortitudinem, quæ passionem timoris refrenat ac moderatur, et quæ ardua facit viriliter aggredi, et circa pericula mortis se strenue gerit.
paras.en: [[8:7|And if a man love justice|Et si justitiam quis diligit]], that is, if anyone desires to be virtuous. For in one sense justice is said to be every virtue, or any virtue whatever, since by each virtue a man behaves as is fitting and as he ought, and renders to God the service due to him: which is clear even of mercy, because by it our neighbours are helped, which God commands. [[8:7|her labours have great virtues|Labores hujus magnas habent virtutes]]: that is, the acts by which one labours to obtain and possess wisdom have joined to them, and merit, the chief virtues, or their good works, or increases of progress, as was said above: [[Wis 3:15|the fruit of good labours is glorious|Bonorum laborum gloriosus est fructus]]. The uncreated Wisdom herself also pours virtues, or spiritual progress, into those who labour so. Therefore it is added: [[8:7|for she teacheth temperance|Sobrietatem enim]] [the Latin has *sobrietatem*, "sobriety"], that is, temperance, [[8:7|and prudence|et sapientiam]] [Denis reads *sapientiam*, "wisdom", where the Vulgate has *prudentiam*], that is, prudence, she teaches: because she bestows them, and inspires how they are to be used; [[8:7|and justice|et justitiam]], which is a special virtue, [[8:7|and fortitude|et virtutem]] [Latin *virtutem*, "strength" or "virtue"], that is, fortitude, which reins in and moderates the passion of fear, and which makes one undertake hard things manfully, and bears itself bravely in the dangers of death.

paras.t: Hæ sunt quatuor cardinales virtutes. De quibus subjungitur: quibus nihil utilius est in vita hominibus: quia istæ quatuor virtutes præcipue conferunt homini ad obtinendum salutem. Verumtamen virtutes theologicæ, et etiam septem dona, sunt eis præstantiores. Sed inter virtutes morales, istæ præfulgent ac utiliores censentur. Unde et in ordine harum, cardinales (id est principales) dicuntur; vel, cardinales, quoniam aliæ virtutes morales circa ipsas versantur et reducuntur, sicut ostium in cardine vertitur. De harum quatuor virtutum cardinalium sufficientia, ratione, proprietate, et distinctione, diffuse loquitur Thomas in prima secundæ, quæstione 61.
paras.en: These are the four cardinal virtues. Of which it is added: [[8:7|which are such things as men can have nothing more profitable in life|quibus nihil utilius est in vita hominibus]]: because these four virtues especially help man to obtain salvation. Yet the theological virtues, and also the seven gifts, are more excellent than they. But among the moral virtues these shine out and are reckoned more profitable. Hence too, in the order of these, they are called cardinal (that is, principal); or cardinal, because the other moral virtues turn about them and are reduced to them, as a door turns on its hinge [Latin *cardo*, "hinge", from which *cardinalis* comes]. Of the sufficiency, nature, property and distinction of these four cardinal virtues Thomas speaks at length in the First of the Second Part, question 61.

paras.t: De quibus et Seneca in libro de Copia verborum, seu Quatuor virtutibus, pulchre tractat: Si prudentiam, inquiens, amplecteris, ubique idem eris, et prout rerum ac temporis varietas exigit, ita te illis accommodabis; nec in aliquibus te mutabis, sed magis aptabis: sicut manus eadem est, quum in palmam extenditur, et dum in pugnum restringitur. Prudentis proprium est examinare consilia, nec credulitate incauta ac facili falli. Denique fortitudinem vocat magnanimitatem. De qua scribit: Magnanimitas, quæ et fortitudo dicitur, si insit animo tuo, cum magna fiducia vives liber, intrepidus, alacer: quæ tamen si modum suum excedat, faciet virum minacem, inflatum, turbidum, inquietum, et in quascumque extollentias verborum atque factorum, neglecta honestate, festinum. Porro justitia est tacita naturæ conventio, in adjutorium multorum inventa. Justitia non nostra institutio, sed divina lex est, et vinculum societatis humanæ. Quisquis hanc sectari desideras, Deum time prius et ama, ut ameris ab eo. Amabis Deum, si eum in hoc imiteris, ut omnibus velis prodesse, nulli nocere: et tunc omnes te virum justum appellabunt, sequentur, venerabuntur ac diligent. Justus autem ut sis, non solum aliis non nocebis, sed nocentes pro viribus prohibebis. Temperantia demum a brutis te dividet, et a fœdis separabit inquinamentis, ut ratione, non passione, te regas. Hæc Seneca.
paras.en: Seneca too treats finely of them in his book On Abundance of Words, or On the Four Virtues [the work, also called *Formula vitæ honestæ*, is by Martin of Braga, though long ascribed to Seneca]: If you embrace prudence, he says, you will be the same everywhere, and as the variety of things and times requires, so you will adapt yourself to them; you will not change yourself in anything, but rather fit yourself: as the hand is the same when it is stretched out into an open palm and when it is closed into a fist. It is the mark of the prudent man to examine counsels, and not to be deceived by heedless and easy credulity. Next, he calls fortitude magnanimity. Of which he writes: If magnanimity, which is also called fortitude, is in your soul, you will live with great confidence, free, fearless, eager: yet if it exceeds its measure, it will make a man threatening, puffed up, turbulent, restless, and hasty, with no regard for what is honourable, towards every kind of vaunting in word and deed. Further, justice is a tacit agreement of nature, devised for the help of many. Justice is not an institution of ours, but a divine law, and the bond of human society. Whoever you are that desire to follow it, first fear and love God, that you may be loved by him. You will love God if you imitate him in this, that you wish to profit all and harm none: and then all will call you a just man, will follow, revere and love you. And that you may be just, you will not only not harm others, but will restrain those who do harm as far as you can. Lastly, temperance will divide you from the brutes and separate you from foul defilements, so that you govern yourself by reason, not by passion. So far Seneca.

paras.t: Et si multitudinem scientiæ, id est scientiam copiosam, desiderat quis, scit præterita, et de futuris æstimat, id est, prænoscit, et quibusdam certam, quibusdam probabilem, dat futurorum notitiam; scit versutias sermonum, id est contortas sententias, astutiasque verborum, quibus nequaquam poterit falli, et dissolutiones argumentorum. De quibus omnibus instruit suos, quibus promisit: Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri. Hinc quum quidam surrexissent de synagoga, disputantes cum beatissimo Stephano, non poterant resistere sapientiæ et Spiritui, qui loquebatur per primicerium martyrum. Signa et monstra scit, antequam fiant, id est, futura mirabilia et insolita, aliquid designantia, monstratione admirationeque digna, prænoscit. De quibus in Evangelio loquitur: Erunt signa in sole et luna. Rursus: Surget gens contra gentem, et regnum adversus regnum; et terræ motus magni erunt per loca, et pestilentiæ, et fames, terroresque de cælo, et signa magna erunt. Et apud Joelem: Dabo prodigia in cælo et in terra, sanguinem et ignem et vaporem fumi: sol convertetur in tenebras et luna in sanguinem, antequam veniat dies Domini magnus et horribilis. Et eventus temporum et seculorum, id est, quid in singulis quibusque temporibus et certis durationibus ac generationibus, fiet sive eveniet.
paras.en: [[8:8|And if a man desire much knowledge|Et si multitudinem scientiæ]], that is, abundant knowledge, [[8:8|she knoweth things past, and judgeth of things to come|desiderat quis, scit præterita, et de futuris æstimat]], that is, she knows them beforehand, and gives knowledge of things to come, certain to some, probable to others; [[8:8|she knoweth the subtilties of speeches|scit versutias sermonum]], that is, twisted sayings and cunning words, by which she can in no way be deceived, [[8:8|and the solutions of arguments|et dissolutiones argumentorum]]. In all these she instructs her own, to whom she promised: [[Luke 21:15|I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist and gainsay|Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri]]. Hence when some had risen up from the synagogue, disputing with the most blessed Stephen[[Acts 6:9||]], [[Acts 6:10|they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit that spoke|non poterant resistere sapientiæ et Spiritui, qui loquebatur]] through the first of the martyrs [Latin *primicerius*, "the first on the list", "the chief"]. [[8:8|she knoweth signs and wonders before they be done|Signa et monstra scit, antequam fiant]], that is, she knows beforehand future marvels and unwonted things, signifying something, worthy to be shown and wondered at.
