Of which he speaks in the Gospel: [[Luke 21:25|there shall be signs in the sun and in the moon|Erunt signa in sole et luna]]. Again: [[Luke 21:10|Nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom|Surget gens contra gentem, et regnum adversus regnum]]; [[Luke 21:11|there shall be great earthquakes in divers places and pestilences and famines and terrors from heaven: and there shall be great signs|et terræ motus magni erunt per loca, et pestilentiæ, et fames, terroresque de cælo, et signa magna erunt]] [the margin gives Luke xxi, 25 only; this second quotation is Luke 21:10–11]. And in Joel: [[Joel 2:30|I will shew wonders in heaven; and in earth, blood, and fire, and vapour of smoke|Dabo prodigia in cælo et in terra, sanguinem et ignem et vaporem fumi]]: [[Joel 2:31|The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood: before the great and dreadful day of the Lord doth come|sol convertetur in tenebras et luna in sanguinem, antequam veniat dies Domini magnus et horribilis]]. [[8:8|and the events of times and ages|Et eventus temporum et seculorum]], that is, what will be done or happen in each and every time, and in fixed durations and generations.

paras.t: Proposui ergo hanc Sapientiam increatam adducere mihi ad convivandum, id est, gratiosam ejus præsentiam, inhabitationem, adventum, decrevi promereri ac adipisci, orando et alia bona agendo, ut spiritualiter epuler secum, et ipsa mecum, delectando in ea, et per ejus contemplationem, cultum, amorem, me reficiendo: quoniam ipsa in Apocalypsi testatur: Ego sto ante ostium, et pulso: si quis aperuerit mihi januam, intrabo ad illum, et cœnabo cum eo, et ipse mecum. Sciens quoniam mecum communicabit de bonis, id est, dona gratiæ suæ mihi distribuet, et spiritualiter me ditabit: quia quanto quis frequentius et affectuosius ipsam contemplatur, et ei se applicat, tanto plus crescit in donis ipsius; et erit allocutio cogitationis et tædii mei, id est, sua inspiratione et illustratione cogitationes meas diriget et purgabit, meaque tædia consolabitur et excludet: quoniam ejus irradiatio mundat, exhilarat, ac dirigit mentem, et vana atque phantastica ejicit tædia.
paras.en: [[8:9|I purposed, therefore, to take her|Proposui ergo hanc]], the uncreated Wisdom, [[8:9|to me to live with me|adducere mihi ad convivandum]] [Denis reads *convivandum*, "to feast with", where the Vulgate has *convivendum*, "to live with"; his gloss follows his reading]: that is, I resolved to merit and obtain her gracious presence, indwelling and coming, by praying and doing other good works, that I might feast with her spiritually, and she with me, by delighting in her and refreshing myself through contemplating, worshipping and loving her: for she testifies in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:20|I stand at the gate and knock|Ego sto ante ostium, et pulso]]: if any man [[Apoc 3:20|open to me the door, I will come in to him and will sup with him: and he with me|aperuerit mihi januam, intrabo ad illum, et cœnabo cum eo, et ipse mecum]]. [[8:9|knowing that she will communicate to me of her good things|Sciens quoniam mecum communicabit de bonis]], that is, she will distribute to me the gifts of her grace and will enrich me spiritually: because the more often and the more lovingly one contemplates her and applies oneself to her, the more one grows in her gifts; [[8:9|and will be a comfort in my cares and grief|et erit allocutio cogitationis et tædii mei]] [Latin *allocutio*, "a speaking to", "consolation"], that is, by her inspiration and enlightening she will direct and purify my thoughts, and will console and drive away my wearinesses: for her shining cleanses, gladdens and directs the mind, and casts out vain and fanciful wearinesses.

paras.t: Habebo propter hanc claritatem ad turbas, id est, magnæ reputationis ac famæ ero inter homines, propter sapientiam mihi infusam a Sapientia increata; et honorem apud seniores: quia eos qui in sapientia clare præfulgent, reputant honorandos.
paras.en: [[8:10|For her sake I shall have glory among the multitude|Habebo propter hanc claritatem ad turbas]], that is, I shall be of great repute and fame among men, because of the wisdom infused into me by the uncreated Wisdom; [[8:10|and honour with the ancients|et honorem apud seniores]]: because they deem those who shine out brightly in wisdom worthy of honour.

paras.t: Juvenis et acutus inveniar in judicio, id est vigorosus et subtilis ad judicandum de causis etiam arduis; et in conspectu potentium admirabilis ero, et facies principum mirabuntur me: id est, principes signa admirationis de eminentia sapientiæ meæ ostendent in vultu suo, se invicem ac me cum apparatu attonito intuendo.
paras.en: [[8:10|though I be young|Juvenis]], [[8:11|And I shall be found of a quick conceit in judgment|et acutus inveniar in judicio]], that is, vigorous and subtle in judging even difficult cases; [[8:11|and shall be admired in the sight of the mighty, and the faces of princes shall wonder at me|et in conspectu potentium admirabilis ero, et facies principum mirabuntur me]]: that is, princes will show in their faces signs of wonder at the eminence of my wisdom, looking at one another and at me with an astonished air.

paras.t: Tacentem me sustinebunt, id est, patienter ferent et præstolabuntur, quousque loqui incipiam, aut verbum interruptum resumam; et loquentem me respicient, verba sapientiæ meæ diligentissime auscultando, meamque facundiam ac peritiam admirando; et sermocinante me plura, manus ori suo imponent, id est, loqui non præsument, verba mea interrumpendo.
paras.en: [[8:12|They shall wait for me when I hold my peace|Tacentem me sustinebunt]], that is, they will bear it patiently and wait until I begin to speak, or take up again a word broken off; [[8:12|and they shall look upon me when I speak|et loquentem me respicient]], listening most attentively to the words of my wisdom, and admiring my eloquence and skill; [[8:12|and if I talk much, they shall lay their hands on their mouth|et sermocinante me plura, manus ori suo imponent]], that is, they will not presume to speak by interrupting my words.

paras.t: Propterea habebo per hanc, immortalitatem, id est, increatæ Sapientiæ ero conjunctus in vita hac, per caritatem vitamque gratiæ, et in futuro, per vitam gloriæ; et memoriam æternam his, qui post me futuri sunt, relinquam, id est, in sæculo isto per generationum successiones ero famosus usque in sæculi finem. Disponam, id est, regam, ordinabo, erudiam, populos: ad quorum gubernationem fit homo per sapientiæ eminentiam præcipue aptus; et nationes mihi erunt subditæ: quia tam caritative ac discrete ad subditos me habebo, quod libenter obedient mihi. Timebunt me audientes reges horrendi, id est, audiendo profunditatem verborum meorum, concipient reverentialem ac formidolosum affectum ad me: quemadmodum Nabuchodonosor rex metuendissimus, auditis verbis sancti Danielis, prostravit se, adoravitque eum. Et in multitudine bonus videbor: id est, tam sapienter et juste loquar, quod omnes audientes me, reputabunt me virtuosum; et in bello fortis: quia ad prævalendum invisibilibus ac visibilibus præcipue valet sapientia: quæ facit hominem ordinate procedere ac divino inniti auxilio, custoditumque esse, et consideranda considerare. Hinc in Proverbiis dictum est: Cum dispositione initur bellum; et denuo, Gubernaculis tractanda sunt bella.
paras.en: [[8:13|Moreover, by the means of her I shall have immortality|Propterea habebo per hanc, immortalitatem]] [Denis's text reads *Propterea*, "therefore"; a marginal note gives *Præterea*, "moreover", the Vulgate's reading], that is, I shall be joined to the uncreated Wisdom in this life by charity and the life of grace, and in the life to come by the life of glory; [[8:13|and shall leave behind me an everlasting memory to them that come after me|et memoriam æternam his, qui post me futuri sunt, relinquam]], that is, in this world I shall be famous through the succession of generations until the end of the world. [[8:14|I shall set|Disponam]], that is, I shall rule, order and instruct, [[8:14|the people in order|populos]]: for the governing of whom a man is made especially fit by eminence in wisdom; [[8:14|and nations shall be subject to me|et nationes mihi erunt subditæ]]: because I shall bear myself so lovingly and discreetly towards my subjects that they will gladly obey me. [[8:15|Terrible kings hearing, shall be afraid of me|Timebunt me audientes reges horrendi]], that is, on hearing the depth of my words they will conceive a reverent and fearful feeling towards me: as Nabuchodonosor, a most dreaded king, on hearing the words of holy Daniel, prostrated himself and worshipped him[[Dan 2:46||]]. [[8:15|among the multitude I shall be found good|Et in multitudine bonus videbor]]: that is, I shall speak so wisely and justly that all who hear me will reckon me virtuous; [[8:15|and valiant in war|et in bello fortis]]: because wisdom avails above all for prevailing over things invisible and visible: for it makes a man proceed in good order, and lean on divine help, and be guarded, and consider what must be considered. Hence it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 24:6|war is managed by due ordering|Cum dispositione initur bellum]]; and again, [[Prov 20:18|wars are to be managed by governments|Gubernaculis tractanda sunt bella]].

paras.t: Præterea omnia ista fuerunt ad litteram in Salomone completa, propter excellentiam sapientiæ ejus. Qui, ut tertio Regum et secundo Paralipomenon legitur, undique famosissimus erat: ita quod omnes reges per gyrum desiderabant vultum ejus conspicere, et verba sapientiæ ejus audire, deferebantque ei munera, et fuerunt ei subjecti. Sed et sanctus Job vir sapientissimus testatur, hæc magna ex parte completa in se, dicens: In platea parabant cathedram mihi. Principes cessabant loqui, et digitum superponebant ori suo; vocem suam cohibebant duces; auris audiens beatificabat me.
paras.en: Moreover, all these things were fulfilled to the letter in Solomon, because of the excellence of his wisdom. He, as we read in the third book of Kings and the second of Paralipomenon, was most famous everywhere[[3 Kings 4:31||]], so that all the kings round about desired to see his face and hear the words of his wisdom[[3 Kings 4:34||]][[2 Par 9:23||]], and brought him gifts[[2 Par 9:24||]], and were subject to him[[2 Par 9:26||]][[2 Par 9:22||]] [the margin gives 3 Kings iv, 31, 34; 2 Par. ix, 22–24, 26]. And holy Job too, a most wise man, testifies that these things were in great part fulfilled in himself, saying: [[Job 29:7|in the street they prepared me a chair|In platea parabant cathedram mihi]]. [[Job 29:9|The princes ceased to speak, and laid the finger on their mouth|Principes cessabant loqui, et digitum superponebant ori suo]]; [[Job 29:10|The rulers held their peace|vocem suam cohibebant duces]]; [[Job 29:11|The ear that heard me blessed me|auris audiens beatificabat me]].

paras.t: Intrans in domum meam, conquiescam cum illa: id est, post occupationes externas, redeundo ad cordis proprii discussionem, atque ingrediens mentis cubiculum, conscientiæ thalamum, ecclesiam, seu habitationem quietam, vacabo per contemplationem, cum grandi tranquillitate, Sapientiæ increatæ, et ab omni exteriori strepitu ac tumultu quiescam in hoc invariabili tranquillissimoque objecto, in quo solo est pax pectoris sancta ac salutaris. De quo dixit Propheta: In pace in id ipsum dormiam, et requiescam. Hinc loquitur Dominus: Sedebit populus meus in pulchritudine pacis, et in tabernaculis fiduciæ, et in requie opulenta. Non enim habet amaritudinem conversatio illius, id est, occupatio mentis in Deo per contemplationem, dilectionem, et laudem ipsius, non habet amaricationem sibi annexam directe, nec inordinatam amaricationem, nec tædium convictus illius, id est, vivifica et contemplativa unio cum Sapientia summa, non est tædiosa, sed gaudiosa. Propter quod subditur: sed lætitiam in contemplando, et gaudium spirituale in diligendo, vel lætitiam redundantem in partem sensitivam ex plenitudine gaudii existentis in superiori animæ parte, juxta illud Prophetæ: Cor meum et caro mea exsultaverunt in Deum vivum. Nempe, quum delectatio oriatur ex unione potentiæ cum objecto convenienti, sitque diffusio animi in conceptu adeptioneque boni, dum mens sincere conjungitur summo et incomparabili bono illi, habet copiosæ delectationis incitamentum, rationem, materiam, et beatitudini Dei sui congratulatur, atque ex spe beatificæ ejus fruitionis exhilaratur: et quanto spirituales deliciæ istæ plus gustantur, tanto plus appetuntur, ac complacent, et relevant mentem; corporales vero delectationes cito vertuntur in nauseam, et aggravant corpus. Ideo Sapientia loquitur: Qui edunt me, adhuc esurient. Aristoteles quoque fatetur, quod philosophia habet mirabiles delectationes sibi admixtas. Et rursus: Delectationi, inquit, quæ est in consideratione, non est tristitia contraria. Itemque: Homo contemplativus plenus est jucundis theorematibus; nec extra se expetit delectari, quia in se habet delectationis puræ materiam.
paras.en: [[8:16|When I go into my house, I shall repose myself with her|Intrans in domum meam, conquiescam cum illa]]: that is, after outward occupations, returning to the examination of my own heart, and entering the chamber of the mind, the bridal room of conscience, the church, or a quiet dwelling, I shall give myself by contemplation, with great tranquillity, to the uncreated Wisdom, and shall rest from all outward noise and tumult in this unchanging and most tranquil object, in which alone is the holy and saving peace of the breast. Of which the Prophet said: [[Ps 4:9|In peace in the self same I will sleep, and I will rest|In pace in id ipsum dormiam, et requiescam]]. Hence the Lord says: [[Is 32:18|my people shall sit in the beauty of peace, and in the tabernacles of confidence, and in wealthy rest|Sedebit populus meus in pulchritudine pacis, et in tabernaculis fiduciæ, et in requie opulenta]]. [[8:16|for her conversation hath no bitterness|Non enim habet amaritudinem conversatio illius]], that is, the occupation of the mind in God by contemplation, love and praise of him has no bitterness joined to it directly, nor any inordinate bitterness, [[8:16|nor her company any tediousness|nec tædium convictus illius]], that is, the life-giving and contemplative union with the highest Wisdom is not wearisome but joyful. Wherefore it is added: [[8:16|but joy|sed lætitiam]] in contemplating, [[8:16|and gladness|et gaudium]], spiritual, in loving; or a gladness overflowing into the sensitive part from the fullness of the joy that is in the higher part of the soul, according to that saying of the Prophet: [[Ps 83:3|My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God|Cor meum et caro mea exsultaverunt in Deum vivum]]. Indeed, since delight arises from the union of a power with a fitting object, and is an expansion of the soul in conceiving and attaining a good, when the mind is sincerely joined to that highest and incomparable good, it has the incentive, the reason and the matter of abundant delight, and rejoices with its God in his beatitude, and is gladdened by the hope of enjoying him in bliss; and the more these spiritual delights are tasted, the more they are desired, and please, and lift up the mind; whereas bodily delights quickly turn to nausea and weigh down the body. Therefore Wisdom says: [[Ecclus 24:29|They that eat me, shall yet hunger|Qui edunt me, adhuc esurient]]. Aristotle too confesses that philosophy has wonderful delights mingled with it. And again: To the delight, he says, that is in contemplation, no sorrow is contrary. And likewise: The contemplative man is full of pleasant theorems [that is, truths contemplated]; nor does he seek delight outside himself, because he has within himself the matter of pure delight.

paras.t: Sed his objici potest quod in Ecclesiaste habetur: In multa sapientia multa est indignatio, et qui addit scientiam, addit et dolorem; et iterum, Cor sapientium ubi tristitia. Et respondendum, quod contemplationi seu considerationi sapientiæ, bene adjungitur bona amaritudo, contritio, dolor concomitanter, ex hoc quod homo Deum contemplando reflectitur ad sui ipsius considerationem, et ad calamitatem iniquitatemque propriam intuendam, ad considerandum quoque statum hujus exsilii, ac distantiam sui a beatifica visione: et sic suis vitiis indignatur, et cum Sancto exclamat: Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est: et cum Paulo: Infelix ego homo! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?
paras.en: But against this may be objected what is found in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 1:18|in much wisdom there is much indignation|In multa sapientia multa est indignatio]], [[Eccles 1:18|and he that addeth knowledge, addeth also labour|et qui addit scientiam, addit et dolorem]] [Denis reads *dolorem*, "sorrow", where the Vulgate has *laborem*, "labour"]; and again, [[Eccles 7:5|The heart of the wise is where there is mourning|Cor sapientium ubi tristitia]]. And the answer is that to the contemplation or consideration of wisdom there is well joined, as a concomitant, a good bitterness, contrition and sorrow, from this: that a man, in contemplating God, is turned back to the consideration of himself, and to looking upon his own wretchedness and iniquity, and also to considering the state of this exile and his distance from the beatific vision: and so he is indignant at his vices, and cries out with the Saint [that is, the Psalmist]: [[Ps 119:5|Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!|Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est]] and with Paul: [[Rom 7:24|Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?|Infelix ego homo! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?]]

paras.t: Hæc cogitans apud me, id est in me: juxta quem modum fertur, Verbum erat apud Deum; et commemorans, id est frequenter revolvens, in corde meo, quoniam immortalitas est in cogitatione sapientiæ, id est, quod homo contemplationi sapientiæ immorando, immortalitatem gloriæ promeretur, et ipsa contemplatio, quæ hic inchoatur, in futuro perficitur ac perpetuatur: prout Christus in Evangelio dixit, Maria optimam partem elegit, quæ non auferetur ab ea; et in amicitia illius delectatio bona, id est, quod virtuosa sit delectatio quæ in dilectione Sapientiæ increatæ consistit: quam diligere sanctum est, et quæ quanto ferventius puriusque amatur, tanto amplius diligentem delectat. Nulla etenim virtus, nulla forma tam delectabiliter operatur, ut caritas. Et in operibus manuum illius, honestas sine defectione, id est, quod in operibus et creaturis, seu effectibus justis et sanctis, sit Sapientiæ æternalis indeficiens honestas, et irreprehensibilis probitas: quia nil reprehensibile ab ea procedit; sed, sicut ait Psalmista, Justus Dominus in omnibus viis suis, et sanctus in omnibus operibus suis. Unde iterum protestatur: Delectasti me, Domine, in factura tua: et in operibus manuum tuarum exsultabo. Et in certamine loquelæ illius, id est, quod in conflictu seu disceptatione sapientialium verborum ac Scripturarum, a Sapientia increata procedentium, sit sapientia, id est instructio doctrinalis: quia dum sapientes inter se caritative et sapientialiter disputant ac conferunt de Scripturis, et contra perfidorum errores ac hæreses arguunt, instruunt audientes. Unde ait Apostolus: Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata, utilis est ad docendum, ad arguendum, ad corripiendum in justitia. De episcopo quoque loquens: Potens sit, inquit, exhortari in doctrina sana, et eos qui contradicunt, arguere. Et præclaritas in communicatione sermonum ipsius, id est, quod magna sinceritas ac lucida veritas sit in verbis et eruditionibus, quibus Sapientia erudit suos, et quæ communicat suis fidelibus, sicut in Proverbiis contestatur: Justi sunt omnes sermones mei, et non est in eis pravum quid, neque perversum.
paras.en: [[8:17|Thinking these things with myself|Hæc cogitans apud me]], that is, within me [Latin *apud me*, "with me"]: in which sense it is said, [[John 1:1|the Word was with God|Verbum erat apud Deum]]; [[8:17|and pondering them|et commemorans]], that is, often turning them over, [[8:17|in my heart, that to be allied to wisdom is immortality|in corde meo, quoniam immortalitas est in cogitatione sapientiæ]] [Denis reads *in cogitatione sapientiæ*, "in the thought of wisdom", where the Vulgate has *in cognatione*, "in kinship with wisdom", which the Douay-Rheims renders "to be allied to wisdom"; his gloss follows his reading], that is, that a man, by dwelling in the contemplation of wisdom, merits the immortality of glory, and that contemplation itself, which is begun here, is perfected and made everlasting in the life to come: as Christ said in the Gospel, [[Luke 10:42|Mary hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her|Maria optimam partem elegit, quæ non auferetur ab ea]]; [[8:18|And that there is great delight in her friendship|in amicitia illius delectatio bona]], that is, that the delight which consists in the love of the uncreated Wisdom is virtuous: to love whom is holy, and who, the more fervently and purely she is loved, the more she delights the one who loves her. For no virtue, no form, works so delightfully as charity. [[8:18|and inexhaustible riches in the works of her hands|Et in operibus manuum illius, honestas sine defectione]] [Latin *honestas sine defectione*, "unfailing honourableness", where the Douay-Rheims has "inexhaustible riches"], that is, that in the works and creatures, or the just and holy effects, of the eternal Wisdom there is an unfailing honourableness and irreproachable uprightness: because nothing blameworthy proceeds from her; but, as the Psalmist says, [[Ps 144:17|The Lord is just in all his ways: and holy in all his works|Justus Dominus in omnibus viis suis, et sanctus in omnibus operibus suis]]. Hence he declares again: [[Ps 91:5|thou hast given me, O Lord, a delight in thy doings: and in the works of thy hands I shall rejoice|Delectasti me, Domine, in factura tua: et in operibus manuum tuarum exsultabo]]. [[8:18|and in the exercise of conference with her|Et in certamine loquelæ illius]], that is, that in the contest or debate of wise words and of the Scriptures, which proceed from the uncreated Wisdom, there is [[8:18|wisdom|sit sapientia]], that is, doctrinal instruction: because when wise men dispute and confer among themselves charitably and wisely about the Scriptures, and argue against the errors and heresies of the faithless, they instruct those who hear. Hence the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 3:16|All scripture, inspired of God, is profitable to teach, to reprove, to correct|Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata, utilis est ad docendum, ad arguendum, ad corripiendum]] [[2 Tim 3:16|in justice|in justitia]]. Speaking also of a bishop: [[Tit 1:9|that he may be able|Potens sit]], he says, [[Tit 1:9|to exhort in sound doctrine and to convince the gainsayers|exhortari in doctrina sana, et eos qui contradicunt, arguere]]. [[8:18|and glory in the communication of her words|Et præclaritas in communicatione sermonum ipsius]], that is, that there is great sincerity and shining truth in the words and teachings by which Wisdom instructs her own, and which she communicates to her faithful, as she declares in Proverbs: [[Prov 8:8|All my words are just, there is nothing wicked, nor perverse|Justi sunt omnes sermones mei, et non est in eis pravum quid, neque perversum]].

paras.t: Circuibam quærens, id est, undique investigans, cuncta occurrentia consideravi, ut mihi illam assumerem, id est, Sapientiam invenirem, et inventam, ut sponsam brachiis pii purique amoris amplecterer. In cunctis etenim rebus creatis Sapientia prima relucet, sicut artifex in opere suo. Ideo fertur in Canticis: Surgam, et circuibo civitatem; per vicos et plateas quæram quem diligit anima mea. Iste est bonus circuitus, qui a Deo incipit, et terminatur ad ipsum. Est autem et pravus circuitus, qui est inordinata evagatio per creata: de qua ait Propheta, In circuitu impii ambulant.
paras.en: [[8:18|I went about seeking|Circuibam quærens]], that is, searching on every side, I considered everything I came upon, [[8:18|that I might take her to myself|ut mihi illam assumerem]], that is, that I might find Wisdom, and having found her, embrace her as a bride with the arms of a devout and pure love. For the first Wisdom shines forth in all created things, as a craftsman in his work. Therefore it is said in the Canticles: [[Cant 3:2|I will rise, and will go about the city: in the streets and the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth|Surgam, et circuibo civitatem; per vicos et plateas quæram quem diligit anima mea]]. This is the good going about, which begins from God and ends in him. But there is also a wicked going about, which is a disordered wandering among created things: of which the Prophet says, [[Ps 11:9|The wicked walk round about|In circuitu impii ambulant]].

paras.t: Puer autem eram ingeniosus, id est acuti atque capacis intellectus. Unde in libro de Civitate Dei asserit Augustinus: Ingeniosum nasci, felicitatis est; et rursus, Faciliter intelligere, et intellecta bene implere, plena felicitas est. Et sortitus sum animam bonam, id est egregiæ indolis, utpote ex naturali dispositione ad sapientiam ac virtutes fortiter inclinatam.
paras.en: [[8:19|And I was a witty child|Puer autem eram ingeniosus]] [Latin *ingeniosus*, "gifted", "of good wit"], that is, of a keen and capacious intellect. Hence Augustine asserts in the book of the City of God: To be born gifted is a matter of good fortune; and again, To understand easily, and to carry out well what is understood, is full happiness. [[8:19|and had received a good soul|Et sortitus sum animam bonam]], that is, of excellent disposition, as being strongly inclined by natural disposition to wisdom and the virtues.

paras.t: Et quum essem magis bonus, id est melior factus, proficiendo in virtutibus atque ingenitam inclinationem assidue actuando, veni ad corpus incoinquinatum, id est mundum; et corpus meum in puritate, puta in castitate conjugali, servavi, et rationi subjeci, mundans me ab omni inquinamento animæ et corporis. Salomon enim per multos annos fuit vir virtuosus, justus, ac continens, quamvis in senectute ad extremam fœditatem dilapsus sit.
paras.en: [[8:20|And whereas I was more good|Et quum essem magis bonus]], that is, having become better, by advancing in the virtues and constantly putting my inborn inclination into act, [[8:20|I came to a body undefiled|veni ad corpus incoinquinatum]], that is, clean; and I kept my body in purity, namely in conjugal chastity, and subjected it to reason, cleansing myself from all defilement of soul and body. For Solomon was for many years a virtuous, just and continent man, although in his old age he fell into the utmost foulness.

paras.t: Et ut scivi, id est, statim postquam cognovi, quoniam aliter non possem esse continens a vitiis et concupiscentiis, nisi Deus det gratiam continendi: quia non est volentis, neque currentis, sed Dei miserentis, qui ait, Sine me nihil potestis facere. Et hoc ipsum erat sapientiæ, id est actus seu consideratio sapientiæ infusæ, et donum ac inspiratio et illuminatio Sapientiæ increatæ, scire cujus esset hoc donum. Unde ait Apostolus: Non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis. Adii Dominum, id est, Deum ubique præsentem mente accessi, dirigendo cor meum in ipsum: juxta illud, Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini; et deprecatus sum illum, et dixi ex totis præcordiis meis, id est intimis affectibus mentis, seu cum tota attentione intellectus, affectioneque integra voluntatis: secundum illud, Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo.
paras.en: [[8:21|And as I knew|Et ut scivi]], that is, as soon as I came to know, [[8:21|that I could not otherwise be continent|quoniam aliter non possem esse continens]] from vices and concupiscences, [[8:21|except God gave it|nisi Deus det]] the grace of continence [Denis's text adds *a vitiis et concupiscentiis* and *gratiam continendi*, words not in the Vulgate]: because [[Rom 9:16|it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy|non est volentis, neque currentis, sed Dei miserentis]], who says, [[John 15:5|without me you can do nothing|Sine me nihil potestis facere]]. [[8:21|and this also was a point of wisdom|Et hoc ipsum erat sapientiæ]], that is, an act or consideration of infused wisdom, and a gift, inspiration and enlightening of the uncreated Wisdom, [[8:21|to know whose gift it was|scire cujus esset hoc donum]]. Hence the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 2:12|we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is of God: that we may know the things that are given us from God|Non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis]]. [[8:21|I went to the Lord|Adii Dominum]], that is, I approached in mind God who is present everywhere, directing my heart towards him: according to that saying, [[Ps 33:6|Come ye to him and be enlightened|Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini]]; [[8:21|and besought him|et deprecatus sum illum]], [[8:21|and said with my whole heart|et dixi ex totis præcordiis meis]], that is, with the inmost affections of the mind, or with the whole attention of the intellect and the entire affection of the will: according to that saying, [[Ps 110:1|I will praise thee, O Lord, with my whole heart|Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo]][[Ps 137:1||]] [the margin gives Ps. cx, 1 and cxxxvii, 1, which both begin with these words].

9.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI NONI : DEUS PATRUM MEORUM, ET DOMINE MISERICORDIÆ.
9.title_en: Elucidation of the ninth chapter: God of my fathers, and Lord of mercy

paras.t: Oratio Salomonis hic ponitur. Deus patrum meorum, scilicet patriarcharum Abrahæ, Isaac, Jacob, et David. Et quamvis sit Deus universorum jure creationis, conservationis, et gubernationis, specialiter tamen per gratiam præcipuæ electionis voluit Deus illorum trium Patriarcharum vocari, quemadmodum in Exodo legitur: Dixit Dominus ad Moysen: Hæc dices filiis Israel: Dominus Deus patrum vestrorum, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, et Deus Jacob, misit me ad vos; hoc nomen mihi est in æternum, et hoc memoriale meum in generationem et generationem. Et Domine misericordiæ, id est dominator misericors, et Dominus omnium miserationum. Dicitur ergo Dominus misericordiæ, sicut in Actibus dicitur Deus gloriæ, et in Psalmo, Rex gloriæ, id est Dominus misericordiam habens, et misericordes effectus producens. Qui fecisti omnia verbo tuo, id est per unigenitum Filium tuum: secundum illud, Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Vel, Verbo, id est imperio tuo: sicut cantamus: Quoniam ipse dixit, et facta sunt; ipse mandavit, et creata sunt.
paras.en: Here the prayer of Solomon is set down. [[9:1|God of my fathers|Deus patrum meorum]], that is, of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and of David. And although God is the God of all things by right of creation, preservation and government, yet by the grace of a special election he willed to be called the God of those three Patriarchs in particular, as we read in Exodus: The Lord said to Moses: [[Ex 3:15|Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: The Lord God of your fathers the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob hath sent me to you; this is my name for ever, and this is my memorial unto all generations|Hæc dices filiis Israel: Dominus Deus patrum vestrorum, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, et Deus Jacob, misit me ad vos; hoc nomen mihi est in æternum, et hoc memoriale meum in generationem et generationem]]. [[9:1|and Lord of mercy|Et Domine misericordiæ]], that is, merciful ruler, and Lord of all mercies. So he is called *Lord of mercy* as in the Acts he is called [[Acts 7:2|The God of glory|Deus gloriæ]], and in the Psalm [[Ps 23:7|the King of Glory|Rex gloriæ]]: that is, the Lord who has mercy and brings about the works of mercy. [[9:1|who hast made all things with thy word|Qui fecisti omnia verbo tuo]], that is, by thy only-begotten Son, according to the text, [[John 1:3|All things were made by him|Omnia per ipsum facta sunt]]. Or, [[9:1|thy word|Verbo]], that is, thy command, as we sing: [[Ps 32:9|For he spoke and they were made: he commanded and they were created.|Quoniam ipse dixit, et facta sunt; ipse mandavit, et creata sunt]] [the margin gives no reference here; these are the words of Ps 32:9, and almost the same stand in Ps 148:5]

paras.t: Et sapientia tua, id est per sapientiam tuam, constituisti hominem. Omnia enim in sapientia fecit; et sicut in Proverbiis dictum est, Dominus sapientia fundavit terram, stabilivit cœlos prudentia. Ut dominaretur creaturæ tuæ, quæ a te facta est: quemadmodum loquitur Dominus: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram; et præsit piscibus maris, et volatilibus cœli, et bestiis, universæque terræ, omnique reptili quod movetur super terram.
paras.en: [[9:2|And by thy wisdom|Et sapientia tua]], that is, through thy wisdom, [[9:2|hast appointed man|constituisti hominem]]. For [[Ps 103:24|thou hast made all things in wisdom|Omnia enim in sapientia fecit]] [Denis has *fecit*, "he made"; the margin's Ps. cii, 24 is Ps 103:24]; and as is said in Proverbs, [[Prov 3:19|The Lord by wisdom hath founded the earth, hath established the heavens by prudence.|Dominus sapientia fundavit terram, stabilivit cœlos prudentia]] [[9:2|that he should have dominion over the creature that was made by thee|Ut dominaretur creaturæ tuæ, quæ a te facta est]]: as the Lord says: [[Gen 1:26|Let us make man to our image and likeness: and let him have dominion over the fishes of the sea, and the fowls of the air, and the beasts, and the whole earth, and every creeping creature that moveth upon the earth|Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram; et præsit piscibus maris, et volatilibus cœli, et bestiis, universæque terræ, omnique reptili quod movetur super terram]].

paras.t: Hinc additur: ut disponat orbem terrarum in æquitate et justitia, id est, elemento terræ et contentis in eo, utatur sicut est divinitus institutum; vel potius, ut genus hominum a se propagatum, recte gubernet. Hoc autem dominium super inferiores creaturas homo plenius habuisset, nisi peccasset. Adhuc tamen aliqualiter habet illud, secundum illud in Psalmo: Omnia subjecisti sub pedibus ejus, oves et boves universas. Et in directione cordis judicium judicet, id est, de judicandis sententiam proferat cum diligenti cordis intuitu, et elevatione mentis ad te, habendo te Judicem summum semper præ oculis, certus quod et ipse judicandus sit a te, qui male judicata rejudicabis. Hinc secundo Paralipomenon rex Josaphat ait judicibus suæ plebis: Quodcumque judicaveritis, in vos redundabit; sit timor Domini vobiscum, et cum diligentia cuncta facite.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[9:3|That he should order the world according to equity and justice|ut disponat orbem terrarum in æquitate et justitia]], that is, that he should use the element of earth and the things it contains as God has ordained; or rather, that he should rightly govern the human race propagated from him. Now man would have had this dominion over the lower creatures more fully had he not sinned. Yet he still has it in some measure, according to the words of the Psalm: [[Ps 8:8|Thou hast subjected all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen|Omnia subjecisti sub pedibus ejus, oves et boves universas]]. [[9:3|and execute justice with an upright heart|Et in directione cordis judicium judicet]] [literally, "and judge judgment in uprightness of heart"], that is, that he should pass sentence on what is to be judged with a careful looking of the heart and a lifting of the mind to thee, keeping thee, the supreme Judge, always before his eyes, sure that he himself is to be judged by thee, who wilt judge again what has been judged amiss. Hence in the second book of Paralipomenon king Josaphat says to the judges of his people: [[2 Par 19:6|whatsoever you judge, it shall redound to you|Quodcumque judicaveritis, in vos redundabit]]; [[2 Par 19:7|Let the fear of the Lord be with you, and do all things with diligence|sit timor Domini vobiscum, et cum diligentia cuncta facite]].

paras.t: Da mihi sedium tuarum adsistricem sapientiam, id est Sapientiam tuam tibi æternaliter vere præsentem, et thronis cœlestibus jugiter adsistentem, omniumque judicialium soliorum cœlestium atque terrestrium directivam. Quæ in Evangelio protestabatur: Vos qui secuti estis me, sedebitis super sedes, judicantes duodecim tribus Israel. Sedes quoque Dei, sunt cœli, prout fatur Propheta: Cœlum mihi sedes est. Sed et animæ justæ, sunt sedes et throni ipsius, quum scriptum supra sit: Anima justi, sedes est sapientiæ. Est item unus chorus angelorum, qui specialiter Throni vocatur, per quos Omnipotens sua decernit judicia: quibus Thronis infallibiliter directrix est sapientia ista. Et noli me reprobare a pueris tuis, id est, de numero electorum servorum tuorum non auferas me, neque condemnes ut reprobum.
paras.en: [[9:4|Give me wisdom, that sitteth by thy throne|Da mihi sedium tuarum adsistricem sapientiam]] [literally, "the wisdom that standeth by thy thrones": Denis goes on to speak of seats and thrones in the plural], that is, thy Wisdom, truly present to thee from eternity, ever standing by the heavenly thrones, and directing all the judgment seats of heaven and earth. She it is who declared in the Gospel: [[Matt 19:28|you who have followed me|Vos qui secuti estis me]], shall sit upon seats, [[Matt 19:28|judging the twelve tribes of Israel|judicantes duodecim tribus Israel]]. The seats of God are also the heavens, as the Prophet says: [[Is 66:1|Heaven is my throne|Cœlum mihi sedes est]]. But just souls too are his seats and thrones, since it has been written above: The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom[[Prov 14:33||]] [the margin gives "cf. Prov. xiv, 33" (In the heart of the prudent resteth wisdom); the saying in these words, often quoted by the Fathers, is not found in the Vulgate]. There is also one choir of angels which is called in particular the Thrones, through whom the Almighty decrees his judgments; and to these Thrones this wisdom is an unerring guide. [[9:4|and cast me not off from among thy children|Et noli me reprobare a pueris tuis]] [*pueri*, "children", can also mean "servants", and Denis takes it so], that is, do not take me away from the number of thy chosen servants, nor condemn me as reprobate.

paras.t: Quoniam servus tuus ego sum: id est, jam tibi devote deservio, et precor ne deseras me, sed hanc cordis mei devotionem semper pie attendas; et filius ancillæ tuæ, videlicet Synagogæ, aut Bethsabee, quæ de suo excessu pœnitens, deinceps fuit devota: sicque meritis matris meæ deprecor exaudiri; homo infirmus, id est fragilis, et ad mala proclivis, et exigui temporis: prout primo Paralipomenon David fatetur: Dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora. Ideo sanctus Job dixit: Homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore, repletur multis miseriis. Et minor ad intellectum judicii et legum, id est ex me ipso insufficiens ad intelligendum quid de singulis occurrentibus sit judicandum, nec valens ex me pertingere ad intelligentiam legum, id est præceptorum tuorum judicialium, cæremonialium atque moralium, legisque naturalis, ac divinæ, et positivæ. Hinc tertio Regum Salomon recitatur dixisse ad Dominum: Quis potest judicare hunc populum? Itemque: Ego sum puer parvulus, nesciens introitum meum et exitum meum.
paras.en: [[9:5|For I am thy servant|Quoniam servus tuus ego sum]]: that is, I already serve thee devoutly, and I pray thee not to forsake me, but ever kindly to regard this devotion of my heart; [[9:5|and the son of thy handmaid|et filius ancillæ tuæ]], namely of the Synagogue, or of Bethsabee, who, repenting of her sin, was devout from then on: and so I pray to be heard through the merits of my mother; [[9:5|a weak man|homo infirmus]], that is, frail and prone to evil, [[9:5|and of short time|et exigui temporis]]: as David confesses in the first book of Paralipomenon: [[1 Par 29:15|Our days upon earth are as a shadow, and there is no stay|Dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora]]. Therefore holy Job said: [[Job 14:1|Man born of a woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries.|Homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore, repletur multis miseriis]] [[9:5|and falling short of the understanding of judgment and laws|Et minor ad intellectum judicii et legum]], that is, of myself unable to understand what is to be judged in each case that arises, and unable of myself to attain to the understanding of the laws, that is, of thy judicial, ceremonial and moral precepts, and of the natural, divine and positive law. Hence in the third book of Kings Solomon is recorded as saying to the Lord: [[3 Kings 3:9|who shall be able to judge this people|Quis potest judicare hunc populum]]? And again: [[3 Kings 3:7|I am but a child, and know not how to go out and come in|Ego sum puer parvulus, nesciens introitum meum et exitum meum]].

paras.t: Et si quis erit consummatus inter filios hominum, id est perfectus inter homines, si ab illo fugerit sapientia tua, id est, si Sapientia tua æterna reliquerit eum, et sapientiam salutarem, quæ est donum, subtraxerit ei, in nihilum reputabitur, id est, nullius erit momenti aut ponderis coram Deo, imo stultus ab eo censebitur, dicente Apostolo: Nonne stultam fecit Deus sapientiam hujus mundi?
paras.en: [[9:6|For if one be perfect among the children of men|Et si quis erit consummatus inter filios hominum]], that is, perfect among men, [[9:6|yet if thy wisdom be not with him|si ab illo fugerit sapientia tua]] [literally, "if thy wisdom flee from him"], that is, if thy eternal Wisdom has left him and withdrawn from him saving wisdom, which is a gift, [[9:6|he shall be nothing regarded|in nihilum reputabitur]], that is, he will be of no moment or weight before God, nay he will be judged a fool by him, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 1:20|Hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?|Nonne stultam fecit Deus sapientiam hujus mundi?]]

paras.t: Consequenter auctor hujus voluminis in persona Salomonis apertissime loquitur. Tu autem elegisti me regem populo tuo, id est ad profectum Israelitici populi: unde David, Salomonem (inquit) filium meum elegit Dominus adhuc puerum et tenellum; et judicem filiorum tuorum et filiarum: quibus in Deuteronomio Moyses ait, Filii estote Domini Dei vestri: filii scilicet adoptivi.
paras.en: Next the author of this book speaks most openly in the person of Solomon. [[9:7|Thou hast chosen me to be king of thy people|Tu autem elegisti me regem populo tuo]], that is, for the good of the people of Israel; whence David: [[1 Par 29:1|Solomon|Salomonem]], he says, [[1 Par 29:1|my son|filium meum]] the Lord hath chosen, [[1 Par 29:1|as yet young and tender|adhuc puerum et tenellum]] [the margin gives I Par. xxiv, 1; the words are in 1 Par 29:1]; [[9:7|and a judge of thy sons and daughters|et judicem filiorum tuorum et filiarum]]: to whom Moses says in Deuteronomy, [[Deut 14:1|Be ye children of the Lord your God|Filii estote Domini Dei vestri]]: adoptive children, that is.

paras.t: Et dixisti me, id est, præcepisti mihi, ædificare templum in monte sancto tuo, puta in monte Moria: in quo Abraham voluit Isaac immolare, et in quo Jacob vidit in somno scalam pertingentem ad cœlum; et in civitate habitationis tuæ altare, id est altaria templi, videlicet altare holocausti in atrio, et altare thymiamatis, quod erat in prima et exteriori templi parte, prout tertio Regum describitur; similitudinem tabernaculi tui sancti: quia templum factum per Salomonem, constructum est ad imitationem tabernaculi Moysis, secundum expositores; quod præparasti ab initio, id est, in monte Sinai loquens Moysi, fieri præcepisti secundum exemplar ei in monte monstratum.
paras.en: [[9:8|And hast commanded me|Et dixisti me]] [literally, "and thou hast told me"], that is, thou hast instructed me, [[9:8|to build a temple on thy holy mount|ædificare templum in monte sancto tuo]], namely on mount Moria[[2 Par 3:1||]], on which Abraham was willing to sacrifice Isaac[[Gen 22:10||]], and on which Jacob saw in his sleep a ladder reaching to heaven[[Gen 28:12||]]; [[9:8|and an altar in the city of thy dwelling place|et in civitate habitationis tuæ altare]], that is, the altars of the temple, namely the altar of holocaust in the court[[3 Kings 9:25||]], and the altar of incense, which was in the first and outer part of the temple, as is described in the third book of Kings[[3 Kings 7:48||]]; [[9:8|a resemblance of thy holy tabernacle|similitudinem tabernaculi tui sancti]]: for the temple made by Solomon was built in imitation of the tabernacle of Moses, according to the expositors; [[9:8|which thou hast prepared from the beginning|quod præparasti ab initio]], that is, speaking to Moses on mount Sinai thou didst command it to be made according to the pattern shewn him on the mount[[Ex 26:30||]].

paras.t: Et tecum sapientia tua increata ac genita, scilicet unigenitus Filius tuus, o Pater æterne. Opera etenim superbeatissimæ Trinitatis ad extra, sunt indivisa. Quæ novit opera tua, quæ et adfuit tunc quum orbem terrarum faceres: imo quum totum conderes universum, quia coæterna, consubstantialis, et coæqualis est tibi. Quæ in Proverbiis attestatur: Quando præparabat cœlos, aderam; quando certa lege et gyro vallabat abyssos, quando appendebat fundamenta terræ, cum eo eram cuncta componens. Hinc et affirmat ipsa Sapientia: Quæcumque facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit; Pater enim diligit Filium, et omnia demonstrat ei quæ ipse facit. Et sciebat quid placitum esset oculis tuis, id est intellectui tuo, atque justitiæ ac providentiæ tuæ, et quid directum, id est vere rectum, et ad te rite relatum, in præceptis tuis, et in executionibus eorumdem. In Patre namque et Filio est una eademque sapientia.
paras.en: [[9:9|And thy wisdom with thee|Et tecum sapientia tua]], uncreated and begotten, namely thy only-begotten Son, O eternal Father. For the works of the most blessed Trinity outside itself are undivided [that is, every work of God upon creatures is the work of the three Persons together]. [[9:9|which knoweth thy works|Quæ novit opera tua]], [[9:9|which then also was present when thou madest the world|quæ et adfuit tunc quum orbem terrarum faceres]]: nay, when thou didst found the whole universe, for she is coeternal, consubstantial and coequal with thee. She bears witness to this in Proverbs: [[Prov 8:27|When he prepared the heavens, I was present: when with a certain law, and compass, he enclosed the depths|Quando præparabat cœlos, aderam; quando certa lege et gyro vallabat abyssos]], [[Prov 8:29|when he balanced the foundations of the earth|quando appendebat fundamenta terræ]], [[Prov 8:30|I was with him forming all things|cum eo eram cuncta componens]]. Hence Wisdom herself also affirms: [[John 5:19|what things soever he doth, these the Son also doth in like manner|Quæcumque facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit]]; [[John 5:20|For the Father loveth the Son and sheweth him all things which himself doth|Pater enim diligit Filium, et omnia demonstrat ei quæ ipse facit]]. [[9:9|and knew what was agreeable to thy eyes|Et sciebat quid placitum esset oculis tuis]], that is, to thy intellect, and to thy justice and providence, [[9:9|and what was right|et quid directum]], that is, truly right, and duly referred to thee, [[9:9|in thy commandments|in præceptis tuis]], and in the carrying out of them. For in the Father and the Son there is one and the same wisdom.

paras.t: Mitte illam de cœlis sanctis tuis, id est, Sapientiam increatam ac genitam mitte mihi invisibili missione, non ut illa variet locum, sed per effectum, infundendo mihi charismata ejus. Porro, per sanctos cœlos, possunt intelligi cives superni, spiritusque angelici: in quibus Sapientia ista, sicut et Pater, esse specialiter perhibetur, quia in illis præclarius operatur, et se ipsam evidentius gloriosiusque demonstrat. Vel orbes cœlestes. Hinc quotidie dicimus: Pater noster qui es in cœlis. Et a sede magnitudinis tuæ, id est a throno majestatis tuæ immensæ: juxta illud, A summo cœlo egressio ejus. De quo accipi potest illud Apostoli: Raptus est usque ad tertium cœlum. Ut mecum sit per gratiam et illuminationem piissimam, et mecum laboret, id est, efficaciter laborare me faciat, meque in laboribus meis dirigat et conservet; ut sciam quid acceptum sit apud te, id est, quid vere complaceat tibi, ne in particularibus errem, aut sub specie boni fallar, aut vitiis passionibusque cæcatus, erronee judicem: quia, ut ait Scriptura, Est via quæ videtur homini bona, et novissima ejus ducunt ad mortem.
paras.en: [[9:10|Send her out of thy holy heaven|Mitte illam de cœlis sanctis tuis]] [literally, "from thy holy heavens"], that is, send me the uncreated and begotten Wisdom by an invisible mission [that is, the sending of a divine Person into the soul by grace, without any visible sign], not that she changes place, but by her effect, pouring her gifts into me. Further, by the holy heavens may be understood the citizens on high and the angelic spirits, in whom this Wisdom, like the Father, is said to be in a special way, because in them she works more splendidly and shows herself more clearly and more gloriously. Or the heavenly spheres. Hence we say daily: [[Matt 6:9|Our Father who art in heaven|Pater noster qui es in cœlis]]. [[9:10|and from the throne of thy majesty|Et a sede magnitudinis tuæ]] [literally, "from the seat of thy greatness"], that is, from the throne of thy boundless majesty, according to the text, [[Ps 18:7|His going out is from the end of heaven|A summo cœlo egressio ejus]]. Of this may be understood the Apostle's words: He [[2 Cor 12:4|was caught up|Raptus est]] [[2 Cor 12:2|to the third heaven|usque ad tertium cœlum]] [the margin gives II Cor. xii, 2, 4: Denis joins *raptus est* of v. 4 to the third heaven of v. 2]. [[9:10|that she may be with me|Ut mecum sit]] by grace and most gracious enlightenment, [[9:10|and may labour with me|et mecum laboret]], that is, make me labour to good effect, and guide and keep me in my labours; [[9:10|that I may know what is acceptable with thee|ut sciam quid acceptum sit apud te]], that is, what truly pleases thee, lest I err in particular matters, or be deceived under the appearance of good, or, blinded by vices and passions, judge wrongly: for, as Scripture says, [[Prov 16:25|There is a way that seemeth to a man right: and the ends thereof lead to death|Est via quæ videtur homini bona, et novissima ejus ducunt ad mortem]][[Prov 14:12||]] [Denis reads *bona*, "good", where Prov 16:25 has *recta*, "right", and Prov 14:12 *justa*, "just"].

paras.t: Scit enim illa omnia, et intelligit, tanquam universorum creatrix; et deducet me in operibus meis sobrie, id est, moderate ac discrete faciet me in cunctis quæ ago, procedere, ita ut dicere possim: Tenuisti manum dexteram meam, et in voluntate tua deduxisti me; et rursus, Deduxit me super semitas justitiæ, propter nomen suum: et custodiet me in sua potentia, id est, a ruina me præservabit sua propria potestate, cui nullus potest resistere. Ipse quippe est principalis custos electorum suorum: qui et per angelos ac prælatos custodit oves suas.
paras.en: [[9:11|For she knoweth and understandeth all things|Scit enim illa omnia, et intelligit]], as the maker of all things; [[9:11|and shall lead me soberly in my works|et deducet me in operibus meis sobrie]], that is, she will make me go forward with moderation and discretion in all that I do, so that I can say: [[Ps 72:24|Thou hast held me by my right hand; and by thy will thou hast conducted me|Tenuisti manum dexteram meam, et in voluntate tua deduxisti me]]; and again, [[Ps 22:3|He hath led me on the paths of justice, for his own name's sake|Deduxit me super semitas justitiæ, propter nomen suum]]: [[9:11|and shall preserve me by her power|et custodiet me in sua potentia]], that is, she will keep me from falling by her own power, which no one can resist. For he himself is the chief keeper of his elect, who also keeps his sheep through angels and prelates.

paras.t: Et erunt accepta opera mea; et disponam, id est, regam ac ordinabo, populum tuum juste, et ero dignus sedilium patris mei, id est, dignus ero sedere ac præsidere populo Israel, residendo in throno regali ac solio judiciali, atque in cathedra doctorali, in quibus David pater meus digne consedit, faciens judicium et justitiam omni populo suo, et dixit: Docebo iniquos vias tuas.
paras.en: [[9:12|So shall my works be acceptable|Et erunt accepta opera mea]]; [[9:12|and I shall govern|et disponam]], that is, rule and order, [[9:12|thy people justly|populum tuum juste]], [[9:12|and shall be worthy of the throne of my father|et ero dignus sedilium patris mei]], that is, I shall be worthy to sit and preside over the people of Israel, sitting on the royal throne and the judgment seat, and in the teacher's chair, in which David my father sat worthily, who [[2 Kings 8:15|did judgment and justice to all his people|faciens judicium et justitiam omni populo suo]][[Ps 118:121||]] [the margin gives Ps. cxviii, 121, "I have done judgment and justice"; Denis's words are those of 2 Kings 8:15], and who said: [[Ps 50:15|I will teach the unjust thy ways|Docebo iniquos vias tuas]] [the margin's Ps. i, 15 is Ps 50:15].

paras.t: Quis enim hominum poterit scire consilium Dei? quasi dicat: Nullus, nisi quantum fuerit ei mediate vel immediate desuper revelatum. Sicque scimus consilium superadorandæ et supersapientissimæ Trinitatis super modo salvationis generis humani per incarnationem et passionem Verbi æterni. Sic quoque loquitur in Actibus Paulus: Non subterfugi quominus annuntiarem vobis omne consilium Dei.
paras.en: [[9:13|For who among men is he that can know the counsel of God?|Quis enim hominum poterit scire consilium Dei?]] As if to say: No one, except so far as it has been revealed to him from above, mediately or immediately. And so we know the counsel of the most adorable and most wise Trinity concerning the manner of saving mankind through the incarnation and passion of the eternal Word. So too Paul speaks in the Acts: [[Acts 20:27|For I have not spread to declare unto you all, the counsel of God|Non subterfugi quominus annuntiarem vobis omne consilium Dei]] [Denis's Latin: "I have not shrunk from declaring to you the whole counsel of God"].

paras.t: Præterea quæri potest, qualiter Deo adscribatur consilium, quum asserat Damascenus, consilium esse ignorantis naturæ. Et respondendum, quod consilium proprie sumptum, dicitur inquisitio de agendis vel omittendis: et ita ex ignorantia quadam procedit. Deo igitur non adscribitur, nisi imperfectione ista seclusa, et quantum ad id quod perfectionis in ipso est, scilicet quoad diligentem considerationem. Itaque nemo scit consilium Dei, nisi divinitus reveletur. Propterea scriptum est: Quis adfuit in consilio Domini, et vidit, et audivit sermonem ejus? Et tamen eodem capitulo Dominus asserit: In novissimis diebus intelligetis consilium meum. Sic et Apostolus dixit: Quis cognovit sensum Domini? aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit?
paras.en: Further, it may be asked how counsel can be ascribed to God, since the Damascene asserts that counsel belongs to a nature that does not know. The answer is that counsel, taken properly, means an inquiry into what is to be done or left undone, and so it proceeds from a certain ignorance. It is therefore ascribed to God only with that imperfection set aside, and as to what of perfection there is in it, namely careful consideration. So no one knows the counsel of God unless it be revealed by God. Therefore it is written: [[Jer 23:18|who hath stood in the counsel of the Lord, and hath seen and heard his word?|Quis adfuit in consilio Domini, et vidit, et audivit sermonem ejus?]] And yet in the same chapter the Lord asserts: [[Jer 23:20|in the latter days you shall understand his counsel|In novissimis diebus intelligetis consilium meum]] [Denis has "my counsel"]. So too the Apostle said: [[Rom 11:34|who hath known the mind of the Lord? Or who hath been his counsellor?|Quis cognovit sensum Domini? aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit?]]

paras.t: Aut quis poterit cogitare quid velit Deus? Certum est quod Deus gloriosus et sanctus vult omne bonum virtutum, et quidquid præcepit atque consuluit. Unde et Paulus: Hæc est, inquit, voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra; et rursus, Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri, et ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Hinc scriptum est: Beati sumus nos, quoniam quæ Deo placita sunt, manifesta sunt nobis. Quomodo ergo nemo potest cogitare quid velit Deus, nisi in quantum Deus illud manifestat? Denique quædam sunt indifferentia, id est nec bona nec mala moraliter, sed prodesse possunt atque obesse: et de talibus latet nos quid velit Deus, aut quid magis expediat nobis. De quibus etiam intelligendum censetur quod Apostolus loquitur: Quid oremus sicut oportet, nescimus.
paras.en: [[9:13|or who can think what the will of God is?|Aut quis poterit cogitare quid velit Deus?]] It is certain that God, glorious and holy, wills all the good of the virtues, and whatever he has commanded and counselled. Whence Paul too: [[1 Thess 4:3|this is|Hæc est]], he says, [[1 Thess 4:3|the will of God, your sanctification|voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra]]; and again, God [[1 Tim 2:4|will have all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth|vult omnes homines salvos fieri, et ad agnitionem veritatis venire]]. Hence it is written: [[Bar 4:4|We are happy, O Israel: because the things that are pleasing to God, are made known to us|Beati sumus nos, quoniam quæ Deo placita sunt, manifesta sunt nobis]]. How then can no one think what God wills, save so far as God makes it known? Now, some things are indifferent, that is, neither good nor bad morally, but they can help or harm; and in such things it is hidden from us what God wills, or what is more expedient for us. Of these too, it is held, is to be understood what the Apostle says: [[Rom 8:26|we know not what we should pray for as we ought|Quid oremus sicut oportet, nescimus]].

paras.t: Cogitationes enim mortalium timidæ. Constat quod cogitationes multorum hominum sint audaces, præsumptuosæ, et quorumdam securæ et firmæ. Attamen circa particularia multa agenda, sunt formidolosæ: quia pro certo non patet quid amplius conferat ad salutem seu finem intentum, et quia nescimus an simus in caritate finaliterve salvandi. Propter quod, sicut in Ecclesiastico legitur, Sapiens in omnibus metuit. Beatus enim homo qui semper est pavidus. Unde et sanctus Job: Verebar, ait, omnia opera mea. Et incerta sunt providentiæ nostræ: quia non possumus omnia prævidere in particulari, quæ possunt occurrere. Ideo sæpe putamus esse expedire, quod potius nocet, et e converso. Hinc in talibus indigemus dono consilii, quo a Spiritu Sancto dirigimur ac juvamur ad consulendum, inquirendum, et providendum quid magis expediat. Hinc quoque in legibus humanis et positivis oportet frequenter fieri dispensationes, quia non potest legislator prævidere aut exprimere universos casus qui possunt emergere.
paras.en: [[9:14|For the thoughts of mortal men are fearful|Cogitationes enim mortalium timidæ]]. It is plain that the thoughts of many men are bold and presumptuous, and those of some secure and firm. Yet about many particular things to be done they are fearful: because it is not clear for certain what will do more for salvation or for the end intended, and because we do not know whether we are in charity, or are to be saved in the end[[Eccles 9:1||]]. For this reason, as we read in Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 18:27|A wise man will fear in every thing|Sapiens in omnibus metuit]]. For [[Prov 28:14|Blessed is the man that is always fearful|Beatus enim homo qui semper est pavidus]]. Hence holy Job too: [[Job 9:28|I feared|Verebar]], he says, [[Job 9:28|all my works|omnia opera mea]]. [[9:14|and our counsels uncertain|Et incerta sunt providentiæ nostræ]] [literally, "our foresights are uncertain"]: for we cannot foresee in particular all that may happen. Therefore we often think that expedient which rather does harm, and the reverse. Hence in such things we need the gift of counsel, by which we are directed and helped by the Holy Ghost to take counsel, inquire, and provide for what is more expedient. Hence too in human and positive laws dispensations must often be made, because the lawgiver cannot foresee or express every case that may arise.

paras.t: Corpus enim quod corrumpitur, id est corpus corruptibile, quod et quotidie tendit ad corruptionem, aggravat animam, id est, a spiritualibus exercitiis et considerationibus intellectualibus frequenter retrahit ac impedit eam, propter multas et varias quotidianasque necessitudines suas, infirmitates ac fragilitates, atque ob fomitis infectionem. Unde caro concupiscit adversus spiritum. De hoc pulchre loquitur Plato in Phædone, ostendens qualiter decem millia impedimenta vacationum seu contemplationum caro adducat spiritui: quæ nunc somno, nunc cibo et potu, nunc veste, nunc domicilio indiget. De hoc beatissimus Andreas apostolus in suo martyrio devotissime, prout in sua legenda narratur, locutus est. Verumtamen in statu innocentiæ corpus non ita animam aggravasset: et multo minus post resurrectionem generalem, quum fuerit glorificatum, eam gravabit; imo ornabit lætificabitque animam, et in omnibus ei promptissime erit obediens. Et quamvis corpus corruptibile sic animam gravet, anima tamen naturaliter ei conjungitur: quia in multis utile ac necessarium est animæ, cui naturale est cognitionem intellectivam a sensitiva accipere.
paras.en: [[9:15|For the corruptible body|Corpus enim quod corrumpitur]] [literally, "the body that is corrupted"], that is, the corruptible body, which also tends daily towards corruption, [[9:15|is a load upon the soul|aggravat animam]], that is, it often draws the soul back and hinders it from spiritual exercises and intellectual considerations, because of its many, varied and daily needs, its infirmities and frailties, and because of the infection of the *fomes* [that is, the tinder of sin, the inclination to evil left in fallen nature]. Whence [[Gal 5:17|the flesh lusteth against the spirit|caro concupiscit adversus spiritum]]. Of this Plato speaks finely in the *Phaedo*, showing how the flesh brings ten thousand hindrances to the spirit's leisure, that is, to its contemplation, needing now sleep, now food and drink, now clothing, now a dwelling [Phaedo 66b–d]. Of this the most blessed apostle Andrew spoke most devoutly in his martyrdom, as is told in his legend. Yet in the state of innocence the body would not have weighed so upon the soul; and much less, after the general resurrection, when it has been glorified, will it weigh upon it; nay, it will adorn and gladden the soul, and obey it most readily in all things. And although the corruptible body thus weighs upon the soul, the soul is nevertheless naturally joined to it: because the body is useful and necessary in many things to the soul, whose nature it is to receive its intellectual knowledge from the knowledge of the senses.

paras.t: Et terrena inhabitatio deprimit sensum multa cogitantem: id est, detentio seu commoratio animæ in corpore isto terreno mortali, frequenter trahit deorsum, et obtundit ac fuscat intellectum plurima meditantem, quem variis imaginationibus, curis, occupationibusque externis involvit. Ideo clamavit Apostolus: Infelix ego homo! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus? Et Propheta: Educ de carcere animam meam ad confitendum nomini tuo. Unde in Job fertur: Hi qui habitant domos luteas, qui terrenum habent fundamentum, consumentur velut a tinea.
paras.en: [[9:15|and the earthly habitation presseth down the mind that museth upon many things|Et terrena inhabitatio deprimit sensum multa cogitantem]], that is, the detention or dwelling of the soul in this earthly, mortal body often drags down, and dulls and darkens the understanding that meditates on very many things, entangling it in various imaginings, cares and outward occupations. Therefore the Apostle cried out: [[Rom 7:24|Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?|Infelix ego homo! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?]] And the Prophet: [[Ps 141:8|Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name|Educ de carcere animam meam ad confitendum nomini tuo]]. Whence it is said in Job: [[Job 4:19|they that dwell in houses of clay, who have an earthly foundation|Hi qui habitant domos luteas, qui terrenum habent fundamentum]] shall [[Job 4:19|be consumed as with the moth|consumentur velut a tinea]].

paras.t: Et difficile æstimamus quæ in terra sunt: id est, inferiora ista caduca ac vilia difficulter et cum incertitudine quadam cognoscimus: ita quod ea perfecte agnoscere non valemus, quantum ad omnia quæ circumstant, accidentaliterque inhærent, et de eis possunt inquiri; proprias vero et essentiales eorum differentias difficillimum est invenire. Quod totum pandit opinionum diversitas, quibus inter se diversificantur atque contendunt philosophi, tam gentiles quam christiani, et item Hebræi. Et quæ in prospectu sunt, id est, quæ sensibus nostris objiciuntur, sensibiliterque videntur, invenimus, id est, inquirendo seu addiscendo cognoscimus, cum labore, imo et frequenter cum erroris deceptione, juxta illud: Cunctæ res difficiles; non potest eas homo explicare sermone. Et iterum Salomon dixit: Intellexi quod omnium operum Dei nullam potest homo invenire rationem. Hoc tamen dixit ut concionator. Hinc scriptum est: Nos quippe involvimur tenebris.
paras.en: [[9:16|And hardly do we guess aright at things that are upon earth|Et difficile æstimamus quæ in terra sunt]], that is, we know these lower, perishable and base things with difficulty and with a certain uncertainty: so that we cannot know them perfectly as to all that surrounds them and inheres in them accidentally and can be asked about them; and their proper and essential differences are very hard indeed to find. All this is shown by the diversity of opinions in which the philosophers differ and contend among themselves, gentile as well as Christian, and the Hebrews likewise. And [[9:16|the things that are before us|Et quæ in prospectu sunt]], that is, the things that are presented to our senses and are seen by the senses, [[9:16|do we find|invenimus]], that is, come to know by inquiring or learning, [[9:16|with labour|cum labore]], nay often with the deceit of error, according to the text: [[Eccles 1:8|All things are hard: man cannot explain them by word|Cunctæ res difficiles; non potest eas homo explicare sermone]]. And again Solomon said: [[Eccles 8:17|I understood that man can find no reason of all those works of God|Intellexi quod omnium operum Dei nullam potest homo invenire rationem]]. Yet he said this as the Preacher [*Concionator*, the Latin name of the author of Ecclesiastes, who often voices views not simply his own]. Hence it is written: [[Job 37:19|we are wrapped up in darkness|Nos quippe involvimur tenebris]].

paras.t: Quæ autem in cœlis sunt, id est cœlestia et separata a materia ac invisibilia, quis investigabit? quasi dicat: Nemo potest illa investigare in lumine naturali, nisi valde defectuose ac penitus imperfecte: quemadmodum Aristoteles, Plato et alii subtiliores philosophi aliqua inde scrutati sunt. Nam et Aristoteles ait: Sunt ibi entia quædam simplicia, optimam vitam ducentia, et de suis sufficientia. Similiter de ordinibus, naturis, proprietatibus et actionibus intellectualium substantiarum multa locutus est Plato. Sed dicta ac scripta eorum, a veritate in pluribus defecerunt. Unde et ipse discretus ac prudentissimus Aristoteles fassus est, quod intellectus noster ad illorum cognitionem se habet sicut oculus vespertilionis ad lucem solis.
paras.en: [[9:16|But the things that are in heaven|Quæ autem in cœlis sunt]], that is, heavenly things, separate from matter and invisible, [[9:16|who shall search out|quis investigabit]]? As if to say: No one can search them out by natural light, except very defectively and altogether imperfectly, in the way that Aristotle, Plato and other subtler philosophers examined something of them. For Aristotle too says: There are there certain simple beings, leading the best life, and sufficient of themselves [Aristotle, *On the Heavens* I, 9]. Likewise Plato said much about the orders, natures, properties and actions of the intellectual substances. But their sayings and writings fell short of the truth in many points. Whence even the discerning and most prudent Aristotle himself confessed that our intellect stands to the knowledge of those things as the eye of the bat to the light of the sun [Aristotle, *Metaphysics* II, 1].

paras.t: Sensum autem tuum, id est intellectus tui sapientiam, judicia, consilia et decreta, quis sciet, nisi tu dederis sapientiam, id est, de talibus illuminaveris et docueris hominem, et miseris spiritum sanctum tuum de altissimis, id est, de throno gloriæ tuæ, et de summo cœlo infuderis eum menti ad illustrandam eam de supernaturalibus illis? Inspiratio namque Omnipotentis dat intelligentiam, et unctio Spiritus Sancti docet de omnibus. Dicitur autem Spiritus Sanctus mitti, infundi, ac dari per suos effectus gratiosos et gratum facientes. Denique in verbis hujus versiculi, superbenedicta trinitas Personarum in simplicissimo Deo evidenter insinuatur. Huic quoque verbo consonat quod asserit Christus: Quum autem venerit ille Spiritus veritatis, docebit vos omnem veritatem.
paras.en: [[9:17|thy thought|Sensum autem tuum]] [Denis takes *sensus* as the mind of God], that is, the wisdom, judgments, counsels and decrees of thy intellect, [[9:17|who shall know|quis sciet]], [[9:17|except thou give wisdom|nisi tu dederis sapientiam]], that is, unless thou enlighten and teach man about such things, [[9:17|and send thy holy Spirit from above|et miseris spiritum sanctum tuum de altissimis]], that is, from the throne of thy glory, and pour him from the highest heaven into the mind, to enlighten it about those supernatural things? For [[Job 32:8|the inspiration of the Almighty giveth understanding|Inspiratio namque Omnipotentis dat intelligentiam]], and the [[1 John 2:27|unction|unctio]] of the Holy Ghost [[1 John 2:27|teacheth you of all things|docet de omnibus]]. Now the Holy Ghost is said to be sent, poured in and given through his gracious effects, which make us pleasing to God [*gratum facientes*: that is, sanctifying grace and its gifts]. Lastly, in the words of this little verse the most blessed trinity of Persons in the most simple God is plainly suggested [the Father, to whom the prayer is made, his wisdom, and his holy Spirit]. With this saying also agrees what Christ asserts: [[John 16:13|But when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will teach you all truth|Quum autem venerit ille Spiritus veritatis, docebit vos omnem veritatem]].

paras.t: Ex quibus omnibus elucescit, quam necessaria sit hominibus gratiosa et supernaturalis illuminatio Dei, præsertim quum sine ea agnoscere nequeamus an actiones nostræ sint veraciter virtuosæ ac meritoriæ. Unde subjungitur: et si correcta sint semitæ eorum, qui in terris sunt, id est, an operationes hominum in terra viventium sint a vitiis emendatæ, et per justitiam ac fidem formatam directæ, et quæ tibi placent, didicerint homines, id est, an homines sint vere salubriter informati. Ista, inquam, sciri non queunt, nisi per illuminationem tuam, et Spiritus Sancti missionem, quum scriptum sit: Sunt justi atque sapientes, et opera eorum in manu Dei sunt; et tamen nescit homo utrum amore an odio dignus sit.
paras.en: From all this it is clear how necessary to men is the gracious and supernatural enlightenment of God, especially since without it we cannot know whether our actions are truly virtuous and meritorious. Whence it is added: and whether [[9:18|the ways of them that are upon earth|semitæ eorum, qui in terris sunt]] [[9:18|may be corrected|correcta sint]] [Denis reads *et si*, "and whether", where the Vulgate has *et sic*, "and so"], that is, whether the works of men living on earth have been amended from vices, and set right through justice and formed faith [that is, faith given its form by charity]; [[9:18|and men may learn the things that please thee|et quæ tibi placent, didicerint homines]] [in Denis's reading, "and whether men have learned the things that please thee"], that is, whether men are truly instructed unto salvation. These things, I say, cannot be known except through thy enlightenment and the sending of the Holy Ghost, since it is written: [[Eccles 9:1|there are just men and wise men, and their works are in the hand of God: and yet man knoweth not whether he be worthy of love, or hatred|Sunt justi atque sapientes, et opera eorum in manu Dei sunt; et tamen nescit homo utrum amore an odio dignus sit]].

paras.t: Nam per sapientiam sanati sunt, id est, a vitiis expurgati, a passionum immoderantiis reformati, ab originali peccato mundati, quicumque placuerunt tibi, Domine, a principio, id est ab exordio mundi, post primorum transgressionem parentum. Nam et ipsi primi parentes et posteri eorumdem electi, per fidem et per sapientiæ donum sunt recuperati, nec sine divina illuminatione pœnituerunt : et totum istud ab æterna et increata Sapientia misericorditer perceperunt, quæ in fine sæculorum incarnata, perfecte recuperavit et sanavit genus humanum, juxta illud : Ecce Agnus Dei, ecce qui tollit peccata mundi. Et per Isaiam dicitur : Vere languores nostros ipse tulit : cujus livore sanati sumus.
paras.en: [[9:19|For by wisdom they were healed|Nam per sapientiam sanati sunt]], that is, purged of vices, set right from the excesses of the passions, cleansed of original sin, [[9:19|whosoever have pleased thee, O Lord, from the beginning|quicumque placuerunt tibi, Domine, a principio]], that is, from the beginning of the world, after the transgression of our first parents. For the first parents themselves, and the elect among their descendants, were restored through faith and the gift of wisdom, and did not repent without divine illumination; and all this they received in mercy from the eternal and uncreated Wisdom, who, made flesh at the end of the ages, perfectly restored and healed the human race, according to that: [[John 1:29|Behold the Lamb of God. Behold him who taketh away the sin of the world|Ecce Agnus Dei, ecce qui tollit peccata mundi]]. And by Isaias it is said: [[Is 53:4|Surely he hath borne our infirmities|Vere languores nostros ipse tulit]]: [[Is 53:5|by his bruises we are healed|cujus livore sanati sumus]].

10.title: DECLARATIO CAPITULI DECIMI : HÆC ILLUM, QUI PRIMUS FORMATUS EST A DEO, ETC.
10.title_en: Declaration of the tenth chapter: She preserved him, that was first formed by God, etc.

paras.t: Excellentiam, pietatem, et operationem summæ et increatæ Sapientiæ hic ostendit per historias rerum gestarum.
paras.en: Here he shows the excellence, the loving-kindness and the working of the highest and uncreated Wisdom through the histories of things that were done.

paras.t: Hæc sapientia illum, qui primus inter individua speciei humanæ, formatus est a Deo pater orbis terrarum, id est ipsum Adam a Deo procreatum, qui fuit productivum principium totius humani generis ipsum sequentis, quum solus esset creatus, id est ante aliorum hominum productionem, non angelorum, qui simul cum cœlo empyreo sunt plasmati, custodivit, id est, in innocentia conservavit, quousque per feminam et serpentem est victus; et eduxit illum de delicto suo, id est, gratiam contritionis concessit, per quam de sua transgressione pœnituit. Et eduxit illum de limo terræ, id est, corpus ejus formavit de limo, prout habetur in Genesi : Formavit igitur Deus hominem de limo terræ; et dedit illi virtutem continendi omnia, id est facultatem regendi cuncta inferiora; vel, Virtutem continendi omnia : quia sic dedit ei originalem justitiam, quod si ipse mansisset in ea, non perdidisset suam posteritatem. Dedit quoque ei virtutem continendi omnia, id est naturam per quam in se continet universa, habendo aliquid commune cum qualibet creatura : quia per intellectum et rationem convenit cum Creatore et angelis; per sentire, cum brutis; per vivere, cum plantis; per esse, cum ceteris inanimatis. Continet etiam omnia per intellectum atque memoriam, quia intellectivus et memorativus est omnium.
paras.en: [[10:1|She|Hæc sapientia]], this wisdom, [[10:1|preserved|custodivit]], that is, kept in innocence until he was overcome through the woman and the serpent, [[10:1|him, that was first|illum, qui primus]] among the individuals of the human species [[10:1|formed by God, the father of the world|formatus est a Deo pater orbis terrarum]] [Denis reads *pater*, so that "the father of the world" is Adam himself; the Vulgate has *patre*], that is, Adam himself, brought forth by God, who was the productive principle of the whole human race that followed him, [[10:1|when he was created alone|quum solus esset creatus]], that is, before the production of other men; not before that of the angels, who were fashioned together with the empyrean heaven. [[10:2|And she brought him out of his sin|et eduxit illum de delicto suo]], that is, she granted him the grace of contrition, by which he repented of his transgression. And she brought him out of the slime of the earth [this clause, which stands in Denis's text of the verse, is not in the Clementine Vulgate or the Douay-Rheims], that is, she formed his body of slime, as we have it in Genesis: [[Gen 2:7|the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth|Formavit igitur Deus hominem de limo terræ]]. [[10:2|and gave him power to govern all things|et dedit illi virtutem continendi omnia]] [literally "power of containing all things", on which Denis gives several readings], that is, the faculty of ruling all lower things[[Gen 1:28||]]; or, power of containing all things, because he gave him original justice in such a way that, had he remained in it, he would not have lost his posterity. He also gave him power of containing all things, that is, a nature by which he contains all things in himself, having something in common with every creature: for by intellect and reason he agrees with the Creator and the angels; by sensing, with the brute beasts; by living, with the plants; by being, with the other, inanimate things. He contains all things also by intellect and memory, since he is able to understand and to remember all things.

paras.t: Ab hac sapientia, ut, id est postquam, recessit injustus, videlicet Cain, qui post lapsum non pœnituit, sed desperavit : Major est (inquiens) iniquitas mea, quam ut veniam merear; in ira sua, id est per iracundiam quam contra Abel justum concepit : cui et invidit ; per iram homicidii, id est per iram ejus vitiosam, ex qua fratricidium perpetravit, ipsum Abel necando, fraternitas deperiit, id est, frater ejus exstinctus est, dilectio quoque fraterna ex parte ipsius destructa fuit.
