paras.en: Hence it is added: [[11:8|And|Qui]] they, namely the children of Israel, [[11:8|whilst they were diminished for a manifest reproof of their murdering the infants|quum minuerentur in traductione infantium occisorum]] [the Douay-Rheims renders *in traductione* "for a manifest reproof"; Denis takes the words of the Hebrews being made fewer by the slaying of their infants], that is, became fewer in number because their infants were slain by drowning in the Nile, [[11:8|thou gavest|dedisti]] to them, namely to the Hebrews, [[11:8|abundant water|abundantem aquam]] to drink, [[11:8|unlooked for|insperate]], that is, beyond hope, either by not turning the waters of the land of Gessen into blood, or by bringing back the blood they drew to the nature of water;

paras.t: ostendens per sitim quæ tunc fuit in Ægyptiis, quemadmodum tuos, scilicet filios Israel, exaltares per diversa beneficia atque miracula, et adversarios illorum necares, utpote Ægyptios, qui vel siti, vel corrupti sanguinis potatione letaliter sunt afflicti.
paras.en: [[11:9|Shewing by the thirst that was then|ostendens per sitim quæ tunc fuit]] in the Egyptians, [[11:9|how thou didst exalt thine|quemadmodum tuos]], namely the children of Israel, by divers benefits and miracles, [[11:9|and didst kill their adversaries|et adversarios illorum necares]], that is, the Egyptians, who were mortally stricken either by thirst or by drinking corrupt blood.

paras.t: Quum enim tentati sunt, id est, quum etiam filii Israel per adversa et sitim probati sunt, et paternaliter castigati, et quidem, id est certe seu utique, cum misericordia disciplinam accipientes, id est correctionem a Deo clementer, quia ad suam emendationem, et quia post disciplinam consecuti sunt consolationem; scierunt, id est cognoverunt, quemadmodum cum ira judicati impii, id est Ægyptii a Deo severiter puniti sine consolatione sequente, tormenta paterentur: quia de temporali pœna ad æternam prolapsi sunt. Frequenter tamen, Moyse exorante, Deus abstulit inflictam plagam Ægyptiis, juxta illud in Psalmo: Et non exacerbavit sermones suos. Sed illis in sua obstinatione manentibus, statim durius sunt plagati, quousque totaliter perierunt.
paras.en: [[11:10|For when they were tried|Quum enim tentati sunt]], that is, when the children of Israel too were proved by adversity and thirst, and chastised as by a father, [[11:10|and|et quidem]] indeed, that is, certainly or assuredly, [[11:10|chastised with mercy|cum misericordia disciplinam accipientes]], that is, receiving correction from God mercifully, since it was for their amendment, and since after the chastisement they obtained consolation; [[11:10|they knew|scierunt]], that is, they came to know, [[11:10|how the wicked were judged with wrath|quemadmodum cum ira judicati impii]], that is, the Egyptians, punished severely by God with no consolation following, [[11:10|and tormented|tormenta paterentur]]: for from temporal punishment they fell into eternal. Often, however, at Moses's entreaty[[Ex 8:12||]][[Ex 8:30||]][[Ex 9:33||]][[Ex 10:18||]], God took away the plague laid on the Egyptians[[Ex 8:13||]][[Ex 8:31||]][[Ex 10:19||]], according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 104:28|and grieved not his words|Et non exacerbavit sermones suos]]. But since they remained in their obstinacy, they were at once stricken more harshly, until they perished altogether.

paras.t: Hinc subditur: Hos quidem, puta Hebræos, tanquam pater monens probasti, id est, paternaliter per adversa exercitasti: juxta quod dictum est supra, Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit illos. Illos autem, scilicet Ægyptios, tanquam durus rex interrogans condemnasti, id est, rigorose peremisti, sicut rex per tormenta extorquet confessionem excessus a reo, et damnat confessum. Sic et Apostolus loquitur: Vide severitatem et bonitatem Dei: severitatem in eis qui perierunt; in te autem bonitatem, si tamen permanseris in bonitate.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[11:11|For thou didst admonish and try|monens probasti]] [[11:11|them|Hos quidem]], namely the Hebrews, [[11:11|as a father|tanquam pater]], that is, thou didst exercise them through adversities in a fatherly way: as was said above, [[Wis 3:6|As gold in the furnace, he hath proved them|Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit illos]]. [[11:11|but the others|Illos autem]], namely the Egyptians, [[11:11|as a severe king, thou didst examine and condemn|tanquam durus rex interrogans condemnasti]], that is, thou didst destroy them with rigour, as a king wrings from a guilty man by torture the confession of his crime, and condemns him once he has confessed [*interrogans*, "examining": the questioning of an accused man under torture]. So too the Apostle speaks: [[Rom 11:22|See then the goodness and the severity of God: towards them indeed that are fallen, the severity; but towards thee, the goodness of God, if thou abide in goodness|Vide severitatem et bonitatem Dei: severitatem in eis qui perierunt; in te autem bonitatem, si tamen permanseris in bonitate]].

paras.t: Absentes enim et præsentes similiter torquebantur: id est, tam illi Ægyptii qui non erant cum Pharaone, quam præsentes eidem, eisdem plagis puniebantur.
paras.en: [[11:12|For whether absent or present, they were tormented alike|Absentes enim et præsentes similiter torquebantur]]: that is, those Egyptians who were not with Pharao, as much as those who were with him, were punished with the same plagues.

paras.t: Deinde subditur de Hebræis, propter quorum oppressionem iniquam sic puniebantur Ægyptii. Duplex enim illos acceperat tædium, id est, duplici tædio affligebantur: et gemitus cum memoria præteritorum: id est, tædium et gemitus fuit in eis, propter mala seu adversa præsentia, juxta illud, Ingemiscentes filii Israel propter opera; et etiam ex recordatione præteritarum afflictionum, quas diu sustinuerunt, quia jam ante proprios amiserunt infantulos. Vel, Cum memoria præteritorum, id est ex recordatione prosperitatum, quas patres eorum tempore Joseph in Ægypto habebant. Qui enim adversitatibus premitur, gravius affligitur, quando se quandoque prosperatum fuisse reminiscetur. Unde sanctus Job dixit: Ego quondam ille opulentus, repente ad nihilum redactus sum. Boetius quoque: Infelicissimum, inquit, infortunii genus est, fuisse felicem.
paras.en: Next it is added of the Hebrews, for whose wicked oppression the Egyptians were punished in this way: [[11:13|For a double affliction came upon them|Duplex enim illos acceperat tædium]] [*tædium*: weariness or loathing], that is, they were afflicted with a twofold weariness: [[11:13|and a groaning for the remembrance of things past|et gemitus cum memoria præteritorum]]: that is, there was weariness and groaning in them, because of their present evils or adversities, according to that text, [[Ex 2:23|the children of Israel groaning, cried out because of the works|Ingemiscentes filii Israel propter opera]]; and also from the remembrance of past afflictions which they had long endured, for already before this they had lost their own little ones[[Ex 1:22||]]. Or, [[11:13|for the remembrance of things past|Vel, Cum memoria præteritorum]], that is, from the remembrance of the prosperity which their fathers had in Egypt in the time of Joseph[[Gen 47:6||]][[Gen 47:11||]][[Gen 47:12||]][[Gen 50:21||]]. For he who is pressed by adversity is afflicted more heavily when he remembers that he once prospered. Hence holy Job said: [[Job 16:13|I that was formerly so wealthy, am all on a sudden|Ego quondam ille opulentus, repente]] [[Job 16:8|brought to nothing|ad nihilum redactus sum]]. And Boethius: The most unhappy kind of misfortune, he says, is to have been happy.

paras.t: Quum enim audirent per sua tormenta bene secum agi, id est, quum filii Israel didicissent, quod Deus eos paternaliter sic probaret ad profectum eorum, commemorati sunt Dominum, id est, Deum et ejus pietatem utiliter consideraverunt, admirantes in finem exitus, id est obstupescentes de sua pia eductione finali ex Ægypto et tribulationibus illis.
paras.en: [[11:14|For when they heard|Quum enim audirent]] [[11:14|that by their punishments|per sua tormenta]] they themselves [[11:14|were benefited|bene secum agi]] [Denis reads *secum*, "with themselves", and takes the words of the Israelites: that it went well with them through their own torments], that is, when the children of Israel had learned that God was thus proving them in a fatherly way for their profit, [[11:14|they remembered the Lord|commemorati sunt Dominum]], that is, they considered God and his kindness to their profit, [[11:14|wondering at the end of what was come to pass|admirantes in finem exitus]], that is, astonished at their merciful final deliverance out of Egypt and out of those tribulations.

paras.t: Quem enim in expositione prava projectum deriserunt, id est Moysen, ex iniquo Pharaonis præcepto in aquis expositum: quem irriserunt, tam Ægyptii, quando primo venit ad Pharaonem ad educendum Hebræos, quam Hebræi, quorum unus dixit ad eum: Quis te constituit judicem aut principem super nos? Et alii dixerunt Moysi, Recede a nobis, ut serviamus Ægyptiis. In finem eventus mirati sunt. Non similiter justis faciens, id est, Deus fuit ipsis Hebræis suis cultoribus, non taliter faciens sicut Ægyptiis, ut patet ex dictis: quod et generaliter accipi potest, quoniam aliter agit Deus cum justis, aliter cum injustis, sicut et diversimode peccant. Nam, teste Scriptura, Septies cadit justus, et resurgit; impius autem, quum in profundum venerit peccatorum, contemnit.
paras.en: [[11:15|For whom they scorned before, when he was thrown out at the time of his being wickedly exposed to perish|Quem enim in expositione prava projectum deriserunt]], that is, Moses, exposed in the waters by the wicked command of Pharao[[Ex 1:22||]][[Ex 2:3||]]: whom both the Egyptians mocked, when he first came to Pharao to lead the Hebrews out, and the Hebrews, one of whom said to him: [[Ex 2:14|Who hath appointed thee prince and judge over us?|Quis te constituit judicem aut principem super nos?]] And others said to Moses, [[Ex 14:12|Depart from us, that we may serve the Egyptians|Recede a nobis, ut serviamus Ægyptiis]]. [[11:15|him they admired in the end, when they saw the event|In finem eventus mirati sunt]]. [[11:15|unlike to that of the just|Non similiter justis faciens]] [Denis reads *non similiter justis faciens*, "not doing alike to the just", where the Vulgate has *sitientes*, "thirsting", rendered by the Douay-Rheims "their thirsting being unlike to that of the just"]: that is, God was not acting towards the Hebrews, his worshippers, as towards the Egyptians, as is plain from what has been said. This may also be taken generally, since God deals in one way with the just and in another with the unjust, as they also sin in different ways. For, as Scripture witnesses, [[Prov 24:16|a just man shall fall seven times, and shall rise again|Septies cadit justus, et resurgit]]; but [[Prov 18:3|The wicked man, when he is come into the depths of sins, contemneth|impius autem, quum in profundum venerit peccatorum, contemnit]].

paras.t: Consequenter tangitur causa derelictionis et punitionis Ægyptiorum. Pro cogitationibus autem insensatis, iniquitates illorum: id est, propter insipientissimas Ægyptiorum cogitationes, quibus senserunt creaturis cultum latriæ exhibendum, permissi sunt ad pravissima facta corruere, atque in suis obdurari excessibus. Quæ quidem, id est quæ iniquitates, fuerunt, quod errantes per incredulitatem, colebant mutos serpentes et bestias supervacuas, id est viles atque inutiles, seu earum imagines, nullam vocem formare potentes. Unde dicitur per Prophetam: Ut adorarent talpas et vespertiliones. Quæ dicuntur mutæ, vel quia raucum et modicum sonum, aut quia non articulatam vocem producunt. Hinc quoque ait Apostolus: Mutaverunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei, in similitudinem corruptibilis hominis, et volucrum, et serpentium, et quadrupedum. Ob tantam impietatem, immisisti illis multitudinem mutorum animalium in vindictam, videlicet ranas, scinifes, muscas, locustas, bruchos: ut patet in Exodo et in Psalmo;
paras.en: Next is touched on the cause of the Egyptians' abandonment and punishment. [[11:16|But for the foolish devices of their iniquity|Pro cogitationibus autem insensatis, iniquitates illorum]] [Denis reads *iniquitates illorum*, "their iniquities", where the Vulgate has *iniquitatis*, "of their iniquity"]: that is, on account of the most senseless thoughts of the Egyptians, by which they held that the worship of latria [the worship due to God alone] was to be given to creatures, they were permitted to rush into the most wicked deeds and to be hardened in their excesses. And these, that is, these iniquities, were that, [[11:16|being deceived|errantes]] through unbelief, they [[11:16|worshipped dumb serpents and worthless beasts|colebant mutos serpentes et bestias supervacuas]], that is, vile and useless ones, or images of them, that could form no voice. Hence it is said through the Prophet: [[Is 2:20|to adore, moles and bats|Ut adorarent talpas et vespertiliones]] [the margin's Is. ii, 20 is printed so that it reads "Is. n, 20"]. These are called *dumb* either because they give a hoarse and slight sound, or because they give no articulate voice. Hence too the Apostle says: [[Rom 1:23|they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of a corruptible man and of birds, and of fourfooted beasts and of creeping things|Mutaverunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei, in similitudinem corruptibilis hominis, et volucrum, et serpentium, et quadrupedum]]. For so great an impiety [[11:16|thou didst send upon them a multitude of dumb beasts for vengeance|immisisti illis multitudinem mutorum animalium in vindictam]], namely frogs[[Ex 8:6||]], sciniphs[[Ex 8:17||]], flies[[Ex 8:24||]], locusts[[Ex 10:13||]] and bruchus, as is plain in Exodus and in the Psalm[[Ps 104:30||]][[Ps 104:31||]][[Ps 104:34||]] [the margin gives Ps. cv, 30, 31, 34; the verses are Ps 104:30, 31, 34];

paras.t: ut scirent, id est, ex qualitate suarum pœnarum adverterent, quia per quæ quis peccat, per hæc, id est eadem vel similia, et punitur, ut pœna correspondeat culpæ: sicut Sodomitæ, qui per ardorem et fœtorem sceleratissimæ immunditiæ peccaverunt, per ardorem intensissimum et fœtorem teterrimum ignis sulfurei sunt puniti.
paras.en: [[11:17|That they might know|ut scirent]], that is, might take note from the kind of their punishments, [[11:17|that by what things a man sinneth, by the same|quia per quæ quis peccat, per hæc]], that is, by the same or like things, [[11:17|also he is tormented|et punitur]] [the print has *punitur*, "is punished"; the margin gives the Vulgate's *torquetur*, "is tormented"], so that the punishment may answer to the fault: as the Sodomites, who sinned through the heat and stench of a most wicked uncleanness[[Gen 19:4||]], were punished through the most intense heat and the foulest stench of sulphurous fire[[Gen 19:24||]].

paras.t: Non enim impossibilis, id est impotens, erat omnipotens manus, id est virtus tua, quæ creavit orbem terrarum ex invisa materia, id est ex materia primo informi et confusa ac tenebrosa, juxta illud: Terra autem erat inanis et vacua, et tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi. Quod qualiter intelligendum sit, ibi diffuse expositum est.
paras.en: For [[11:18|thy almighty hand|omnipotens manus]], that is, thy might, [[11:18|was not unable|Non enim impossibilis]], that is, was not powerless, [[11:18|which made the world of matter without form|quæ creavit orbem terrarum ex invisa materia]] [*ex invisa materia*, literally "of unseen matter"], that is, of matter at first formless, confused and dark, according to that text: [[Gen 1:2|And the earth was void and empty, and darkness was upon the face of the deep|Terra autem erat inanis et vacua, et tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi]]. How this is to be understood has been set out at length there.

paras.t: Vel dicitur orbis terrarum creatus ex invisa materia, quia materia prima secundum se, non est quid, nec quanta, nec qualis, quum sit expers omnis substantialisque accidentalisque formæ. Sed quum creare, sit ex nihilo facere, quomodo orbis terrarum dicitur creatus ex materia? Et respondendum, quia ut in exordio Genesis legitur, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram. Sicque elementum terræ immediate a Deo productum est in sua forma atque materia. Idcirco, quod dicitur creatum ex informi invisaque materia, intelligendum est, quod factum sit ex forma et materia, tanquam ex substantialibus partibus, non quasi ex præjacenti materia, quamvis aliqui aliter opinentur, ut super Genesim dictum est. Creare autem frequenter sumitur extense, pro Facere. Unde et Deus dicitur omnium Creator, quamvis multa ex materia facta sint præjacenti.
paras.en: Or the world is said to be made [[11:18|of matter without form|ex invisa materia]] because prime matter in itself is neither a what, nor of any quantity, nor of any quality, since it is without any form, whether substantial or accidental. But since to create is to make out of nothing, how is the world said to be created out of matter? The answer is that, as we read at the beginning of Genesis, [[Gen 1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]. And so the element of earth was produced immediately by God in its form and its matter. Therefore when it is said to be created out of formless and unseen matter, this is to be understood to mean that it was made of form and matter as of its substantial parts, not as out of pre-existing matter, although some think otherwise, as was said on Genesis [the margin refers to Denis's commentary on Genesis, art. VI]. *To create*, moreover, is often taken in a wider sense for *to make*. Hence God too is called the Creator of all things, although many things were made out of pre-existing matter.

paras.t: Immittere illis multitudinem ursorum, aut audaces leones, aut novi generis ira plenas et ignotas bestias, id est feras iracundissimas, ante non visas, aut vaporem ignium spirantes, ut dracones, aut fumi odorem, id est afflictivum fœtorem, proferentes, aut horrendas ab oculis suis scintillas emittentes: quarum non solum læsura, id est vulneratio, morsus, intoxicatio, poterat illos, scilicet Ægyptios, exterminare, sed et adspectus per timorem occidere, id est, tam excessivum timorem poterant Ægyptiis incutere, quod ex timore obissent. Passiones namque partis sensitivæ, fiunt cum corporali transmutatione; et quanto sunt intensiores ac magis prædominantes, tanto plus lædunt complexionem: et sua nimietate possunt mortem inducere, sicut et in Ecclesiastico legitur: Multos occidit tristitia. Et Daniel ex visione perterritus: Domine, inquit, in visione tua dissolutæ sunt compages meæ; sed et halitus meus intercluditur, et nihil in me remansit virium, et emarcui.
paras.en: [[11:18|to send upon them a multitude of bears, or fierce lions|Immittere illis multitudinem ursorum, aut audaces leones]], [[11:19|Or unknown beasts of a new kind, full of rage|aut novi generis ira plenas et ignotas bestias]], that is, most wrathful wild beasts never seen before, [[11:19|either breathing out a fiery vapour|aut vaporem ignium spirantes]], like dragons, [[11:19|or sending forth a stinking smoke|aut fumi odorem]], that is, giving out an afflicting stench, [[11:19|or shooting horrible sparks out of their eyes|aut horrendas ab oculis suis scintillas emittentes]]: [[11:20|Whereof not only the hurt|quarum non solum læsura]], that is, their wounding, biting and poisoning, [[11:20|might be able to destroy them|poterat illos]], namely the Egyptians, [[11:20|but also the very sight might kill them through fear|sed et adspectus per timorem occidere]], that is, they could have struck such excessive fear into the Egyptians that they would have died of fear. For the passions of the sensitive part come about with a bodily change; and the more intense and the more dominant they are, the more they harm the constitution [*complexio*: the balance of the humours in the body], and by their excess they can bring on death, as we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 30:25|sadness hath killed many|Multos occidit tristitia]]. And Daniel, terrified by the vision: [[Dan 10:16|O my lord|Domine]], he says, [[Dan 10:16|at the sight of thee my joints are loosed|in visione tua dissolutæ sunt compages meæ]]; [[Dan 10:17|moreover, my breath is stopped|sed et halitus meus intercluditur]], [[Dan 10:16|and no strength hath remained in me|et nihil in me remansit virium]], and [[Dan 10:8|I fainted away|emarcui]].

paras.t: Sed et sine his, id est absque læsione ferarum istarum, uno spiritu, id est in sola indignatione jussioneve tua, aut ministerio unius angelici spiritus, poterant occidi ipsi Ægyptii, persecutionem passi ab ipsis factis suis, id est, propter impia opera sua plagati; vel, Ab ipsis factis suis, id est propter manufacta idola sua, ac idololatrias, et præsertim propter excessus eorum in filios Israel; et dispergi, id est, diversimode perdi, per spiritum virtutis tuæ, id est per imperium omnipotentiæ tuæ, vel per spiritum angelicum tua virtute creatum.
paras.en: [[11:21|Yea, and without these|Sed et sine his]], that is, without being hurt by those wild beasts, [[11:21|with one blast|uno spiritu]] [*spiritus* means both "breath" and "spirit"], that is, by thy indignation or thy command alone, or by the ministry of one angelic spirit, [[11:21|they might have been slain|poterant occidi]], the Egyptians themselves, [[11:21|persecuted by their own deeds|persecutionem passi ab ipsis factis suis]], that is, stricken for their wicked works; or, [[11:21|by their own deeds|vel, Ab ipsis factis suis]], that is, for the idols made by their hands, and their idolatries, and above all for their excesses against the children of Israel; [[11:21|and scattered|et dispergi]] [Denis reads *dispergi*, "to be scattered", where the Vulgate has *dispersi*], that is, destroyed in divers ways, [[11:21|by the breath of thy power|per spiritum virtutis tuæ]], that is, by the command of thy omnipotence, or by an angelic spirit created by thy power.

paras.t: Sed omnia in mensura, et numero, et pondere constituisti. Hoc ad litteram videtur inductum, ad assignandum causam cum Deus justus ac sapiens punivit Ægyptios per minuta ac vilia animalia: quia videlicet talia coluerunt. Et ita omnia Ægyptiorum tormenta disposuit et effecit ministerio angelorum, in mensura, id est certa proportione: ut quo majora erant peccata, eo et majora essent supplicia, juxta illud in Apocalypsi: Quantum glorificavit se, et in deliciis fuit; tantum date illi tormentum et luctum. Unde per Isaiam testatur Altissimus: In mensura contra mensuram, quum abjecta fuerint, judicabo eam: id est, in mensura justitiæ seu pœnæ, judicabo eam, contra mensuram, id est ad puniendum ejus iniquitatem secundum ipsius quantitatem. Sic quoque supplicia inferuntur in numero certo, prout meretur et exigit numerositas culpæ, eo quod nulla culpa maneat impunita; atque in pondere, quoniam quanto quis peccat ex majori libidine, et intentiori pravitatis affectu, eo acutiorem meretur ac sortitur punitionem. Potest etiam per mensuram certa duratio pœnæ intelligi: quamvis enim pœnæ inferni sint æternales, pœnæ tamen vitæ præsentis sunt temporales: quæ divinitus moderantur ac dispensantur. Sicque plagæ Ægyptiorum fuerunt sibi invicem succedentes, ac tempore certo durantes, secundum quod Pharao petiit sibi et suis ignosci, et plagas auferri.
paras.en: [[11:21|but thou hast ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight|Sed omnia in mensura, et numero, et pondere constituisti]] [Denis reads *constituisti*, "thou hast established"; the margin gives the Vulgate's *disposuisti*]. In the literal sense this seems to be brought in to give the reason why God, just and wise, punished the Egyptians by tiny and vile animals: namely because they worshipped such things. And so he ordered and carried out all the torments of the Egyptians by the ministry of angels, *in measure*, that is, in a fixed proportion: so that the greater the sins were, the greater too were the punishments, according to that in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 18:7|As much as she hath glorified herself and lived in delicacies, so much torment and sorrow give ye to her|Quantum glorificavit se, et in deliciis fuit; tantum date illi tormentum et luctum]]. Hence the Most High testifies through Isaias: [[Is 27:8|In measure against measure, when it shall be cast off, thou shalt judge it|In mensura contra mensuram, quum abjecta fuerint, judicabo eam]] [Denis reads *judicabo*, "I will judge", where the Vulgate has *judicabis*]: that is, in the measure of justice or of punishment I will judge it, *against measure*, that is, so as to punish its iniquity according to its quantity. So too punishments are inflicted *in number*, a fixed number, as the number of the faults deserves and requires, since no fault remains unpunished; and *in weight*, since the greater the lust and the more intense the love of wickedness with which a man sins, the sharper the punishment he deserves and receives. By *measure* may also be understood a fixed duration of punishment: for although the pains of hell are eternal, the pains of the present life are temporal, and are tempered and dispensed by God. And so the plagues of the Egyptians followed one upon another and lasted a fixed time, according as Pharao asked that he and his people be forgiven and the plagues taken away[[Ex 8:8||]][[Ex 8:28||]][[Ex 9:28||]][[Ex 10:17||]].

paras.t: Præterea verba ista per se sumpta profundius possunt exponi. In primis etenim dicere possumus, quod omnia simul sumpta, id est totum universum, constitutum et factum sit in mensura, quia finitum est in dignitate et esse specifico, in quantitate et potestate; et item in numero, quoniam unus est mundus, non multi aut innumerabiles, ut quidam imaginati sunt; in pondere quoque, quo omnia tendunt ad centrum, inclinationemque habent ad proprium finem. Insuper quælibet res subsistens, facta est in mensura, quoniam habet esse limitatum ac determinatam naturam. Facta est quoque in numero, in quantum constat ex essentialibus suis partibus aut principiis, ut ex forma et materia, vel ex actu et potentia, sive ex quod est et quo est, et certam differentiam habet, qua ad gradum aliquem essentialis perfectionis suæ contrahitur; et in pondere, id est in naturali inclinatione ad proprium finem. Hinc Augustinus asserit, omnia facta in modo, specie et ordine: per modum, intelligens mensuram; per speciem, numerum, nam et species rerum se habent ut numeri; per ordinem, pondus. Ad quæ reducuntur tria, quæ in libro LXXXIII Quæstionum inducit, dicendo: Quod constat, quod discernitur, quod congruit. Unumquodque etenim per suum esse constat, per naturam specificam seu formam cognoscitur, per ordinem congruit. Amplius, quum Deus dicatur causa universorum efficiens et exemplaris atque finalis, causat hæc tria in rebus secundum quamdam appropriationem. Nam in quantum causa efficiens, dat esse; in quantum causa exemplaris, largitur speciem; in quantum causa finalis, imprimit pondus seu ordinem ad proprium finem. De hac materia possunt multa introduci subtilia: quæ in opusculo de Venustate mundi et pulchritudine Dei induxi.
paras.en: Moreover, these words taken by themselves can be expounded more deeply. First, we can say that all things taken together, that is, the whole universe, was established and made *in measure*, since it is finite in dignity and specific being, in quantity and in power; and likewise *in number*, since the world is one, not many or innumerable, as some have imagined; and *in weight*, by which all things tend to the centre and have an inclination to their proper end. Further, every subsisting thing was made *in measure*, since it has a limited being and a determinate nature. It was made also *in number*, inasmuch as it consists of its essential parts or principles, as of form and matter, or of act and potency, or of *that which is* and *that by which it is* [the scholastic distinction of the subject and its being], and has a fixed difference by which it is narrowed to some degree of its essential perfection; and *in weight*, that is, in a natural inclination to its proper end. Hence Augustine asserts that all things were made in mode, species and order: by *mode* meaning measure; by *species*, number, for the species of things are related as numbers are; by *order*, weight. To these are brought back the three things he puts forward in the book of the Eighty-three Questions, saying: That by which it stands, that by which it is distinguished, that by which it agrees. For each thing stands by its own being, is known by its specific nature or form, and agrees by its order. Further, since God is called the efficient, exemplar and final cause of all things, he causes these three in things by a certain appropriation [that is, the ascribing of something common to the whole Trinity to one Person or aspect]. For as efficient cause he gives being; as exemplar cause he bestows species; as final cause he imprints weight, or order to their proper end. Many subtle things can be brought in on this matter, which I have set out in the little work On the Beauty of the World and the Comeliness of God.

paras.t: Hinc ait Scriptura de Creatore: Qui numerat multitudinem stellarum. Et in libro Job: Qui fecit ventis pondus, et aquas appendit in mensura. Unde dixit Boetius: Omnia quæ a primæva rerum origine processerunt, ratione numerorum sunt condita. In his Deus mundum constituit, regit, ac judicabit. In his justus Judex nec comprehendi potest, nec reprehendi. Omnia in clausura horum trium latent abscondita: quæ clavibus sapientiæ, justitiæ, ac judicii Dei reserabuntur, quando illuminabuntur abscondita tenebrarum, et revelabuntur consilia cordium.
paras.en: Hence Scripture says of the Creator: [[Ps 146:4|Who telleth the number of the stars|Qui numerat multitudinem stellarum]]. And in the book of Job: [[Job 28:25|Who made a weight for the winds, and weighed the waters by measure.|Qui fecit ventis pondus, et aquas appendit in mensura]] [the margin gives Job xxviii, 23; the words are Job 28:25]. Hence Boethius said: All things that have come forth from the first origin of things were founded by the reckoning of numbers. In these God established the world, rules it, and will judge it. In these the just Judge can be neither comprehended nor reproved. All things lie hidden within the enclosure of these three, which will be unlocked by the keys of God's wisdom, justice and judgement, when [[1 Cor 4:5|the hidden things of darkness|abscondita tenebrarum]] shall be brought to light, and [[1 Cor 4:5|the counsels of the hearts|consilia cordium]] revealed.

paras.t: Multum enim valere, tibi soli supererat semper: id est, non ex impotentia immisisti Ægyptiis animalia illa minima in vindictam, quoniam æternaliter omnipotens es, et semper facere potes majora ac plura quam facis, imo infinities plura, quum sis infinitæ potentiæ. Et virtuti brachii tui quis resistet? id est, potestati majestatis tuæ nullus potest resistere. Potest etiam per brachium Dei, Filius ejus intelligi, juxta illud: Salvavit sibi dextera ejus, et brachium sanctum ejus; itemque, Fecit potentiam in brachio suo.
paras.en: [[11:22|For great power always belonged to thee alone|Multum enim valere, tibi soli supererat semper]]: that is, it was not from want of power that thou didst send those tiniest animals upon the Egyptians for vengeance, since thou art eternally almighty, and canst always do greater things and more than thou doest, nay, infinitely more, since thou art of infinite power. [[11:22|and who shall resist the strength of thy arm?|Et virtuti brachii tui quis resistet?]] that is, no one can resist the power of thy majesty. By the arm of God his Son may also be understood, according to that text: [[Ps 97:1|His right hand hath wrought for him salvation, and his arm is holy|Salvavit sibi dextera ejus, et brachium sanctum ejus]]; and again, [[Luke 1:51|He hath shewed might in his arm|Fecit potentiam in brachio suo]].

paras.t: Quoniam tanquam momentum, id est stilus seu lingua, stateræ, sic ante te est orbis terrarum, id est parvæ et modicæ reputationis, imo dependens incessanter a te, et tanquam pulvis exiguus respectu majestatis tuæ immensæ: juxta quem modum loquitur Isaias, Ecce gentes quasi stilla situlæ, et quasi momentum stateræ reputatæ sunt: et tanquam gutta roris antelucani, id est roris qui ante lucem descendit, et solis ardore mox desiccatur.
paras.en: [[11:23|For|Quoniam]] [[11:23|as the least grain|tanquam momentum]], that is, the pointer or tongue, [[11:23|of the balance|stateræ]] [Denis takes *momentum* as the tongue of the balance; the Douay-Rheims has "the least grain"], so [[11:23|the whole world before thee is|sic ante te est orbis terrarum]], that is, of small and slight account, nay, hanging on thee without ceasing, and like a little dust in regard of thy boundless majesty: in which manner Isaias speaks, [[Is 40:15|Behold the Gentiles are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the smallest grain of a balance|Ecce gentes quasi stilla situlæ, et quasi momentum stateræ reputatæ sunt]]: [[11:23|and as a drop of the morning dew|et tanquam gutta roris antelucani]], that is, of the dew that comes down before daylight and is soon dried up by the heat of the sun.

paras.t: Sed misereris omnium: nam Creator universa pie conservat in esse, et providet creaturis, viatoribus quoque misericors est: quoniam omnia potes: sicque omnipotentia tua plena est pietate ac sapientia, non tyrannide, nec violentia. Imo substantialiter est ipsa bonitas, pietas, et sapientia tua, quæ etiam damnatos punit citra condignum. Et dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam, id est, ea punire differs, et habes te quasi non videas, quatenus interim pœniteant, et salventur: juxta illud Isaiæ, Propterea exspectat Dominus, ut misereatur vestri. Unde ait Apostolus: Ignoras quoniam benignitas Dei ad pœnitentiam te adducit? Vel, Dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam, id est, per pœnitentiam hominum ea dimittis, et impunita transire permittis, non infligendo saltem pœnam æternam, sed illam mutando in temporalem. Possetque esse tanta contritio, quod tota pœna dimitteretur: quoniam ipsa contritio, est magna spontaneaque sui ipsius interior punitio.
paras.en: [[11:24|But thou hast mercy upon all|Sed misereris omnium]]: for the Creator lovingly keeps all things in being, and provides for his creatures, and is merciful also to wayfarers [*viatores*: men still on the way, in this life, not yet at their end]: [[11:24|because thou canst do all things|quoniam omnia potes]]; and so thy omnipotence is full of kindness and wisdom, not of tyranny or violence. Nay, it is in substance thy very goodness, kindness and wisdom, which punishes even the damned less than they deserve. [[11:24|and overlookest the sins of men for the sake of repentance|Et dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam]] [*dissimulas*: thou dost act as though thou didst not see], that is, thou puttest off punishing them, and bearest thyself as though thou didst not see, so that meanwhile they may repent and be saved: according to that of Isaias, [[Is 30:18|Therefore the Lord waiteth that he may have mercy on you|Propterea exspectat Dominus, ut misereatur vestri]]. Hence the Apostle says: [[Rom 2:4|Knowest thou not that the benignity of God leadeth thee to penance?|Ignoras quoniam benignitas Dei ad pœnitentiam te adducit?]] Or, [[11:24|overlookest the sins of men for the sake of repentance|Vel, Dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam]], that is, through men's repentance thou dost remit them and lettest them pass unpunished, at least by not inflicting eternal punishment but changing it into temporal. And contrition could be so great that the whole punishment would be remitted, since contrition itself is a great and voluntary inward punishment of oneself.

paras.t: Diligis enim omnia quæ sunt, in quantum sunt, et tuam bonitatem participant: sic enim tibi aliqualiter assimilantur, et amabilia, non odibilia, exstant. Natura quippe secundum se considerata, pura est atque amabilis. Propter quod frequenter in Prophetis tota gens, etiam iniqua, nomine filiæ et nomine virginis designatur: sicut dicitur per Isaiam: Descende, sede in pulvere, virgo filia Babylon: ad insinuandum quod natura hominum in se instar virginis pura sit, et instar filiæ exsistat amabilis, ut super Isaiam tangit Hieronymus. Et nihil odisti eorum quæ fecisti, quantum ad id quod habet creatura a te: sed quantum ad id quod habet ex libera voluntate, potest odibilis fieri, non in se, sed per comparationem ad culpam: prout infra habetur, Odio sunt Deo impius et impietas ejus: et in Psalmo, Odisti omnes qui operantur iniquitatem. Iste est amor Dei ad creaturas naturalis. Porro amore prædestinationis amat solos electos. Unde testatur per Prophetam: Jacob dilexi, Esau autem odio habui. Universos quoque qui in caritate exsistunt, amat amore præsentis justitiæ. Nec enim odiens aliquid constituisti, aut fecisti. Omnia enim fecit propter bonum convenientemque finem, ut suo modo bona sint, et bene sit eis.
paras.en: [[11:25|For thou lovest all things that are|Diligis enim omnia quæ sunt]], inasmuch as they are and share in thy goodness: for so they are in some way made like to thee, and stand forth as lovable, not hateful. For nature considered in itself is pure and lovable. For this reason in the Prophets a whole nation, even a wicked one, is often called by the name of daughter and the name of virgin, as is said through Isaias: [[Is 47:1|Come down, sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon|Descende, sede in pulvere, virgo filia Babylon]]: to suggest that the nature of men in itself is pure like a virgin and lovable like a daughter, as Jerome touches on in his commentary on Isaias. [[11:25|and hatest none of the things which thou hast made|Et nihil odisti eorum quæ fecisti]], as regards what the creature has from thee: but as regards what it has from its free will, it can become hateful, not in itself, but in relation to its fault: as is found below, [[Wis 14:9|to God the wicked and his wickedness are hateful|Odio sunt Deo impius et impietas ejus]]; and in the Psalm, [[Ps 5:7|Thou hatest all the workers of iniquity|Odisti omnes qui operantur iniquitatem]]. This is God's natural love for his creatures. But with the love of predestination he loves the elect alone. Hence he testifies through the Prophet: [[Mal 1:2|I have loved Jacob|Jacob dilexi]], [[Mal 1:3|But have hated Esau|Esau autem odio habui]]. All those too who are in charity he loves with the love of present justice. [[11:25|for thou didst not appoint, or make any thing hating it|Nec enim odiens aliquid constituisti, aut fecisti]]. For he made all things for a good and fitting end, that each in its own way might be good, and that it might be well with them.

paras.t: Quomodo autem posset aliquid permanere, nisi tu voluisses? quasi dicat, Nequaquam: quoniam tanta est dependentia creaturæ ad Creatorem, ut nec ad momentum queat subsistere aut durare sine illius voluntate et conservatione. Imo plus dependet ab illo, quam splendor a luce, aut dies a sole, aut quævis creatura ab alia. Aut quod a te vocatum non esset, conservaretur? id est, impossibile est aliquid conservari, nisi te imperante.
paras.en: [[11:26|And how could any thing endure, if thou wouldst not?|Quomodo autem posset aliquid permanere, nisi tu voluisses?]] as if to say, In no way: for so great is the dependence of the creature on the Creator that it could not subsist or last even for a moment without his will and keeping. Nay, it depends on him more than brightness on light, or the day on the sun, or any creature on another. [[11:26|or be preserved, if not called by thee?|Aut quod a te vocatum non esset, conservaretur?]] that is, it is impossible for anything to be preserved unless thou command it.

paras.t: Parcis autem omnibus: eo modo quo dictum est, Misereris omnium; quoniam tua sunt, Domine: causa enim naturaliter amat et conservat suum effectum, et bonus Creator propriæ creaturæ libenter propitiatur, dummodo illa non se figat in malo: qui amas animas, id est, rationales animas specialiter diligis, quoniam ad æternam beatitudinem, ad tui ipsius beatificam fruitionem eas creasti et ordinasti, saltem antecedente voluntate, et quantum in te est, qui omnes homines vis fieri salvos; verumtamen quosdam, non omnes, prædestinasti. Corpora vero propter animas dilexisti et condidisti.
paras.en: [[11:27|But thou sparest all|Parcis autem omnibus]], in the way in which it was said, [[11:24|thou hast mercy upon all|Misereris omnium]]; [[11:27|because they are thine, O Lord|quoniam tua sunt, Domine]]: for a cause naturally loves and preserves its effect, and the good Creator is gladly appeased towards his own creature, provided it does not fix itself in evil: [[11:27|who lovest souls|qui amas animas]], that is, thou lovest rational souls in a special way, since thou didst create and ordain them for eternal beatitude, for the blessed enjoyment of thyself, at least by thy antecedent will [God's will considered before the circumstances of each case, by which he wills all to be saved; it is distinguished from his consequent will] and as far as lies in thee, [[1 Tim 2:4|Who will have all men to be saved|qui omnes homines vis fieri salvos]]; yet some, not all, thou hast predestined. Bodies, again, thou hast loved and made for the sake of souls.

paras.t: Juxta mysticum intellectum, sicut filii Israel iter fecerunt per deserta inhabitabilia, sic veri Christifideles per vastitatem sæculi hujus tendunt ad patriam regni cœlestis. Stantque spiritualibus armis accincti contra hostes suæ salutis: de quibus se vindicant, dum tanto instantius serviunt Deo, quanto acrius ab illis tentantur ac impugnantur ut recedant ab eo. Sitiunt quoque esuriuntque justitiam, et invocant Deum Patrem: qui de petra altissima tribuit eis aquam, id est, de plenitudine gratiæ Christi eis propinat, ac meritis Salvatoris virtuteque suæ salutiferæ passionis spiritualiter reficit eos.
paras.en: In the mystical sense, as the children of Israel [[11:2|went through wildernesses|iter fecerunt per deserta]] that were not inhabited, so the true faithful of Christ make their way through the waste of this world to the fatherland of the heavenly kingdom. And they stand girt with spiritual arms against the enemies of their salvation: and they revenge themselves of them while they serve God the more earnestly, the more fiercely they are tempted and assailed by them to make them draw back from him. They thirst also and hunger after justice[[Matt 5:6||]], and call upon God the Father, who gives them water [[11:4|out of the high rock|de petra altissima]]: that is, he gives them to drink of the fullness of the grace of Christ, and refreshes them spiritually by the merits of the Saviour and the power of his saving passion.

paras.t: Quemadmodum etiam reprobi, perfidi, hæretici, schismatici, atque in vitiis obstinati, moriuntur in præsenti morte peccati, deinde morte infernalis supplicii, ex spiritualis inopia defectuque poculi, de quo loquitur Filius Dei, Qui sitit, veniat ad me, et bibat; sic electi et veri Christiani misericordiam consequuntur finalem, et aqua sapientiæ, poculo consolationis internæ, rore illustrationis supernæ potantur. Quibus clamat Salvator: Venite ad me, omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos. Porro iniquis et reprobis dat pro fonte sempiterni fluminis, id est pro communicatione et infusione donorum gratiæ et gloriæ Unigeniti Dei (de quo in Psalmo: Inebriabuntur ab ubertate domus tuæ, et torrente voluptatis tuæ potabis eos; quoniam apud te est fons vitæ), humanum sanguinem bibere, id est sanguinolentis ac turpibus operibus delectari, et persecutione justorum gaudere; aut trucidare se invicem, ita quod sanguis sanguinem tangit, ut in Osee habetur.
paras.en: And as the reprobate, the faithless, heretics, schismatics and those hardened in vice die now the death of sin, and afterwards the death of the punishment of hell, through the want and failing of the spiritual drink of which the Son of God speaks, [[John 7:37|If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink|Qui sitit, veniat ad me, et bibat]]; so the elect and true Christians obtain final mercy, and are given to drink the water of wisdom, the cup of inward consolation, the dew of heavenly enlightenment. To them the Saviour cries: [[Matt 11:28|Come to me all you that labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you|Venite ad me, omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos]]. But to the wicked and reprobate he gives, [[11:7|instead of a fountain of an ever running river|pro fonte sempiterni fluminis]], that is, instead of the sharing and pouring in of the gifts of grace and glory of the Only-begotten of God (of whom it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 35:9|They shall be inebriated with the plenty of thy house; and thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure|Inebriabuntur ab ubertate domus tuæ, et torrente voluptatis tuæ potabis eos]]; [[Ps 35:10|For with thee is the fountain of life|quoniam apud te est fons vitæ]]), [[11:7|human blood|humanum sanguinem]] to drink: that is, to delight in bloody and shameful works, and to rejoice in the persecution of the just; or to slaughter one another, so that [[Osee 4:2|blood hath touched blood|sanguis sanguinem tangit]], as we have it in Osee.

paras.t: Postremo, sicut Ægyptii sunt puniti per parva et vilia animalia, qualia coluerunt; sic indurati Judæi, pagani, hæretici, schismatici, qui fabularum suarum et vanitatum atque errorum colunt figmenta magis, quam Deum atque catholicam veritatem, infernalibus traduntur bestiis devorandi, et exterminat eos multitudo vilissimorum spirituum immundorum.
paras.en: Lastly, as the Egyptians were punished by small and vile animals such as they worshipped, so hardened Jews, pagans, heretics and schismatics, who worship the inventions of their fables, vanities and errors rather than God and the Catholic truth, are handed over to the beasts of hell to be devoured, and a multitude of the vilest unclean spirits destroys them.

12.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI DUODECIMI : O QUAM BONUS ET SUAVIS EST, DOMINE, SPIRITUS TUUS !
12.title_en: Exposition of the twelfth chapter: O how good and sweet is thy spirit, O Lord

paras.t: RECITANTUR hic beneficia filiis Israel præstita tempore ingressionis in terram promissionis sub Josue. O quam bonus et suavis est, Domine, spiritus tuus, scilicet Spiritus Sanctus, in omnibus! Ipse enim est substantialiter et incircumscriptibiliter bonus et dulcis in se, bonus quoque et dulcis in omnium gubernatione, et suorum charismatum communicatione. Hoc auctor admirative præmittit ex consideratione pietatis et gratiæ Dei circa Israeliticum populum.
paras.en: Here are recounted the benefits bestowed on the children of Israel at the time of their entry into the land of promise under Josue. [[12:1|O how good and sweet is thy Spirit, O Lord|O quam bonus et suavis est, Domine, spiritus tuus]], namely the Holy Ghost, [[12:1|in all things|in omnibus]]! For he is substantially and uncircumscribably good and sweet in himself, and good and sweet also in the governing of all things and in the imparting of his gifts [Latin *charismata*, the gifts of grace]. This the author sets first, in wonder, from considering the mercy and grace of God toward the people of Israel.

paras.t: Ideoque hos qui exerrant, id est, a via veritatis et salutis ac gratiæ deviant, partibus corripis, id est, particulariter et segregatim castigas et punis, quatenus unus emendetur exemplo alterius, atque pœniteat: et quamvis interdum plures simul corripiantur, raro tamen aut nunquam iniquorum collectio, universæve gentes et nationes iniquæ. Et de quibus peccant admonens alloqueris: id est, per instinctum divinum et angelicum, per flagella et beneficia, per miracula et doctrinas, exhortaris iniquos de his in quibus peccant: ut scilicet cessent peccare, nec abutantur rebus creatis. Ideo subditur: ut relicta malitia infidelitatis, idololatriæ, ac habitus vitiosi, credant in te, Domine, per fidem formatam.
paras.en: [[12:2|And therefore|Ideoque]] [[12:2|them that err|hos qui exerrant]], that is, those who stray from the way of truth, of salvation and of grace, [[12:2|thou chastisest|corripis]] [[12:2|by little and little|partibus]] [Latin *partibus*, "by parts"], that is, thou correctest and punishest them one part at a time and separately, so that one may be amended by the example of another, and repent: and though several are sometimes chastised together, yet rarely or never the whole company of the wicked, or whole wicked peoples and nations; [[12:2|and admonishest them, and speakest to them|admonens alloqueris]], [[12:2|concerning the things wherein they offend|Et de quibus peccant]] [Denis reads *admonens alloqueris*, "admonishing, thou speakest to them"]: that is, by divine and angelic prompting, by scourges and benefits, by miracles and teachings, thou exhortest the wicked concerning the things in which they sin: namely, that they may cease to sin, and not misuse created things. Therefore it is added: [[12:2|that leaving their wickedness|ut relicta malitia]] of unbelief, of idolatry and of vicious habit, [[12:2|they may believe in thee, O Lord|credant in te, Domine]], by formed faith [that is, faith given its form by charity].

paras.t: Illos enim antiquos inhabitatores terræ tuæ sanctæ, videlicet septem, vel potius decem gentes Chananæorum, habitantes olim in terra promissionis: quæ sancta vocatur, quia in ea tempore veteris Testamenti viguit cultus Dei; et in fine veteris legis, inchoante novi temporis Testamenti, completa sunt ibi mysteria Christi, et primitiva Ecclesia conversata est ibi sanctissime. Quos exhorruisti, non ob id quod erant, sed quod fecerant, sicut subjungitur: quoniam odibilia tibi opera, id est peccata gravissima, faciebant per medicamina, id est sortilegia atque auguria, per quæ sibi quærebant mederi, et sacrificia injusta idolis immolata, imo dæmonibus, dicente Apostolo: Quæ immolant gentes, dæmoniis immolant.
paras.en: [[12:3|For those ancient inhabitants of thy holy land|Illos enim antiquos inhabitatores terræ tuæ sanctæ]], namely the seven, or rather ten, nations of the Chanaanites who once dwelt in the land of promise: which is called holy because in it, in the time of the Old Testament, the worship of God flourished; and at the end of the old law, as the time of the New Testament began, the mysteries of Christ were accomplished there, and the primitive Church lived there most holily; [[12:3|whom thou didst abhor|Quos exhorruisti]], not for what they were, but for what they had done, as is added: [[12:4|Because they did works hateful to thee|quoniam odibilia tibi opera]], that is, most grievous sins, [[12:4|by their sorceries|per medicamina]], that is, by sorceries and auguries, by which they sought to heal themselves [*medicamina* means "remedies", hence "to heal"], [[12:4|and wicked sacrifices|et sacrificia injusta]] offered to idols, nay rather to devils, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 10:20|the things which the heathens sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils|Quæ immolant gentes, dæmoniis immolant]].

paras.t: Et filiorum suorum necatores sine misericordia: quia propriam sobolem offerebant in holocaustum idolis suis, juxta illud in Psalmo: Et effuderunt sanguinem innocentem, sanguinem filiorum suorum et filiarum suarum, quas sacrificaverunt dæmoniis; et comestores viscerum hominum: quia de carnibus sacrificatis aliquid comedebant, ut aliqui dicunt, juxta illud in Psalmo: Comederunt sacrificia mortuorum. Aliqui vero opinantur oppositum, asserentes quod iste sit metaphoricus sermo: quemadmodum de oppressore et cupido officiato communiter dicitur, quod hominum sit comestor. Secundum quod Dominus loquitur per Prophetam: Qui comedunt carnem populi mei; et in Psalmo, Dum appropiant super me nocentes, ut edant carnes meas. Et alibi dicitur per Job: Quare persequimini me sicut Deus, et carnibus meis saturamini? Et devoratores sanguinis: quia ex sanguine pecorum immolato sumpserunt in usum suum; et auctores parentes, id est generativa principia, animarum inauxiliatarum, id est sobolis suæ auxilio parentum propriorum destitutæ. Nam contra legem naturalem ac divinam, occidebant et diis suis offerebant propriam prolem, quam potius a morte debebant defendere.
paras.en: [[12:5|And those merciless murderers of their own children|Et filiorum suorum necatores sine misericordia]]: because they offered their own offspring as a holocaust to their idols, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 105:38|And they shed innocent blood: the blood of their sons and of their daughters which they sacrificed|Et effuderunt sanguinem innocentem, sanguinem filiorum suorum et filiarum suarum, quas sacrificaverunt]] [[Ps 105:37|to devils|dæmoniis]]; [[12:5|and eaters of men's bowels|et comestores viscerum hominum]]: because they ate something of the flesh offered in sacrifice, as some say, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 105:28|ate the sacrifices of the dead|Comederunt sacrificia mortuorum]]. Others, however, hold the opposite, asserting that this is a metaphorical way of speaking: as it is commonly said of an oppressor, or of a greedy official, that he is an eater of men. In this sense the Lord speaks by the Prophet: [[Mich 3:3|Who have eaten the flesh of my people|Qui comedunt carnem populi mei]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 26:2|Whilst the wicked draw near against me, to eat my flesh|Dum appropiant super me nocentes, ut edant carnes meas]]. And elsewhere it is said by Job: [[Job 19:22|Why do you persecute me as God, and glut yourselves with my flesh?|Quare persequimini me sicut Deus, et carnibus meis saturamini?]] [[12:5|and devourers of blood|Et devoratores sanguinis]]: because they took of the blood of the cattle sacrificed for their own use; [[12:6|And those parents|et auctores parentes]] [Latin *auctores parentes*, "parents who were the authors"], that is, those who begot [[12:6|helpless souls|animarum inauxiliatarum]], that is, their offspring, left destitute of the help of their own parents. For against the natural and the divine law they killed their own children and offered them to their gods, whom they ought rather to have defended from death.

paras.t: Perdere, id est occidere et auferre, voluisti a medio sacramento tuo, id est a Terra sancta in medio terræ habitabilis situata, in qua sacra implesti mysteria, per manus parentum nostrorum, scilicet duodecim tribuum sub Josue, sicut in libro ejus describitur.
paras.en: [[12:6|it was thy will|voluisti]] [[12:6|to destroy|Perdere]], that is, to kill and to take away, [[12:5|from the midst of thy consecration|a medio sacramento tuo]] [in the Vulgate these words end v. 5; Denis reads them with "it was thy will to destroy"], that is, from the Holy Land, situated in the middle of the habitable earth, in which thou didst accomplish the sacred mysteries, [[12:6|by the hands of our parents|per manus parentum nostrorum]], namely of the twelve tribes under Josue, as is described in his book[[Jos 12:1||]].

paras.t: ut dignam perciperent peregrinationem puerorum Dei, id est, merito acciperent Terram sanctam in hereditatem: in qua pueri Dei, Abraham, Isaac et Jacob, fuerunt peregrinati, secundum illud: Dedit illam Jacob puero suo, et Israel dilecto sibi. Quæ tibi omnium carior est terra: id est, pro tempore illo magis erat electa, ut in ea verus Deus coleretur, et Christi mysteria complerentur, ac primitiva conversaretur Ecclesia.
paras.en: That they [[12:7|might receive a worthy colony of the children of God|ut dignam perciperent peregrinationem puerorum Dei]] [Latin *peregrinationem*, "a sojourning", where the Douay-Rheims has "colony"], that is, that they might deservedly receive the Holy Land as an inheritance: the land in which the children of God, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, sojourned as pilgrims[[Gen 12:5||]][[Gen 26:1||]][[Gen 26:23||]][[Gen 33:18||]], according to that: [[Bar 3:37|gave it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved|Dedit illam Jacob puero suo, et Israel dilecto sibi]] [*puer* means both "child" and "servant"; in Baruch "it" is the way of knowledge]. [[12:7|the land which of all is most dear to thee|Quæ tibi omnium carior est terra]]: that is, for that time it was the more chosen, that in it the true God might be worshipped, the mysteries of Christ accomplished, and the primitive Church live.

paras.t: Sed et his tanquam hominibus pepercisti, id est, Chananæis tribuisti pœnitentiæ locum: et quidam eorum fuerunt conversi, ut Gabaonitæ, et aliarum trium urbium habitatores, ut in libro Josue habetur. Et misisti antecessores exercitus tui vespas, id est animalia parva sic dicta, quæ (ut aliqui scribunt) præcesserunt populum Israel, qui vocatur hic exercitus Dei: quæ venenatis suis aculeis multos occiderunt Chananæorum, ut subditur, ut illos paulatim exterminarent. Alii per vespas intelligunt acerrimos timores, atque angustias Chananæorum, formidantium Israelitarum adventum, prout in libro Josue habetur: Irruit in nos terror vester, et elanguerunt omnes habitatores terræ. Unde ex vehementi timore Hevæi dicuntur fugisse a terra illa ante Hebræorum ingressum.
paras.en: [[12:8|Yet even those thou sparedst as men|Sed et his tanquam hominibus pepercisti]], that is, to the Chanaanites thou gavest place of repentance: and some of them were converted, as the Gabaonites and the inhabitants of three other cities, as is related in the book of Josue[[Jos 9:1||]]; [[12:8|and didst send wasps forerunners of thy host|Et misisti antecessores exercitus tui vespas]], that is, the small animals so called, which (as some write) went before the people of Israel, who are here called the host of God: and with their poisoned stings these killed many of the Chanaanites, as is added, [[12:8|to destroy them by little and little|ut illos paulatim exterminarent]]. Others understand by the wasps the sharpest fears and anguish of the Chanaanites, who dreaded the coming of the Israelites, as is related in the book of Josue: [[Jos 2:9|the dread of you is fallen upon us, and all the inhabitants of the land have lost all strength|Irruit in nos terror vester, et elanguerunt omnes habitatores terræ]]. Hence the Hevites are said to have fled from that land out of vehement fear before the Hebrews entered it.

paras.t: Non quia impotens eras in bello subjicere impios justis: id est, non ideo præmisisti sic vespas, quod non potueris per filios Israel aut ministerio angelico subdere Chananæos illos Hebræis, aut bestiis sævis, id est ferocibus, aut verbo duro simul exterminare illos iniquos.
paras.en: [[12:9|Not that thou wast unable to bring the wicked under the just by war|Non quia impotens eras in bello subjicere impios justis]]: that is, thou didst not send the wasps ahead in this way because thou couldst not subdue those Chanaanites to the Hebrews by the children of Israel or by the ministry of angels, [[12:9|or by cruel beasts|aut bestiis sævis]], that is, fierce ones, [[12:9|or with one rough word to destroy them at once|aut verbo duro simul exterminare]], those wicked men.

paras.t: Sed partibus judicans, id est paulatim et per partes illos ejiciens et occidens, dabas pœnitentiæ locum residuis, ut dictum est. Ideo quoque non simul exterminavit illos, ne terra illa tam magna, pro grandi parte redigeretur in solitudinem, et sic bestiæ multiplicarentur in ea contra Israelitas: quoniam filii Israel non poterant totam terram illam sufficienter populare tam cito, ut in Deuteronomio legitur. Non ignorans quoniam iniqua est natio eorum, puta Chananæorum, id est a juventute et pueritia vitiis assueta, et naturalis malitia ipsorum, id est in consuetudinem ducta, quæ est altera natura, et quia ex dispositione suæ complexionis erant multum proni ad vitia. Verumtamen, sicut peccatum est contra rationem, quæ deprecatur et inclinat ad optima; sic est contra naturam bene institutam seu integram, non corruptam, et innaturale. Propter quod Tullius virtutem definiens: Virtus, inquit, est habitus naturæ rationique consentaneus. Et quoniam non poterat mutari cogitatio cordis illorum prava ad bonum, in perpetuum: id est, valde difficulter poterant flecti et emendari, utpote obstinati: non tamen simpliciter inconvertibiles erant, utpote liberum habentes arbitrium, nondum determinate fixum ad unum.
paras.en: [[12:10|But executing thy judgments by degrees|Sed partibus judicans]], that is, casting them out and killing them little by little and part by part, [[12:10|thou gavest them place of repentance|dabas pœnitentiæ locum]]: to those that remained, as has been said. For this reason too he did not destroy them all at once, lest that land, being so great, should for the most part be reduced to a wilderness, and so the beasts should multiply in it against the Israelites: since the children of Israel could not people that whole land sufficiently so quickly, as is read in Deuteronomy[[Deut 7:22||]]; [[12:10|not being ignorant that they were a wicked generation|Non ignorans quoniam iniqua est natio eorum]], namely the Chanaanites, that is, used to vices from youth and childhood, [[12:10|and their malice natural|et naturalis malitia ipsorum]], that is, turned into custom, which is a second nature, and also because by the disposition of their complexion [that is, their bodily temperament] they were much inclined to vices. Nevertheless, as sin is against reason, which pleads for the best things and inclines to them, so it is against nature well constituted, that is, whole and not corrupted, and is unnatural. For which reason Tully, defining virtue, says: Virtue is a habit in harmony with nature and reason [Cicero, *De inventione* II, 53]. [[12:10|and that their thought could never be changed|Et quoniam non poterat mutari cogitatio cordis illorum prava ad bonum, in perpetuum]] [Denis's text reads "and because the depraved thought of their heart could never be changed to good"]: that is, they could be bent and amended only with great difficulty, being obstinate; yet they were not simply inconvertible, since they had free will, not yet determinately fixed on one thing.

paras.t: Semen enim erat maledictum ab initio secundæ ætatis mundi. Nam mox post diluvium, quum Cham filius Noe ostendisset fratribus suis patris sui virilia, locutus est Noe: Maledictus Chanaan, servus servorum erit fratribus suis. Verumtamen maledictio illa Chanaan filii Cham, et Chananæorum natorum ex Chanaan, non fuit nisi addictio ad quædam temporalia mala pœnalia: quoniam filii pro parentum peccatis non maledicuntur quantum ad animam, per spiritualium subtractionem bonorum, ut plenius dixi super Genesim, et super Jeremiam, ac alibi sæpe. Verumtamen ex illa maledictione poterant posteri proniores esse ad vitia, ægre ferentes servituti se esse subjectos. Vel sensus est, quod in præscientia Dei erant maledicti, id est præsciti ac reprobi. Nihilo minus bonus et pius Deus fecit pro illorum conversione, quod erat in se; et quia tam difficulter convertibiles erant, paulatim ac diu admonuit eos.
paras.en: [[12:11|For it was a cursed seed from the beginning|Semen enim erat maledictum ab initio]] of the second age of the world. For soon after the flood, when Cham the son of Noe had shown his father's nakedness to his brothers[[Gen 9:22||]], Noe spoke: [[Gen 9:25|Cursed be Chanaan, a servant of servants shall he be unto his brethren|Maledictus Chanaan, servus servorum erit fratribus suis]]. Yet that curse on Chanaan the son of Cham, and on the Chanaanites born of Chanaan, was nothing but a sentence to certain temporal penal evils: since children are not cursed for their parents' sins as regards the soul, by the withdrawal of spiritual goods, as I have said more fully on Genesis and on Jeremias, and often elsewhere. Yet because of that curse their posterity could be more prone to vices, bearing it ill that they were made subject to servitude. Or the sense is that they were cursed in the foreknowledge of God, that is, foreknown and reprobate [that is, foreseen by God as not to be saved]. Nonetheless the good and merciful God did for their conversion what was in him to do; and because they were so hard to convert, he admonished them little by little and for a long time.

paras.t: Nec timens aliquem, veniam dabas peccatis illorum: id est, non distulisti punitionem Chananæorum, nec pepercisti quibusdam eorum ex timore alicujus superioris aut potentioris, quum tu sis universis ac singulis infinite potentior incomparabiliterque sublimior, nec appellari potest a tuo judicio.
paras.en: [[12:11|neither didst thou for fear of any one give pardon to their sins|Nec timens aliquem, veniam dabas peccatis illorum]]: that is, thou didst not put off the punishment of the Chanaanites, nor spare some of them, out of fear of anyone higher or more powerful, since thou art infinitely more powerful than all and each, and incomparably more exalted, nor can any appeal be made from thy judgment.

paras.t: Quis enim dicet tibi, Quid fecisti? id est, nullus te reprehendere potest: juxta illud ad Romanos: O homo, tu quis es, qui respondeas Deo? Numquid dicit figmentum ei qui se finxit, Quid me fecisti sic? Hoc, inquam, nemo potest dicere de jure, quamvis de facto quis irrationabiliter dicat. Aut quis stabit contra judicium tuum ad resistendum efficaciter ei? secundum illud Isaiæ: Væ qui contradicit factori suo. Numquid dicit lutum figulo suo, Quid facis? Aut quis in conspectu tuo veniet vindex iniquorum hominum? id est, nullus poterit ante te comparere ad vindicandum in te punitionem aut condemnationem iniquorum, quos pœnis adjudicas: quia in ditione tua cuncta sunt posita, et non est qui tuæ possit resistere voluntati, aut tuum reprobare judicium. Ideo in Job fertur: Si fortitudo quæritur, robustissimus est; si æquitas judicii, nemo audet pro me testimonium dicere. Unde rursus sanctus Job fassus est: Vere scio, quod non justificetur homo compositus Deo; si voluerit contendere cum eo, non poterit ei respondere unum pro mille.
paras.en: [[12:12|For who shall say to thee: What hast thou done?|Quis enim dicet tibi, Quid fecisti?]] that is, no one can reproach thee: according to that to the Romans: [[Rom 9:20|O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it: Why hast thou made me thus?|O homo, tu quis es, qui respondeas Deo? Numquid dicit figmentum ei qui se finxit, Quid me fecisti sic?]] This, I say, no one can say by right, though in fact someone may unreasonably say it. [[12:12|or who shall withstand thy judgment|Aut quis stabit contra judicium tuum]], so as to resist it effectually? according to that of Isaias: [[Is 45:9|Woe to him that gainsayeth his maker|Væ qui contradicit factori suo]]. [[Is 45:9|shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it: What art thou making|Numquid dicit lutum figulo suo, Quid facis?]]? [[12:12|or who shall come before thee to be a revenger of wicked men?|Aut quis in conspectu tuo veniet vindex iniquorum hominum?]] that is, no one will be able to appear before thee to take vengeance on thee for the punishment or condemnation of the wicked whom thou sentencest to punishments: because [[Esth 13:9|all things are in thy power, and there is none that can resist thy will|in ditione tua cuncta sunt posita, et non est qui tuæ possit resistere voluntati]], or to reject thy judgment. Therefore it is said in Job: [[Job 9:19|If strength be demanded, he is most strong: if equity of judgment, no man dare bear witness for me.|Si fortitudo quæritur, robustissimus est; si æquitas judicii, nemo audet pro me testimonium dicere]] Hence holy Job again confessed: [[Job 9:2|Indeed I know|Vere scio]] [[Job 9:2|that man cannot be justified, compared with God|quod non justificetur homo compositus Deo]]; [[Job 9:3|If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him one for a thousand.|si voluerit contendere cum eo, non poterit ei respondere unum pro mille]]

paras.t: Aut quis tibi imputabit, si perierint nationes quas tu fecisti? id est, nullus valet tibi juste imputare pereuntium peccata ac tormenta: quoniam quantum in te est, nullum perire permittis; imo per instinctus divinos atque angelicos ac aliis variis modis ad salutem hortaris. Qui per Ezechielem locutus es: Numquid voluntatis meæ est mors impii, et non ut convertatur a viis suis, et vivat? Verumtamen quidam omnino perversi, conantur in Deum retorquere pereuntium culpam. De quibus ait Psalmista: Quoniam declinaverunt in te mala. Contra quos ad Romanos disputat Paulus.
paras.en: [[12:12|or who shall accuse thee, if the nations perish, which thou hast made?|Aut quis tibi imputabit, si perierint nationes quas tu fecisti?]] [Latin *imputabit*, "shall impute it to thee", where the Douay-Rheims has "accuse"]: that is, no one can justly impute to thee the sins and torments of those who perish: since, as far as in thee lies, thou lettest none perish; nay, by divine and angelic promptings and in various other ways thou exhortest them to salvation. Thou who hast spoken by Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:23|Is it my will that a sinner should die|Numquid voluntatis meæ est mors impii]], [[Ezech 18:23|and not that he should be converted from his ways, and live?|et non ut convertatur a viis suis, et vivat?]] Yet some utterly perverse men try to turn the blame of those who perish back upon God. Of whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 20:12|For they have intended evils against thee|Quoniam declinaverunt in te mala]] [Latin "they have turned evils aside upon thee"]. Against these Paul disputes in the Epistle to the Romans[[Rom 9:14||]].

paras.t: Nec enim est alius Deus quam tu: ideo superiorem non habes, neque æqualem a te diversum; cui cura est de omnibus, id est, universorum providentiam habes, specialiter tamen intellectualium creaturarum, potissime electarum. Propter quod dixit Apostolus: Numquid de bobus cura est Deo? Divinæ autem providentiæ dispositio aut præcognitio, ad universa et singula distincte ac plenarie se extendit, sicut cognitionis requirit perfectio; exsequitur autem providentiam suam in multis per causas secundas. Ideo ait Salvator: Nonne quinque passeres venundantur dipondio, et unus ex illis non est in oblivione coram Deo? Vestri autem et capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt. Ut ostendas quoniam non injuste judicas, id est, judicialiter seu sententialiter profers, judicium.
paras.en: [[12:13|For there is no other God but thou|Nec enim est alius Deus quam tu]]: therefore thou hast no superior, nor any equal distinct from thee; [[12:13|who hast care of all|cui cura est de omnibus]], that is, thou hast providence over all things, yet especially over intellectual creatures, and most of all over the elect. For which reason the Apostle said: [[1 Cor 9:9|Doth God take care for oxen?|Numquid de bobus cura est Deo?]] Yet the disposition or foreknowledge of divine providence extends to all things and to each, distinctly and fully, as the perfection of knowledge requires; but he carries out his providence in many things through secondary causes. Therefore the Saviour says: [[Luke 12:6|Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings, and not one of them is forgotten before God?|Nonne quinque passeres venundantur dipondio, et unus ex illis non est in oblivione coram Deo?]] [[Luke 12:7|Yea, the very hairs of your head are all numbered|Vestri autem et capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt]]. [[12:13|that thou shouldst shew that thou dost not give judgment unjustly|Ut ostendas quoniam non injuste judicas]], that is, that thou dost not unjustly pronounce, judicially or by sentence, [[12:13|judgment|judicium]].

paras.t: Neque rex, qui in suo officio sequitur rationem, sapientiam et virtutes, neque tyrannus, qui utitur voluntate pro ratione, et impetum sequitur passionum, in conspectu tuo inquirent de his quos perdidisti, id est, discutere poterunt, aut conqueri valebunt, cur impios perire permisisti, aut condemnasti. Hinc Dominus in Job loquitur: Numquid condemnabis me, ut tu justificeris?
paras.en: [[12:14|Neither shall king|Neque rex]], who in his office follows reason, wisdom and the virtues, [[12:14|nor tyrant|neque tyrannus]], who uses his will in place of reason and follows the impulse of the passions, [[12:14|in thy sight inquire about them whom thou hast destroyed|in conspectu tuo inquirent de his quos perdidisti]], that is, shall be able to call it in question, or have grounds to complain, why thou hast let the impious perish, or hast condemned them. Hence the Lord speaks in Job: Wilt thou [[Job 40:3|condemn me, that thou mayst be justified|condemnabis me, ut tu justificeris]]? [the margin gives Job xi, 3; the words are Job 40:3]

paras.t: Quum ergo sis justus, juste omnia disponis, dando unicuique quod meretur. Nec obstat quod multa pie disponit, et quod universæ viæ ejus misericordia et veritas; quoniam ipse tam bonus est, ut justum sit eum quædam clementer ac pie disponere. Imo miserationes ejus super omnia opera ejus. Unde et Jacobus ait: Superexaltat autem misericordia judicium. Ideo, quum Deus dicitur omnia juste disponere, intelligendum est quod universa decenter, et sicut dictat sapientia ejus, disponit. Sicque cantatur in Psalmo: Justus Dominus in omnibus viis suis. Sed et quantum ad finalem retributionem, omnia juste disponit, et injustitiam culpæ per æquitatem supplicii recompensat atque instaurat.
paras.en: [[12:15|For so much then, as thou art just, thou orderest all things justly|Quum ergo sis justus, juste omnia disponis]], giving to each what he deserves. Nor does it stand in the way that he disposes many things mercifully, and that [[Ps 24:10|All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth|universæ viæ ejus misericordia et veritas]]; for he is so good that it is just for him to dispose some things clemently and mercifully. Nay, [[Ps 144:9|his tender mercies are over all his works|miserationes ejus super omnia opera ejus]] [the margin gives Ps. cxlv, 9; the verse is Ps 144:9]. Hence James too says: [[Jas 2:13|And mercy exalteth itself above judgment|Superexaltat autem misericordia judicium]]. Therefore, when God is said to dispose all things justly, it is to be understood that he disposes all things fittingly, and as his wisdom dictates. And so it is sung in the Psalm: [[Ps 144:17|The Lord is just in all his ways|Justus Dominus in omnibus viis suis]] [the margin gives Ps. cxlv, 17]. But also as regards the final retribution he disposes all things justly, and by the equity of the punishment recompenses and makes good the injustice of the fault.

paras.t: Ipsum quoque qui non debet puniri, id est innocentem ac justum, condemnas, id est, temporalibus pœnis quandoque adjudicas, ad majus meritum suum, et ad aliorum ædificationem, et ad patientiæ suæ exercitationem, probationem, et coronationem: ut Job, Tobiam, et Paulum. Unde sanctus Job: Multiplicabit (inquit) vulnera mea, etiam sine causa, id est sine culpa mea. Et exterum æstimas a tua virtute, id est, permittis reputari extraneum a tua protectione: quia secundum exteriorem apparentiam, ita te habes ad eum, quasi non pertineat ad te. Unde amici Job et Tobiæ insultaverunt eis tanquam hypocritis et a Deo relictis. Propter quod Job dixit: Deridetur justi simplicitas; et rursus, Nunc in eorum canticum versus sum; itemque, Fratres mei elongaverunt a me, et noti mei quasi alieni recesserunt a me. Denique istud in Christo maxime patet: qui quæ non rapuit, exsolvit; quem propter scelus populi sui Pater percussit in tantum, quod reputatus fuit tanquam leprosus, et percussus a Deo, et humiliatus.
paras.en: Him also [[12:15|who deserveth not to be punished|qui non debet puniri]], that is, the innocent and just man, thou dost [[12:15|condemn|condemnas]], that is, thou sometimes sentencest him to temporal punishments, for his greater merit, for the edification of others, and for the exercise, proof and crowning of his patience: as with Job, Tobias[[Tob 2:12||]] and Paul[[2 Cor 11:23||]][[2 Cor 12:7||]]. Whence holy Job: He shall [[Job 9:17|multiply|Multiplicabit]] (he says) [[Job 9:17|my wounds even without cause|vulnera mea, etiam sine causa]], that is, without fault of mine. And [[12:15|thinking it not agreeable to the power|Et exterum æstimas a tua virtute]] [Denis reads *exterum æstimas a tua virtute*, "thou accountest him a stranger to thy power", and takes the whole verse of the just man whom God lets suffer; the Douay-Rheims follows another sense: "thinking it not agreeable to the power to condemn him who deserveth not to be punished"], that is, thou permittest him to be reckoned a stranger to thy protection: because, to outward appearance, thou dost behave toward him as if he did not belong to thee. Hence the friends of Job and of Tobias insulted them as hypocrites and as men forsaken by God. For which reason Job said: [[Job 12:4|the simplicity of the just man is laughed to scorn|Deridetur justi simplicitas]]; and again, [[Job 30:9|Now I am turned into their song|Nunc in eorum canticum versus sum]]; and likewise, [[Job 19:13|He hath put my brethren far from me, and my acquaintance like strangers have departed from me.|Fratres mei elongaverunt a me, et noti mei quasi alieni recesserunt a me]] [Denis reads "my brethren have gone far from me"]. Lastly, this is most evident in Christ, who paid back what he did not take away[[Ps 68:5||]]; whom the Father struck for the wickedness of his people[[Is 53:8||]] so far that he was reckoned [[Is 53:4|as it were a leper, and as one struck by God and afflicted|tanquam leprosus, et percussus a Deo, et humiliatus]].

paras.t: Virtus enim tua, justitiæ initium est: id est, tu ipse, seu sanctitas aut omnipotentia tua, est causa, regula, et mensura omnis justitiæ ac virtutis. Ideo eo ipso quod tu judicas aliquid esse justum, sequitur quod sit justum. Et quidquid agis, eo ipso quod illud a te, qui essentialiter bonus et sanctus es, agitur, bonum et irreprehensibile est. Ideo loquitur Isaias: Cum quo iniit consilium, et instruxit eum, et docuit eum semitam justitiæ, et erudivit eum scientia, et viam prudentiæ ostendit illi? Ideo ait: An non licet mihi quod volo facere? Et ob hoc quod omnium Dominus es auctoritate creationis, judiciaria potestate, et omnipotenti imperio. Non tamen omnium Dominus est per debitam inferiorum subjectionem atque obsequium. Propter quod in Evangelio loquitur: Quid dicitis mihi, Domine, Domine, et non facitis quæ dico? Etiam dicitur per Prophetam: Si Dominus ego sum, ubi est timor meus? Omnibus te parcere facis, id est, propria voluntate ac pietate cunctis te exhibes pium. Nam et reprobos in præsenti a multis retrahis vitiis instinctu divino et per angelorum custodiam, multa quoque beneficia tribuis impiis et ingratis; damnatos etiam minus quam meruerunt, affligis. Ideo asserit Christus: Altissimus, benignus et misericors est super ingratos et malos.
paras.en: [[12:16|For thy power is the beginning of justice|Virtus enim tua, justitiæ initium est]] [Latin *virtus*, both "power" and "virtue"]: that is, thou thyself, or thy holiness or omnipotence, art the cause, rule and measure of all justice and virtue. Therefore, by the very fact that thou judgest a thing to be just, it follows that it is just. And whatever thou doest is good and blameless by the very fact that it is done by thee, who art essentially good and holy. Therefore Isaias says: [[Is 40:14|With whom hath he consulted, and who hath instructed him, and taught him the path of justice, and taught him knowledge, and shewed him the way of understanding?|Cum quo iniit consilium, et instruxit eum, et docuit eum semitam justitiæ, et erudivit eum scientia, et viam prudentiæ ostendit illi?]] Therefore he says [in the Gospel parable]: [[Matt 20:15|is it not lawful for me to do what I will?|An non licet mihi quod volo facere?]] [[12:16|and because thou art Lord of all|Et ob hoc quod omnium Dominus es]] by the authority of creation, by judicial power and by almighty command.
