Yet he is not Lord of all by the due subjection and service of those beneath him. For which reason he says in the Gospel: [[Luke 6:46|why call you me, Lord, Lord; and do not the things which I say?|Quid dicitis mihi, Domine, Domine, et non facitis quæ dico?]] It is also said by the Prophet: [[Mal 1:6|if I be a master, where is my fear|Si Dominus ego sum, ubi est timor meus]]? [Latin *Dominus*, "Lord", where the Douay-Rheims has "master"] [[12:16|thou makest thyself gracious to all|Omnibus te parcere facis]] [Latin "thou makest thyself spare all"], that is, of thine own will and kindness thou showest thyself merciful to all. For even the reprobate thou drawest back in this present life from many vices, by divine prompting and by the guardianship of angels; many benefits too thou bestowest on the impious and ungrateful; and even the damned thou afflictest less than they deserved. Therefore Christ asserts: The Most High [[Luke 6:35|is kind to the unthankful and to the evil|benignus et misericors est super ingratos et malos]] [Denis reads "is kind and merciful", taking "merciful" from the next verse][[Luke 6:36||]].

paras.t: Virtutem enim ostendis, id est, omnipotentiam tuam variis modis declaras, in operibus naturæ ac gratiæ, in naturalibus et supernaturalibus, in actibus justitiæ et pietatis; tu qui non crederis in virtute esse consummatus, id est, quem perfidi quidam putant non esse omnipotentem, et in omni potestate perfectum. De quibus in libro Job fertur: Quasi nihil possit facere Omnipotens, ita æstimaverunt eum. Et hos qui te nesciunt esse, et in omni perfectione esse immensum, in audaciam traducis, id est, propter eorum stultam audaciam, qua se putant impune peccare, et audacter provocant Deum, ducis de culpis eorum ad debitas pœnas. Interdum tamen aliquos tales misericorditer traducit de tanta ignorantia ac perfidia, ad fidei veritatem ac gratiam. Traducit quoque et tales, dum justo judicio permittit eos de vitiis in vitia prolabi.
paras.en: [[12:17|For thou shewest thy power|Virtutem enim ostendis]], that is, thou declarest thy omnipotence in various ways: in the works of nature and of grace, in natural and supernatural things, in acts of justice and of mercy; [[12:17|when men will not believe thee to be absolute in power|tu qui non crederis in virtute esse consummatus]] [Latin "thou who art not believed to be perfect in power"], that is, thou whom certain faithless men think not to be almighty and perfect in all power. Of whom it is said in the book of Job: They [[Job 22:17|looked upon the Almighty as if he could do nothing|Quasi nihil possit facere Omnipotens, ita æstimaverunt eum]]. [[12:17|and thou convincest the boldness|in audaciam traducis]] [[12:17|of them that know thee not|Et hos qui te nesciunt]] to be, and to be immeasurable in all perfection [Denis reads "and them that know not that thou art … thou leadest over into boldness"; *traducis*, "thou leadest across", also means "thou exposest", whence the Douay-Rheims "convincest"], that is, on account of their foolish boldness, by which they think they sin with impunity and boldly provoke God, thou leadest them over from their faults to the punishments due to them. Yet at times he mercifully leads some such men over from so great ignorance and faithlessness to the truth of faith and to grace. He also leads such men over when by a just judgment he permits them to slip from vice into vice.

paras.t: Tu autem dominator virtutis, id est dominator virtuosus ac potens, vel, dominator, causa omnis creatæ virtutis, cum tranquillitate judicas, id est cum pace imperturbabili et summa quiete. Nam sine occupatione et inquietudine regit et judicat universa, quum sit potentiæ et sapientiæ penitus infinitæ. Verumtamen in Scripturis adscribuntur Deo quædam animi passiones, ut quod cum ira, furore, indignatioque judicet: quæ omnia intelligenda sunt tropice, quantum ad similitudinem operis, non quoad inquietudinem mentis. Propter quod ait per Jeremiam: Numquid me ad iracundiam provocant? nonne semetipsos in confusionem vultus sui? Et cum magna reverentia disponis nos, id est magnifice et præclare, prout tuam condecet majestatem. Vel etiam, Cum reverentia magna, quia multum honorificas homines, quod tam benigne eos gubernas, et eorum pœnitentiam præstolaris, ac jugiter eis offers gratiam et amicitiam tuam, sanctosque angelos ad eorum custodiam deputas. Ideo ait Psalmista: Minuisti eum paulo minus ab angelis. Subest enim tibi, quum volueris, posse: id est, potestas ad omnia tibi placentia peragenda, adest tibi juxta libitum tuum.
paras.en: [[12:18|But thou being master of power|Tu autem dominator virtutis]], that is, a ruler mighty and powerful, or, a ruler who is the cause of all created power, [[12:18|judgest with tranquillity|cum tranquillitate judicas]], that is, with imperturbable peace and the highest quiet. For he rules and judges all things without toil or disquiet, since he is of altogether infinite power and wisdom. Yet in the Scriptures certain passions of the soul are ascribed to God, as that he judges with wrath, fury and indignation[[Is 13:9||]]: all of which are to be understood figuratively, as to the likeness of the work, not as to any disquiet of mind. For which reason he says by Jeremias: [[Jer 7:19|Do they provoke me to anger|Numquid me ad iracundiam provocant]]? [[Jer 7:19|is it not themselves, to the confusion of their own countenance?|nonne semetipsos in confusionem vultus sui?]] [[12:18|and with great favour disposest of us|Et cum magna reverentia disponis nos]] [Latin *cum magna reverentia*, "with great reverence"], that is, magnificently and gloriously, as befits thy majesty. Or else, [[12:18|with great favour|Cum reverentia magna]], because thou greatly honourest men, in that thou governest them so kindly, and awaitest their repentance, and constantly offerest them thy grace and friendship, and appointest the holy angels to guard them. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 8:6|Thou hast made him a little less than the angels|Minuisti eum paulo minus ab angelis]]. [[12:18|for thy power is at hand when thou wilt|Subest enim tibi, quum volueris, posse]]: that is, the power to accomplish all things pleasing to thee is present to thee at thy good pleasure.

paras.t: Docuisti autem populum tuum per talia opera, id est per opera tuæ pietatis et æquitatis, quoniam oportet justum esse et humanum, id est, ut ipsi exemplo tui, sint justi simul et pii, justitiam et clementiam contemperando per discretionem. Unde in Evangelio ait Salvator: Estote misericordes, sicut et Pater vester cœlestis misericors est. Apostolus quoque: Estote, inquit, imitatores Dei sicut filii carissimi. Et istud ad præsidentes præcipue spectat; omnium tamen intellectualium creaturarum perfectio est, suo Creatori in virtutibus assimilari. Et bonæ spei fecisti filios tuos, id est, filiis Israel dedisti spem veniæ impetrandæ dum peccarent; qui judicans, das locum in peccatis pœnitentiæ, id est, tempus et facultatem pœnitendi das hominibus quando peccant, quia non statim eos condemnas, sed ad pœnitentiam exhortaris.
paras.en: [[12:19|But thou hast taught thy people by such works|Docuisti autem populum tuum per talia opera]], that is, by the works of thy mercy and equity, [[12:19|that they must be just and humane|quoniam oportet justum esse et humanum]], that is, that they themselves, after thy example, should be just and merciful at once, tempering justice and clemency together with discretion. Hence the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Luke 6:36|Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.|Estote misericordes, sicut et Pater vester cœlestis misericors est]] [Denis adds "heavenly": "as your heavenly Father also is merciful"]. The Apostle too: [[Eph 5:1|Be ye|Estote]], he says, [[Eph 5:1|followers of God, as most dear children|imitatores Dei sicut filii carissimi]]. And this concerns those who preside above all; yet it is the perfection of all intellectual creatures to be made like their Creator in the virtues. [[12:19|and hast made thy children to be of a good hope|Et bonæ spei fecisti filios tuos]], that is, thou gavest the children of Israel hope of obtaining pardon when they sinned; [[12:19|because in judging, thou givest place for repentance for sins|qui judicans, das locum in peccatis pœnitentiæ]], that is, thou givest men time and means of repenting when they sin, because thou dost not condemn them at once, but exhortest them to repentance.

paras.t: Si enim, id est quia, inimicos servorum tuorum, id est Ægyptios et Chananæos, adversarios filiorum Israel, et debitos morti, quia mortem temporalem ac infernalem promeruerunt, cum tanta cruciasti attentione, id est cum tam pio moderamine et consideratione fragilitatis humanæ, puniendo eos paulatim, et cum interpolatione, ut interim pœniterent, et liberasti eos a plagis inflictis, Moyse exorante, et pœnam differendo, ac aliquos convertendo, ut dictum est: nam et vulgus promiscuum Ægyptiacum innumerabile exivit cum filiis Israel de Ægypto; dans tempus et locum, per quæ possent mutari a malitia, vexatione eis intellectum præbente:
paras.en: [[12:20|For if|Si enim]], that is, since, [[12:20|the enemies of thy servants|inimicos servorum tuorum]], that is, the Egyptians and the Chanaanites, the adversaries of the children of Israel, [[12:20|and that deserved to die|et debitos morti]], because they had merited temporal and infernal death, thou didst punish them [[12:20|with so great deliberation|cum tanta cruciasti attentione]], that is, with such merciful restraint and such consideration of human frailty, punishing them little by little and with intervals, so that meanwhile they might repent, *and didst deliver* them [Denis's text adds *et liberasti*, "and didst deliver"] from the plagues inflicted on them, at the prayer of Moses[[Ex 8:12||]][[Ex 8:30||]][[Ex 9:33||]][[Ex 10:18||]], both by deferring the punishment and by converting some, as has been said: for a mixed Egyptian multitude without number went out of Egypt with the children of Israel[[Ex 12:38||]]; [[12:20|giving them time and place whereby they might be changed from their wickedness|dans tempus et locum, per quæ possent mutari a malitia]], vexation giving them understanding[[Is 28:19||]]:

paras.t: cum quanta diligentia judicasti filios tuos? id est, utique cum ampliori miseratione disposuisti filios Israel, et peccantes paternaliter corripuisti, et castigasti pro eorum salute, quorum parentibus, scilicet Abrahæ, Isaac, et Jacob, juramenta et conventiones dedisti bonarum promissionum, id est, cum juramento eis promisisti, dare eorum posteritati terram promissionis: imo et bona gratiæ ac gloriæ promisisti eisdem, sicut in Missa cantatur: Michael repræsentet animas in lucem sanctam, quam olim Abrahæ promisisti et semini ejus. Nam Abrahæ dixit: Merces tua magna nimis. Dedit quoque Patriarchis illis conventiones harum promissionum, quia multa præcepit eis, cum hujus conditionis adjectione, quod si facerent ea, daret eis hujusmodi bona.
paras.en: [[12:21|With what circumspection hast thou judged thy own children|cum quanta diligentia judicasti filios tuos?]]? that is, thou didst surely dispose the children of Israel with ampler mercy, and when they sinned didst rebuke them as a father, and chastise them for their salvation, [[12:21|to whose parents|quorum parentibus]], namely Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, [[12:21|thou hast sworn, and made covenants of good promises|juramenta et conventiones dedisti bonarum promissionum]] [Latin "thou gavest oaths and covenants of good promises"], that is, thou didst promise them with an oath to give their posterity the land of promise: nay, thou didst also promise them the goods of grace and of glory, as is sung in the Mass: May Michael bring the souls into the holy light, which thou didst promise of old to Abraham and to his seed [from the Offertory of the Mass for the Dead]. For to Abraham he said: [[Gen 15:1|thy reward exceeding great|Merces tua magna nimis]]. He also gave those Patriarchs covenants of these promises, because he commanded them many things[[Gen 17:9||]][[Gen 17:8||]][[Gen 26:2||]][[Gen 28:13||]], with this condition added, that if they did them, he would give them such goods.

paras.t: Quum ergo nobis disciplinam das, paternaliter castigando in vita hac, ne æternaliter pereamus: juxta illud, Quia quem diligit Dominus, corripit, et quasi pater in filio complacet sibi; inimicos nostros, scilicet infideles, multipliciter flagellas, eos in sua duritia relinquendo, et non solum temporaliter, sed æternaliter puniendo. Unde et Salomon ait: Si justus in terra recipit, quanto magis impius et peccator?
paras.en: [[12:22|Therefore whereas thou chastisest us|Quum ergo nobis disciplinam das]] [Latin "whereas thou givest us discipline"], chastising us as a father in this life, lest we perish eternally: according to that: [[Prov 3:12|For whom the Lord loveth, he chastiseth: and as a father in the son he pleaseth himself|Quia quem diligit Dominus, corripit, et quasi pater in filio complacet sibi]]; [[12:22|our enemies|inimicos nostros]], namely the unbelievers, [[12:22|thou scourgest|flagellas]] [[12:22|very many ways|multipliciter]], leaving them in their hardness, and punishing them not only in time but eternally. Hence Solomon too says: [[Prov 11:31|If the just man receive in the earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner.|Si justus in terra recipit, quanto magis impius et peccator?]]

paras.t: Ut bonitatem tuam cogitemus, considerando quam paterne ac pie agas nobiscum, judicantes, id est, prudenter discernentes correctionem nostram a reproborum punitione; vel, Judicantes, id est, dum proximos judicamus, ut simus eis benigni et indulgentes, sicut Deus nobiscum misericorditer egit. Unde in Evangelio dicitur servo iniquo: Serve nequam, omne debitum dimisi tibi, quia rogasti me: nonne ergo oportuit et te misereri conservi tui, sicut et ego tui misertus sum? Hinc hortatur Apostolus: Donantes vobismetipsis, sicut et Deus in Christo donavit vobis. Et quum de nobis judicatur, id est, quum pro nostris culpis judicamur et punimur in vita præsenti, speremus misericordiam tuam obtinere: quia non judicas bis in id ipsum, et pœnæ vitæ præsentis sunt medicinales.
paras.en: To the end that [[12:22|we may think on thy goodness|Ut bonitatem tuam cogitemus]], considering how fatherly and mercifully thou dealest with us, [[12:22|when we judge|judicantes]], that is, prudently distinguishing our correction from the punishment of the reprobate; or, [[12:22|when we judge|Judicantes]], that is, when we judge our neighbours, that we may be kind and indulgent to them, as God has dealt mercifully with us. Hence in the Gospel it is said to the wicked servant: [[Matt 18:32|Thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all the debt, because thou besoughtest me|Serve nequam, omne debitum dimisi tibi, quia rogasti me]]: [[Matt 18:33|Shouldst not thou then have had compassion also on thy fellow servant, even as I had compassion on thee?|nonne ergo oportuit et te misereri conservi tui, sicut et ego tui misertus sum?]] Hence the Apostle exhorts: [[Eph 4:32|forgiving one another, even as God hath forgiven you in Christ|Donantes vobismetipsis, sicut et Deus in Christo donavit vobis]]. [[12:22|and when we are judged|Et quum de nobis judicatur]], that is, when for our faults we are judged and punished in this present life, [[12:22|we may hope for thy mercy|speremus misericordiam tuam]] [Denis's text adds *obtinere*, "to obtain"]: because thou dost not judge twice for the same thing[[Job 33:14||]] [the margin gives Job 33:14, "God speaketh once, and repeateth not the selfsame thing the second time"; the saying is usually drawn from Nah 1:9, "there shall not rise a double affliction"], and the punishments of the present life are medicinal.

paras.t: Unde et illis qui in vita sua insensate et injuste vixerunt, videlicet Ægyptiis, qui insipienter se habuerunt ad Deum, et injuste ad Hebræos, quos oppresserunt, per hæc quæ coluerunt, id est per parva et vilia animalia, quæ adoraverunt, dedisti summa tormenta, id est valde magna supplicia, immittendo eis ranas, muscas, scinifes, bruchos, locustas, quoniam talpas, vespertiliones, serpentesque coluerunt: et quia non pœnituerunt in pœnis his, adepti sunt pœnas æternas. Ideo subditur:
paras.en: [[12:23|Wherefore|Unde et]] [[12:23|them, who, in their life, have lived foolishly and unjustly|illis qui in vita sua insensate et injuste vixerunt]], namely the Egyptians, who behaved foolishly toward God and unjustly toward the Hebrews, whom they oppressed, [[12:23|by the same things which they worshipped|per hæc quæ coluerunt]], that is, by the small and vile animals which they adored, [[12:23|thou hast also greatly tormented|dedisti summa tormenta]] [Latin "thou hast given the greatest torments"], that is, very great punishments, sending upon them frogs[[Ex 8:6||]], flies[[Ex 8:24||]], sciniphs[[Ex 8:17||]], the bruchus[[Ps 104:34||]] and locusts[[Ex 10:13||]] [the margin gives Ps. cv, 34; the bruchus is named in Ps 104:34], since they worshipped moles, bats and serpents: and because they did not repent under these punishments, they came to eternal punishments. Therefore it is added:

paras.t: Etenim in erroris via diutius erraverunt, id est, in sua idololatria ac ceteris vitiis permanserunt pro majori parte usque ad mortem, deos æstimantes hæc, quæ in animalibus sunt supervacua, id est vilia et inutilia bruta præfata, infantium insensatorum more viventes, id est stulte et pueriliter, non pensantes tam vilia non esse colenda.
paras.en: [[12:24|For they went astray for a long time in the ways of error|Etenim in erroris via diutius erraverunt]], that is, they remained in their idolatry and other vices, for the most part until death, [[12:24|holding those things for gods which are the most worthless among beasts|deos æstimantes hæc, quæ in animalibus sunt supervacua]], that is, the vile and useless brute beasts already mentioned, [[12:24|living after the manner of children without understanding|infantium insensatorum more viventes]], that is, foolishly and childishly, not considering that things so vile are not to be worshipped.

paras.t: Propter hoc tanquam pueris insensatis judicium in derisum dedisti: id est, Ægyptiis intulisti derisibile illud supplicium muscarum et similium bestiolarum, sicut pueri insensati solent derisibiliter corrigi.
paras.en: [[12:25|Therefore|Propter hoc]] [[12:25|as senseless children|tanquam pueris insensatis]] [[12:25|thou hast sent a judgment upon them|judicium]] [[12:25|to mock them|in derisum dedisti]]: that is, thou didst bring upon the Egyptians that laughable punishment of flies and like little beasts, as senseless children are wont to be corrected in a way that makes them a laughing-stock.

paras.t: Qui autem ludibriis, id est pœnis illis irrisione aspernationeque dignis, et increpationibus Moysis, seu Dei punientis, non sunt correcti, id est, non pœnituerunt veraciter et constanter, dignum judicium Dei experti sunt: quia in mari Rubro submersi seu aliter mortui, perpetuo sunt damnati.
paras.en: [[12:26|But they that|Qui autem]] [[12:26|by mockeries|ludibriis]], that is, by those punishments worthy of derision and scorn, [[12:26|and reprehensions|et increpationibus]] of Moses, or of God punishing them, [[12:26|were not amended|non sunt correcti]], that is, did not truly and steadfastly repent, [[12:26|experienced the worthy judgment of God|dignum judicium Dei experti sunt]]: because, drowned in the Red Sea or dying otherwise, they are damned for ever.

paras.t: In his enim quæ patiebantur, molestè ferebant, id est, ipsas suas punitiones ægre et impatienter sustinuerunt; in quibus patientes, id est, pœnam magnam habentes, indignabantur contra Deum Hebræorum eos sic punientem, cujus omnipotentiæ invidebant: sicut in Apocalypsi scribitur de quibusdam: Manducaverunt linguas suas præ doloribus, et non egerunt pœnitentiam, ut darent gloriam Deo; sed blasphemaverunt nomen Dei habentis potestatem super has plagas. Per hæc, quæ putabant deos, in ipsis quum exterminarentur, videntes illum quem olim negabant se nosse, verum Deum agnoverunt.
paras.en: For in those things [[12:27|that they suffered|quæ patiebantur]] they were vexed [Denis's text reads *In his enim quæ patiebantur, moleste ferebant*, "for in the things which they suffered they bore it ill"], that is, they bore their very punishments grievously and impatiently; in which [[12:27|they suffered|patientes]], that is, bearing great punishment, they were filled [[12:27|with indignation|indignabantur]] against the God of the Hebrews who so punished them, whose almighty power they envied: as it is written of some in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 16:10|they gnawed their tongues for pain|Manducaverunt linguas suas præ doloribus]]; [[Apoc 16:9|Neither did they penance to give him glory|et non egerunt pœnitentiam, ut darent gloriam Deo]]; but [[Apoc 16:9|they blasphemed the name of God, who hath power over these plagues|blasphemaverunt nomen Dei habentis potestatem super has plagas]]. [[12:27|by those very things which they took for gods|Per hæc, quæ putabant deos]], [[12:27|when they were destroyed by the same|in ipsis quum exterminarentur]], [[12:27|seeing|videntes]] [[12:27|whom in time past they denied that they knew|illum quem olim negabant se nosse]], [[12:27|they acknowledged him the true God|verum Deum agnoverunt]].

paras.t: Littera intricata est. Est igitur sensus et ordo verborum: Ægyptii aut etiam Chananæi, videntes, id est aliqualiter cognoscentes, illum quem olim negabant se nosse, scilicet Deum Israel: de quo Pharao dixit: Quis est Dominus, ut audiam vocem ejus, et dimittam Israel? Nescio Dominum, et Israel non dimittam. Cognoscentes, inquam, illum per hæc flagella, quum exterminarentur quæ putabant esse deos, id est, idola eorum (quæ putabant esse deos suos, seu deos inter ipsos) destruerentur a Deo qui in diis Ægyptiorum exercuerat ultionem, ut fertur in Exodo, vel a filiis Israel qui idola Chananæorum dissipaverunt, sicut in Deuteronomio sæpissime jussum fuit; agnoverunt verum Deum: quia experiebantur eum esse potentiorem omnibus diis ipsorum, a quibus juvari non poterant, imo et omnipotentem in multis prodigiis, sicut in statione solis et lunæ, et maris Rubri divisione. Non tamen honoraverunt eum ut Deum: idcirco inexcusabiles erant. Ideo subditur: propter quod et finis condemnationis eorum, id est finalis seu ultima et plena condemnatio illorum, veniet super illos: et hoc in die generalis judicii, quando cum corpore et anima damnabuntur.
paras.en: The wording is intricate. This, then, is the sense and order of the words: The Egyptians, or the Chanaanites too, [[12:27|seeing|videntes]], that is, in some way knowing, him [[12:27|whom in time past they denied that they knew|illum quem olim negabant se nosse]], namely the God of Israel, of whom Pharao said: [[Ex 5:2|Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice, and let Israel go? I know not the Lord, neither will I let Israel go|Quis est Dominus, ut audiam vocem ejus, et dimittam Israel? Nescio Dominum, et Israel non dimittam]]. Knowing him, I say, [[12:27|by those very things|per hæc]], that is, by these scourges, [[12:27|when they were destroyed|quum exterminarentur]] [[12:27|which they took for gods|quæ putabant esse deos]], that is, when their idols (which they thought to be their gods, or gods among themselves) were destroyed by God, who had executed vengeance on the gods of the Egyptians[[Ex 12:12||]], as is related in Exodus, or by the children of Israel, who scattered the idols of the Chanaanites, as was very often commanded in Deuteronomy[[Deut 7:5||]][[Deut 7:25||]][[Deut 12:3||]]; [[12:27|they acknowledged him the true God|agnoverunt verum Deum]]: because they found him to be mightier than all their gods, from whom they could get no help, nay, and almighty in many prodigies, as in the standing still of the sun and moon[[Jos 10:13||]] and in the dividing of the Red Sea[[Ex 14:21||]]. Yet they did not honour him as God[[Rom 1:21||]]: therefore they were inexcusable[[Rom 1:20||]]. Therefore it is added: [[12:27|for which cause the end also of their condemnation|propter quod et finis condemnationis eorum]], that is, the final or last and full condemnation of them, [[12:27|came upon them|veniet super illos]] [Denis reads *veniet*, "shall come"]: and this on the day of the general judgment, when they shall be damned in body and soul.

13.title: DECLARATIO CAPITULI TERTIIDECIMI : VANI AUTEM SUNT OMNES HOMINES IN QUIBUS NON SUBEST SCIENTIA DEI.
13.title_en: Declaration of the thirteenth chapter: But all men are vain, in whom there is not the knowledge of God

paras.t: Reprobatur hic idololatria, non solum Ægyptiorum aut Chananæorum, sed gentium universarum. Vani autem sunt omnes homines in quibus non subest scientia Dei, id est, qui veri Dei carent notitia. Vanum namque vocatur, quod ad finem propter quem institutum est, non pertingit : quemadmodum vana est medicina quæ ad sanitatem non confert. Quum ergo finis et salus hominum sit Dei cognitio, sicut asserit Veritas, Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum; homines qui ad Dei notitiam non pertingunt, recte vani censentur. Et horum triplex est genus. Quidam enim habent cognitionem Dei, non solum naturalem, sed etiam theologicam et supernaturalem illam quæ est donum gratiæ gratis datæ, et studio potest acquiri; tamen non habent scientiam Dei quæ est donum, et caritati semper conjuncta est : et isti sunt vani, quum sint extra caritatem et statum salutis, seu in peccato mortali. Alii solum habent cognitionem Dei naturalem, philosophicam, acquisitam, ignorantes sacram Scripturam, et fide carentes : et isti sunt vaniores, ut infideles. Alii nesciunt unum summum universorum principium esse, et omni Deitatis notitia destituuntur, ut quidam idololatræ, de quibus hic agitur : et isti perhibentur vanissimi. Porro primum genus potest subdividi. Nam aliqui habentes supernaturalem scientiam Dei traditam in Scripturis, et quæ est donum gratiæ gratis datæ, habent veram fidem, ut mali Catholici; alii carent fide, sicut hæretici.
paras.en: Here idolatry is condemned: not only that of the Egyptians or the Chanaanites, but that of all the nations. [[13:1|But all men are vain, in whom there is not the knowledge of God|Vani autem sunt omnes homines in quibus non subest scientia Dei]], that is, who lack the knowledge of the true God. For that is called vain which does not reach the end for which it was instituted, as that medicine is vain which does nothing for health. Since, then, the end and the salvation of men is the knowledge of God, as the Truth declares: [[John 17:3|this is eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God|Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum]]; men who do not attain to the knowledge of God are rightly judged vain. And of these there are three kinds. For some have a knowledge of God, not only natural but also theological and supernatural: that knowledge which is a gift of grace freely given [*gratia gratis data*: a grace given chiefly for the good of others, such as learning or prophecy, which does not of itself make its bearer holy], and can be acquired by study; yet they have not the knowledge of God which is a gift [the gift of knowledge, one of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost] and is always joined to charity. And these are vain, since they are outside charity and the state of salvation, that is, in mortal sin. Others have only a natural, philosophical, acquired knowledge of God, not knowing Holy Scripture and lacking faith: and these are vainer, as unbelievers. Others do not know that there is one supreme principle of all things, and are destitute of all knowledge of the Godhead, as are certain idolaters, of whom this passage treats: and these are declared the vainest of all. The first kind, moreover, can be subdivided. For some who have the supernatural knowledge of God handed down in the Scriptures, which is a gift of grace freely given, have the true faith, as bad Catholics; others lack faith, as heretics.

paras.t: Et de his quæ videntur bona, id est ex rerum creatarum notitia, quæ aliquid bonitatis participant, et quibusdam meliora apparent quam sunt, non potuerunt, id est, non curaverunt, nec studuerunt, seu facili conatu nequibant, intelligere eum qui est, scilicet verum Deum, qui solus est ipsum esse separatum, plenum, independens, incircumscriptum, purum, simplicissimum, infinite perfectum, in se ipso incommutabiliter æternaliterque consistens: quod tantæ est excellentiæ, ut ejus comparatione omne creatum esse, sit quasi non esse. Ideo primum nomen Dei ponitur, Esse, seu, Qui est. Qui Moysi nomen suum sciscitanti legitur respondisse : Ego sum qui sum. Hæc dices filiis Israel : Qui est, misit me ad vos. Cui sanctus Job dixit : Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine? Nonne tu qui solus es? De quo legitur in Propheta : Qui fecit omnia, ipse est; Dominus exercituum nomen ejus.
paras.en: [[13:1|and who by these good things that are seen|Et de his quæ videntur bona]], that is, from the knowledge of created things, which share in some goodness and seem to some better than they are, [[13:1|could not|non potuerunt]], that is, did not care to, nor apply themselves, or could not with slight effort, [[13:1|understand him that is|intelligere eum qui est]]: namely the true God, who alone is being itself: separate, full, independent, uncircumscribed, pure, most simple, infinitely perfect, abiding in himself unchangeably and eternally; which is of such excellence that in comparison with it all created being is as it were not being. Therefore the first name of God is given as Being, or He Who Is. We read that when Moses asked his name, he answered: [[Ex 3:14|I AM WHO AM|Ego sum qui sum]]. [[Ex 3:14|Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you|Hæc dices filiis Israel : Qui est, misit me ad vos]]. To him holy Job said: [[Job 14:4|Who can make him clean that is conceived of unclean seed? is it not thou who only art?|Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine? Nonne tu qui solus es?]] Of him we read in the Prophet: [[Jer 51:19|he that made all things he it is|Qui fecit omnia, ipse est]]; [[Jer 51:19|the Lord of hosts is his name|Dominus exercituum nomen ejus]] [the margin gives Jer. ii, 19; the words are those of Jer 51:19 (li, 19), and nearly so of Jer 10:16].

paras.t: Neque operibus attendentes, agnoverunt quis esset artifex, id est, creaturarum considerationi vacantes, non agnoverunt quod productæ essent ab uno summo artifice.
paras.en: [[13:1|neither by attending to the works have acknowledged who was the workman|Neque operibus attendentes, agnoverunt quis esset artifex]], that is, while giving themselves to the consideration of creatures, they did not acknowledge that these had been produced by one supreme workman.

paras.t: Sed aut ignem, aut spiritum, id est ventum seu ætherem, aut citatum, id est commotum aut mobilem, aerem, aut gyrum stellarum, id est circulum siderum, seu zodiacum (qui est circulus obliquus, in quo moventur planetæ, habens duodecim signa : unde legitur, Delevit Josias eos qui adolebant soli et lunæ et duodecim signis), aut nimiam, id est abundantissimam, aquam, videlicet elementum aquæ, sive Oceanum, aut solem et lunam, rectores orbis terrarum deos putaverunt, id est, æstimaverunt esse principales rectores inferiorum, ac deos. Nempe aliquo modo verum censetur, quod Aristoteles ait : Oportet hunc mundum esse contiguum lationibus superiorum, ut tota ejus virtus inde gubernetur. Sicque cœlestia corpora agunt et influunt in elementa ac mixta, et instrumentaliter regunt ea; non tamen directe agunt in superiorem partem animæ rationalis, nec eam necessitant. Hinc sol suo accessu in zodiaco, dicitur causa generationis in inferioribus; et sua elongatione, causa corruptionis. Ad quod etiam super secundum Sententiarum Thomas divinum Dionysium allegat et sequitur.
paras.en: [[13:2|But have imagined either the fire, or the wind|Sed aut ignem, aut spiritum]], that is, the wind or the ether, [[13:2|or the swift|aut citatum]], that is, moved or movable, [[13:2|air|aerem]], [[13:2|or the circle of the stars|aut gyrum stellarum]], that is, the round of the heavenly bodies, or the zodiac (which is the oblique circle in which the planets move, and has twelve signs; whence we read that Josias [[4 Kings 23:5|destroyed|Delevit]] [[4 Kings 23:5|them also that burnt incense|eos qui adolebant]] [[4 Kings 23:5|to the sun, and to the moon, and to the twelve signs|soli et lunæ et duodecim signis]]), [[13:2|or the great|aut nimiam]], that is, most abundant, [[13:2|water|aquam]], namely the element of water, or the Ocean, [[13:2|or the sun and moon, to be the gods that rule the world|aut solem et lunam, rectores orbis terrarum deos putaverunt]], that is, they reckoned them to be the chief rulers of the lower things, and gods. Indeed what Aristotle says is held to be true in some way: This world must be contiguous to the motions of the higher bodies, so that all its power may be governed from there. And so the heavenly bodies act and flow into the elements and the mixed bodies, and govern them as instruments; yet they do not act directly on the higher part of the rational soul, nor do they necessitate it. Hence the sun, by its approach in the zodiac, is said to be the cause of generation in lower things, and by its withdrawal, the cause of corruption. On this point Thomas too, on the second book of the Sentences, cites and follows the divine Dionysius.

paras.t: Quorum enim creatorum, si, pro quia, specie, id est decore, delectati idololatræ, deos putaverunt, sciant quanto his dominator eorum speciosior est, id est, advertant et sciant, quod creator et rector eorum, utique infinite sit speciosior ipsis. Denique summi philosophi, planetas et stellas ac orbes cœlestes, dixerunt esse animatos, et deos. Nihilo minus cognoverunt primam causam, scilicet Deum, esse incomparabiliter digniorem ac pulchriorem, utpote purum actum, et infinitam virtutem. Unde in primo Timæi Plato inducit opificem universi, stellis orbibusque loquentem : O dii deorum! quorum pater et opifex ego. Aristoteles quoque tertio de Anima, solem appellat patrem virorum ac deorum. Et quamvis isti in aliquibus erraverunt, minus tamen, quam illi qui istis creatis attribuebant principalem auctoritatem, deitatem, et formositatem. Speciei enim generator, id est Deus omnis pulchritudinis institutor et auctor, hæc omnia constituit, id est, fecit : ideo quidquid perfectionis ac pulchritudinis inest istis, multo præclarius est in illo.
paras.en: [[13:3|With whose|Quorum enim creatorum]] [Denis reads *quorum creatorum*, "of which created things"] [[13:3|beauty|specie]], that is, comeliness, [[13:3|if|si]] (put here for *because*) the idolaters, [[13:3|being delighted|delectati]], [[13:3|took them to be gods|deos putaverunt]]: [[13:3|let them know how much the Lord of them is more beautiful than they|sciant quanto his dominator eorum speciosior est]], that is, let them consider and know that their creator and ruler is beyond doubt infinitely more beautiful than they. Indeed the greatest philosophers said that the planets and stars and the heavenly spheres were animate, and gods. Nevertheless they knew that the first cause, namely God, is incomparably worthier and more beautiful, as being pure act and infinite power. Whence in the first book of the Timæus Plato brings in the maker of the universe speaking to the stars and spheres: O gods of gods, whose father and maker am I! Aristotle too, in the third book On the Soul, calls the sun the father of men and of gods. And though these erred in some things, they erred less than those who attributed to these created things the chief authority, godhead and beauty. Then follows: [[13:3|for the first author of beauty|Speciei enim generator]], that is, God, the founder and author of all beauty, [[13:3|made all those things|hæc omnia constituit]]: therefore whatever perfection and beauty is in these things is far more glorious in him.

paras.t: Aut si virtutem et opera eorum mirati sunt, id est, quia causalitatem et effectus solis ac lunæ, aut consimilium, sunt admirati, intelligant ab ipsis, id est ex consideratione ipsorum, quoniam qui hæc constituit, id est, creavit, fortior, id est causalior atque potentior, est illis; et quidquid efficaciæ habent, ab illo sortiti sunt, et ab eodem incessanter dependent.
paras.en: [[13:4|Or if they admired their power, and their effects|Aut si virtutem et opera eorum mirati sunt]], that is, because they wondered at the causality and the effects of the sun and moon, or of the like, [[13:4|let them understand by them|intelligant ab ipsis]], that is, from the consideration of them, [[13:4|that he that made them|quoniam qui hæc constituit]], that is, created them, [[13:4|is mightier|fortior]], that is, more a cause and more powerful, [[13:4|than they|est illis]]; and whatever efficacy they have, they have received from him, and they depend on him unceasingly.

paras.t: A magnitudine enim speciei et creaturæ, id est ex consideratione magni decoris rerum et ipsarum creaturarum, cognoscibiliter poterit creator horum videri, id est, Deus omnium causa intelligi. Quamvis enim incomprehensibilis sit, quantum ad quid est, nec cognosci possit per causam, id est, sciri non possit a priori; tamen cognoscibilis est, quia est, et a posteriori, per suos effectus, quum omne causatum sit quædam similitudo suæ causæ. Sic et omnis creatura est quædam participata similitudo, et velut quidam radius Creatoris. Ex ordine quoque causarum, et mobilium et moventium, atque regentium, et ex ordine universi, et decentissima concatenatione et coordinatione specierum ipsius, atque ex aliis multis concluditur, quod sit unum primum et summum ens, prima omnium causa, primus rector et motor. Rursus, quum non sit processus in infinitum, et videamus multa suum esse aliunde sortiri, necesse est devenire ad unum primum et increatum. Et quia nihil est imperfectum, nisi in quantum distat a fonte suæ perfectionis, oportet hoc primum ens fateri omnino perfectum atque æternum. Unde ex his considerationibus cognoverunt meliores philosophi multa vera et alta de Deo, quemadmodum scribit Apostolus: Invisibilia Dei a creatura mundi, per ea quæ facta sunt, intellecta conspiciuntur; sempiterna quoque virtus ejus et divinitas, ita ut sint inexcusabiles: quia quod notum est Dei, manifestum est in illis. Verumtamen isti, qui nobiles creaturas dixerunt deos, sunt minus reprehensibiles quam qui vilissimas bestiolas deos putabant. Ideo subditur:
paras.en: [[13:5|For by the greatness of the beauty, and of the creature|A magnitudine enim speciei et creaturæ]], that is, from the consideration of the great comeliness of things and of the creatures themselves, [[13:5|the creator of them may be seen, so as to be known thereby|cognoscibiliter poterit creator horum videri]], that is, God may be understood as the cause of all things. For though he is incomprehensible as to what he is, and cannot be known through a cause, that is, cannot be known a priori, yet he is knowable as to the fact that he is, and a posteriori, through his effects, since everything caused is a certain likeness of its cause. So too every creature is a certain participated likeness, and as it were a ray, of the Creator. From the order of causes, too, of things moved, of movers and of rulers, and from the order of the universe and the most fitting linking and co-ordination of its species, and from many other things, it is concluded that there is one first and highest being, the first cause of all things, the first ruler and mover. Again, since there is no going on to infinity, and we see that many things receive their being from another, we must come to one that is first and uncreated. And since nothing is imperfect except in so far as it is distant from the source of its perfection, this first being must be confessed to be altogether perfect and eternal. Hence from these considerations the better philosophers knew many true and lofty things about God, as the Apostle writes: [[Rom 1:20|the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made. His eternal power also and divinity: so that they are inexcusable|Invisibilia Dei a creatura mundi, per ea quæ facta sunt, intellecta conspiciuntur; sempiterna quoque virtus ejus et divinitas, ita ut sint inexcusabiles]]: [[Rom 1:19|Because that which is known of God is manifest in them|quia quod notum est Dei, manifestum est in illis]]. Yet those who called the noble creatures gods are less to be blamed than those who took the vilest little beasts for gods. Therefore it is added:

paras.t: Sed tamen adhuc in his ita errantibus, minor est querela, id est culpa seu reprehensio, quam in aliis, de quibus dicetur. Et hi enim fortassis errant, Deum quærentes, et volentes invenire. Non dubium quin errent: idcirco quod ait, Fortassis, referendum est ad participia illa, Quærentes, et, Volentes. Forsitan enim, dicendo nobiliora quæque esse deos, quærunt, invenireque volunt Deum, quem æstimant aliquem magnum.
paras.en: [[13:6|But yet as to these|Sed tamen adhuc in his]] who so err, [[13:6|they are less to be blamed|minor est querela]] [*querela*, literally "complaint"], that is, the fault or reproach is less than in the others, of whom he will speak. [[13:6|For they perhaps err, seeking God, and desirous to find him|Et hi enim fortassis errant, Deum quærentes, et volentes invenire]]. There is no doubt that they err; so what he says, *perhaps*, is to be referred to those participles, *seeking* and *desirous*. For perhaps, in saying that all the nobler things are gods, they are seeking God and wish to find him, whom they reckon to be some great one.

paras.t: Etenim quum in operibus illius conversentur, id est, quum occupent se in considerationibus creaturarum Dei, inquirunt scire, et persuasum habent, id est, tanquam probabile tenent, quoniam bona sunt quæ videntur: et sic aliquo modo bene sentiunt de creatis, et de Deo, quoad hoc quod nobilioribus et causabilioribus rebus attribuunt deitatem. Non tamen sunt totaliter excusabiles. Propterea sequitur:
paras.en: [[13:7|For being conversant among his works|Etenim quum in operibus illius conversentur]], that is, since they busy themselves in considering the creatures of God, [[13:7|they search|inquirunt scire]] [Denis reads *inquirunt scire*, "they seek to know"], [[13:7|and they are persuaded|et persuasum habent]], that is, they hold it as probable, [[13:7|that the things are good which are seen|quoniam bona sunt quæ videntur]]: and so in some way they think rightly of created things and of God, in that they attribute godhead to the nobler things and those more powerful as causes. Yet they are not wholly excusable. Therefore there follows:

paras.t: Iterum autem nec his debet ignosci error eorum: imo damnatione sunt digni.
paras.en: [[13:8|But then again they are not to be pardoned|Iterum autem nec his debet ignosci]] their error: nay, they are worthy of damnation.

paras.t: Si enim tantum potuerunt scire, id est in scientia proficere, ut possent æstimare sæculum, id est probabilem habere cognitionem de mundo, et de ordine, cursu, successioneque rerum; quomodo hujus Dominum facilius non invenerunt? id est, in hoc negligenter et irrationabiliter se habebant, quod ex rebus creatis et præactis earum considerationibus, statim non attenderunt omnia ista ab uno primo principio profluxisse, quum omnis multitudo procedat ab uno, et omne participatum ac dependens et imperfectum, reducatur finaliter ad aliquod imparticipatum, independens ac perfectum. Denique, sicut nihil est incomprehensibilius Deo, quantum ad quid est; sic nihil facilius aut certius est Deo, quantum ad quia est. Imo multi magni dixerunt, quod Deum esse, sit per se notum. Verumtamen Deum cognoscere quantum ad aliqua attributa ipsius, difficile est: sicque verificatur quod asserit Plato, Genitorem opificemque universi, tam difficile inveniri, quam inventum impossibile digne effari. Et hoc consonat ei quod scriptum est: Digne eum invenire non possumus, et enarrari non potest. Quod tamen de inventione Dei quoad quid est, potest intelligi.
paras.en: [[13:9|For if they were able to know so much|Si enim tantum potuerunt scire]], that is, to advance in knowledge, [[13:9|as to make a judgment of the world|ut possent æstimare sæculum]], that is, to have a probable knowledge of the world, and of the order, course and succession of things: [[13:9|how did they not more easily find out the Lord thereof?|quomodo hujus Dominum facilius non invenerunt?]] That is, in this they behaved negligently and unreasonably, that from created things and from the considerations of them which they had already made, they did not at once see that all these things flowed from one first principle; since every multitude proceeds from one, and everything participated, dependent and imperfect is finally led back to something unparticipated, independent and perfect. Indeed, as nothing is more incomprehensible than God as to what he is, so nothing is easier or more certain than God as to the fact that he is. Indeed many great men have said that God's existence is self-evident [*per se notum*: known of itself, needing no proof]. Yet to know God as to some of his attributes is difficult; and so what Plato asserts is borne out, that the Begetter and Maker of the universe is as hard to find as, once found, he is impossible to speak of worthily. And this agrees with what is written: [[Job 37:23|We cannot find him worthily|Digne eum invenire non possumus]], [[Job 37:23|and he is ineffable|et enarrari non potest]] [no margin reference; the words are Job 37:23]. This, however, may be understood of finding God as to what he is.

paras.t: Consequenter ostenditur, quod prædicti infeliciores sunt, qui rebus inanimatis ac vilibus deitatem attribuebant. Infelices autem sunt, id est æternaliter condemnati, aut digni damnari, et inter mortuos spes illorum est, id est, non plus sperandum de eorum salute, quam de mortuorum, id est rerum non viventium, seu in vitiis defunctorum, felicitate; qui appellaverunt deos opera manuum hominum, id est idola fabrefacta, aurum et argentum, id est idola facta ex auro et argento, consimilibusve materiis: quæ opera manuum hominum sunt, quantum ad formam eorum artificialem: unde subjungitur, artis inventionem, quia per humanæ artis excogitationem ita formata sunt; et similitudines animalium deos dixerunt, aut lapidem inutilem, id est lapideam statuam factam de saxo vili, quod conculcatur velut inutile : omne tamen creatum est ad aliquid utile; opus manus antiquæ, id est formatum a manu in vitiis veterati. Vel additur hoc, quoniam idola vetustiora amplius honorabant.
paras.en: Next it is shown that those who attributed godhead to lifeless and vile things are more unhappy than the aforesaid. [[13:10|But unhappy are they|Infelices autem sunt]], that is, eternally condemned, or worthy to be damned, [[13:10|and their hope is among the dead|et inter mortuos spes illorum est]], that is, no more is to be hoped for their salvation than for the happiness of the dead, that is, of things not living, or of those dead in vices; [[13:10|who have called gods the works of the hand of men|qui appellaverunt deos opera manuum hominum]], that is, idols made by craftsmen, [[13:10|gold and silver|aurum et argentum]], that is, idols made of gold and silver or of like materials: which are works of men's hands as to their artificial form; whence it is added, [[13:10|the inventions of art|artis inventionem]], because they were so formed by the devising of human art; [[13:10|and the resemblances of beasts|et similitudines animalium]] they called gods, [[13:10|or an unprofitable stone|aut lapidem inutilem]], that is, a stone statue made of vile rock, which is trodden underfoot as useless (yet every created thing is made for some use); [[13:10|the work of an ancient hand|opus manus antiquæ]], that is, formed by a hand grown old in vices. Or this is added because they honoured the older idols the more.

paras.t: Deinde ad ostendendum idololatrarum fatuitatem, exemplificatur. Aut si quis artifex faber, id est faber lignarius, de silva lignorum rectum secuerit, id est, cum securi absciderit, et hujus docte eradat omnem corticem, id est, perite deponat vel purget corticem ejus, et arte sua usus, diligenter fabricet vas inutile, id est valde utile, juxta Glossam : secundum illud Virgilianum : Nunquam imprudentibus (id est multum prudentibus) imber obfuit. Vel, Inutile, id est intus utile, puta ad usus domesticos. In conversationem vitæ, id est ad humanum convictum, ad quem vasa lignea requiruntur. Posset quoque sic legi : Vas in utile, id est in vas utile, ut, in utile, duæ sint dictiones.
paras.en: Then, to show the folly of the idolaters, an example is given. [[13:11|Or if an artist, a carpenter|Aut si quis artifex faber]], that is, a worker in wood, [[13:11|hath cut down a tree proper for his use in the wood|de silva lignorum rectum secuerit]], that is, has cut it off with an axe, [[13:11|and skilfully taken off all the bark thereof|et hujus docte eradat omnem corticem]], that is, expertly strips or cleans off its bark, [[13:11|and with his art, diligently formeth a vessel|et arte sua usus, diligenter fabricet vas]] *inutile* [Denis's text has *vas inutile*, "an unprofitable vessel", where the Douay-Rheims has "profitable"; he gives three ways of taking it], that is, very profitable, according to the Gloss, after that line of Virgil: Never did the rain harm the *imprudentes* (that is, the very prudent) [the gloss takes the *in-* of *inutile* as strengthening the word, not denying it]. Or *inutile*, that is, profitable within (*intus utile*), say for household uses, [[13:11|for the common uses of life|In conversationem vitæ]], that is, for men's life together, for which wooden vessels are needed. It could also be read thus: *vas in utile*, that is, *in vas utile*, "into a profitable vessel", so that *in utile* is two words.

paras.t: Reliquiis autem hujus operis, id est reliqua parte ligni ita erasi, ad præparationem escæ abutatur, id est, ignem ex ea faciat pro cibo coquendo.
paras.en: [[13:12|And useth the chips of his work|Reliquiis autem hujus operis]], that is, the remaining part of the wood thus stripped, [[13:12|to dress his meat|ad præparationem escæ abutatur]], that is, makes a fire of it to cook food.

paras.t: Et reliquum horum, id est residuum partium ligni hujus, quod ad nullum usum fecit, id est, de quo non format vas aut instrumentum in usus humanos, videlicet lignum curvum, et verticibus, id est globosis eminentiis seu nodis apparentibus, plenum, sculpat diligenter per vacuitatem suam, id est per propriam vanitatem et mentem inanem; et per scientiam artis suæ figuret illud, imprimendo ei formam artificialem, et assimilet illud imagini hominis, id est figuræ humanæ,
paras.en: [[13:13|And taking what was left thereof|Et reliquum horum]], that is, the remainder of the parts of this wood, [[13:13|which is good for nothing|quod ad nullum usum fecit]], that is, of which he does not form a vessel or tool for human uses, namely [[13:13|being a crooked piece of wood, and full of knots|lignum curvum, et verticibus]], that is, [[13:13|full|plenum]] of round swellings or knots standing out, [[13:13|carveth it diligently when he hath nothing else to do|sculpat diligenter per vacuitatem suam]], that is, through his own vanity and empty mind [*vacuitas* means both leisure and emptiness; Denis takes it as emptiness of mind]; [[13:13|and by the skill of his art fashioneth it|et per scientiam artis suæ figuret illud]], impressing on it an artificial form, [[13:13|and maketh it like the image of a man|et assimilet illud imagini hominis]], that is, a human figure,

paras.t: aut alicui ex animalibus irrationabilibus comparet, id est conformet, illud, imprimendo ei figuram bestialem; perliniens rubrica, id est rubeo colore, et rubicundum faciens fucum, id est tinctura, quæ fit de herba quæ etiam fucus vocatur (sed et quidam superpositus color dicitur fucus; interdum quoque fraus, mendacium, astutia, dicitur fucus, quia supponitur veritati aut falsitati coloranda), colorem illius, et omnem maculam quæ in illo est perliniens;
paras.en: [[13:14|Or the resemblance of some beast|aut alicui ex animalibus irrationabilibus comparet]], that is, he conforms it to some irrational animal, impressing on it the figure of a beast; [[13:14|laying it over with vermilion|perliniens rubrica]], that is, with red colour, [[13:14|and painting it red|et rubicundum faciens fucum]] [literally "making its colour red with *fucus*"], that is, with a dye made from a plant that is also called *fucus* (but a colour laid on top of something is also called *fucus*; and sometimes fraud, a lie or cunning is called *fucus*, because it is laid over the truth, or over a falsehood that is to be coloured), [[13:14|and covering every spot that is in it|et omnem maculam quæ in illo est perliniens]];

paras.t: et faciat ei dignam habitationem, scilicet templum, altare, aut alium locum quem arbitratur congruere hujusmodi deo suo; et in pariete ponens illud, et confirmans, id est, fortiter figens in loco, ferro, id est cum clavis, ne forte cadat, prospiciens illi, id est, providens periculo casus illius, sciens quoniam non potest adjuvare se, id est, ipso facto suo ostendit se id scire, quamvis aliunde deceptus, putet aliquid numinis esse in illo; imago enim est inanimata, et opus est illi adjutorium, id est, adjutorio sustentationis hujusmodi indigeat, ne ruat ex loco suo.
paras.en: [[13:15|And maketh a convenient dwelling place for it|et faciat ei dignam habitationem]], namely a temple, an altar, or some other place that he thinks fitting for such a god of his; [[13:15|and setting it in a wall, and fastening it|et in pariete ponens illud, et confirmans]], that is, fixing it firmly in its place, [[13:15|with iron|ferro]], that is, with nails, [[13:16|lest it should fall|ne forte cadat]], [[13:16|Providing for it|prospiciens illi]], that is, guarding against the danger of its falling, [[13:16|knowing that it is unable to help itself|sciens quoniam non potest adjuvare se]], that is, by his very deed he shows that he knows this, although, deceived on another side, he thinks there is something of divinity in it; [[13:16|for it is an image|imago enim est inanimata]] [Denis's text adds *inanimata*, "without life"], [[13:16|and hath need of help|et opus est illi adjutorium]], that is, it needs the help of such a support, lest it fall from its place.

paras.t: Et de substantia sua, id est facultatibus, et de filiis suis, et de nuptiis votum faciens, ut scilicet bona sua aut prolem consecret diis, aut alio modo de eis disponat, inquirit ab illa imagine, quid agere debeat. Non erubescit loqui cum illo, qui sine anima est, id est cum homine sculpto inanimato; et pro sanitate quidem obtinenda aut conservanda, infirmum, id est impotentem, deprecatur; et pro vita sua conservanda mortuum rogat, id est non viventem; et in adjutorium inutilem invocat; et pro itinere petit ab eo, qui ambulare non potest; et de acquirendo lucro, et de operando, et de omnium rerum eventu petit ab eo, qui in omnibus inutilis est: quia nec se, nec alios potest defendere aut juvare.
paras.en: And [[13:17|concerning his substance|Et de substantia sua]], that is, his means, [[13:17|and his children, or his marriage|et de filiis suis, et de nuptiis]], he [[13:17|maketh prayer to it|votum faciens]] [*votum faciens*, "making a vow"], namely to consecrate his goods or his offspring to the gods, or to dispose of them in some other way, and goes [[13:17|enquiring|inquirit]] of that image what he ought to do. [[13:17|And he is not ashamed to speak to that which hath no life|Non erubescit loqui cum illo, qui sine anima est]], that is, with a carved and lifeless man; [[13:18|And for health|et pro sanitate quidem]] to be obtained or preserved [[13:18|he maketh supplication to the weak|infirmum]], that is, the powerless; [[13:18|and for life|et pro vita sua]] to be preserved [[13:18|prayeth to that which is dead|mortuum rogat]], that is, to what is not living; [[13:18|and for help calleth upon that which is unprofitable|et in adjutorium inutilem invocat]]; [[13:19|And for a good journey he petitioneth him that cannot walk|et pro itinere petit ab eo, qui ambulare non potest]]; [[13:19|and for getting, and for working, and for the event of all things he asketh him|et de acquirendo lucro, et de operando, et de omnium rerum eventu petit ab eo]] [Denis's text adds *lucro*: "for getting gain"] [[13:19|that is unable to do any thing|qui in omnibus inutilis est]]: for it can neither defend nor help itself or others.

paras.t: Verumtamen Trismegistus erronee posuit statuas animatas, sensu et spiritu plenas, imbecillitatem aut incolumitatem hominibus facientes : quod penitus falsum est, prout in Summa contra gentiles, S. Thomas diffuse prosequitur ac demonstrat. Dæmones vero per idola dabant responsa, et hominibus multipliciter illudebant, ac quosdam fecerunt infirmos, qui ad invocationem deorum videbantur sanari, dæmonibus a vexatione cessantibus : quorum deceptiones per gloriosos Apostolos patefactæ sunt et convictæ.
paras.en: Trismegistus, however, erroneously held that statues are animate, full of sense and spirit, and bring weakness or soundness upon men: which is altogether false, as St. Thomas treats at length and demonstrates in the Summa contra Gentiles. But the demons gave answers through the idols and mocked men in many ways, and made some sick, who seemed to be healed at the invocation of the gods when the demons ceased from troubling them: and their deceits were laid bare and refuted by the glorious Apostles.

paras.t: Postremo, dictis in isto capitulo consonant quæ per Isaiam de ista materia plene scribuntur : Plastæ, inquit, idoli omnes nihil sunt. Ipsi sunt testes eorum, quia non vident, neque intelligunt, ut confundantur : et cetera quæ ibi sequuntur. Unde Psalmista : Oculos habent, et non videbunt ; aures habent, et non audient.
paras.en: Lastly, with what is said in this chapter agree the things that are written fully on this matter by Isaias: [[Is 44:9|The makers|Plastæ]], he says, [[Is 44:9|of idols are all of them nothing|idoli omnes nihil sunt]]. [[Is 44:9|They are their witnesses, that they do not see, nor understand, that they may be ashamed|Ipsi sunt testes eorum, quia non vident, neque intelligunt, ut confundantur]], and the rest that follows there [the margin gives Is. xliv, 9–20; Denis quotes only verse 9 and points to the rest, the passage on the carpenter who carves an idol from the wood he burns]. Whence the Psalmist: [[Ps 113:13|they have eyes and see not|Oculos habent, et non videbunt]]; [[Ps 113:14|They have ears and hear not|aures habent, et non audient]] [the margin gives Ps. cxiii, 5, 6, counting from the second part of the psalm (Ps. cxv in the Hebrew); in the Vulgate numbering used here these are Ps 113:13–14].

14.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI QUARTIDECIMI : ITERUM ALIUS NAVIGARE COGITANS.
14.title_en: Elucidation of the fourteenth chapter: Again, another designing to sail

paras.t: Vanitatem et impietatem idololatrarum, in marinis negotiis ac periculis idola invocantium, hic ostendit. Iterum alius navigare cogitans, et per feros, id est crudeles, quantum ad effectum, seu periculosos, fluctus iter facere incipiens, ligno portante se, fragilius lignum, id est idolum ligneum frangibilius nave qua vehitur, invocat: quod prorsus stultissimum est et iniquum, utpote non invocare Creatorem, qui navigantibus dedit rationem et artem fabricandi navigia, sed idolum humana arte formatum.
paras.en: Here he shows the vanity and impiety of idolaters who call upon idols in their business and perils at sea. [[14:1|Again, another designing to sail|Iterum alius navigare cogitans]], [[14:1|and beginning to make his voyage|iter facere incipiens]] [[14:1|through the raging|et per feros]], that is, cruel as to their effect, or dangerous, [[14:1|waves|fluctus]], [[14:1|calleth upon|invocat]] [[14:1|a piece of wood more frail|fragilius lignum]], that is, a wooden idol more breakable than the ship in which he is carried, [[14:1|than the wood that carrieth him|ligno portante se]]: which is utterly most foolish and wicked, since it means calling not upon the Creator, who gave seafarers the reason and the art of building ships, but upon an idol shaped by human art.

paras.t: Illud enim, scilicet idolum, cupiditas acquirendi excogitavit: id est, una causa formationis culturæque idolorum, avaritia fuit artificum, qui ut plus lucrarentur, fecerunt imagines multum formosas et quasi vitales. Hinc in Actis, Demetrius artifex idolorum, concitans suos collegas adversus Paulum: Scitis, inquit, quia de hoc artificio acquisitio est nobis. Et artifex sapientia, id est arte, sua practica formavit.
paras.en: [[14:2|For this|Illud enim]], namely the idol, [[14:2|the desire of gain devised|cupiditas acquirendi excogitavit]]: that is, one cause of the making and worship of idols was the avarice of the craftsmen, who, to make more profit, made images very beautiful and as it were alive. Hence in the Acts Demetrius, a maker of idols, stirring up his fellows against Paul: [[Acts 19:25|you know|Scitis]], he says, [[Acts 19:25|that our gain is by this trade|quia de hoc artificio acquisitio est nobis]]. [[14:2|and the workman|Et artifex]] [[14:2|by his skill|sapientia]], that is, by art, [[14:2|built it|sua practica formavit]] [Denis's text reads *sapientia sua practica formavit*, "fashioned it by his practical wisdom"; *sapientia*, "wisdom", is the word he glosses as "art"].

paras.t: Tu autem, Pater, gubernas providentia, id est, o Pater cœlestis, tu per providentiam tuam gubernas homines in terra et mari: quod patet, quoniam dedisti in mari viam, id est, per fundum maris Rubri hinc inde divisi, dedisti populo Israel iter, et inter fluctus semitam firmissimam, quando duxisti filios Israel per Jordanem, una parte aquarum Jordanis stante fixa in tumulo uno instar turris, et alia decurrente deorsum;
paras.en: [[14:3|But thy providence, O Father, governeth it|Tu autem, Pater, gubernas providentia]] [Denis's text reads *Tu autem, Pater, gubernas providentia*, "But thou, O Father, governest by providence"], that is, O heavenly Father, thou by thy providence governest men on land and sea: which is plain, [[14:3|for thou hast made a way even in the sea|quoniam dedisti in mari viam]], that is, thou gavest the people of Israel a road across the bed of the Red Sea, divided on this side and on that[[Ex 14:21||]][[Ex 14:22||]], [[14:3|and a most sure path among the waves|et inter fluctus semitam firmissimam]], when thou leddest the children of Israel through the Jordan, one part of the waters of the Jordan standing fixed in one heap like a tower, and the other running down[[Jos 3:15||]][[Jos 3:16||]];

paras.t: ostendens per illos miraculosos effectus, quoniam potens es ex omnibus sanare, id est ab omni periculo maris eripere, etiam si sine rate aliquis adeat mare, id est, quamvis aliquis tentet mare seu aquas perambulare pedester sine navigio: secundum quod Christus ambulavit super mare, et admirabile vas illud infinitæ misericordiæ Dei, contemplativissima atque sanctissima illa Maria Ægyptiaca.
paras.en: [[14:4|Shewing|ostendens]] by those miraculous effects [[14:4|that thou art able to save out of all things|quoniam potens es ex omnibus sanare]] [Denis's text has *sanare*, "to heal", for *salvare*], that is, to rescue from every peril of the sea, [[14:4|yea, though a man went to sea without art|etiam si sine rate aliquis adeat mare]] [Denis reads *sine rate*, "without a vessel", where the Vulgate has *sine arte*, "without art"; hence his gloss], that is, even if someone should try to walk on foot across the sea or the waters without a ship: as Christ walked upon the sea, and that wonderful vessel of the infinite mercy of God, the most contemplative and most holy Mary of Egypt.

paras.t: Sed ut non essent vacua, id est infructuosa, sapientiæ tuæ opera, scilicet divitiæ temporales ad usum ordinatæ humanum; propter hoc etiam et exiguo ligno, id est lignæ navi, credunt homines animas suas, id est se ipsos, sperantes adjutorio navis non periclitari in mari, et vitam suam exponentes eventibus maris valde incertis; et transeuntes mare ad vendendum merces quas deferunt secum, vel ad emendum ea, quæ alibi plus abundant, per ratem, id est per navem, liberati sunt a maris periculis.
paras.en: [[14:5|But that the works of thy wisdom|sapientiæ tuæ opera]] (namely temporal riches, ordered to human use) [[14:5|might not be idle|Sed ut non essent vacua]], that is, fruitless: [[14:5|therefore men also trust their lives|credunt homines animas suas]], that is, themselves, [[14:5|even to a little wood|propter hoc etiam et exiguo ligno]], that is, to a wooden ship, hoping not to come into danger at sea by the help of the ship, and exposing their life to the very uncertain chances of the sea; [[14:5|and passing over the sea|et transeuntes mare]] to sell the wares they carry with them, or to buy what is more plentiful elsewhere, [[14:5|by ship|per ratem]], that is, by a vessel [*ratis* is properly a raft], [[14:5|are saved|liberati sunt]] from the perils of the sea.

paras.t: Sequitur alia navigiorum ac navigationum utilitas. Sed et ab initio secundæ ætatis, quæ cœpit tempore Noe, quum perirent, id est, diluvio mergerentur, superbi gigantes: qui tunc præcipue erant rei, et magna causa diluvii; spes orbis terrarum, scilicet Noe et soboles sua, in quibus mansit genus humanum, et spes recuperationis illius, ad ratem, id est ad arcam, quæ et navis vocatur, confugiens ex Dei præcepto, remisit sæculo semen nativitatis, id est, post diluvium propagavit filios ac filias, per quas recuperata est hominum multitudo, quæ nativitas manu tua erat gubernata, id est, processum habuit et propagationem secundum potentiam et sapientiam tuam.
paras.en: There follows another benefit of ships and of voyages. [[14:6|And from the beginning also|Sed et ab initio]] of the second age, which began in the time of Noe, [[14:6|when the proud giants|superbi gigantes]] [[14:6|perished|quum perirent]], that is, were drowned by the flood (it was they who were then chiefly guilty, and a great cause of the flood), [[14:6|the hope of the world|spes orbis terrarum]], namely Noe and his offspring, in whom the human race remained, and the hope of its recovery, [[14:6|fleeing|confugiens]] at God's command [[14:6|to a vessel|ad ratem]], that is, to the ark, which is also called a ship, [[14:6|left to the world seed of generation|remisit sæculo semen nativitatis]], that is, after the flood brought forth sons and daughters, through whom the multitude of men was restored; [[14:6|which was governed by thy hand|quæ nativitas manu tua erat gubernata]] [Denis takes *quæ* of the generation, "which generation was governed by thy hand"; the Douay-Rheims refers it to the vessel], that is, it had its course and increase according to thy power and wisdom.

paras.t: Benedictum est enim lignum, id est suo modo laudibus dignum Deoque consecratum, per quod fit justitia, id est, tua justa ordinatio adimpletur, sicut exstitit arca, quæ fuit typus Ecclesiæ. In qua arca, principe Apostolorum testante, pauci, id est octo animæ seu personæ, salvæ factæ sunt per aquam: quæ aqua fuit Baptismi figura, per quem animæ electorum salvantur. Potissime autem benedictum est lignum salvificæ crucis, per quod Christus per viam cujusdam justitiæ redemit genus humanum, sustinens amarissimam mortis pœnam ex ardentissima caritate et obedientia summa, ad satisfaciendum pro humani generis culpis.
paras.en: [[14:7|For blessed is the wood|Benedictum est enim lignum]], that is, worthy of praise in its own way and consecrated to God, [[14:7|by which justice cometh|per quod fit justitia]], that is, by which thy just ordinance is fulfilled, as was the ark, which was a type of the Church. In this ark, as the prince of the Apostles testifies, [[1 Pet 3:20|a few, that is, eight souls|pauci, id est octo animæ]] or persons, [[1 Pet 3:20|were saved by water|salvæ factæ sunt per aquam]]: and that water was a figure of Baptism, by which the souls of the elect are saved[[1 Pet 3:21||]]. But most of all [[14:7|blessed is the wood|benedictum est lignum]] of the saving cross, by which Christ, by the way of a certain justice, redeemed the human race, enduring the most bitter penalty of death out of most burning charity and supreme obedience, to make satisfaction for the sins of the human race.

paras.t: Per manus autem quod fit idolum, id est, idolum quod fit per artificis manum, maledictum, id est vituperatum ac detestandum, est et ipsum idolum, et qui fecit illud, scilicet artifex, qui fecit illud ut coleretur: quia ille quidem, scilicet artifex, operatus est materiam tantorum facinorum, intentione perversa ac prava radice: illud autem idolum, quum esset fragile, id est faciliter corruptibile, deus cognominatus est: et ita fuit peccandi occasio, et idololatrandi materia.
paras.en: [[14:8|But the idol that is made by hands|Per manus autem quod fit idolum]], that is, the idol that is made by the craftsman's hand, [[14:8|is cursed|maledictum]], that is, reproved and to be detested, [[14:8|as well it|est et ipsum idolum]], [[14:8|as he that made it|et qui fecit illud]], namely the craftsman, who made it to be worshipped: [[14:8|he because|quia ille quidem]], namely the craftsman, [[14:8|he made it|operatus est]], that is, wrought the matter of such great crimes, with a perverse intention and from an evil root; [[14:8|and it because being frail|illud autem idolum, quum esset fragile]], that is, easily corrupted, [[14:8|it is called a god|deus cognominatus est]]: and so it was an occasion of sin and the matter of idolatry.

paras.t: Similiter autem odio, id est odibiles, Deo, secundum præsentem justitiam, ut dictum est supra, sunt impius et impietas ejus: impius propter impietatem, et impietas propter se ipsam. Unde per Isaiam testatur: Festivitates vestras odivit anima mea. Et per Jeremiam dicit: Facta est mihi hereditas mea quasi leo in silva; dedit contra me vocem suam, ideo odivi eam. Atque per Osee dicitur: Exosos habui eos, propter malitiam adinventionum ipsorum.
paras.en: [[14:9|But to God|Deo]] [[14:9|the wicked and his wickedness|sunt impius et impietas ejus]] [[14:9|are hateful alike|Similiter autem odio]], that is, odious, according to present justice, as was said above: the wicked man because of his wickedness, and the wickedness for its own sake. Hence he testifies through Isaias: [[Is 1:14|My soul hateth your new moons, and your solemnities|Festivitates vestras odivit anima mea]] [Denis's text has only "your festivals my soul hath hated"]. And through Jeremias he says: [[Jer 12:8|My inheritance is become to me as a lion in the wood: it hath cried out against me, therefore have I hated it.|Facta est mihi hereditas mea quasi leo in silva; dedit contra me vocem suam, ideo odivi eam]]. And through Osee it is said: [[Osee 9:15|I hated them|Exosos habui eos]], [[Osee 9:15|for the wickedness of their devices|propter malitiam adinventionum ipsorum]].

paras.t: Etenim quod factum est, scilicet idolum, vel potius dæmonium in idolo habitans ac respondens, cum illo qui fecit idolum manu propria, aut per artificem fieri procuravit aut jussit, tormenta patietur æterna, tanto acerbiora, quanto gravius scelus est idololatria.
paras.en: [[14:10|For that which is made|Etenim quod factum est]], namely the idol, or rather the devil dwelling in the idol and giving answers from it, [[14:10|together with him that made it|cum illo qui fecit]] with his own hand, or procured or ordered it to be made by a craftsman, [[14:10|shall suffer torments|tormenta patietur]], and eternal ones, the more bitter as idolatry is the graver crime.

paras.t: Propter hoc et in idolis nationum non erit respectus: id est, Deus oculo pietatis et indulgentiæ non adspiciet idola, id est dæmonia eis præsidentia, juxta quod scriptum est: Quoniam omnes dii gentium dæmonia. Indurati enim sunt dæmones, et irremissibilia sunt eorum peccata; et peccant gravissime, procurantes ac usurpantes sibi divinos honores, avertentesque a Creatoris obsequio creaturas rationales.
paras.en: [[14:11|Therefore there shall be no respect had even to the idols of the Gentiles|Propter hoc et in idolis nationum non erit respectus]]: that is, God will not look with the eye of kindness and pardon upon the idols, that is, upon the devils who preside over them, as it is written: [[Ps 95:5|For all the gods of the Gentiles are devils|Quoniam omnes dii gentium dæmonia]]. For the devils are hardened, and their sins are unforgivable; and they sin most grievously, procuring and usurping divine honours for themselves, and turning rational creatures away from the service of the Creator.

paras.t: Quoniam creaturæ Dei in odium factæ sunt. Istud ad litteram, juxta textus connexionem, de dæmonibus dictum videtur: qui secundum suam bonam naturam creaturæ sunt Dei; sed concomitanter, et per propriæ voluntatis perversitatem, facti sunt in odium, quia se ipsos fecerunt Deo odibiles, et eos quos vincunt et ad idololatriam trahunt, Deo faciunt odiosos. Et in tentationem animæ hominum: quia ex sua invidia assidue tentant animas, ad eam beatitudinem quam ipsi perdiderunt creatas. Unde præhabitum est: Invidia autem diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum. Et in muscipulam pedibus insipientium, id est in deceptionem affectibus ac gressibus iniquorum, qui capiuntur, et irretiti tenentur a malignis spiritibus. Quibus qui consentiunt, vere sunt insipientes, quia atrocissimis hostibus suis præbent consensum: quod agendo occidunt atque æternæ damnationi adstringunt se ipsos. Sapientibus vero et justis tentamenta vincentibus, facti sunt dæmones in exercitium et coronam.
paras.en: [[14:11|because the creatures of God are turned to an abomination|Quoniam creaturæ Dei in odium factæ sunt]] [*in odium*, literally "into hatred"]. Literally, according to the connexion of the text, this seems to be said of the devils: who by their good nature are creatures of God; but consequently, and through the perversity of their own will, they have been turned to an abomination, because they have made themselves hateful to God, and those whom they overcome and draw into idolatry they make odious to God. [[14:11|and a temptation to the souls of men|Et in tentationem animæ hominum]]: because out of their envy they continually tempt souls, which were created for that beatitude which they themselves have lost. Hence it was said before: [[Wis 2:24|But by the envy of the devil, death came into the world|Invidia autem diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum]]. [[14:11|and a snare to the feet of the unwise|Et in muscipulam pedibus insipientium]] [*muscipula* is properly a mousetrap], that is, a deception to the affections and steps of the wicked, who are caught and held entangled by the evil spirits. Those who consent to them are truly unwise, since they give their consent to their most cruel enemies: by doing which they slay themselves and bind themselves over to eternal damnation. But to the wise and just, who overcome their temptations, the devils have become a means of exercise and a crown.

paras.t: Insuper verba hæc per se sumpta, sic possunt intelligi, quod creaturæ istæ hujus mundi inferioris, puta divitiæ, deliciæ et honores, sensuumque objecta, factæ sunt in odium, et in tentationem animarum hominum, et in muscipulam pedibus insipientium: quia in istis rebus creatis est aliquid boni delectabilis, utilis, et honesti, videlicet aliquid pulchritudinis, et utilitatis, et voluptatis, et honorabilitatis, per quod appetibiles sunt, et humanum alliciunt appetitum. Sapientes vero et virtuosi, non afficiuntur ad eas, nec eis utuntur, nisi secundum legem divinam, rectamque rationem: ideo creaturæ hæ eis deserviunt atque proficuæ sunt. Homines vero carnales, cupidi, libidinosi, ambitiosi attrahuntur ab eis, sicut mures alliciuntur a nucleo nucis in muscipula positæ. Non enim considerant eas per comparationem ad Deum, ad ultimum finem, ad animarum suarum salutem, sed solum quoad propriam voluptatem, aut transitoriam utilitatem, seu temporalem honorem. Ideo sicut mures capiuntur muscipula, sic ipsi per objecta creata, circumventione diabolica. Hinc fertur in Job: Abscondita est in terra pedica ejus, et decepula ejus juxta semitam. Ad quod pertinere mystice potest illud in Psalmo: Cogitaverunt supplantare gressus meos, et funes extenderunt in laqueum; juxta iter scandalum posuerunt mihi.
paras.en: Moreover, these words taken by themselves can be understood thus: that the creatures of this lower world, such as riches, delights and honours, and the objects of the senses, [[14:11|are turned to an abomination|factæ sunt in odium]], [[14:11|and a temptation to the souls of men|et in tentationem animarum hominum]], [[14:11|and a snare to the feet of the unwise|et in muscipulam pedibus insipientium]]: because in these created things there is something of the good that is delightful, useful and honourable [*honestum*, the good that is worthy in itself], namely something of beauty, of usefulness, of pleasure and of honour, through which they are desirable and allure the human appetite. The wise and virtuous are not attached to them, and do not use them except according to the divine law and right reason: so these creatures serve them and are profitable to them. But carnal men, the covetous, the lustful and the ambitious, are drawn by them as mice are lured by the kernel of a nut set in a mousetrap. For they do not consider them in relation to God, to the last end, to the salvation of their souls, but only as regards their own pleasure, or passing usefulness, or temporal honour. So, as mice are caught by a mousetrap, so are they by created objects, through the devil's snares. Hence it is said in Job: [[Job 18:10|A gin is hidden for him in the earth, and his trap upon the path.|Abscondita est in terra pedica ejus, et decepula ejus juxta semitam]]. To which may mystically belong that in the Psalm: [[Ps 139:5|Who have proposed to supplant my steps|Cogitaverunt supplantare gressus meos]], [[Ps 139:6|And they have stretched out cords for a snare: they have laid for me a stumblingblock by the wayside|et funes extenderunt in laqueum; juxta iter scandalum posuerunt mihi]].

paras.t: Initium enim fornicationis spiritualis, scilicet superstitionis idololatricæ, est exquisitio, id est excogitatio, procuratio, formatio, idolorum; et adinventio illorum corruptio vitæ est, id est infectio et maculatio conversationis humanæ, et directe formaliterque destructio vitæ caritatis ac gratiæ, quæ consistit in amore et cultu summi boni: cui vitæ directe contrariatur amor et adoratio idolorum. Denique, quum omnis anima sit sponsa Dei, aut adultera diaboli, et desponsatio illa cum Deo per omne mortale peccatum tollatur: constat quod omne peccatum mortale sit fornicatio spiritualis, id est recessus mentis a Sponso cœlesti, et unio quædam cum diabolo, ac constupratio mentis ab illo. Hinc avaritiam appellat Apostolus idolorum servitutem. Specialissime tamen idololatria est fornicatio spiritualis, quoniam creaturam pro Creatore assumit in Deum. Similiter hæretica pravitate corrumpi, est spiritualiter fornicari.
