paras.en: [[14:12|For the beginning of fornication|Initium enim fornicationis]] (spiritual fornication, namely idolatrous superstition) [[14:12|is the devising|est exquisitio]], that is, the thinking out, procuring and fashioning, [[14:12|of idols|idolorum]]; [[14:12|and the invention of them is the corruption of life|et adinventio illorum corruptio vitæ est]], that is, the infection and staining of human conduct, and directly and formally the destruction of the life of charity and grace, which consists in the love and worship of the highest good: to which life the love and adoration of idols is directly contrary. Lastly, since every soul is either the bride of God or the adulteress of the devil, and that espousal with God is taken away by every mortal sin, it is clear that every mortal sin is a spiritual fornication, that is, a withdrawal of the mind from the heavenly Bridegroom, and a kind of union with the devil, and a defilement of the mind by him. Hence the Apostle calls avarice the service of idols[[Col 3:5||]]. Yet idolatry is spiritual fornication most especially, since it takes the creature for God in place of the Creator. Likewise to be corrupted by heretical depravity is to commit spiritual fornication.

paras.t: Non enim erant ab initio: quia in prima mundi ætate non erant, propter recentem memoriam creationis mundi, ex qua patuit cunctis unum esse verum Deum, solum adorandum; neque erunt in perpetuum. Nam per Christi Apostolos et eorum discipulos, idololatria pro maxima parte exstincta fuit. Nunquam tamen ex quo incepit, fuit in toto destructa: nam et in aquilonaribus quibusdam partibus mundi viget adhuc, ut in libro de Fide et legibus refert Guillelmus Parisiensis. Sed et post Mahometi detestabilem legem, imo potius fæcem et sordem, multum invaluit idololatria in populo Tartarorum. Sed ante sæculi finem totaliter destruenda asseritur, præsertim quando Antichristo occiso, totum pene genus humanum convertetur ad Christum, paucissimis induratis Antichristi demptis ministris: qui tamen non putantur fore idololatræ, quia Antichristus idololatriam reprobabit, simulans se Moysis legem servare. Et de illis dixit Apostolus: Quum dixerint, Pax et securitas, repentinus eis superveniet interitus. Sicque verificatur quod subditur: neque erunt in perpetuum, id est, semper non erunt.
paras.en: [[14:13|For neither were they from the beginning|Non enim erant ab initio]]: because in the first age of the world they did not exist, on account of the fresh memory of the creation of the world, from which it was plain to all that there is one true God, who alone is to be adored; [[14:13|neither shall they be for ever|neque erunt in perpetuum]]. For through the Apostles of Christ and their disciples idolatry was for the most part extinguished. Yet since it began it has never been wholly destroyed: for it still flourishes in certain northern parts of the world, as William of Paris relates in his book On Faith and Laws. And after the detestable law of Mahomet, or rather its dregs and filth, idolatry grew very strong among the people of the Tartars. But it is held that it is to be wholly destroyed before the end of the world, especially when, Antichrist having been slain, almost the whole human race will be converted to Christ, except for a very few hardened ministers of Antichrist: and these, however, are not thought likely to be idolaters, since Antichrist will condemn idolatry, pretending to keep the law of Moses. And of them the Apostle said: [[1 Thess 5:3|when they shall say: Peace and security; then shall sudden destruction come upon them|Quum dixerint, Pax et securitas, repentinus eis superveniet interitus]]. And so what follows is made true: [[14:13|neither shall they be for ever|neque erunt in perpetuum]], that is, they will not be always.

paras.t: Supervacuitas enim hominum, id est vanitas et defectus veræ sapientiæ, hæc adinvenit in orbem terrarum, et ideo brevis illorum, scilicet idolorum, finis inventus est. Philo enim creditur libri hujus conscriptor: qui Alexandriæ habitavit tempore quo beatissimus princeps Apostolorum Romæ sedit, et Marcus in Alexandria prædicavit; tuncque per gloriosos Apostolos et eorum cooperatores, idololatria undique valde exstinguebatur.
paras.en: [[14:14|For by the vanity of men|Supervacuitas enim hominum]], that is, vanity and the lack of true wisdom, [[14:14|they came into the world|hæc adinvenit in orbem terrarum]] [Denis reads *adinvenit*, "devised these", for *advenit*, "came"], [[14:14|and therefore they|et ideo brevis illorum]] (namely the idols) [[14:14|shall be found to come shortly to an end|finis inventus est]]. For Philo is believed to have been the writer of this book: who lived at Alexandria at the time when the most blessed prince of the Apostles held his see at Rome and Mark preached in Alexandria; and then, through the glorious Apostles and their fellow workers, idolatry was being greatly extinguished everywhere.

paras.t: Consequenter docetur qualiter idololatria sumpsit exordium. Acerbo enim luctu dolens pater de morte filii sui ante se defuncti, cito sibi rapti, id est per mortem subtracti, filii fecit imaginem pro sua consolatione et filii veneratione; et illum qui tunc quasi, id est vere ut homo mortuus fuerat: sicque, Quasi, hic denotat veritatem, non similitudinem tantum; nunc, scilicet facta ejus imagine, tanquam deum, quum non esset aliquid habens deitatis, colere cœpit, propter aliquam eminentiam quæ videbatur esse in filio, quando vixit, et constituit inter servos suos sacra et sacrificia. Per sacra, intelliguntur festa, templa, vel altaria, aut ritus colendi, consecrata filio mortuo aut ejus imagini, cui sacrificia jussit pater offerri.
paras.en: Next he teaches how idolatry took its beginning. [[14:15|For a father being afflicted with bitter grief|Acerbo enim luctu dolens pater]] at the death of his son, who died before him, [[14:15|who was quickly taken away|cito sibi rapti]], that is, taken from him by death, [[14:15|made to himself the image of his son|filii fecit imaginem]] for his own consolation and the veneration of his son; [[14:15|and him who then|et illum qui tunc]] (*as*, that is, truly as) [[14:15|had died as a man|homo mortuus fuerat]]: and so *as* here denotes the reality, not a likeness only [*quasi* can mean "as if" or "as being"]; [[14:15|he began now to worship|colere cœpit]] (*now*, that is, once his image had been made) [[14:15|as a god|tanquam deum]], though he had nothing of godhead, because of some eminence which seemed to be in the son while he lived, [[14:15|and appointed him rites and sacrifices among his servants|et constituit inter servos suos sacra et sacrificia]]. By *rites* [*sacra*, "sacred things"] are meant feasts, temples or altars, or ceremonies of worship, consecrated to the dead son or to his image, to which the father ordered sacrifices to be offered.

paras.t: Deinde interveniente tempore, convalescente iniqua consuetudine taliter sacrificandi, hic error superstitiosus colendi defunctum, aut ejus imaginem, tanquam lex custoditus est, et tyrannorum imperio colebantur figmenta, videlicet idola. Nam quidam tyranni jusserunt sui ipsorum imagines coli, ut subditur.
paras.en: [[14:16|Then, in process of time|Deinde interveniente tempore]], [[14:16|wicked custom prevailing|convalescente iniqua consuetudine]] of sacrificing in this way, [[14:16|this error|hic error]], the superstitious error of worshipping the dead man or his image, [[14:16|was kept as a law|tanquam lex custoditus est]], [[14:16|and statues were worshipped by the commandment of tyrants|et tyrannorum imperio colebantur figmenta]] [*figmenta*, "things fashioned"], namely idols. For certain tyrants ordered images of themselves to be worshipped, as follows.

paras.t: Et hos tyrannos, quos in palam, id est præsentialiter, homines subditi eis honorare non poterant, propter hoc quod longe essent, id est, ob hoc quod longa locorum distantia erant absentes ab invicem, e longinquo figura illorum allata, id est imagine talium tyrannorum apportata ad subditos longe absentes, evidentem imaginem regis, quem honorare volebant, fecerunt, juxta formam imaginis eis missæ; ut illum qui aberat, tanquam præsentem colerent sua sollicitudine.
paras.en: [[14:17|And those|Et hos]] tyrants [[14:17|whom men could not honour in presence|quos in palam]], that is, face to face (the men being their subjects), [[14:17|because they dwelt far off|propter hoc quod longe essent]], that is, because they were absent from one another by a long distance between their places, [[14:17|they brought their resemblance from afar|e longinquo figura illorum allata]], that is, an image of such tyrants having been brought to their subjects far away, [[14:17|and made an express image of the king, whom they had a mind to honour|evidentem imaginem regis, quem honorare volebant, fecerunt]], according to the form of the image sent to them, [[14:17|that by this their diligence, they might honour as present, him that was absent|ut illum qui aberat, tanquam præsentem colerent sua sollicitudine]].

paras.t: Auxit autem idololatriam pulchritudo imaginum. Ideo subditur: Provexit autem, id est promovit, ad horum idolorum culturam et hos qui ignorabant, id est simplices et indoctos, nescientes nihil esse numinis in illis figmentis, artificis eximia diligentia ad faciendum formosam imaginem.
paras.en: The beauty of the images increased idolatry. So it is added: [[14:18|helped to set forward|Provexit autem]], that is, advanced, [[14:18|to the worshipping of these|ad horum idolorum culturam]] idols [[14:18|the ignorant|et hos qui ignorabant]], that is, the simple and unlearned, not knowing that there was nothing of the divine in those figments, [[14:18|the singular diligence also of the artificer|artificis eximia diligentia]] in making a beautiful image.

paras.t: Ille enim artifex volens placere illi qui se assumpsit, id est principi a quo inductus fuit ad formandum imaginem, elaboravit arte sua pictoria, ut similitudinem in melius figuraret, id est, idolum faceret pulchrius quo valebat.
paras.en: [[14:19|For he|Ille enim]], the artificer, [[14:19|being willing to please him that employed him|volens placere illi qui se assumpsit]], that is, the prince by whom he was engaged to fashion the image, [[14:19|laboured with all his art|elaboravit arte sua pictoria]] [Denis's text has *arte sua pictoria*, "with his painter's art"] [[14:19|to make the resemblance in the best manner|ut similitudinem in melius figuraret]], that is, to make the idol as beautiful as he could.

paras.t: Multitudo autem hominum indoctorum abducta per speciem operis, id est per pulchritudinem idoli facti decepta, eum qui ante tempus, scilicet nondum facta ejus imagine, tanquam homo honoratus fuit cultu duliæ tanquam parens, aut princeps, seu judex, nunc deum æstimaverunt, facta ejus imagine, impendentes ei latriæ cultum.
paras.en: [[14:20|And the multitude of men|Multitudo autem hominum]], unlearned men, [[14:20|carried away by the beauty of the work|abducta per speciem operis]], that is, deceived by the beauty of the idol that was made, [[14:20|took him now for a god|nunc deum æstimaverunt]] once his image had been made, paying him the worship of latria [the worship due to God alone]: him who [[14:20|that little before|eum qui ante tempus]], that is, while his image was not yet made, [[14:20|was but honoured as a man|tanquam homo honoratus fuit]] with the worship of dulia [the honour paid to creatures], as a parent, or prince, or judge.

paras.t: Et hæc fuit vitæ humanæ deceptio, quoniam aut affectui, aut regibus deservientes homines, id est, subditi cupientes regibus suis placere, vel adulari, aut propria commoda consequi ex idolorum formatione aut cultu, ut dictum est, incommunicabile nomen, id est Deitatem, seu ejus appellationem, quæ pluribus substantialiter diversis convenire non potest, lapidibus et lignis, id est idolis ligneis ac saxeis, imposuerunt.
paras.en: [[14:21|And this was the occasion of deceiving human life|Et hæc fuit vitæ humanæ deceptio]], [[14:21|for men serving either their affection, or their kings|quoniam aut affectui, aut regibus deservientes homines]], that is, subjects desiring to please their kings or to flatter them, or to gain their own advantage from the making or worship of idols, as has been said, [[14:21|gave|imposuerunt]] [[14:21|the incommunicable name|incommunicabile nomen]], that is, the Godhead, or its name, which cannot belong to several beings substantially different, [[14:21|to stones and wood|lapidibus et lignis]], that is, to idols of wood and stone.

paras.t: Verumtamen per quamdam imitationem et participationem divinarum proprietatum, aliqui appellati sunt dii, imo et deus, sicut ad Moysen Dominus dixit: Constitui te deum Pharaonis. Et Christus in Evangelio: Illos, inquit, dixit deos, ad quos sermo Dei factus est. Et Psalmista: Deus stetit in synagoga deorum. Sicque in lege Moysis præsidentes ac judices, dii vocantur, juxta illud in Exodo: Diis non detrahes; et rursus ibidem, Dominus domus applicabitur ad deos. Vera autem deitas et cultus latriæ creaturis nequeunt convenire. Propter quod Dominus ait per Isaiam: Ego Dominus: hoc est nomen meum: gloriam meam alteri non dabo, et laudem meam sculptilibus. Ideoque incommunicabilitatem divini nominis tangit Psalmista, dicendo: Quoniam quis Deus præter Deum nostrum? Unde asserit Jeremias: Stultus factus est omnis homo a scientia sua, confusus est omnis conflator in sculptili, quia mendax conflatio ejus, nec spiritus est in eis. Vana sunt opera ejus, et risu digna; in tempore visitationis suæ peribunt. Et denuo: Dii, inquit, qui non fecerunt cœlum et terram, pereant de terra.
paras.en: Yet by a certain imitation and sharing of the divine properties some have been called gods, and even god, as the Lord said to Moses: [[Ex 7:1|I have appointed thee the god of Pharao|Constitui te deum Pharaonis]]. And Christ in the Gospel: [[John 10:35|he called them|Illos]], he says, [[John 10:35|gods to whom the word of God was spoken|dixit deos, ad quos sermo Dei factus est]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 81:1|God hath stood in the congregation of gods|Deus stetit in synagoga deorum]]. And so in the law of Moses rulers and judges are called gods, according to that in Exodus: [[Ex 22:28|Thou shalt not speak ill of the gods|Diis non detrahes]]; and again in the same place: [[Ex 22:8|the master of the house shall be brought to the gods|Dominus domus applicabitur ad deos]]. But true godhead and the worship of latria cannot belong to creatures. For which reason the Lord says through Isaias: [[Is 42:8|I the Lord, this is my name: I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to graven things.|Ego Dominus: hoc est nomen meum: gloriam meam alteri non dabo, et laudem meam sculptilibus]]. And therefore the Psalmist touches on the incommunicability of the divine name, saying: [[Ps 17:32|For who is God|Quoniam quis Deus]] [[Ps 17:32|but our God|præter Deum nostrum]]? Hence Jeremias declares: [[Jer 51:17|Every man is become foolish by his knowledge: every founder is confounded by his idol, for what he hath cast is a lie, and there is no breath in them.|Stultus factus est omnis homo a scientia sua, confusus est omnis conflator in sculptili, quia mendax conflatio ejus, nec spiritus est in eis]] [[Jer 51:18|They are vain works, and worthy to be laughed at, in the time of their visitation they shall perish.|Vana sunt opera ejus, et risu digna; in tempore visitationis suæ peribunt]] [the margin gives Jer. x, 14, 15 and li, 17, 18: the same words stand in both places, and Denis's wording is that of Jer 51:17–18][[Jer 10:14||]][[Jer 10:15||]]. And again: [[Jer 10:11|The gods|Dii]], he says, [[Jer 10:11|that have not made heaven and earth, let them perish from the earth|qui non fecerunt cœlum et terram, pereant de terra]].

paras.t: Deinceps tanguntur facinora idololatriam consecuta. Et non suffecerat errasse eos circa Dei scientiam: id est, perversitati idololatrarum satis non fuit, tam insipienter sentire de Deo, seu nomen ejus communicare vilibus rebus; sed et in magno viventes inscitiæ bello, id est in grandi insipientia, per quam Deo, et omni veritati ac honestati, veræque beatitudini repugnabant, tot et tam magna mala, id est tam enormia scelera, quæ mox exprimentur, pacem appellant, id est, salubria reputant sibi.
paras.en: Next the crimes that followed upon idolatry are touched on. [[14:22|And it was not enough for them to err about the knowledge of God|Et non suffecerat errasse eos circa Dei scientiam]]: that is, it was not enough for the perversity of the idolaters to think so foolishly of God, or to share his name with base things; [[14:22|but whereas they lived in a great war of ignorance|sed et in magno viventes inscitiæ bello]], that is, in great folly, by which they fought against God, and against all truth and honour, and true beatitude, [[14:22|they call|appellant]] [[14:22|so many and so great evils|tot et tam magna mala]], that is, such enormous crimes, which will shortly be set out, [[14:22|peace|pacem]], that is, they reckon them wholesome for themselves.

paras.t: Aut enim filios suos sacrificantes idolis: quibus quandoque propriam sobolem offerebant in holocaustum: aut obscura sacrificia facientes: sicut in sacris Isidis Ægyptiæ et Cereris, quæ fiebant nocturnis temporibus; aut insaniæ plenas vigilias habentes: quia in nocturnis suis vigiliis turpissima et insensatissima opera commiserunt; et interdum sacerdotes reddebantur arrepticii, ex diabolico spiritu loquentes, et quasi vaticinantes, seu quædam occulta pandentes;
paras.en: [[14:23|For either they sacrifice their own children|Aut enim filios suos sacrificantes]] to idols, to whom they sometimes offered their own offspring as a holocaust; [[14:23|or use hidden sacrifices|aut obscura sacrificia facientes]], as in the rites of the Egyptian Isis and of Ceres, which were performed at night-time; [[14:23|or keep watches full of madness|aut insaniæ plenas vigilias habentes]]: because in their night watches they committed the foulest and most senseless deeds; and at times the priests became possessed, speaking from the devil's spirit and as it were prophesying, or revealing certain hidden things;

paras.t: neque vitam, neque nuptias mundas jam custodiunt: quoniam vitam suam spiritualibus atque carnalibus maculant vitiis, et connubia per adulteria fœdant. Sed alius alium per invidiam occidit, aut adulterans contristat, polluendo conjugem ejus;
paras.en: [[14:24|So that now they neither keep life, nor marriage undefiled|neque vitam, neque nuptias mundas jam custodiunt]]: since they stain their life with spiritual and carnal vices, and befoul marriages by adulteries. [[14:24|but one killeth another through envy, or grieveth him by adultery|Sed alius alium per invidiam occidit, aut adulterans contristat]], by defiling his wife;

paras.t: et omnia, quæ sequuntur peccata, commixta sunt: sanguis, id est effusio sanguinis, homicidium, furtum et fictio, corruptio, id est violatio fidelitatis, seu defloratio virginum, et infidelitas, turbatio et perjurium, tumultus, id est inquietudo passionum, sive seditio, bonorum Dei immemoratio, id est oblivio beneficiorum Dei, animarum inquinatio, nativitatis immutatio, id est innaturalis et sodomitica commixtio, aut animalium diversarum specierum illicita conjunctio, nuptiarum inconstantia, id est repudiatio contoralis, vel mutua uxorum mutatio ad fruendum, inordinatio mœchiæ, id est adulterationis, et impudicitiæ.
paras.en: [[14:25|And all things|et omnia]], namely the sins that follow, [[14:25|are mingled together|commixta sunt]]: [[14:25|blood|sanguis]], that is, the shedding of blood, [[14:25|murder, theft, and dissimulation|homicidium, furtum et fictio]], [[14:25|corruption|corruptio]], that is, the violation of fidelity, or the deflowering of virgins, [[14:25|and unfaithfulness, tumults and perjury|et infidelitas, turbatio et perjurium]], [[14:25|disquieting|tumultus]], that is, the restlessness of the passions, or sedition, [[14:25|of the good|bonorum]] [[14:26|forgetfulness of God|Dei immemoratio]], that is, forgetfulness of the benefits of God [Denis takes *bonorum* with what follows, "forgetfulness of the good things of God"; the Douay-Rheims reads "disquieting of the good, forgetfulness of God"], [[14:26|defiling of souls|animarum inquinatio]], [[14:26|changing of nature|nativitatis immutatio]] [literally "changing of birth"], that is, unnatural and sodomitical intercourse, or the unlawful coupling of animals of different species, [[14:26|disorder in marriage|nuptiarum inconstantia]], that is, the putting away of a wife, or the mutual exchange of wives for enjoyment, [[14:26|and the irregularity of adultery|inordinatio mœchiæ]], that is, of adulterous intercourse, [[14:26|and uncleanness|et impudicitiæ]].

paras.t: Infandorum, id est innominandorum, enim idolorum cultura, omnis mali causa est: quia omnia vitia possunt oriri, et quasi oriuntur ex ea, similiter multa mala pœnalia in præsenti et in futuro; et initium: non quod sit prius tempore omnibus aliis vitiis, quia, ut patuit, in prima mundi ætate non fuit; sed gravitate quodammodo primum est, et in certo genere; et finis, id est consummatio vitiorum, quia per alia vitia merentur homines tandem in illud corruere. Et ita secundum diversas considerationes, vocatur causa, initium, et finis omnium vitiorum: et eadem specie, non numero, idololatria hæc recipit prædicata.
paras.en: [[14:27|For the worship|cultura]] [[14:27|of abominable|Infandorum]], that is, not to be named, [[14:27|idols|enim idolorum]] [[14:27|is the cause|omnis mali causa est]] of all evil: because all vices can arise, and as it were do arise, from it, and likewise many penal evils, in the present and in the future; [[14:27|and the beginning|et initium]]: not that it is prior in time to all other vices, since, as has appeared, it did not exist in the first age of the world; but in gravity it is in a manner first, and in a certain kind; [[14:27|and end|et finis]], that is, the consummation of vices, because through other vices men at last deserve to fall into it. And so, under different considerations, it is called the cause, beginning and end of all vices: and it is idolatry one in species, not in number, that receives these predicates [that is, not the same single act of idolatry is at once cause, beginning and end].

paras.t: Aut enim dum lætantur idololatræ, insaniunt, irrationaliter aut arrepticie se habendo; aut certe vaticinantur falsa, ex inspiratione diabolica, aut vivunt injuste, aut perjurant cito.
paras.en: [[14:28|For either|Aut enim]] the idolaters [[14:28|are mad|insaniunt]] [[14:28|when they are merry|dum lætantur]], behaving irrationally or like men possessed; [[14:28|or they prophesy lies|aut certe vaticinantur falsa]] by diabolical inspiration, [[14:28|or they live unjustly, or easily forswear themselves|aut vivunt injuste, aut perjurant cito]].

paras.t: Dum enim confidunt in idolis, quæ sine intellectu et sine anima sunt, male jurantes noceri se non sperant, id est, non putant, nec metuunt se lædendos aut puniendos.
paras.en: [[14:29|For whilst they trust in idols|Dum enim confidunt in idolis]], [[14:29|which are without life|quæ sine intellectu et sine anima sunt]] [Denis's text reads "without understanding and without life"], [[14:29|though they swear amiss, they look not to be hurt|male jurantes noceri se non sperant]], that is, they do not think or fear that they will be harmed or punished.

paras.t: Utraque ergo illis evenient digne: id est, bina supplicia merito patientur, unum pro idololatria, aliud pro perjurio; vel pro perjurio, et pro eo quod putabant se perjurare ac peccare impune.
paras.en: [[14:30|But for both these things they shall be justly punished|Utraque ergo illis evenient digne]] [literally "both things shall befall them deservedly"]: that is, they will deservedly suffer two punishments, one for idolatry, the other for perjury; or for perjury, and for thinking that they could forswear themselves and sin with impunity.

paras.t: Non enim jurantium est virtus, id est, jurare non est commendabile, nec juranti imputatur in laudem jurare. Ideo ait Salvator: Ego dico vobis, non jurare omnino. Non quod jurare sit semper illicitum, sed quia ruinæ vicinum est, nec sine rationabili aut necessaria causa assumendum: pro qua, si admittatur, actus virtutis est, quæ latria nuncupatur. Sic enim juravit Apostolus: Ego, inquiens, Deum testem invoco in animam meam; et iterum, Deus mihi testis est. Unde scriptum est: Dominum Deum timebis, et per nomen ejus jurabis. Sed peccantium pœna perambulat semper, id est, pœna iniquorum continuo augmentatur, injustorum prævaricationem, id est, per hoc quod prævaricantur quæ justa sunt, videlicet divina præcepta. Pœna quoque peccantium est, quod demerito culpæ prioris permittuntur cadere in sequens peccatum: et ita hæc perambulat semper, id est, assidue crescit, dum de vitiis cadunt in vitia, et de minoribus ad majora.
paras.en: [[14:31|For it is not the power of them, by whom they swear|Non enim jurantium est virtus]] [Denis reads *jurantium*, "of those who swear", for *juratorum*, "of those sworn by", and takes *virtus* as "virtue": swearing is no virtue], that is, to swear is not commendable, nor is swearing counted to the swearer's praise. So the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:34|I say to you not to swear at all|Ego dico vobis, non jurare omnino]]. Not that swearing is always unlawful, but because it is close to ruin, and is not to be undertaken without a reasonable or necessary cause: for such a cause, if it is admitted, it is an act of the virtue that is called latria [the worship of God; the oath is an act of religion]. For so the Apostle swore: [[2 Cor 1:23|I|Ego]], he says, [[2 Cor 1:23|call God to witness upon my soul|Deum testem invoco in animam meam]]; and again: [[Rom 1:9|God is my witness|Deus mihi testis est]][[Phil 1:8||]]. Hence it is written: [[Deut 6:13|Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God|Dominum Deum timebis]], [[Deut 6:13|and thou shalt swear by his name|et per nomen ejus jurabis]]. [[14:31|but the just vengeance of sinners always punisheth|Sed peccantium pœna perambulat semper]] [*perambulat*, literally "walks through" or "goes about", which Denis takes as "keeps advancing"], that is, the punishment of the wicked is continually increased, [[14:31|the transgression of the unjust|injustorum prævaricationem]], that is, through their transgressing what is just, namely the divine precepts. It is also a punishment of sinners that, by the demerit of an earlier fault, they are allowed to fall into a further sin: and so this punishment *goes about always*, that is, grows continually, as they fall from vice into vice, and from lesser to greater.

paras.t: Amplius, sicut Magister in historiis refert, Nemrod compulit homines ignem adorare. Judæi autem dicunt, quod Ismael fecit de luto simulacra. Alii dicunt, quod Ninus rex Assyriorum, de morte Beli patris sui vehementissime dolens, fecit ei imaginem, quam coli præcepit, et confugientibus ad eam tribuit libertatem. De ista materia, et de origine ac reprobatione idololatriæ, subtiliter scribit Lactantius in libro adversus gentes; Thomas quoque in secunda secundæ, quæstione 94. In Itinerario vero S. Clementis diffuse tractatur, qualiter gentiles diversimode idola coluerunt. Quidam etenim posuerunt totum mundum esse unum deum, non propter corporalem substantiam, sed propter animam ejus, dicentes, Deum non esse nisi animam mundum ratione ac motu regentem. Propterea toti mundo et omnibus ejus partibus æstimabant divinum exhibendum honorem: cujus opinionis videtur et Varro fuisse.
paras.en: Further, as the Master relates in the Histories [Peter Comestor, *Historia scholastica*], Nemrod compelled men to worship fire. The Jews say that Ismael made images out of clay. Others say that Ninus, king of the Assyrians, grieving most bitterly at the death of his father Belus, made an image of him, which he commanded to be worshipped, and he granted freedom to those who took refuge at it. Of this matter, and of the origin and condemnation of idolatry, Lactantius writes acutely in his book Against the Gentiles; and Thomas too, in the Second Part of the Second Part, question 94. And in the Itinerary of St. Clement [the *Recognitions* ascribed to Clement of Rome] it is treated at length how the gentiles worshipped idols in various ways. For some held that the whole world is one god, not on account of its bodily substance but on account of its soul, saying that God is nothing but the soul that rules the world by reason and motion. Therefore they thought that divine honour was to be shown to the whole world and to all its parts: and Varro seems to have been of this opinion too.

15.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI QUINTIDECIMI : TU AUTEM, DEUS NOSTER, SUAVIS ET VERUS ES.
15.title_en: Exposition of the fifteenth chapter: But thou, our God, art gracious and true

paras.t: Recitatur hic devotio Judæorum ad Deum sub lege. Tu autem, Deus noster, qui quamvis sis omnium Deus per creationem, generalemque providentiam et conservationem, specialiter tamen es Deus noster, per multiplicem pietatem et gratiam tuam in nobis, per cultum quoque et devotionem nostram, quos tibi impendimus; suavis et verus es, imo suavitas infinita, et veritas per essentiam, verus quoque in omnibus verbis tuis atque promissis, patiens, id est longanimis, non statim ulciscens, sed clementer peccantium pœnitentiam præstolans. Patientia autem, prout est virtus moralis, passionem tristitiæ moderans ac refrenans, non competit Deo, nisi quantum ad similitudinem operis. Et in misericordia disponens omnia, id est, mundum pie misericorditerque gubernans, quia miserationes tuæ super omnia opera tua : qui pluis super justos et injustos, et solem tuum facis oriri super bonos ac malos, multaque beneficia largiris ingratis. Nihilo minus Deus disponit omnia in sua justitia. et item in sapientia sua. Justus enim Dominus in omnibus viis suis : qui et omnia in sapientia fecit. Hæc namque in eisdem concurrunt effectibus, et sapienter contemperantur, ut dictum est plenius.
paras.en: Here is recited the devotion of the Jews to God under the Law. [[15:1|But thou, our God|Tu autem, Deus noster]]: who, though thou art the God of all by creation and by general providence and preservation, art nevertheless in a special way our God, by thy manifold kindness and grace towards us, and also by the worship and devotion which we pay thee; [[15:1|art gracious and true|suavis et verus es]] [suavis, literally "sweet"], nay, infinite sweetness, and truth by essence, true also in all thy words and promises; [[15:1|patient|patiens]], that is, long-suffering, not taking vengeance at once, but mercifully awaiting the repentance of sinners. Now patience, taken as a moral virtue that moderates and reins in the passion of sorrow, does not belong to God, except as regards a likeness in the work. [[15:1|And ordering all things in mercy|Et in misericordia disponens omnia]], that is, governing the world kindly and mercifully, because [[Ps 144:9|his tender mercies are over all his works|miserationes tuæ super omnia opera tua]] [Denis puts the Psalm in the second person: "thy tender mercies are over all thy works"]: thou who [[Matt 5:45|raineth upon the just and the unjust|pluis super justos et injustos]], and [[Matt 5:45|maketh his sun to rise upon the good, and bad|solem tuum facis oriri super bonos ac malos]], and bestowest many benefits on the ungrateful. Nevertheless God orders all things in his justice, and likewise in his wisdom. For [[Ps 144:17|The Lord is just in all his ways|Justus enim Dominus in omnibus viis suis]], he of whom it is said, [[Ps 103:24|thou hast made all things in wisdom|omnia in sapientia fecit]]. For these concur in the same effects, and are wisely tempered together, as has been said more fully.

paras.t: Etenim si peccaverimus, tui sumus, id est, adhuc in tua potestate, quam nusquam evadere possumus, permanemus, teque vere Deum et Creatorem nostrum esse agnoscimus et fatemur, saltem informi notitia : et sic tui manemus adhuc per fidem, atque facilius recuperari poterimus quam infideles fidei fundamento carentes. Sicut in Evangelio testatur : Qui ceciderit super lapidem istum, confringetur : super quem vero ceciderit, conteret eum. Scientes magnitudinem tuam, id est majestatem et pietatem tuam, qua potes et paratus es nobis ignoscere : idcirco non desperamus, nec idola adoramus. Et si non peccaverimus, mortalia evitando et in bonis perseverando, scimus quoniam apud te sumus computati, id est inter electos numerati, atque in libro vitæ et prædestinationis æternæ conscripti, in quo certus est numerus electorum. Unde dixisti : Gaudete, quia nomina vestra scripta sunt in cœlis.
paras.en: [[15:2|For if we sin, we are thine|Etenim si peccaverimus, tui sumus]], that is, we remain still in thy power, which we can nowhere escape, and we acknowledge and confess that thou art truly our God and Creator, at least with an unformed knowledge [that is, a knowledge of faith not yet quickened by charity]; and so we still remain thine by faith, and shall be able to be recovered more easily than unbelievers who lack the foundation of faith. As he testifies in the Gospel: [[Matt 21:44|whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it shall grind him to powder|Qui ceciderit super lapidem istum, confringetur : super quem vero ceciderit, conteret eum]]. [[15:2|knowing thy greatness|Scientes magnitudinem tuam]], that is, thy majesty and kindness, by which thou art able and ready to pardon us: therefore we do not despair, nor do we worship idols. [[15:2|and if we sin not|Et si non peccaverimus]], by avoiding mortal sins and persevering in good, [[15:2|we know that we are counted with thee|scimus quoniam apud te sumus computati]], that is, numbered among the elect, and written in the book of life and of eternal predestination, in which the number of the elect is fixed. Whence thou hast said: Rejoice, [[Luke 10:20|that your names are written in heaven|quia nomina vestra scripta sunt in cœlis]].

paras.t: Nosse enim te per fidem formatam, et per sapientiæ donum, consummata justitia est, id est perfectio vitæ præsentis, et felicitas inchoata. Et sumitur hic justitia, prout est virtus communis. Porro nosse te clare per speciem, est consummata et plena perfectio omnis mentis creatæ. Unde Dominus loquitur : Non glorietur sapiens in sapientia sua, et non glorietur fortis in fortitudine sua, et non glorietur dives in divitiis suis; sed in hoc glorietur, qui gloriatur, scire et nosse me. Et scire, modo prætacto per fidem et sapientiam, justitiam tuam increatam, et virtutem, id est omnipotentiam tuam, radix est immortalitatis, id est actio meritoria futuræ felicitatis ac beatæ incorruptibilitatis : quæ est immortalitas gloriæ, qua mens creata inavertibiliter est Deo unita per fruitionem felicem, corpus quoque dotem immortalitatis habebit. Vel : Scire, per scientiam actualem et operosam, justitiam et virtutem tuam, id est sciendo exercere actus justitiæ ac virtutum infusarum, radix est immortalitatis, quia ad immortalitatem beatam perducit.
paras.en: [[15:3|For to know thee|Nosse enim te]] by faith formed [that is, faith quickened by charity] and by the gift of wisdom [[15:3|is perfect justice|consummata justitia est]], that is, the perfection of the present life, and happiness begun. And justice is taken here as the general virtue [that is, justice in the wide sense, the whole of virtue, not the particular virtue that gives each his due]. But to know thee clearly by sight is the consummate and full perfection of every created mind. Whence the Lord says: [[Jer 9:23|Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches|Non glorietur sapiens in sapientia sua, et non glorietur fortis in fortitudine sua, et non glorietur dives in divitiis suis]]; [[Jer 9:24|But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me|sed in hoc glorietur, qui gloriatur, scire et nosse me]]. [[15:3|and to know|Et scire]], in the manner touched on above, by faith and wisdom, [[15:3|thy justice|justitiam tuam]] uncreated, [[15:3|and thy power|et virtutem]], that is, thy omnipotence, [[15:3|is the root of immortality|radix est immortalitatis]], that is, the meritorious act of future happiness and of blessed incorruptibility: which is the immortality of glory, by which the created mind is united to God, never to be turned away, in happy fruition, and the body too will have the endowment of immortality. Or: [[15:3|to know|Scire]], by an actual and working knowledge, [[15:3|thy justice, and thy power|justitiam et virtutem tuam]] [virtutem taken here as "virtue"], that is, to exercise, by knowing them, the acts of justice and of the infused virtues, [[15:3|is the root of immortality|radix est immortalitatis]], because it leads to blessed immortality.

paras.t: Non enim in errorem idololatriæ induxit nos hominum malæ artis excogitatio, id est adinventio hominum impiorum, qui arte prava operati sunt idola, nec umbra picturæ, id est apparentia imaginis, labor sine fructu, id est, quæ pictura facta est infructuoso labore, et effigies, id est similitudo, sculpta et decorata per varios colores : cujus adspectus insensato dat concupiscentiam, id est, affectum insipientis inspectoris inclinat ad idoli cultum atque amorem.
paras.en: [[15:4|For the invention of mischievous men hath not deceived us|Non enim in errorem idololatriæ induxit nos hominum malæ artis excogitatio]] [literally "hath not led us into the error" (Denis adds "of idolatry") "the contrivance of men of evil art"], that is, the invention of impious men, who wrought idols with a depraved art, [[15:4|nor the shadow of a picture|nec umbra picturæ]], that is, the appearance of an image, [[15:4|a fruitless labour|labor sine fructu]], that is, a picture which was made with fruitless labour, and the [[15:4|figure|effigies]], that is, the likeness, [[15:4|graven|sculpta]] and adorned [[15:4|with divers colours|per varios colores]]: [[15:5|The sight whereof enticeth the fool to lust after it|cujus adspectus insensato dat concupiscentiam]], that is, it inclines the affection of the foolish beholder to the worship and love of the idol.

paras.t: Istud ad litteram recitat auctor hujus voluminis de populo Judæorum temporis sui. Nam tempore judicum et regum sæpius idola coluerunt, etiam pro parte ad aliquod tempus post reditum a Babylonica captivitate sub Antiocho rege. Sed a tempore quo præfuerunt Jonathas ac Simon fratres Judæ Machabæi, ac deinde, non videntur in idololatriam lapsi; nec statuam Caii imperatoris missam eis ad adorandum, adorare acquierunt. Propter quod Caius eis vehementer indignans, ab Herode, qui S. Jacobum decollavit, placatus est.
paras.en: This, according to the letter, the author of this book recites of the Jewish people of his own time. For in the time of the judges and of the kings they often worshipped idols, and in part also for some time after the return from the Babylonian captivity, under King Antiochus. But from the time when Jonathas and Simon, the brothers of Judas Machabeus, were rulers, and thereafter, they do not seem to have fallen into idolatry; nor would they consent to worship the statue of the emperor Caius sent to them to be worshipped. For which reason Caius, vehemently angered against them, was appeased by Herod, who beheaded St James[[Acts 12:2||]].

paras.t: Et diligit ipse insensatus mortuæ imaginis effigiem sine anima, id est inanimatam formam imaginis non viventis, seu idoli.
paras.en: [[15:5|and he loveth the lifeless figure of a dead image|Et diligit ipse insensatus mortuæ imaginis effigiem sine anima]] (he, the fool), that is, the inanimate form of an image that does not live, or of an idol.

paras.t: Malorum, id est vitiorum, amatores, digni sunt morte æternæ damnationis, imo et temporali : quum enim quis peccat mortaliter, meretur a Deo relinqui, et a diabolo perimi; qui spem habent in talibus, puta in idolis, seu hominibus impiis, quorum sunt idola illa repræsentativa; et qui faciunt illos, et qui diligunt eorum imagines ut colantur, et qui colunt. Sic et Apostolus ait : Digni sunt morte, non solum qui faciunt ea, sed et qui consentiunt facientibus.
paras.en: [[15:6|The lovers|amatores]] [[15:6|of evil things|Malorum]], that is, of vices, [[15:6|deserve|digni sunt]] the death of eternal damnation, and indeed temporal death too: for when anyone sins mortally, he deserves to be abandoned by God and slain by the devil; and so do those [[15:6|to trust in|qui spem habent in talibus]] such things [Denis reads the verse as "the lovers of evil things are worthy of death, and those who put their hope in such things"; the Vulgate's sense, as in the Douay-Rheims, is "are worthy to have such things to trust in"], for instance in idols, or in the impious men whom those idols represent; [[15:6|both they that make them|et qui faciunt illos]], and [[15:6|they that love|et qui diligunt]] their images so that they may be worshipped, [[15:6|and they that worship them|et qui colunt]]. So too the Apostle says: they that do such things [[Rom 1:32|are worthy of death|Digni sunt morte]]: [[Rom 1:32|not only they that do them, but they also that consent to them that do them|non solum qui faciunt ea, sed et qui consentiunt facientibus]].

paras.t: Deinde per exemplum ostendit idololatriæ fatuitatem. Sed et figulus mollem terram, scilicet lutum, premens manibus, aptando illud ad vasis formationem, laboriose fingit, id est format, ad usus nostros unumquodque vas; et de eodem luto, id est de una parte ejusdem luti, fingit quæ munda sunt in usum vasa, id est vasa apta et ordinata ad usum honestum, ut quod manducetur ex eis, et similiter quæ his sunt contraria, id est, de alia ejusdem luti parte, format vasa ad viles usus. Horum autem vasorum quis sit usus, id est, ad quem usum sint aptiora, judex est figulus : quia unicuique in sua arte perito et experto credendum est. Iis consonat illud Apostoli : Annon habet potestatem figulus ex eadem massa faciendi vas aliud in honorem, aliud in contumeliam?
paras.en: Next, by an example, he shows the folly of idolatry. [[15:7|The potter also|Sed et figulus]], [[15:7|tempering|premens]] [[15:7|soft earth|mollem terram]], that is, clay, with his hands, fitting it for the forming of a vessel, [[15:7|with labour fashioneth|laboriose fingit]], that is, forms, [[15:7|every vessel for our service|ad usus nostros unumquodque vas]]; [[15:7|and of the same clay|et de eodem luto]], that is, from one part of the same clay, [[15:7|he maketh both vessels that are for clean uses|fingit quæ munda sunt in usum vasa]], that is, vessels fit and ordered for a decent use, such as that food be eaten from them, [[15:7|and likewise such as serve to the contrary|et similiter quæ his sunt contraria]], that is, from another part of the same clay he forms vessels for base uses. [[15:7|but what is the use of these vessels|Horum autem vasorum quis sit usus]], that is, for what use they are the more fit, [[15:7|the potter is the judge|judex est figulus]]: for everyone skilled and experienced in his own art is to be believed. With these words agrees that saying of the Apostle: [[Rom 9:21|hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump, to make one vessel unto honour and another unto dishonour?|Annon habet potestatem figulus ex eadem massa faciendi vas aliud in honorem, aliud in contumeliam?]]

paras.t: Et cum labore vano, id est prorsus inutili, deum fingit de eodem luto, id est luteum idolum, quod ipse aliique idololatræ nominant deum. Pauperes quippe, qui de pretiosis materiis non poterant sibi idola procurare, de vilioribus materiis, scilicet ligno, saxo, luto, ea procuraverunt. Ille, scilicet figulus, qui paulo ante de terra factus fuerat, id est ex elementis compositus, in quibus in corpore humano terra prædominatur, et post pusillum reducit se unde acceptus est, id est, ex intrinseco principio tendit ad mortem : per quam resolvitur in ea ex quibus corpus suum fuit compositum, quoniam ex contrariis constat ; repetitus animæ debitum quam habebat, id est exactus, Deo jubente, propriam animam exhalare, sicut requirit humana conditio. Unde legitur : Hac nocte animam tuam repetunt a te. Et alibi dicit Scriptura : Revertatur pulvis in terram suam, unde erat, et spiritus redeat ad Deum qui dedit illum.
paras.en: And [[15:8|by a vain labour|Et cum labore vano]], that is, one altogether useless, [[15:8|he maketh a god|deum fingit]] [[15:8|of the same clay|de eodem luto]], that is, a clay idol, which he and other idolaters call a god. For the poor, who could not procure idols for themselves of precious materials, procured them of baser materials, namely wood, stone and clay. [[15:8|he who a little before was made of earth himself|Ille, scilicet figulus, qui paulo ante de terra factus fuerat]], namely the potter, that is, compounded of the elements, among which earth predominates in the human body, [[15:8|and a little after returneth to the same out of which he was taken|et post pusillum reducit se unde acceptus est]], that is, from a principle within him he tends towards death, by which he is resolved into the things of which his body was composed, since it is made up of contraries; [[15:8|when his life, which was lent him, shall be called for again|repetitus animæ debitum quam habebat]] [literally "asked back for the debt of the soul which he had", as a loan is called in], that is, required, at God's bidding, to breathe out his own soul, as the human condition demands. Whence we read: [[Luke 12:20|this night do they require thy soul of thee|Hac nocte animam tuam repetunt a te]] [repetunt, "they ask back", the same word as in the verse]. And elsewhere Scripture says: [[Eccles 12:7|And the dust return into its earth, from whence it was, and the spirit return to God, who gave it|Revertatur pulvis in terram suam, unde erat, et spiritus redeat ad Deum qui dedit illum]].

paras.t: Sed est illi, videlicet figulo, cura, non quia laboraturus est, idola faciendo, nec quoniam brevis illi vita est, id est de hoc quod vita sua non diu durabit : hoc est, non solum sollicitatur propter laborem quem habebit in idolorum formatione, nec propter vitæ suæ incertissimam brevitatem ; sed concertatur aurificibus et argentariis, id est, contendit et arguit cum artificibus operantibus ex auro et argento : non quod artificiata sua sint magis pretiosa quam artificiata illorum ; sed quod vel subtilius facta sint, seu magis accommode, quia parvo sumptu possunt formari, et a cunctis etiam pauperibus faciliter obtineri. Sed et ærarios, id est artifices operantes ex ære, imitatur, faciendo idola similia imaginibus factis ab illis : et quia illi quoque concertantur aurificibus ac argentariis, secundum sensum jam tactum ; et quoniam idola illorum ærea possunt a communi populo satis faciliter adipisci. Et gloriam præfert, id est, in hoc præponit artem suam arti ærariorum, quod idola sua lutea facilius emuntur et acquiruntur quam ærea : quoniam res supervacuas fingit, videlicet luteas imagines.
paras.en: [[15:9|But his care is|Sed est illi, videlicet figulo, cura]] (his, that is, the potter's), [[15:9|not that he shall labour|non quia laboraturus est]] in making idols, [[15:9|nor that his life is short|nec quoniam brevis illi vita est]], that is, about the fact that his life will not last long: that is, he is not only anxious about the labour he will have in forming the idols, nor about the most uncertain shortness of his life; [[15:9|but he striveth with the goldsmiths and silversmiths|sed concertatur aurificibus et argentariis]], that is, he contends and argues with the craftsmen who work in gold and silver: not that his handiwork is more precious than theirs, but that it is either more finely made or more serviceable, because it can be formed at small cost and easily obtained by all, even the poor. [[15:9|and he endeavoureth to do like|imitatur]] [[15:9|the workers in brass|Sed et ærarios]], that is, the craftsmen who work in bronze, making idols like the images made by them: both because they too contend with the goldsmiths and silversmiths, in the sense already touched on, and because their bronze idols can be had fairly easily by the common people. [[15:9|and counteth it a glory|Et gloriam præfert]] [præfert, "he puts forward" or "prefers"], that is, in this he prefers his own art to the art of the bronze-workers, that his clay idols are bought and acquired more easily than bronze ones: [[15:9|to make vain things|quoniam res supervacuas fingit]], namely clay images.

paras.t: Cinis est enim cor ejus, id est, propter amorem suum inordinatum ad terrena, cor ipsius figuli cinis vocatur, et vile ut cinis, cinerique conforme : sicut qui adhæret meretrici, unum corpus fit cum illa; et qui Deo adhæret, unus est spiritus per amorem. Per adhæsionem namque affectionis, unum alteri assimilatur, sicut Augustinus testatur : Si terram amas, terra es. Hinc expositorie subditur : et terra supervacua, spes illius : id est, in terrenis figit spem suam, imo in luteo idolo, et in luto de quo efficit statuam : et luto vilior, vita ejus, id est, propter peccata sua, ipse et conversatio sua viliores sunt luto : sicut et Aristoteles asserit, impium hominem brutis mille viliorem. Nam et eo ipso quo figit spem suam in re vili, facit ea se viliorem : quia facit se medium, et illud finem. Finis autem ponitur dignior his quæ ordinantur in ipsum.
paras.en: [[15:10|For his heart is ashes|Cinis est enim cor ejus]], that is, because of his disordered love of earthly things the heart of this potter is called ashes, and is base as ashes and made like to ashes: just as [[1 Cor 6:16|he who is joined to a harlot is made one body|qui adhæret meretrici, unum corpus fit]] with her, and [[1 Cor 6:17|he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit|qui Deo adhæret, unus est spiritus]] through love. For by the clinging of the affections one thing is made like to another, as Augustine testifies: "If thou lovest the earth, thou art earth." Hence, by way of explanation, is added: [[15:10|and his hope vain earth|et terra supervacua, spes illius]], that is, he fixes his hope on earthly things, nay, on a clay idol, and on the clay of which he makes the statue; [[15:10|and his life more base than clay|et luto vilior, vita ejus]], that is, because of his sins he himself and his way of life are baser than clay: as Aristotle too asserts, that a wicked man is a thousand times baser than the brutes. For by the very fact that he fixes his hope on a base thing, he makes himself baser than it: for he makes himself the means, and that thing the end. And the end is held to be of more worth than the things that are ordered to it.

paras.t: Quoniam ignoravit qui se finxit, id est Deum, a quo tanquam a prima principalique causa formatus est, etiam quantum ad corporis formaturam, sicut sanctus Job protestatur : Manus tuæ fecerunt me, et plasmaverunt me totum in circuitu; memento, quæso, quod sicut lutum feceris me; et qui inspiravit illi animam : quam Deus creando infundit. Denique non solum tam vilis est, qui nullam penitus habet Dei notitiam, etiam nec informem; sed item qui non habet notitiam Dei formatam, id est caritati conjunctam : qui etsi dicat nosse se Deum, factis tamen negat. Et amat quæ operatus est, id est idola a se facta, tanquam deos; et qui inspiravit ei spiritum vitalem, id est Deum, a quo habet animam intellectualem, non agnovit : idcirco justo Dei judicio permissus est cadere in tantam vesaniam, ut neglecta salute animæ suæ, lutum adoret, et solum quæ carnis sunt quærat.
paras.en: [[15:11|Forasmuch as he knew not his maker|Quoniam ignoravit qui se finxit]], that is, God, by whom, as by the first and principal cause, he was formed, even as regards the shaping of his body, as holy Job declares: [[Job 10:8|Thy hands have made me, and fashioned me wholly round about|Manus tuæ fecerunt me, et plasmaverunt me totum in circuitu]]; [[Job 10:9|Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay|memento, quæso, quod sicut lutum feceris me]]; [[15:11|and him that inspired into him the soul|et qui inspiravit illi animam]], which God pours in by creating it. Moreover, not only is he so base who has no knowledge of God at all, not even an unformed one, but so too is he who has no formed knowledge of God, that is, knowledge joined to charity: who, though he say that he knows God, yet denies him by his deeds[[Tit 1:16||]]. And he loves the things he has wrought[[15:11||]] [Denis's text reads et amat quæ operatus est where the Vulgate has animam quæ operatur, "the soul that worketh"], that is, the idols made by him, as if they were gods; [[15:11|and that breathed into him a living spirit|et qui inspiravit ei spiritum vitalem]], that is, God, from whom he has his intellectual soul, he has not acknowledged: therefore by the just judgment of God he has been allowed to fall into such madness that, neglecting the salvation of his soul, he adores clay and seeks only the things of the flesh.

paras.t: Sed æstimaverunt lusum esse vitam nostram : id est, vitam nostram non æstimabant a Creatore institutam ac ordinatam ad veram beatitudinem in futuro, ad quam per virtutum exercitia pertingeretur; sed ad præsentia bona, videlicet voluptates et opes terrenas tantummodo ordinatam, et esse leve quid tanquam ludum, atque in luxu et lusibus consistere summum vitæ nostræ bonum, non in spiritualibus rebus. Hinc supra dixisse narrantur iniqui : Non est qui agnitus sit reversus ab inferis : quia ex nihilo nati sumus, et post hæc erimus tanquam si non fuerimus. Fruamur ergo bonis quæ sunt; nullum pratum sit quod non pertranseat luxuria nostra : ubique relinquamus signa lætitiæ. Et conversationem vitæ compositam ad lucrum, id est, humanæ vitæ convictum et operationem arbitrati sunt datos ac constitutos ad augendum temporalia bona : et oportere undecumque, id est quocumque modo, sive per fas, sive per nefas : ideo subditur, etiam ex malo, id est injuste, seu per fraudem violentiamque, acquirere transitoria bona, non ponentes providentiam Dei, nec futurum judicium, imo nec vitam aliam post præsentem. Unde superius dicunt : Opprimamus pauperem justum; sit autem fortitudo nostra lex justitiæ.
paras.en: [[15:12|Yea, and they have counted our life a pastime|Sed æstimaverunt lusum esse vitam nostram]], that is, they did not reckon that our life was instituted and ordered by the Creator to true beatitude in the life to come, to be reached by the practice of the virtues, but that it was ordered only to present goods, namely pleasures and earthly riches, and was a light thing, like a game, and that the highest good of our life consists in luxury and sport, not in spiritual things. Hence above the wicked are related to have said: [[Wis 2:1|no man hath been known to have returned from hell|Non est qui agnitus sit reversus ab inferis]]: [[Wis 2:2|For we are born of nothing, and after this we shall be as if we had not been|quia ex nihilo nati sumus, et post hæc erimus tanquam si non fuerimus]]. [[Wis 2:6|let us enjoy the good things that are present|Fruamur ergo bonis quæ sunt]]; [[Wis 2:8|let no meadow escape our riot|nullum pratum sit quod non pertranseat luxuria nostra]]: [[Wis 2:9|let us every where leave tokens of joy|ubique relinquamus signa lætitiæ]]. [[15:12|and the business of life to be gain|Et conversationem vitæ compositam ad lucrum]], that is, they judged that the common life and work of men were given and appointed for increasing temporal goods; [[15:12|and that we must be getting every way|et oportere undecumque]], that is, in any manner whatever, whether by right or by wrong: therefore is added, [[15:12|even out of evil|etiam ex malo]], that is, unjustly, or by fraud and violence, to acquire transitory goods, not admitting the providence of God, nor the judgment to come, nay, nor any other life after the present one. Whence above they say: [[Wis 2:10|Let us oppress the poor just man|Opprimamus pauperem justum]]; [[Wis 2:11|But let our strength be the law of justice|sit autem fortitudo nostra lex justitiæ]].

paras.t: O quam multi, adhuc tales esse non verentur! qui furto, rapina, taxillatione, usura, fraude, mendacio, perjurio, aut simoniaca pravitate student temporalia congregare. Verumtamen hos errores etiam nobiliores philosophi, Plato, Aristoteles, Socrates, reprobaverunt : docentes hominem, quantum ad meliorem sui partem, habere convenientiam quamdam, communionem atque consortium cum intellectualibus, immortalibus, incorporeisque substantiis ; et virtutibus debere vacare, justitiam, sapientiamque amplecti, et per has ad beatitudinem proficisci : prout Plato in Phædone et Menone ac Timæo disseruit ; Aristoteles quoque decimo tetigit Ethicorum, disputans contra poetam Simonidem, asserentem quod homo, quum sit mortalis, mortalia sapere ac quærere debeat.
paras.en: O how many still do not fear to be such! who strive to heap up temporal things by theft, robbery, dicing, usury, fraud, lying, perjury, or the wickedness of simony. And yet even the nobler philosophers, Plato, Aristotle, Socrates, condemned these errors, teaching that man, as regards the better part of himself, has a certain kinship, communion and fellowship with the intellectual, immortal and incorporeal substances; and that he ought to give himself to the virtues, embrace justice and wisdom, and by them advance towards beatitude: as Plato discoursed in the Phædo, the Meno and the Timæus; and Aristotle too touched on it in the tenth book of the Ethics, arguing against the poet Simonides, who asserted that man, since he is mortal, ought to savour and seek mortal things.

paras.t: Hic enim, utpote figulus idolifex, scit, id est, merito scire debet, et faciliter potest perpendere, se super omnes delinquere, id est, præ cunctis hominibus quodammodo gravius peccare, qui ex terræ materia, puta ex luto, fragilia vasa et sculptilia, id est idola, fingit : quæ idola, quum fuerint formata, ornantur ac complanantur quadam sculptura.
paras.en: [[15:13|For that man|Hic enim]], namely the idol-making potter, [[15:13|knoweth|scit]], that is, rightly ought to know, and can easily weigh, [[15:13|that he offendeth above all others|se super omnes delinquere]], that is, that he sins in a manner more grievously than all men, [[15:13|who of earthly matter|qui ex terræ materia]], for instance of clay, [[15:13|maketh|fingit]] [[15:13|brittle vessels, and graven gods|fragilia vasa et sculptilia]], that is, idols: and these idols, when they have been formed, are adorned and smoothed with a certain carving.

paras.t: Omnes enim insipientes et infelices, scilicet idololatræ, et ceteri vitiosi : qui nunc miseri sunt, miseria culpæ ad æternæ pœnæ miseriam pertrahente ; supra modum animæ suæ superbi, id est, ultra propriam conditionem et potestatem se extollentes : sicut in Isaia et Jeremia fertur de Moab, Superbus est valde, superbia et arrogantia ejus plus quam fortitudo ipsius ; sunt inimici populi tui. Tales enim persequuntur ac odiunt justos, et sæpe dominantur eis per fastum atque tyrannidem : quia per tales Deus exercet, probat, purgat, coronat suos electos, sicut ait Scriptura : Pascua divitum pauperes. Hinc subditur, et imperantes illi : juxta illud, Impius prævalet adversus justum. Quoniam omnia idola nationum deos æstimaverunt : in quo patet eorum insipientia; quibus idolis nec oculorum visus est, neque nares ad percipiendum spiritum, id est ad attrahendum aerem, vel ad sentiendum odoris vaporem ; neque aures ad audiendum, neque digiti ad tractandum ; sed et pedes eorum pigri, id est impotentes, ad ambulandum.
paras.en: [[15:14|But all|Omnes enim]] [[15:14|are foolish, and unhappy|insipientes et infelices]], namely idolaters and other vicious men, who are wretched now, the wretchedness of guilt dragging them to the wretchedness of eternal punishment; [[15:14|and proud beyond measure|supra modum animæ suæ superbi]] [literally "proud beyond the measure of their soul"], that is, exalting themselves beyond their own condition and power: as is said of Moab in Isaias, and in Jeremias[[Jer 48:29||]][[Jer 48:30||]]: [[Is 16:6|he is exceeding proud: his pride and his arrogancy|Superbus est valde, superbia et arrogantia ejus]] [[Is 16:6|is more than his strength|plus quam fortitudo ipsius]]; they are [[15:14|the enemies of thy people|sunt inimici populi tui]]. For such men persecute and hate the just, and often lord it over them in haughtiness and tyranny: for by such men God exercises, proves, purges and crowns his elect, as the Scripture says: [[Ecclus 13:23|the poor are devoured by the rich|Pascua divitum pauperes]] [literally "the poor are the pasture of the rich"]. Hence is added, [[15:14|that hold them in subjection|et imperantes illi]]: according to that saying, [[Hab 1:4|the wicked prevaileth against the just|Impius prævalet adversus justum]]. [[15:15|For they have esteemed all the idols of the heathens for gods|Quoniam omnia idola nationum deos æstimaverunt]]: in which their folly is plain; [[15:15|which neither have the use of eyes to see|quibus idolis nec oculorum visus est]] [Denis reads visus, "sight", for the Vulgate's usus, "use"], [[15:15|nor noses to draw breath|neque nares ad percipiendum spiritum]], that is, to draw in the air, or to perceive the vapour of a smell; [[15:15|nor ears to hear|neque aures ad audiendum]], [[15:15|nor fingers of hands to handle|neque digiti ad tractandum]]; [[15:15|and as for their feet, they are slow|sed et pedes eorum pigri]], that is, powerless, [[15:15|to walk|ad ambulandum]].

paras.t: Homo enim fecit illos ; et qui spiritum mutuatus est, scilicet ipse artifex homo : qui animam quasi mutuo accepit a Deo, ut eam virtutibus ditet, et ipsam sic exornatam suo restituat Creatori; is finxit illos, id est, idola illa formavit : idcirco non vivunt, nec sentiunt ; nec sensus nec membra humana conveniunt eis univoce, sed metaphorice potius. Nemo enim sibi similem homo poterit deum fingere, id est, nullus homo potest formare deum similem sibi, vitalem et intellectualem, præsertim quum de ratione dei sit, esse quid altius homine. Quum sit enim mortalis ipse homo idolifex, mortuum, id est non viventem, fingit manibus iniquis, id est per manus suas sceleratas, quas exhibet arma iniquitatis tanto peccato. Melior est enim ipse his quos colit, id est falsis diis seu idolis ; quia ipse quidem vixit, quum esset mortalis, illi autem, scilicet idola, nunquam. Vivum autem et intellectuale, est melius entibus quæ non vivunt.
paras.en: [[15:16|For man made them|Homo enim fecit illos]]: [[15:16|and he that borroweth his own breath|et qui spiritum mutuatus est]], namely the craftsman himself, a man, who has received his soul from God as a loan, as it were, that he may enrich it with virtues and, so adorned, give it back to its Creator, [[15:16|fashioned them|is finxit illos]], that is, formed those idols: therefore they do not live, nor feel; and neither the senses nor human members belong to them univocally, but rather metaphorically. [[15:16|For no man can make a god like to himself|Nemo enim sibi similem homo poterit deum fingere]], that is, no man can form a god like himself, living and intellectual, especially since it belongs to the notion of a god to be something higher than man. [[15:17|For being mortal himself|Quum sit enim mortalis]], the idol-making man himself [[15:17|formeth a dead thing|mortuum]], that is, a thing not living, [[15:17|with his wicked hands|fingit manibus iniquis]], that is, with his own criminal hands, which he yields as [[Rom 6:13|instruments of iniquity|arma iniquitatis]] to so great a sin. [[15:17|For he is better than they whom he worshippeth|Melior est enim ipse his quos colit]], that is, than the false gods or idols; [[15:17|because he indeed hath lived, though he were mortal|quia ipse quidem vixit, quum esset mortalis]], [[15:17|but they|illi autem]], namely the idols, [[15:17|never|nunquam]]. And what is living and intellectual is better than beings that do not live.

paras.t: Sed obviare videtur, quod dixit jam paulo ante : Luto vilior, vita ejus. Et respondendum, quod bonitate ac dignitate naturæ specificæ, melior est artifex idolis, sed moribus pejor ac vitiis vilior est quam illa.
paras.en: But what he said a little before seems to stand against this: [[15:10|his life more base than clay|Luto vilior, vita ejus]]. And the answer is that in the goodness and dignity of the nature of his species the craftsman is better than the idols, but in his morals he is worse and in his vices baser than they.

paras.t: Sed et animalia irrationalia miserrimi idololatræ colunt. Qui merito appellantur Miserrimi, quoniam colunt ea quibus ipsi sunt digniores : idcirco tali cultu non salutem, sed calamitatem mercantur. Hoc est quod subditur : Insensata enim, videlicet animalia irrationalia, comparata his idololatris, illis, id est præfatis idololatris, deteriora sunt, id est viliora in natura et specie.
paras.en: [[15:18|Moreover, they worship also the vilest creatures|Sed et animalia irrationalia miserrimi idololatræ colunt]] [Denis reads miserrimi, so that it is the idolaters who are "most wretched", where the Vulgate has miserrima, "most wretched animals"], that is, the most wretched idolaters worship irrational animals. They are rightly called most wretched, since they worship things than which they themselves are of more worth: therefore by such worship they purchase not salvation, but calamity. This is what is added: [[15:18|but things without sense|Insensata enim]], namely irrational animals, [[15:18|compared to these|comparata his]] idolaters, [[15:18|are worse|deteriora sunt]] [[15:18|than they|illis]], that is, than the aforesaid idolaters, that is, baser in nature and species.

paras.t: Sed nec adspectu, aliquod ex his animalibus, id est nullum horum irrationalium animalium, suo adspectu sensitivo, bona potest conspicere, id est, ea quæ vere bona sunt ac salutaria valet discernere, quum careat ratione. Idcirco nec proprios noscit cultores : ideo stultum est colere illud. Vel sensus est, quod homo suo adspectu seu consideratione, non potest perpendere aliquod irrationalium animalium esse bonum, seu bona includere, propter quæ colendum exsistat. Effugerunt autem Dei laudem, id est, miserrimi idololatræ recesserunt a laudibus Creatoris, et fugerunt ab ejus obsequio, servientes creaturæ magis, quam Creatori : ideo effugerunt et benedictionem ejus, id est, dona gratiæ Dei non sunt consecuti, quia averterunt se inde, dilexeruntque maledictionem, et veniet eis.
paras.en: [[15:19|Yea, neither by sight|Sed nec adspectu]] can any one [[15:19|of these beasts|ex his animalibus]], that is, none of these irrational animals, by its own sense of sight, [[15:19|see good|bona potest conspicere]], that is, it is not able to discern the things that are truly good and wholesome, since it lacks reason [Denis reads aliquod, "any one" of the animals, where the Vulgate has aliquis, "any man"; his second reading below keeps the Vulgate's sense]. Therefore it does not even know its own worshippers: and so it is foolish to worship it. Or the sense is that man, by his sight or consideration, cannot judge any of the irrational animals to be good, or to contain good things, on account of which it should be worshipped. [[15:19|But they have fled from the praise of God|Effugerunt autem Dei laudem]], that is, the most wretched idolaters have withdrawn from the praises of the Creator, and fled from his service, as men who [[Rom 1:25|served the creature rather than the Creator|servientes creaturæ magis, quam Creatori]]: therefore they have fled [[15:19|and from his blessing|et benedictionem ejus]], that is, they have not obtained the gifts of God's grace, because they turned themselves away from them, and [[Ps 108:18|he loved cursing, and it shall come unto him|dilexeruntque maledictionem, et veniet eis]] [Denis puts the Psalm in the plural: "they loved cursing, and it shall come unto them"].

16.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI SEXTIDECIMI : PROPTER HÆC ET HIS SIMILIA, ETC.
16.title_en: Explanation of the sixteenth chapter: For these things, and by the like to these, etc.

paras.t: Historiæ quædam veteris Testamenti in isto capitulo, sicut et in quibusdam aliis, breviter recitantur cum declarationibus earumdem. Propter hæc et his similia, id est prætacta in præcedenti capitulo scelera, et potissime idololatriæ crimina, passi sunt digne tormenta, id est, idololatriæ juste perpessi sunt diversa supplicia : atque ad litteram fit de Ægyptiis sermo, sicut ex consequentibus innotescit; et per multitudinem bestiarum exterminati sunt, id est valde afflicti, puta per ranas, muscas, scinifes : a quibus tamen non leguntur occisi.
paras.en: Certain histories of the Old Testament are briefly recounted in this chapter, as also in some others, together with explanations of them. [[16:1|For these things, and by the like things to these|Propter hæc et his similia]], that is, the crimes touched on in the preceding chapter, and above all the crimes of idolatry, [[16:1|they were worthily punished|passi sunt digne tormenta]], that is, the idolaters [the print has *idololatriæ*, "of idolatry"; read *idololatræ*, "the idolaters"] justly suffered various punishments; and literally the passage speaks of the Egyptians, as is clear from what follows; [[16:1|and were destroyed by a multitude of beasts|et per multitudinem bestiarum exterminati sunt]], that is, sorely afflicted, for instance by frogs, flies and sciniphs [gnats, the third plague of Egypt]: by which, however, we do not read that they were killed.

paras.t: Pro quibus tormentis, id est vice et loco tormentorum illorum Ægyptiis inflictorum, bene disposuisti populum tuum Israel, quibus dedisti concupiscentiam delectamenti sui, id est rem ab eis concupitam boni saporis : ideo subditur, novum saporem, id est cibum novi saporis, quem antea non erant experti, escam parans, id est mittens ac providens, eis ortygometram, id est coturnicem (juxta illud in Psalmo, Petierunt, et venit coturnix), hoc est avium illarum multitudinem copiosam. Unde in Numeris legitur : Ventus egrediens a Domino, arreptas trans mare coturnices detulit, et demisit in castra.
paras.en: [[16:2|Instead of which punishment|Pro quibus tormentis]], that is, in the stead and place of those punishments inflicted on the Egyptians, [[16:2|dealing well with thy people|bene disposuisti populum tuum Israel]] Israel, [[16:2|thou gavest them their desire of delicious food|quibus dedisti concupiscentiam delectamenti sui]], that is, a thing of good savour that they longed for; therefore it adds, [[16:2|of a new taste|novum saporem]], that is, a food of a new savour, which they had not tasted before, [[16:2|preparing|escam parans]] food, that is, sending and providing, [[16:2|for them quails|eis ortygometram]] [*ortygometra*, a Greek word for a kind of quail], that is, the quail (according to that in the Psalm, [[Ps 104:40|They asked, and the quail came|Petierunt, et venit coturnix]]), that is, a plentiful multitude of those birds. Hence we read in Numbers: [[Num 11:31|a wind going out from the Lord, taking quails up beyond the sea brought them, and cast them into the camp|Ventus egrediens a Domino, arreptas trans mare coturnices detulit, et demisit in castra]].

paras.t: Ut illi quidem, puta Ægyptii, concupiscentes escam more consueto, propter ea quæ illis ostensa et missa sunt, id est ex horrore parvorum, venenatorum et vilium animalium, scilicet ranarum, muscarum, etc., per quæ plagati fuerunt, etiam a necessaria concupiscentia, id est appetitione alimentorum, averterentur, in pœnam suorum facinorum : nam ranæ illæ innumerabiles atque fœdissimæ, intraverunt reliquias ciborum Ægyptiorum, ut in Exodo habetur. Sicque cibi illi eis in nauseam vertebantur.
paras.en: [[16:3|To the end, that they indeed|Ut illi quidem]], namely the Egyptians, [[16:3|desiring food|concupiscentes escam]] in their accustomed way, [[16:3|by means of those things that were shewn and sent among them|propter ea quæ illis ostensa et missa sunt]], that is, from loathing of the small, venomous and vile creatures, namely frogs, flies, etc., by which they were plagued, [[16:3|even that which was necessary to satisfy their desire|etiam a necessaria concupiscentia]], that is, the appetite for food, [[16:3|might loath|averterentur]], as a punishment for their crimes: for those frogs, countless and most foul, entered into the remains of the Egyptians' food, as we have in Exodus[[Ex 8:3||]]. And so that food turned to loathing for them.

paras.t: Hi autem, scilicet filii Israel, in brevi inopes facti : quia quæ secum detulerunt ex Ægypto, cito fuerunt comesta, ita quod ex inopia indiguerunt supernaturali Dei provisione; novam gustaverunt escam, id est coturnices, et etiam manna. Verumtamen carnes illas petierunt perversi et ingrati, ipsum manna fastidientes, atque dicentes : Anima nostra arida est; nihil aliud respiciunt oculi nostri nisi man.
paras.en: [[16:3|But these|Hi autem]], namely the children of Israel, [[16:3|after suffering want for a short time|in brevi inopes facti]]: for what they had brought with them out of Egypt was soon eaten up, so that out of want they needed God's supernatural provision; [[16:3|tasted a new meat|novam gustaverunt escam]], that is, the quails, and the manna too. Yet they asked for that flesh perversely and ungratefully, loathing the manna itself and saying: [[Num 11:6|Our soul is dry, our eyes behold nothing else but manna|Anima nostra arida est; nihil aliud respiciunt oculi nostri nisi man]].

paras.t: Oportebat enim, secundum ordinem divinæ justitiæ, illis, utpote Ægyptiis, sine excusatione, id est evasione, quidem superpervenire interitum : potissime his qui in mari Rubro demergebantur, quia induratissimi erant, nec ex tot ac tantis prodigiis fuerunt conversi; propter quod inexcusabiles fuerant : illis, inquam, exercentibus tyrannidem, id est crudelitatem in Israelitas, quos ferociter oppresserunt : his autem, scilicet Hebræis, tantum ostendere per evidentiam facti, quemadmodum inimici illorum, puta Ægyptii, exterminabantur per plagas eis inflictas : quod fuit ad filiorum Israel consolationem, qui zelo justitiæ de Ægypti percussionibus poterant gloriari.
paras.en: [[16:4|For it was requisite|Oportebat enim]], according to the order of divine justice, [[16:4|that inevitable|sine excusatione]], that is, unescapable [Latin *sine excusatione*, literally "without excuse", which Denis glosses *evasione*, "escape"], [[16:4|destruction should come upon them|quidem superpervenire interitum]], that is, upon the Egyptians: above all upon those who were drowned in the Red Sea, since they were utterly hardened and were not converted by so many and such great wonders, for which reason they were without excuse: upon them, I say, [[16:4|that exercised tyranny|exercentibus tyrannidem]], that is, cruelty against the Israelites, whom they fiercely oppressed: [[16:4|but to these|his autem]], namely the Hebrews, [[16:4|it should only be shewn|tantum ostendere]] by the plain evidence of the fact, [[16:4|how their enemies|quemadmodum inimici illorum]], namely the Egyptians, [[16:4|were destroyed|exterminabantur]] by the plagues inflicted on them: which was for the consolation of the children of Israel, who, out of zeal for justice, could glory in the strokes that fell on Egypt.

paras.t: Sed quia his objici posset, quod etiam filii Israel per serpentes plagati sunt, subditur : Etenim quum supervenit illis, puta Hebræis, sæva bestiarum ira, videlicet furor serpentium, qui eos invaserunt eo quod contra Dominum murmurassent, dicentes ad Moysen : Cur eduxisti nos de Ægypto, ut morerentur in solitudine? Deest panis, non sunt aquæ, anima nostra jam nauseat super cibo isto levissimo. Quamobrem misit Dominus in populum ignitos serpentes, ut in Numeris describitur. Unde subjungitur : morsibus perversorum, id est feralium, colubrorum exterminabantur : quia multi de populo Israel, ab illis serpentibus occidebantur.
paras.en: But since it could be objected to this that the children of Israel too were plagued by serpents, it adds: [[16:5|For when|Etenim quum]] [[16:5|the fierce rage of beasts|sæva bestiarum ira]] [[16:5|came upon these|supervenit illis]], namely the Hebrews: that is, the fury of the serpents, which attacked them because they had murmured against the Lord, saying to Moses: [[Num 21:5|Why didst thou bring us out of Egypt, to die in the wilderness? There is no bread, nor have we any waters: our soul now loatheth this very light food|Cur eduxisti nos de Ægypto, ut morerentur in solitudine? Deest panis, non sunt aquæ, anima nostra jam nauseat super cibo isto levissimo]]. [[Num 21:6|Wherefore the Lord sent among the people fiery serpents|Quamobrem misit Dominus in populum ignitos serpentes]], as is described in Numbers. Hence it goes on: [[16:5|they were destroyed by the bitings of crooked|morsibus perversorum]], that is, savage, [[16:5|serpents|colubrorum exterminabantur]]: for many of the people of Israel were killed by those serpents[[Num 21:6||]].

paras.t: Sed non in perpetuum permansit ira tua, id est punitio illa tua justa. Deo namque jubente, Moyses fecit et erexit serpentem æneum, quem intuendo sanabantur percussi. Sed ad correctionem in brevi turbati sunt, id est, ad modicum tempus fuerunt ita plagati, ut de cetero melius se haberent, et qui occisi fuerunt, per temporalem mortem evaderent æternalem : quam et evaserunt, qui in sua temporali punitione pœnituerunt ; signum habentes salutis, videlicet serpentem æneum : qui fuit signum curationis præfatæ, non causa : unde Dominus Moysi dixit, Fac serpentem æneum, et pone eum pro signo; ad commemorationem mandati legis tuæ, id est, quatenus signo illo admoniti, de cetero memores essent præceptorum legis quam dedisti per Moysen.
paras.en: [[16:6|But thy wrath endured not for ever|Sed non in perpetuum permansit ira tua]], that is, that just punishment of thine. For at God's command Moses made and set up a brazen serpent, by looking on which those who had been struck were healed[[Num 21:8||]][[Num 21:9||]]. [[16:6|but they were troubled for a short time for their correction|Sed ad correctionem in brevi turbati sunt]], that is, they were plagued for a little while in such a way that they might behave better thereafter, and that those who were killed might by a temporal death escape the eternal one; which those did escape who repented in their temporal punishment; [[16:6|having a sign of salvation|signum habentes salutis]], namely the brazen serpent, which was the sign of that healing, not its cause: hence the Lord said to Moses, [[Num 21:8|Make a brazen serpent, and set it up for a sign|Fac serpentem æneum, et pone eum pro signo]]; [[16:6|to put them in remembrance of the commandment of thy law|ad commemorationem mandati legis tuæ]], that is, so that, admonished by that sign, they might be mindful thereafter of the precepts of the law which thou gavest through Moses.

paras.t: Qui enim conversus est, id est, quicumque ex filiis Israel pœnituit, et pœnitendo serpentemque æneum intuendo curabatur, non per hoc quod videbat, id est non virtute illius ænei serpentis, sanabatur, sed per te omnium salvatorem, id est virtute tua divina, qui salvas, non omnes, sed cunctos qui salvantur. Juxta quem sensum fertur in Psalmo : Allevat Dominus omnes qui corruunt, et erigit omnes elisos. Porro Deo proprium est salvare. Qui in Isaia testatur : Deus justus et salvans non est præter me. Et alibi per Prophetam dicitur : Ego Dominus Deus tuus, et salvator non est præter me.
