paras.en: [[16:7|For he that turned to it|Qui enim conversus est]], that is, whoever of the children of Israel repented and, by repenting and looking on the brazen serpent, was cured, [[16:7|was not healed by that which he saw|non per hoc quod videbat]], that is, not by the power of that brazen serpent, [[16:7|but by thee, the Saviour of all|sed per te omnium salvatorem]], that is, by thy divine power, who savest, not all men, but all who are saved. In accordance with this sense it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 144:14|The Lord lifteth up all that fall: and setteth up all that are cast down|Allevat Dominus omnes qui corruunt, et erigit omnes elisos]]. Moreover it is proper to God to save; and he testifies in Isaias: [[Is 45:21|A just God and a saviour, there is none besides me|Deus justus et salvans non est præter me]]. And elsewhere it is said through the Prophet: [[Osee 13:4|I am the Lord thy God|Ego Dominus Deus tuus]], and [[Osee 13:4|there is no saviour beside me|salvator non est præter me]].

paras.t: Præterea Deus per serpentem æneum sic voluit subvenire, ad præfigurandum mysterium passionis redemptionisque Christi. Ideo ait Glossa : Non serpens æneus sanavit illos, sed sacramentum mysterii, id est mors Christi in serpente præfigurata. Christus quippe antiquum serpentem triumphavit in cruce, et ejus venenum devicit : ut qui vere imaginem Christi et ejus passionem conspexerit, salvetur. Unde dicitur : Sicut Moyses exaltavit serpentem in deserto, ita exaltari oportet Filium hominis : ut omnis qui credit in ipsum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Recte æneus serpens in ligno suspenditur. Æs enim ceteris durabilius est metallis. In serpente ergo Christus mortuus designatur, in ære, æternus insinuatur : quia mortuus per humanitatem, quasi non mortuus est per divinitatem.
paras.en: Further, God willed to give help in this way, through a brazen serpent, in order to prefigure the mystery of the passion and redemption of Christ. Hence the Gloss says: It was not the brazen serpent that healed them, but the sacrament of the mystery, that is, the death of Christ prefigured in the serpent. For Christ triumphed over the old serpent on the cross and overcame his venom, so that whoever truly looks upon the image of Christ and his passion may be saved. Hence it is said: [[John 3:14|as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of man be lifted up|Sicut Moyses exaltavit serpentem in deserto, ita exaltari oportet Filium hominis]]: [[John 3:15|That whosoever believeth in him may not perish, but may have life everlasting|ut omnis qui credit in ipsum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam]]. Rightly is the brazen serpent hung upon wood. For brass is more lasting than the other metals. In the serpent, then, Christ dead is signified; in the brass, Christ eternal is suggested: for, dead in his humanity, he is as it were not dead in his divinity.

paras.t: In hoc autem miraculo, quo ita sanasti percussos ab ignitis serpentibus, per ænei serpentis intuitum, ostendisti inimicis nostris, puta Ægyptiis, quando hoc ipsum devenit ad eorum notitiam; vel Ægyptiis qui egressi erant Ægyptum cum filiis Israel, et antea quandoque erant adversarii Israelitarum; quia tu es qui liberas ab omni malo.
paras.en: [[16:8|And in this|In hoc autem]] miracle, in which thou didst so heal those struck by the fiery serpents through looking on the brazen serpent, [[16:8|thou didst shew to our enemies|ostendisti inimicis nostris]], namely the Egyptians, when this very thing came to their knowledge; or to the Egyptians who had gone out of Egypt with the children of Israel[[Ex 12:38||]], and had at one time been adversaries of the Israelites; [[16:8|that thou art he who deliverest from all evil|quia tu es qui liberas ab omni malo]].

paras.t: Illos enim, puta Ægyptios, locustarum et muscarum occiderunt morsus. Ex quo elicitur, quod aliqui Ægyptiorum obierunt ex punctionibus morsibusque muscarum ac locustarum : quod tamen in Exodo non legitur evidenter. Et non est inventa sanitas animæ, id est vitæ animali, eorum : quia curati non sunt, sed occisi; nec anima eorum pœnituit. Verumtamen ad tempus suspendit et interrupit Deus plagas Ægyptiorum; sed impœnitentibus paulo post graviores inflixit. Quia digni erant ob duritiam et impœnitentiam suam, ab hujusmodi plagis exterminari.
paras.en: [[16:9|For the bitings of locusts, and of flies, killed them|Illos enim, puta Ægyptios, locustarum et muscarum occiderunt morsus]], namely the Egyptians. From this it is gathered that some of the Egyptians died from the stings and bites of flies and locusts: which, however, is not plainly read in Exodus. [[16:9|and there was found no remedy for their life|Et non est inventa sanitas animæ]] [Latin *sanitas animæ*, literally "health of soul"], that is, for their animal life [that is, the life of the body]: for they were not cured but killed; nor did their soul repent. Yet God for a time suspended and broke off the plagues of the Egyptians; but since they did not repent, he soon inflicted heavier ones. [[16:9|because they were worthy|Quia digni erant]], on account of their hardness and impenitence, [[16:9|to be destroyed by such things|ab hujusmodi plagis exterminari]] [Denis's text adds *plagis*, "by such plagues"].

paras.t: Filios autem tuos adoptivos Hebræos, qui de suo excessu pœnituerant, nec draconum, nec venenatorum, scilicet ignitorum serpentium, viderunt dentes, id est, morsus dentium non occiderunt. Denique draco serpens quidam est, et maximus inter serpentes, sicut elephantus inter bruta terræ, et gryphus inter aves. Misericordia enim tua adveniens, id est illis succurrens per ænei serpentis intuitum, sicut prædictum est, sanabat illos, qui pœnitentes confugerunt ad Moysen, deprecantes ut oraret pro eis.
paras.en: But [[16:10|thy children|Filios autem tuos]], the adopted ones, the Hebrews, who had repented of their excess, [[16:10|not even the teeth|nec draconum]] of dragons, nor [[16:10|of venomous serpents|nec venenatorum]], namely the fiery serpents, [[16:10|overcame|viderunt dentes]] [Denis reads *nec draconum, nec venenatorum … dentes*, "neither the teeth of dragons nor of venomous ones"; the print has *viderunt*, "saw", for the Vulgate's *vicerunt*, "overcame"]: that is, the bites of their teeth did not kill them. Now the dragon is a kind of serpent, and the greatest among serpents, as the elephant is among the beasts of the earth and the griffin among birds. [[16:10|for thy mercy came|Misericordia enim tua adveniens]], that is, succouring them through the sight of the brazen serpent, as was said before, [[16:10|and healed them|sanabat illos]], those who in repentance fled to Moses, begging him to pray for them[[Num 21:7||]].

paras.t: Immemoria enim sermonum tuorum, id est propter oblivionem verborum ac præceptorum tuorum, exterminabantur: sicque quod dicitur, Immemoria, una est dictio. Vel duæ sunt dictiones, ut sit sensus: In memoria, id est ad hoc, ut de cetero memores sint corde et opere sermonum tuorum, exterminabantur, id est, lædebantur. Et velociter sanabantur, qui pœnitebant, per modum præhabitum. Vel, Exterminabantur, id est, quidam occidebantur, ut alii qui sanabantur memores tui essent: et ita quamvis quod dicitur, Exterminabantur, et, Sanabantur, videatur ad eosdem referri, tamen ad diversos refertur, juxta unam regularum Tichonii. Juxta quem modum fertur in Psalmo: Quum occideret eos, quærebant eum; et revertebantur, et diluculo veniebant ad eum.
paras.en: For through forgetfulness [[16:11|of thy words|sermonum tuorum]], that is, on account of forgetting thy words and precepts, they were destroyed [Denis reads *Immemoria … exterminabantur*, "through forgetfulness … they were destroyed", where the Douay-Rheims has "they were examined for the remembrance"]: and so *Immemoria* ["forgetfulness"] as it is written here is one word. Or they are two words, so that the sense is: [[16:11|for the remembrance|In memoria]], that is, to this end, that thereafter they might be mindful of thy words in heart and deed, they were destroyed, that is, harmed. [[16:11|and were quickly healed|Et velociter sanabantur]], those who repented, in the way described before. Or, *they were destroyed*, that is, some were killed, so that others who were healed might be mindful of thee: and so, although *they were destroyed* and *were healed* seem to refer to the same persons, yet they refer to different ones, according to one of the rules of Tichonius [Tyconius, whose seven rules for reading Scripture Augustine adopted]. In accordance with this manner it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 77:34|When he slew them, then they sought him: and they returned, and came to him early in the morning|Quum occideret eos, quærebant eum; et revertebantur, et diluculo veniebant ad eum]].

paras.t: Ne in altam, id est profundam, gravem et obstinatam, incidentes oblivionem majestatis et beneficentiæ tuæ, non possent tuo uti adjutorio, id est, omnino inhabiles fierent et inepti ad impetrandum auxilia pietatis ac gratiæ tuæ. Nempe qui ingratus est de præteritis donis, futuris indignus est.
paras.en: [[16:11|lest falling into deep|Ne in altam]], that is, profound, grievous and obstinate, [[16:11|forgetfulness|incidentes oblivionem]] of thy majesty and goodness, [[16:11|they might not be able to use thy help|non possent tuo uti adjutorio]], that is, become altogether unfit and incapable of obtaining the aids of thy mercy and grace. For he who is ungrateful for past gifts is unworthy of future ones.

paras.t: Etenim neque herba medicinalis naturalis, neque malagma, id est medicamentum seu emplastrum artificiale, sanavit illos a morsu serpentium, et multo minus a vulneribus animarum: sed tuus, Domine, sermo, qui sanat omnia, id est imperium tuum. Sic enim in Scripturis sumitur sermo, seu verbum: juxta illud in Psalmo, Ignis, grando, nix, glacies, spiritus procellarum, quæ faciunt verbum ejus: itemque, Benedicite Domino, angeli ejus, potentes virtute, facientes verbum illius. Et Apostolus dicit: Portansque omnia verbo virtutis suæ. Qui sanat omnia quæ sanantur: vel quædam de omnibus, seu omnia quantum in se est. Etenim dixisse Dei, fecisse est, secundum Hieronymum. Et idem est aliquid fieri Deo volente, et Deo agente, secundum Augustinum. Profundius tamen, per sermonem Dei, intelligitur Verbum Patris æterni: de quo ad Hebræos ait Apostolus: Vivus est sermo Dei, et efficax. Hic sermo, Salvator est mundi: per quem sicut Pater omnia fecit, sic cuncta refecit.
paras.en: [[16:12|For it was neither herb|Etenim neque herba]], that is, a natural medicinal herb, [[16:12|nor mollifying plaster|neque malagma]], that is, a medicine or plaster made by art, [[16:12|that healed them|sanavit illos]] from the bite of the serpents, and much less from the wounds of souls: [[16:12|but thy word, O Lord, which healeth all things|sed tuus, Domine, sermo, qui sanat omnia]], that is, thy command. For so *word* (*sermo* or *verbum*) is taken in the Scriptures, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 148:8|Fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy winds, which fulfil his word|Ignis, grando, nix, glacies, spiritus procellarum, quæ faciunt verbum ejus]]; and again: [[Ps 102:20|Bless the Lord, all ye his angels: you that are mighty in strength, and execute his word|Benedicite Domino, angeli ejus, potentes virtute, facientes verbum illius]]. And the Apostle says: [[Heb 1:3|upholding all things by the word of his power|Portansque omnia verbo virtutis suæ]]. Which healeth all things that are healed; or some of all things; or all things, as far as lies in him. For with God, to have said is to have done, according to Jerome; and it is the same for a thing to be done with God willing it and with God doing it, according to Augustine. More deeply, however, by the word of God is understood the Word of the eternal Father, of whom the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 4:12|the word of God is living and effectual|Vivus est sermo Dei, et efficax]]. This Word is the Saviour of the world: through whom, as the Father made all things, so he has remade all things.

paras.t: Tu es, Domine, qui vitæ et mortis habes potestatem, id est, vitam naturæ, vitam gratiæ, vitamque gloriæ dare, conservare, atque auferre potes. Vitam quippe naturæ aufert directe, tanquam malum pœnæ; vitam gratiæ, indirecte et permissive; vitam gloriæ nunquam aufert a Beatis, quamvis de potentia absoluta hoc possit; sed ab his qui ad horam ad eam admissi credun[…] Paulus et Moyses, abstulit eam. Hinc ait in Apocalypsi: Habeo claves mortis et inferni. Et deducis ad portas, id est ingressum, mortis, et reducis: id est, corporaliter quos vis occidis, et eosdem dum vis, ad nutum rursus vivificas. Quod et Christus inter homines corporaliter conversans, sæpius fecit, et multo frequentius per suos discipulos. Unde: Ego, inquit, occidam, et ego vivere faciam. Ad portas demum spiritualis mortis, non nisi permissive deducit. Portæ vero mortis corporalis, possunt etiam dici infirmitates incurabiles et letales. Insuper ad portas mortis infernales efficienter deducit eos qui in culpa moriuntur mortali; et quos vult, ex speciali gratia inde reducit: juxta illud primo Regum, Deducit ad inferos, et reducit.
paras.en: [[16:13|For it is thou, O Lord, that hast power of life and death|Tu es, Domine, qui vitæ et mortis habes potestatem]], that is, thou canst give, preserve and take away the life of nature, the life of grace and the life of glory. The life of nature he takes away directly, as an evil of punishment [that is, an evil suffered as a penalty, as distinct from the evil of sin]; the life of grace, indirectly and by permission; the life of glory he never takes away from the Blessed, though by his absolute power [that is, God's power considered in itself, apart from the order he has decreed] he could do so; but from those who are believed to have been admitted to it for an hour […] [the transcription runs two words together here, *credun…Paulus*; probably *creduntur, ut*, "are believed, as"] Paul and Moses[[2 Cor 12:2||]][[2 Cor 12:4||]][[Ex 33:11||]], he took it away [that is, those who are held to have seen God in this life for a passing moment]. Hence he says in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 1:18|have the keys of death and of hell|Habeo claves mortis et inferni]]. [[16:13|and leadest down to the gates|Et deducis ad portas]], that is, to the entrance, [[16:13|of death, and bringest back again|mortis, et reducis]]: that is, thou killest bodily whom thou wilt, and the same, when thou wilt, thou quickenest again at a nod. This Christ also did more than once while he lived bodily among men[[Matt 9:18||]][[Matt 9:25||]][[Luke 7:14||]][[John 11:43||]], and much more often through his disciples[[Acts 9:40||]][[Acts 20:9||]]. Hence he says: [[Deut 32:39|I will kill and I will make to live|occidam, et ego vivere faciam]] [the margin gives Deut. xxxi, 39; the words are Deut 32:39]. To the gates of spiritual death, again, he leads down only by permission. The gates of bodily death may also be called incurable and deadly illnesses. Moreover, to the gates of the death of hell he leads down, as its efficient cause, those who die in mortal sin; and those whom he will he brings back thence by special grace: according to that in the first book of Kings: [[1 Kings 2:6|he bringeth down to hell, and bringeth back again|Deducit ad inferos, et reducit]].

paras.t: Homo autem occidit quidem per malitiam, id est per propriam atque spontaneam pravitatem cogitationis, affectionis, locutionis, commissionis, aut omissionis, animam suam, morte culpæ: de qua loquitur Christus, Dimitte mortuos sepelire mortuos suos; atque in Apocalypsi, Nomen habes quod vivas, sed mortuus es. Et ipsa malitia formaliter est mors animæ; sed in quantum ex propria oritur voluntate, dicitur homo per ipsam malitiam suam occidere animam. Nec potest alter occidere animam hominis hujus aut alicujus alterius, nisi dispositive, et homine isto volente, cujus peccatum est aliquo modo voluntarium. Ideo nulla nocebit ei adversitas, nulla tentatio, nulla injuria, si non dominetur ei propria culpa, vel consensus illicitus.
paras.en: [[16:14|A man indeed killeth through malice|Homo autem occidit quidem per malitiam]], that is, through his own spontaneous depravity of thought, affection, speech, commission or omission, his own soul [Denis's text adds *animam suam*, "his own soul"], by the death of sin: of which Christ speaks: [[Matt 8:22|let the dead bury their dead|Dimitte mortuos sepelire mortuos suos]]; and the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:1|thou hast the name of being alive. And thou art dead|Nomen habes quod vivas, sed mortuus es]]. Malice itself is formally the death of the soul; but inasmuch as it springs from his own will, a man is said to kill his soul by his own malice. Nor can another kill the soul of this man or of anyone else, except dispositively [that is, by disposing or inclining him to sin, not by causing it], and with this man willing it, whose sin is in some way voluntary. Therefore no adversity, no temptation, no injury will harm him, if his own fault or unlawful consent does not have dominion over him.

paras.t: Et quum exierit spiritus, non revertetur : id est, quum anima de corpore per mortem exierit, non redibit in illud de lege communi, naturalique cursu : quamvis supernaturaliter possit corpori suo rursus uniri. Ideo sanctus Job dixit : Viam per quam non revertar, ambulo. Nec revocabit quis animam quæ recepta est a Deo, qui corpori eam immisit : id est, post exitum a corpore, alicui receptaculo, secundum suorum exigentiam meritorum, deputata est a judice Deo. Porro de receptaculis animarum, quæ et quot sint, quarto Sententiarum tractatur. Jam quidem sunt, infernus, purgatorium, limbus puerorum, et regnum cœlorum. Sed ante Salvatoris adventum, fuit et limbus patrum.
paras.en: [[16:14|and when the spirit is gone forth, it shall not return|Et quum exierit spiritus, non revertetur]]: that is, when the soul has gone out of the body by death, it will not return into it by the common law and the course of nature, though it can be united to its body again supernaturally. Hence holy Job said: [[Job 16:23|I am walking in a path by which I shall not return|Viam per quam non revertar, ambulo]]. [[16:14|neither shall he call back the soul that is received|Nec revocabit quis animam quæ recepta est]] by God, who put it into the body [Denis's text adds *a Deo, qui corpori eam immisit*, "by God, who put it into the body"]: that is, after its going out of the body it has been assigned by God the judge to some abode, as its merits require. Of the abodes of souls, what and how many they are, the fourth book of the Sentences treats [Peter Lombard, Sentences IV, dist. 45]. At present they are hell, purgatory, the limbo of children and the kingdom of heaven; but before the Saviour's coming there was also the limbo of the fathers.

paras.t: Sed tuam manum, id est potestatem, effugere, impossibile est : juxta quod ait Psalmista : Quo ibo a spiritu tuo? et quo a facie tua fugiam? Ideo Jonas, qui fugit a facie Domini, deprehensus fuit in mari. Hinc consultissimum est, ut qui Omnipotentis manum non valemus effugere, non cessemus ad ejus pietatem obedienter humiliterque confugere.
paras.en: [[16:15|But it is impossible to escape|effugere, impossibile est]] [[16:15|thy hand|Sed tuam manum]], that is, thy power: according to what the Psalmist says: [[Ps 138:7|Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy face?|Quo ibo a spiritu tuo? et quo a facie tua fugiam?]] Therefore Jonas, who fled from the face of the Lord[[Jon 1:3||]], was caught in the sea[[Jon 1:15||]]. Hence it is the wisest course that we, who cannot escape the hand of the Almighty, should never cease to flee for refuge, obediently and humbly, to his mercy.

paras.t: Negantes enim te nosse impii, puta Ægyptii, quorum rex dixit, Nescio Dominum, per fortitudinem brachii tui flagellati sunt variis plagis, sicut expositum est; novis aquis, et grandinibus, et pluviis, persecutionem, id est debitam punitionem, passi sunt, et per ignem consumpti, id est per aquas, grandines, pluvias insolito modo generatas et supervenientes. Nam et fluvii Ægyptiorum computruerunt, et suas ripas forsitan exeuntes, damna intulerunt eisdem. Et, ut legitur in Exodo, Dominus pluit super terram Ægypti grandinem copiosam ac maximam, et simul cum grandine descendit ignis et discurrentia fulgura : ex quibus multi Ægyptiorum exstincti sunt.
paras.en: [[16:16|For the wicked that denied to know thee|Negantes enim te nosse impii]], namely the Egyptians, whose king said, [[Ex 5:2|I know not the Lord|Nescio Dominum]], [[16:16|were scourged by the strength of thy arm|per fortitudinem brachii tui flagellati sunt]] with various plagues, as has been explained; [[16:16|by strange waters, and hail, and rain|novis aquis, et grandinibus, et pluviis]] [[16:16|being persecuted|persecutionem]], that is, suffering due punishment, [[16:16|and consumed by fire|et per ignem consumpti]]: that is, by waters, hail and rain produced and coming on in an unwonted way [this explains *novis*, "strange", literally "new"]. For the rivers of the Egyptians also putrefied[[Ex 7:21||]], and, perhaps overflowing their banks, did them damage. And, as we read in Exodus, the Lord rained a plentiful and very great hail upon the land of Egypt[[Ex 9:18||]][[Ex 9:23||]], and together with the hail there came down fire and lightnings running along[[Ex 9:24||]]: by which many of the Egyptians were killed[[Ex 9:25||]].

paras.t: Quod enim mirabile erat, in aqua, quæ omnia exstinguit, specialiter ignem, cui sua frigiditate et humiditate contrariatur, plus ignis valebat : id est, ignis ille qui simul ferebatur cum grandine et pluvia, intensius viguit et gravius nocuit ipsis Ægyptiis, quosdam eorum incendendo, et terræ nascentia quædam vastando. Vindex est enim orbis justorum, id est, universitas creaturarum, te jubente, ulciscitur justorum injurias, et contra injustos consurgit, ac Creatoris inhonorationem parata est vindicare.
paras.en: [[16:17|And which was wonderful, in water, which extinguisheth all things|Quod enim mirabile erat, in aqua, quæ omnia exstinguit]], and especially fire, to which it is contrary by its coldness and moisture, [[16:17|the fire had more force|plus ignis valebat]]: that is, that fire which was borne along together with the hail and rain was the more vigorous and did the more grievous harm to the Egyptians themselves, burning some of them and laying waste some of the produce of the land. [[16:17|for the world fighteth for the just|Vindex est enim orbis justorum]] [Latin *vindex est orbis justorum*, "the world is the avenger of the just"], that is, the whole of creation, at thy command, avenges the wrongs done to the just, rises up against the unjust, and stands ready to avenge the dishonour done to the Creator.

paras.t: Quodam enim tempore, dum scilicet Ægyptii variis plagis puniebantur, mansuetabatur ignis, id est, vim sui caloris non exercebat in quædam, ut subditur, ne comburerentur quæ ad impios missa erant animalia, id est, ne parva ac vilia animalia a Deo missa ad puniendos Ægyptios, læderentur ab illo igne qui ferebatur mixtim cum grandine ; sed ut ipsi videntes, id est, ut Ægyptii conspicientes qualiter ignis ille non egit in illas bestiolas ipsis nocivas, sed eorum jumenta utilia, scilicet equos, boves, vaccas, combussit, scirent quoniam Dei judicio patiuntur persecutionem, id est, ex tanto signo adverterent quod Deo jubente paterentur hujusmodi plagas.
paras.en: [[16:18|For at one time|Quodam enim tempore]], namely while the Egyptians were being punished with various plagues, [[16:18|the fire was mitigated|mansuetabatur ignis]], that is, it did not exercise the force of its heat on certain things, as is added: [[16:18|that the beasts which were sent against the wicked might not be burnt|ne comburerentur quæ ad impios missa erant animalia]], that is, that the small and vile animals sent by God to punish the Egyptians might not be hurt by that fire which was borne along mixed with the hail; [[16:18|but that they might see|sed ut ipsi videntes]], that is, that the Egyptians, seeing how that fire did not act on those little beasts that harmed them, but burnt their useful cattle, namely horses, oxen and cows, [[16:18|and perceive that they were persecuted by the judgment of God|scirent quoniam Dei judicio patiuntur persecutionem]], that is, might take note from so great a sign that it was at God's command that they suffered such plagues.

paras.t: Et quodam tempore in aqua super virtutem, id est ultra naturalem vim suam, ignis ardebat undique, quando videlicet ignis simul cum imbre et grandine ferebatur, ut dictum est, ut iniquam terræ nationem exterminaret, id est, Ægyptios dire vexaret, et quosdam eorum occideret.
paras.en: [[16:19|And at another time|Et quodam tempore]], [[16:19|in the midst of water|in aqua]], [[16:19|the fire, above its own power|super virtutem]], that is, beyond its natural force, [[16:19|burnt|ignis ardebat undique]] on every side, namely when the fire was borne along together with the rain and hail, as has been said, [[16:19|to destroy the fruits of a wicked land|ut iniquam terræ nationem exterminaret]] [Latin *iniquam terræ nationem*, "the wicked nation of the land"], that is, to harass the Egyptians grievously and kill some of them.

paras.t: Pro quibus, id est vice et loco tantarum plagarum, angelorum esca, scilicet manna ministerio angelorum exhibito ac descendente, nutrivisti populum tuum Israel, et paratum panem de cœlo præstitisti illis sine labore. Nam angeli formaverunt manna in cœlo aerio, et fecerunt illud simul cum rore descendere. Filii autem Israel collegerunt manna, quod erat quasi semen coriandri, et inde fecerunt panes: ita quod sine eorum labore manna pervenit ad eos.
paras.en: [[16:20|Instead of which things|Pro quibus]], that is, in the stead and place of such great plagues, [[16:20|with the food of angels|angelorum esca]], namely the manna, furnished and coming down by the ministry of angels, [[16:20|thou didst feed thy people|nutrivisti populum tuum Israel]] Israel, [[16:20|and gavest them bread from heaven, prepared without labour|et paratum panem de cœlo præstitisti illis sine labore]]. For the angels formed the manna in the heaven of the air and made it come down together with the dew. And the children of Israel gathered the manna, which was like coriander seed, and made loaves of it[[Ex 16:21||]][[Ex 16:31||]]: so that the manna came to them without their labour.

paras.t: Omne delectamentum in se habentem, et omnis saporis suavitatem. Naturalis sapor mannæ fuit unus: De quo scriptum est: Mane ros jacuit per circuitum castrorum, et apparuit in solitudine manna minutum, et quasi pilo tusum in similitudinem pruinæ super terram: quod erat quasi semen coriandri album, gustusque ejus quasi similæ cum melle. Idcirco quod dicitur hic, habuisse omne delectamentum et omnis saporis suavitatem, non erat naturale, nec ex natura et vi mannæ, sed divina virtute: quemadmodum etiam ipsum manna in se (ut dictum est) dulce, videbatur iniquis insipidum: qui dixerunt, Anima nostra nauseat super cibo isto levissimo. Justis vero et Deo gratis sapiebat quasi omnium habens saporum suavitatem.
paras.en: [[16:20|having in it all that is delicious, and the sweetness of every taste|Omne delectamentum in se habentem, et omnis saporis suavitatem]]. The natural taste of the manna was one, of which it is written: [[Ex 16:13|in the morning a dew lay round about the camp|Mane ros jacuit per circuitum castrorum]], [[Ex 16:14|it appeared in the wilderness small, and as it were beaten with a pestle, like unto the hoar frost on the ground|et apparuit in solitudine manna minutum, et quasi pilo tusum in similitudinem pruinæ super terram]]: [[Ex 16:31|it was like coriander seed, white, and the taste thereof like to flour with honey|quod erat quasi semen coriandri album, gustusque ejus quasi similæ cum melle]]. Therefore what is said here, that it had all that is delicious and the sweetness of every taste, was not natural, nor from the nature and power of the manna, but by divine power: just as the manna itself, sweet in itself (as has been said), seemed tasteless to the wicked, who said: [[Num 21:5|our soul now loatheth this very light food|Anima nostra nauseat super cibo isto levissimo]]. But to the just and to those pleasing to God it tasted as though it had the sweetness of all tastes.

paras.t: Hinc subditur: substantiam enim, id est opulentiam tuam, et dulcedinem, id est piam et caritativam munificentiam tuam, quam in filios adoptivos, quales tunc erant multi in Israel, habes, ostendebas per tam præclarum miraculum, et delicatam justorum illorum refectionem; et deserviens manna uniuscujusque justi voluntati, ad quod quisque volebat, convertebatur, id est ad præbendum talem saporem, qualem talium quisque optavit, sapiendo nunc ut panis, nunc ut carnes, nunc ut pisces.
paras.en: Hence it adds: [[16:21|For thy sustenance|substantiam enim]], that is, thy wealth, and [[16:21|thy sweetness|et dulcedinem]], that is, thy kind and charitable munificence, which thou hast [[16:21|to thy children|in filios]] by adoption, such as many in Israel then were, [[16:21|shewed|ostendebas]] [Denis reads *substantiam enim tuam et dulcedinem tuam … ostendebas*, "for thou didst shew thy substance and thy sweetness"] by so glorious a miracle and by the dainty refreshment of those just men; [[16:21|and serving every man's will|et deserviens manna uniuscujusque justi voluntati]] [Denis's text has "the manna, serving the will of every just man"], [[16:21|it was turned to what every man liked|ad quod quisque volebat, convertebatur]], that is, to yield such a taste as each of them wished, tasting now like bread, now like flesh, now like fish.

paras.t: Nix autem et glacies, id est nix et grandines (quæ sunt aquæ congelatæ, et cum igne, ut dictum est, descendebant), sustinebant vim ignis, et non tabescebant, id est, absque sua corruptione et liquefactione supernaturaliter ignis illius calorem: ut sciret quoniam fructus inimicorum exterminabat ignis, id est, quatenus filii Israel adverterent, et super hoc gratias Deo referrent zelo justitiæ, quod ignis ille ardens in grandine, et in pluvia coruscans, destruxit terræ nascentia Ægyptiorum.
paras.en: [[16:22|But snow and ice|Nix autem et glacies]], that is, snow and hailstones (which are frozen waters, and came down with the fire, as has been said), [[16:22|endured the force of fire, and melted not|sustinebant vim ignis, et non tabescebant]], that is, they bore the heat of that fire supernaturally, without their own corruption and melting: [[16:22|that they might know that the fire|ut sciret quoniam]] [[16:22|destroyed the fruits of the enemies|fructus inimicorum exterminabat ignis]], that is, so that the children of Israel might take note, and with zeal for justice give thanks to God for it, that that fire, [[16:22|burning in the hail, and flashing in the rain|ardens in grandine, et in pluvia coruscans]], destroyed the produce of the land of the Egyptians.

paras.t: Hoc autem iterum, ut nutrirentur justi, ignis etiam suæ virtutis oblitus est: id est, hoc rursus mirabile fuit, quod ignis suam naturalem actionem non exercuit in quibusdam, ut justi nutrirentur ex his, quæ ignis (ut naturaliter potuisset) non consumpsit. Aliqui autem exponunt istud de Anania, Azaria, Misaele: quos ignis fornacis non læsit, ut nutrirentur, id est, in vita manerent, atque reficerentur. Alii applicant istud ad filios Israel in Ægypto, qui habitabant ibi in terra Gessen: quam ignis ille Ægyptios vastans, non intravit, nec Hebræorum læsit jumenta, quum tamen naturaliter se forsitan diffudisset in terram Gessen, et læsisset ibidem pecora Hebræorum.
paras.en: [[16:23|But this same again, that the just might be nourished|Hoc autem iterum, ut nutrirentur justi]], the fire [[16:23|did even forget its own strength|etiam suæ virtutis oblitus est]]: that is, this again was a marvel, that the fire did not exercise its natural action on certain things, so that the just might be nourished by those things which the fire did not consume (as naturally it could have done). Some, however, expound this of Ananias, Azarias and Misael, whom the fire of the furnace did not hurt[[Dan 3:50||]], that they might be nourished, that is, remain alive and be refreshed. Others apply it to the children of Israel in Egypt, who dwelt there in the land of Gessen: which that fire, as it laid the Egyptians waste, did not enter[[Ex 9:26||]], nor did it hurt the cattle of the Hebrews; though naturally it might perhaps have spread into the land of Gessen and hurt the herds of the Hebrews there.

paras.t: Creatura enim etiam inanimata tibi factori deserviens, exardescit, id est, acuitur, et quasi ira fervens, intense movetur, in tormentum, id est ad inferendum pœnas, adversus injustos, id est ipsis injustis ac reprobis, non ad bonum correctionis, sed ad malum extremæ perditionis eorum; et lenior, id est mitior ac convenientior, fit ad benefaciendum pro his qui in te confidunt, id est sperantibus in te, ad profectum ac salutem ipsorum, finaliter tamen ad honorem et gloriam tui ipsius, qui es universorum ultimus finis, ad quem omne bonum est referendum, qui et propter te ipsum operatus es omnia.
paras.en: [[16:24|For the creature|Creatura enim]], even the inanimate, [[16:24|serving thee, the Creator|tibi factori deserviens]], [[16:24|is made fierce|exardescit]], that is, is sharpened and, as though boiling with anger, is intensely moved, [[16:24|for their punishment|in tormentum]], that is, to inflict penalties, [[16:24|against the unjust|adversus injustos]], that is, on the unjust and reprobate themselves, not for the good of correction but for the evil of their final perdition; [[16:24|and abateth its strength|et lenior]] [Latin *lenior fit*, "becomes gentler"], that is, milder and more fitting, [[16:24|for the benefit of them that trust in thee|ad benefaciendum pro his qui in te confidunt]], that is, of those who hope in thee, for their progress and salvation, yet finally for the honour and glory of thyself, who art the last end of all things, to whom all good is to be referred, and who hast wrought all things for thine own sake[[Prov 16:4||]].

paras.t: Propter hoc et tunc omnia transfigurata, id est ignis, aqua, manna, de quibus jam dictum est, mutata tunc a naturali cursu, proprietate, et actione, ita quod ignis in aqua plus viguit, sicut præhabitum est, omnium nutrici gratiæ tuæ, id est tuæ gratiositati, seu gratiosæ voluntati omnibus providenti, deserviebant, obediendo eidem ad nutum, ad voluntatem horum qui a te desiderati sunt, id est juxta desiderium et petitionem filiorum Israel, quorum profectum et salutem specialiter desiderasti: de quibus locutus es Moysi: Quis det talem eos habere mentem, ut bene sit eis? Et alibi per Prophetam: Utinam attendisses mandata mea.
paras.en: [[16:25|Therefore even then|Propter hoc et tunc]] all things [[16:25|transformed|transfigurata]] [Denis reads *omnia transfigurata … deserviebant*, "all things, transformed, were obedient", where the Douay-Rheims has "it was transformed into all things"], that is, fire, water and manna, of which we have spoken, changed then from their natural course, property and action, so that fire had more force in water, as was said before, [[16:25|to thy grace, that nourisheth all|omnium nutrici gratiæ tuæ]], that is, to thy graciousness, or to thy gracious will that provides for all, [[16:25|was obedient|deserviebant]], obeying it at a nod, [[16:25|according to the will of them|ad voluntatem horum]] [[16:25|that desired it of thee|qui a te desiderati sunt]] [Denis reads *qui a te desiderati sunt*, "who were desired by thee"], that is, according to the desire and petition of the children of Israel, whose progress and salvation thou didst especially desire: of whom thou didst say to Moses: [[Deut 5:29|Who shall give them to have such a mind|Quis det talem eos habere mentem]], [[Deut 5:29|that it may be well with them|ut bene sit eis]]? And elsewhere through the Prophet: [[Is 48:18|O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments|Utinam attendisses mandata mea]].

paras.t: Ut scirent filii tui, quos dilexisti, Domine, id est filii Israel specialiter tibi cari, quibus in veteri Testamento multa et magna beneficia specialia, tam spiritualia quam corporalia tribuisti. De quibus scriptum est : Non est alia natio tam grandis; et rursus, Te elegit Dominus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis qui sunt super terram, quia dilexit vos Dominus. Quoniam non nativitatis fructus pascunt homines, id est, quod non soli fructus nati ex terra, ipsos homines alunt; sed sermo tuus, id est tua instructio et doctrina, hos qui in te crediderunt fide formata, conservat in esse statuque gratiæ ac virtutum : et sic spiritualiter reficit atque vivificat eos, juxta illud : Non in solo pane vivit homo, sed in omni verbo quod procedit de ore Dei. Ideo admonemur per Apostolum : In mansuetudine suscipite insitum verbum, quod potest salvare animas vestras.
paras.en: [[16:26|That thy children, O Lord, whom thou lovedst, might know|Ut scirent filii tui, quos dilexisti, Domine]], that is, the children of Israel, especially dear to thee, on whom in the Old Testament thou didst bestow many great and special benefits, spiritual as well as bodily; of whom it is written: [[Deut 4:7|Neither is there any other nation so great|Non est alia natio tam grandis]]; and again: [[Deut 7:6|The Lord thy God hath chosen thee, to be his peculiar people of all peoples that are upon the earth|Te elegit Dominus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis qui sunt super terram]], [[Deut 7:8|because the Lord hath loved you|quia dilexit vos Dominus]] [the margin gives Deut. vii, 6 and 3; these last words are Deut 7:8]. [[16:26|that it is not the growing of fruits that nourisheth men|Quoniam non nativitatis fructus pascunt homines]], that is, that it is not the fruits born of the earth alone that feed men; [[16:26|but thy word|sed sermo tuus]], that is, thy instruction and teaching, [[16:26|preserveth|conservat]] [[16:26|them that believe in thee|hos qui in te crediderunt]] with formed faith [that is, faith given its form by charity] in the being and state of grace and the virtues: and so it refreshes and quickens them spiritually, according to that: [[Matt 4:4|Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God|Non in solo pane vivit homo, sed in omni verbo quod procedit de ore Dei]][[Deut 8:3||]]. Therefore we are admonished by the Apostle: [[Jas 1:21|with meekness receive the ingrafted word, which is able to save your souls|In mansuetudine suscipite insitum verbum, quod potest salvare animas vestras]].

paras.t: Quod enim ab igne non poterat exterminari, scilicet manna, quod coquebatur et indurabatur ad ignem, statim ab exiguo solis radio calefactum tabescebat, id est liquefiebat, ut notum omnibus esset, quoniam oportet prævenire solem ad benedictionem tuam : id est, quatenus cunctis filiis Israel innotesceret, quod ante solis ortum, adspectum, seu elevationem notabilem super nostrum horizontem, vel antequam sol magnum in terra calorem produceret, oportuit eos accedere ad colligendum manna : quod vocatur benedictio Dei, id est donum ab eo gratis exhibitum. Unde et Abigail primo Regum ait ad David : Accipe benedictionem ancillæ tuæ, id est escam quam attuli ad te. Hinc in Exodo fertur : Colligebant mane singuli, quantum sufficere poterat ad vescendum; quumque incaluisset sol, liquefiebat. Et ad ortum lucis te adorare, id est statim sole oriente, et radios super terram diffundente, te invocare, et grates tibi refundere pro beneficiis tuis.
paras.en: [[16:27|For that which could not be destroyed by fire|Quod enim ab igne non poterat exterminari]], namely the manna, which was baked and hardened at the fire, [[16:27|being warmed with a little sunbeam, presently melted away|statim ab exiguo solis radio calefactum tabescebat]], that is, was liquefied, [[16:28|That it might be known to all, that we ought to prevent the sun to bless thee|ut notum omnibus esset, quoniam oportet prævenire solem ad benedictionem tuam]] [*prævenire*, "to come before"; Latin *ad benedictionem tuam*, "for thy blessing", which Denis takes of the manna]: that is, so that it might be known to all the children of Israel that before the rising of the sun, its appearing or notable elevation above our horizon, or before the sun produced great heat on the earth, they had to come out to gather the manna: which is called the blessing of God, that is, a gift freely bestowed by him. Hence Abigail too, in the first book of Kings, says to David: [[1 Kings 25:27|receive this blessing|Accipe benedictionem]] of thy handmaid, that is, the food which I have brought to thee. Hence it is said in Exodus: [[Ex 16:21|every one of them gathered in the morning, as much as might suffice to eat: and after the sun grew hot, it melted|Colligebant mane singuli, quantum sufficere poterat ad vescendum; quumque incaluisset sol, liquefiebat]]. [[16:28|and adore thee at the dawning of the light|Et ad ortum lucis te adorare]], that is, as soon as the sun rises and spreads its rays over the earth, to call upon thee and render thee thanks for thy benefits.

paras.t: Itaque, quod ait, Oportet ad ortum lucis te adorare, non est intelligendum quod secundum legem Moysis jussum aut licitum fuerit adorare versus orientem, sed ad occidentem : quia et tabernaculum Moysis templumque Salomonis respiciebant ad occidentem, et ab oriente intrabatur in ea. Nam in Exodo jussum fuit, versus occidentem fieri adorationem : et hoc, ut populus Israel veri Dei cultor, a gentibus distingueretur, qui fere omnes versus orientem orabant, ad honorem solis ac planetarum, qui omnes ab illa cœli parte super terram ascendunt. Hinc ab Ezechiele increpantur, qui versus orientem orabant. Hinc, quod dictum est, Ad ortum solis, non denotat situm loci, sed certam temporis horam : de qua loquitur Isaias, De mane vigilabo ad te; et Psalmista, Mane adstabo tibi, et videbo. Unde et in Ecclesiastico legitur : Sapiens cor suum tradet ad vigilandum diluculo, ad Dominum qui fecit illum.
paras.en: Accordingly, when it says, We ought to adore thee at the dawning of the light[[16:28||]], this is not to be understood as if under the law of Moses it was commanded or lawful to adore towards the east; rather, towards the west: for both the tabernacle of Moses and the temple of Solomon faced the west, and were entered from the east. For in Exodus it was commanded that adoration be made towards the west[[Ex 26:22||]][[Ex 26:23||]] [the margin gives "cf. Exod. xxvi, 22, 23", which describe the west end of the tabernacle]: and this so that the people of Israel, worshipper of the true God, might be distinguished from the gentiles, nearly all of whom prayed towards the east, in honour of the sun and the planets, which all rise above the earth from that quarter of the sky. Hence those who prayed towards the east are rebuked by Ezechiel[[Ezech 8:16||]]. Hence what was said, *at the rising of the sun*, does not denote the position of a place but a certain hour of time: of which Isaias speaks: [[Is 26:9|in the morning early I will watch to thee|De mane vigilabo ad te]]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 5:5|In the morning I will stand before thee, and I will see|Mane adstabo tibi, et videbo]]. Hence we read in Ecclesiasticus too: The wise man [[Ecclus 39:6|will give his heart to resort early to the Lord that made him|cor suum tradet ad vigilandum diluculo, ad Dominum qui fecit illum]].

paras.t: Sic ergo oportet adorare, et Deo regratiari. Ingrati enim spes, tanquam hibernalis, id est hiemalis, glacies tabescet : id est, spes ingratorum non consequetur salutem; sed sicut glacies calore cito dissolvitur, sic illa privabitur optato effectu; et disperiet tanquam aqua supervacua : id est, omnino peribit, et ipse ingratus damnationem incurret, sicut aqua superflua defluendo cito percurrit ac deficit. Hinc dictum est supra : Spes impii tanquam lanugo; et in Psalmo, Iter impiorum peribit. In Job quoque legitur de iniquo : Ecce spes ejus frustrabitur eum, et videntibus cunctis præcipitabitur. Sic et spes perfidorum Judæorum, regem Messiam adhuc præstolantium, et Domino Jesu Christo ingratissimorum, quæ spes frigore infidelitatis atque duritia obstinationis instar glaciei constricta est, apparente Sole justitiæ Christo Domino penitus confundetur.
paras.en: So, then, we ought to adore and give thanks to God. [[16:29|For the hope of the unthankful|Ingrati enim spes]] [[16:29|shall melt away as the winter's ice|tanquam hibernalis, id est hiemalis, glacies tabescet]] [Denis glosses *hibernalis*, "wintry", with the commoner *hiemalis*]: that is, the hope of the ungrateful will not attain salvation; but as ice is quickly dissolved by heat, so it will be deprived of the effect it longed for; [[16:29|and shall run off as unprofitable water|et disperiet tanquam aqua supervacua]], that is, it will perish altogether, and the ungrateful man himself will incur damnation, as superfluous water quickly runs off and is gone. Hence it was said above: [[Wis 5:15|the hope of the wicked is as dust|Spes impii tanquam lanugo]] [Latin *lanugo*, "down"]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 1:6|the way of the wicked shall perish|Iter impiorum peribit]]. In Job too we read of the wicked man: [[Job 40:28|Behold his hope shall fail him, and in the sight of all he shall be cast down|Ecce spes ejus frustrabitur eum, et videntibus cunctis præcipitabitur]]. So too the hope of the faithless Jews, who still await the king Messias and are most ungrateful to the Lord Jesus Christ, a hope bound fast like ice by the cold of unbelief and the hardness of obstinacy, will be utterly confounded when Christ the Lord, the Sun of justice, appears.

17.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI SEPTIMIDECIMI : MAGNA ENIM SUNT JUDICIA TUA, DOMINE.
17.title_en: Elucidation of the seventeenth chapter: For thy judgments, O Lord, are great

paras.t: Quam diversimode Deus se habeat circa electos et reprobos, hic docetur.
paras.en: How diversely God deals with the elect and with the reprobate is taught here.

paras.t: Magna enim, id est sancta, justa, sapientialia et præclara, sunt judicia tua, Domine, id est decreta sapientiæ atque justitiæ tuæ, seu earumdem effectus, in rationalibus creaturis, censuræ quoque sapientiæ tuæ in temetipso. Unde ait Psalmista : Justitia tua sicut montes Dei ; judicia tua abyssus multa. Hinc clamat Apostolus : O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei! Quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, et investigabiles viæ ejus! Unde et in Apocalypsi fertur : Magna et mirabilia sunt opera tua, Domine Deus omnipotens: justa et vera, judicia tua. Horum judiciorum ratio potest esse occulta, non autem injusta.
paras.en: [[17:1|For thy judgments, O Lord, are great|Magna enim]]: great, that is, holy, just, full of wisdom and glorious, [[17:1|thy judgments, O Lord|sunt judicia tua, Domine]], that is, the decrees of thy wisdom and justice, or their effects, in rational creatures, and also the sentences of thy wisdom within thyself. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 35:7|Thy justice is as the mountains of God, thy judgments are a great deep|Justitia tua sicut montes Dei ; judicia tua abyssus multa]]. Hence the Apostle cries out: [[Rom 11:33|O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways!|O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei! Quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, et investigabiles viæ ejus!]]! Hence also in the Apocalypse it is said: [[Apoc 15:3|Great and wonderful are thy works, O Lord God Almighty|Magna et mirabilia sunt opera tua, Domine Deus omnipotens]]: just and true are thy judgments [Denis's text has "thy judgments" here, where the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have "thy ways"]. The reason of these judgments may be hidden, but not unjust.

paras.t: Et inenarrabilia verba tua, id est, verba illa interna, quæ tu, Deus, in cordibus loqueris electorum, plene exprimi nequeunt : præsertim profundiora illa eloquia et secreta, quæ melius intelligi possunt quam eloqui. Unde et sanctus Apostolus affirmat se audivisse arcana verba, quæ non licet homini loqui. In Ecclesiastico quoque oratur : Reple Sion inenarrabilibus verbis tuis. Frequenter etiam per verba designantur facta, seu opera quæ significant per verba : quæ Dei opera frequenter inenarrabilia sunt. Propter hæc indisciplinatæ animæ erraverunt : quæ tua judicia non verentur, nec tuis obediunt verbis, sed incultæ sunt moribus atque indomitæ : quales fuerunt Ægyptii, de quibus subjungitur :
paras.en: [[17:1|and thy words cannot be expressed|Et inenarrabilia verba tua]], that is, those inward words which thou, O God, speakest in the hearts of the elect cannot be fully expressed: above all those deeper and secret utterances, which can better be understood than spoken. Hence the holy Apostle too affirms that he [[2 Cor 12:4|heard secret words which it is not granted to man to utter|audivisse arcana verba, quæ non licet homini loqui]]. In Ecclesiasticus also it is prayed: [[Ecclus 36:16|Fill Sion with thy unspeakable words|Reple Sion inenarrabilibus verbis tuis]] [the Latin word rendered "unspeakable" here is the same as the one rendered "cannot be expressed" in this verse]. Often too deeds are meant by words, or the works which are signified by words: and these works of God are often beyond telling. [[17:1|therefore undisciplined souls have erred|Propter hæc indisciplinatæ animæ erraverunt]]: souls that do not fear thy judgments nor obey thy words, but are untilled in their ways and untamed: such were the Egyptians, of whom is added:

paras.t: Dum enim persuasum habent iniqui, id est, quoniam sibi ipsis persuaserunt posse dominari nationi sanctæ, id est Israeliticæ plebi, quam putabant non posse liberari a Deo suo de servitute ipsorum; vinculis tenebrarum, id est infidelitatis et errorum suorum, et longæ noctis, id est obstinatæ excæcationis, compediti, id est mente ligati et capti: vel, Vinculis tenebrarum palpabilium quas sustinuerunt, et longæ noctis, quia tribus diebus duravit illa caligo, ut legitur in Exodo; inclusi sunt tectis : quia intra tantum tempus nullus se movit de loco suo; fugitivi : quia timore imminentium plagarum, quandoque hinc inde fugerunt; perpetuæ providentiæ jacuerunt, id est, divinæ providentiæ erant, vellent nollent, subditi et prostrati, sustinendo inevitabiliter pœnas quas Deus eis inferre præordinavit.
paras.en: [[17:2|For while the wicked thought|Dum enim persuasum habent iniqui]], that is, since they had persuaded themselves [[17:2|to be able to have dominion over the holy nation|posse dominari nationi sanctæ]], that is, over the people of Israel, which they thought could not be set free by its God from their bondage; [[17:2|with the bonds of darkness|vinculis tenebrarum]], that is, of their unbelief and errors, [[17:2|and a long night|et longæ noctis]], that is, of obstinate blindness, [[17:2|being fettered|compediti]], that is, bound and taken captive in mind: or, with the bonds of the palpable darkness which they endured, and of a long night, because that gloom lasted three days, as is read in Exodus[[Ex 10:22||]]; [[17:2|shut up in their houses|inclusi sunt tectis]] [the printed text reads "inclusi sunt tectis", with the reading "sub tectis", "under their roofs", noted in the margin]: because within so long a time no one moved from his place; [[17:2|exiled|fugitivi]]: because for fear of the plagues hanging over them they sometimes fled hither and thither; [[17:2|lay there exiled from the eternal providence|perpetuæ providentiæ jacuerunt]] [Denis takes "fugitivi", "fugitives", on its own, and "perpetuæ providentiæ jacuerunt" as "they lay subject to the eternal providence"], that is, willing or unwilling, they were subject and laid low before the divine providence, inescapably bearing the punishments which God had foreordained to bring upon them.

paras.t: Et dum putant se latere in obscuris peccatis, id est divinæ providentiæ non patere in occultis peccatis, quæ vel secrete, vel in tenebris faciunt, juxta illud : Et dixi : Forsitan tenebræ conculcabunt me; et nox illuminatio mea in deliciis meis. De quibus ait Propheta : Quorum sunt in tenebris opera, et dicunt : Dominus non videt. Tenebroso oblivionis velamento dispersi sunt, id est propter suam tenebrosam oblivionem, qua obliviscebantur Dei: quæ corda eorum erant operta tanquam velamento, sicut ait Apostolus. Tenebris obscuratum habentes cor; paventes horrende, id est, terribiliter formidantes ex plagis imminentibus aut inflictis, et cum admiratione nimia perturbati : quia de tanta sua devastatione ac dejectione maxime mirabantur ac turbabantur, videntes filios Israel, quos paulo ante pro nihilo reputabant et oppresserunt, tam inopinate superiores eis effectos, seu desuper defensatos : ita quod rex Ægypti compulsus est veniam postulare a Moyse, et liberationem a plagis immissis.
paras.en: [[17:3|And while they thought to lie hid in their obscure sins|Et dum putant se latere in obscuris peccatis]], that is, not to lie open to the divine providence in their hidden sins, which they commit either secretly or in the dark, according to that saying: [[Ps 138:11|And I said: Perhaps darkness shall cover me: and night shall be my light in my pleasures|Et dixi : Forsitan tenebræ conculcabunt me; et nox illuminatio mea in deliciis meis]]. Of whom the Prophet says: [[Is 29:15|their works are in the dark, and they say|Quorum sunt in tenebris opera, et dicunt]]: The Lord seeth not [so Denis; the Vulgate of Isaias has "Who seeth us?"]. [[17:3|they were scattered under a dark veil of forgetfullness|Tenebroso oblivionis velamento dispersi sunt]], that is, because of their dark forgetfulness, by which they forgot God: with which their hearts were covered as with a veil, as the Apostle says: [[Eph 4:18|Having their understanding darkened|Tenebris obscuratum habentes cor]] [Denis has "heart", "cor", where the Apostle has "understanding"]; [[17:3|being horribly afraid|paventes horrende]], that is, dreading terribly the plagues hanging over them or already inflicted, [[17:3|and troubled with exceeding great astonishment|et cum admiratione nimia perturbati]]: because they marvelled and were troubled exceedingly at so great a laying waste and casting down of themselves, seeing the children of Israel, whom a little before they counted as nothing and oppressed, so unexpectedly made their superiors, or defended from on high: so that the king of Egypt was forced to beg pardon of Moses[[Ex 8:8||]][[Ex 8:28||]][[Ex 9:28||]][[Ex 10:17||]], and deliverance from the plagues sent upon him.

paras.t: Neque enim quæ continebat illos spelunca, sine timore custodiebat : id est, etiam in suis latibulis in quæ confugerunt, ex plagarum horrore vehementer timebant; quoniam sonitus descendens, id est de aere veniens, puta tonitruum, vel quicumque aeris fragor, perturbabat illos : homines enim in adversitatibus et diffortuniis positi, faciliter perterrentur; et personæ tristes illis apparentes, pavorem illis præstabant. Homines quippe formidolosi et angustiis pleni, patiuntur in somno, imo et in vigilia, tempore noctis præsertim, imaginationes terribiles; et sæpe apparent eis miserabilium personarum phantasmata, timorem eis incutientia : ad quod dæmones sæpe cooperantur. Ideo fertur in Psalmo : Misit in eos iram indignationis suæ, immissiones per angelos malos. Nam et sanctus Job in percussionibus positus, dixit : Terrebis me per somnia.
paras.en: [[17:4|For neither did the den that held them, keep them from fear|Neque enim quæ continebat illos spelunca, sine timore custodiebat]]: that is, even in their hiding places, to which they had fled, they were greatly afraid from the horror of the plagues; [[17:4|for noises coming down|quoniam sonitus descendens]], that is, coming from the air, such as thunder or any crash in the air, [[17:4|troubled them|perturbabat illos]]: for men set in adversities and misfortunes are easily terrified; [[17:4|and sad visions appearing to them, affrighted them|et personæ tristes illis apparentes, pavorem illis præstabant]] [literally "sad persons appearing to them"; hence Denis speaks next of phantoms of persons]. For fearful men, full of anguish, suffer terrible imaginings in sleep, and even awake, above all at night-time; and often phantoms of wretched persons appear to them, striking fear into them: and the demons often work together to this end. Therefore it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 77:49|he sent upon them the wrath of his indignation|Misit in eos iram indignationis suæ]], [[Ps 77:49|which he sent by evil angels|immissiones per angelos malos]]. For holy Job also, set amid his afflictions, said: [[Job 7:14|Thou wilt frighten me with dreams|Terrebis me per somnia]].

paras.t: Et ignis quidem nulla vis poterat illis lumen præbere : id est, ignis nulla sua claritate aut vi poterat Ægyptiis lucem exhibere triduo illarum palpabilium tenebrarum, propter nimiam densitatem earum; nec siderum limpidæ flammæ, id est claræ scintillationes et irradiationes stellarum, illuminare poterant illam noctem horrendam tam diu durantem : vel quia aer capax non fuit, nimium ingrossatus, ut aliqui dicunt; vel, ut potius creditur, quoniam sicut Deo jubente sol radios suæ lucis subtraxit Ægyptiis tribus diebus, sic planetæ et stellæ noctibus illis.
paras.en: [[17:5|And no power of fire could give them light|Et ignis quidem nulla vis poterat illis lumen præbere]]: that is, fire by no brightness or strength of its own could give light to the Egyptians during the three days of that palpable darkness, because of its exceeding thickness; [[17:5|neither could the bright flames of the stars|nec siderum limpidæ flammæ]], that is, the clear twinkling and radiance of the stars, [[17:5|enlighten that horrible night|illuminare poterant illam noctem horrendam]] that lasted so long: either because the air, too much thickened, could not take the light, as some say; or, as is rather believed, because, as at God's command the sun withdrew the rays of its light from the Egyptians for three days, so did the planets and stars on those nights.

paras.t: Apparebat autem illis subitaneus ignis timore plenus. Hoc dispensative contingere potuit ad majorem Ægyptiorum afflictionem, ut suam inspicientes dispositionem et cladem, ad modicam moram gravius angustiarentur. Unde subjungitur : et timore percussi illius, quæ non videbatur, faciei, id est, valde perterriti imaginaria apparitione facierum miserabilium, quæ in veritate non aderant, æstimabant deteriora esse quæ videbantur, id est, putabant quod magis periculosa et nociva essent quæ apparebant, quam erant : sicut communiter putant hi, quibus talia apparent in somno.
paras.en: [[17:6|But there appeared to them a sudden fire, very dreadful|Apparebat autem illis subitaneus ignis timore plenus]]. This could happen by God's dispensation, for the greater affliction of the Egyptians, so that, seeing for a short while their state and their ruin, they might be the more grievously distressed. Hence is added: [[17:6|and being struck with the fear of that face, which was not seen|et timore percussi illius, quæ non videbatur, faciei]], that is, greatly terrified by an imagined appearance of wretched faces, which were not really there, [[17:6|they thought the things which they saw to be worse|æstimabant deteriora esse quæ videbantur]], that is, they thought that the things which appeared were more dangerous and harmful than they were: as those commonly think to whom such things appear in sleep.

paras.t: Et magicæ artis apposita erant derisus : id est, ceteris miseriis et flagellis Ægyptiorum apposuit Deus irrisiones et confusiones magorum et maleficorum : quos Pharao advocavit, ut resisterent Moysi; cœperuntque ei resistere, sed defecerunt, non valendo producere scinifes, ut dicitur in Exodo. Et paulo post fuerunt vulnerati ulceribus vesicarum turgentium, ita quod stare non poterant coram Moyse, nec se ipsos, nec alios adjuvare, ut patet in Exodo. Hinc additur : et sapientiæ gloriæ correctio : id est, Deus addidit illis correctionem vanæ gloriationis, qua de sapientia magorum gloriabantur : quam gloriationem Deus correxit cum contumelia, ostendens magorum insipientiam, per confusibilem ipsorum vulnerationem præfatam.
paras.en: [[17:7|And the delusions of their magic art were put down|Et magicæ artis apposita erant derisus]] [Denis reads this as "the mockeries of the magic art were added", and explains it so], that is, to the other miseries and scourges of the Egyptians God added the mockery and confusion of the magicians and sorcerers, whom Pharao called in to withstand Moses[[Ex 7:11||]][[Ex 7:12||]][[Ex 7:22||]][[Ex 8:7||]]; and they began to withstand him, but failed, not being able to bring forth sciniphs, as is said in Exodus[[Ex 8:18||]]. And a little after they were wounded with boils of swelling blisters, so that they could not stand before Moses, nor help themselves or others, as is plain in Exodus[[Ex 9:11||]]. Hence is added: [[17:7|and their boasting of wisdom|et sapientiæ gloriæ]] [[17:7|rebuked|correctio]]: that is, God added for them the correction of the vain boasting with which they gloried in the wisdom of the magicians: which boasting God corrected [[17:7|reproachfully|cum contumelia]], showing up the folly of the magicians by their shameful wounding spoken of above.

paras.t: Illi enim, scilicet magi, qui promittebant timores et perturbationes expellere se ab anima languente, id est, qui præsumpserunt et asseruerunt quod ab Ægyptiis expellerent anxietates et inquietudines, quas sustinuerunt ex plagis Dei, hi cum derisu pleni timore languebant, id est, sicut et ceteri vulnerati fuerunt, ac territi ex flagellis Altissimi.
paras.en: [[17:8|For they|Illi enim]], namely the magicians, [[17:8|who promised to drive away fears and troubles from a sick soul|qui promittebant timores et perturbationes expellere se ab anima languente]], that is, who took it upon themselves and declared that they would drive out from the Egyptians the anxieties and disquiet which they suffered from the plagues of God, [[17:8|were sick themselves of a fear worthy to be laughed at|hi cum derisu pleni timore languebant]], that is, they too, like the rest, were wounded and terrified by the scourges of the Most High.

paras.t: Nam etsi nihil illos ex monstris perturbabat, id est, quamvis magi illi non terrebantur ex monstrorum terribilium facierum apparitione, quoniam assueti erant talia sæpe videre : quemadmodum Balaam, alloquente eum asina sua, non fuit turbatus, utpote talibus monstris assuetus, secundum Augustinum; transitu animalium, et serpentium sibilatione commoti, tremebundi peribant : quia postquam in se ipsis experti fuerunt acerbitatem plagationis eis inflictæ, cœperunt timere, etiam solo adspectu ac sonitu animalium nocivorum. Hinc ad Timotheum scribit Apostolus : Quemadmodum Jannes et Mambres restiterunt Moysi, ita et hi resistunt veritati. Sed ultra non proficient : insipientia enim eorum manifesta erit omnibus, sicut et illorum fuit. Et aerem quem nulla ratione quis effugere posset, id est, sine cujus respiratione nemo potest vivere, negantes se videre : non quod aer sit exteriori visu directe visibilis, sed mediante luce perceptibilis : quem, durante densitate palpabilium tenebrarum, ita percipere non valebant.
paras.en: [[17:9|For though no terrible thing disturbed them|Nam etsi nihil illos ex monstris perturbabat]], that is, although those magicians were not terrified by the appearing of monsters with terrible faces, since they were used to seeing such things often: just as Balaam, when his ass spoke to him[[Num 22:28||]], was not troubled, being used to such portents, according to Augustine; [[17:9|yet being scared with the passing by of beasts, and hissing of serpents|transitu animalium, et serpentium sibilatione commoti]], [[17:9|they died for fear|tremebundi peribant]]: because after they had felt in themselves the bitterness of the plague inflicted on them, they began to be afraid even at the mere sight and sound of harmful animals. Hence the Apostle writes to Timothy: [[2 Tim 3:8|as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth|Quemadmodum Jannes et Mambres restiterunt Moysi, ita et hi resistunt veritati]]. [[2 Tim 3:9|But they shall proceed no farther: for their folly shall be manifest to all men, as theirs also was|Sed ultra non proficient : insipientia enim eorum manifesta erit omnibus, sicut et illorum fuit]]. And [[17:9|the air, which could by no means be avoided|aerem quem nulla ratione quis effugere posset]], that is, without breathing which no one can live, [[17:9|denying that they saw|negantes se videre]]: not that the air is directly visible to outward sight, but it is perceived by means of light: and while the thickness of the palpable darkness lasted, they could not perceive it in this way.

paras.t: Frequenter enim præoccupant pessima, id est, maxima pœnalia mala sæpe præveniunt, seu citius adesse putantur quam adsint, redarguente conscientia, id est ex remorsu propriæ conscientiæ, qua impius sibi suorum conscius vitiorum suspicatur sibi assidue adversa instare, quæ se noscit promeruisse.
paras.en: “For the worst things often come before their time” [these words, and "conscience reproving" below, stand at this place in Denis's text, before v. 10; they are not in the Clementine Vulgate or the Douay-Rheims], that is, the greatest evils of punishment often come on ahead, or are thought to be at hand sooner than they are, “conscience reproving”, that is, from the remorse of one's own conscience, by which the wicked man, conscious of his own vices, suspects that adversities he knows he has deserved are constantly hanging over him.

paras.t: Quum sit enim timida nequitia, id est, timidum faciat hominem, ratione prætacta : propter quod fures et latrones semper sunt pavidi, metuentes jugiter deprehendi; dat testimonium condemnata, id est, accusat se ipsam, et juste se damnari testatur atque puniri ipsa sua inordinata formidine. Alii habent : Data est in omnium condemnationem, id est, a Deo judice ordinatur ad ipsorum reorum punitionem et condemnationem. Inordinatus etenim animus, sibi ipsi frequenter est gravis; et timor quem parit nequitia in suo subjecto, est quædam ejus punitio.
paras.en: [[17:10|For whereas wickedness is fearful|Quum sit enim timida nequitia]], that is, makes a man fearful, for the reason touched on above: which is why thieves and robbers are always fearful, dreading at every moment to be caught; [[17:10|it beareth witness|dat testimonium]], being condemned [Denis reads "condemnata", "condemned", where the Vulgate has "condemnationis", "of its condemnation"], that is, it accuses itself, and by its very disordered fear testifies that it is justly condemned and punished. Others read: It is given over to the condemnation of all, that is, it is ordained by God the judge for the punishment and condemnation of the guilty themselves. For a disordered mind is often a burden to itself; and the fear that wickedness begets in its subject is a kind of punishment of it.

paras.t: Semper enim præsumit sæva perturbata conscientia : id est, conscientia nequitiosa jugiter suspicatur, præsupponit, seu putat sibi adfutura et propinqua esse dura ferociaque tormenta. Sicque patitur supplicia antequam veniant : sicut et Leo Papa testatur, quod rea conscientia intra se patitur quidquid Dei bonitate differtur.
paras.en: [[17:10|for a troubled conscience always forecasteth grievous things|Semper enim præsumit sæva perturbata conscientia]]: that is, a wicked conscience constantly suspects, takes for granted, or thinks that hard and cruel torments are about to come upon it and are near. And so it suffers punishments before they come: as Pope Leo also testifies, that a guilty conscience suffers within itself whatever is put off by the goodness of God.

paras.t: Nihil enim est timor hujusmodi inordinatus, ex nequitia oriens cum sua matre, puta nequitia, nisi præsumptionis præfatæ, qua quis prava conscientia suspicatur sibi instare tormenta, adjutorium : quia fovet et auget talem præsumptionem, quam causat nequitia. Est quoque timor iste proditio cogitationis auxiliorum : quia ex timore solet procedere tremor corporis, pallorque vultus, adulatio et humiliatio quædam : ex quibus manifestatur, quod timens cogitat qualiter possit obtinere auxilia contra imminentia sibi adversa.
paras.en: [[17:11|For fear is nothing else|Nihil enim est timor]] (such disordered fear, springing from wickedness, together with its mother, namely wickedness) but a help of the presumption spoken of above [Denis's text reads "nisi præsumptionis adjutorium", "but a help of presumption", words not in the Clementine Vulgate or the Douay-Rheims], by which someone of depraved conscience suspects that torments are hanging over him: because it fosters and increases such presumption, which wickedness causes. This fear is also [[17:11|a yielding up of the succours from thought|proditio cogitationis auxiliorum]] ["proditio" can mean a betraying or a disclosing; Denis takes it in the second sense]: because from fear there usually come trembling of the body and paleness of the face, flattery and a kind of self-abasement: and from these it is made plain that the one who is afraid is thinking how he may get help against the adversities hanging over him.

paras.t: Et dum ab intro minor est exspectatio, id est, dum ex se ipso minus confidit se auxilia adepturum, minusque ea exspectat, majorem putat potentiam ejus causæ, de qua tormentum præstat : id est, eum ex cujus consideratione concipit metum et afflictionem in corde, reputat esse potentiorem ad nocendum sibi, quam est, et graviora putat sibi ab illo imminere adversa, quam imminent. Timor namque dejicit eum, pusillanimemque constituit : sed et ipsa irrefrenata passio timoris, a recto abducit judicio rationis, sicut et cæteræ passiones.
paras.en: [[17:12|And while there is less expectation from within|Et dum ab intro minor est exspectatio]], that is, while of himself he has less confidence that he will obtain help, and expects it less, [[17:12|the greater doth it count|majorem putat]] the power [Denis reads "potentiam", "power", where the Vulgate has "inscientiam", "ignorance"] [[17:12|of that cause which bringeth the torment|ejus causæ, de qua tormentum præstat]]: that is, the one from the thought of whom he conceives fear and distress in his heart he reckons more powerful to harm him than he is, and thinks that heavier adversities threaten him from that quarter than in fact do. For fear casts him down and makes him faint-hearted: and besides, the very passion of fear, unbridled, leads away from the right judgment of reason, as the other passions do too.

paras.t: Denique his concordat quod apud Job legitur : Sonitus terroris semper in auribus impii; et quum pax sit, ille insidias suspicatur. Itemque : Angustia vallabit impium, sicut regem qui paratur ad prælium. Quod etenim impius intulit alteri, suspicatur sibi posse inferri. Econtra, nihil quietius innocente sinceraque mente, quæ sicut non nocuit proximis, sic nec sibi præsumit nocendum esse ab illis. Hinc innocentia, justitia, sapientia vera, præstant fiduciam et confidentiam bonam, et imperterritum statuunt animum. Propter quod ait Scriptura : Fugit impius nemine persequente; justus autem quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit. Et rursus Sapientia ait : Qui me audierit, absque terrore quiescet, et abundantia perfruetur, malorum timore sublato. Unde habetur de Juda, qui cum fratribus suis non vere accusabatur de furto : Accedens autem propius, confidenter ait. Aristoteles quoque fatetur, quod hi qui melius habent se in divinis, sunt fiduciæ melioris.
paras.en: Finally, with these words agrees what is read in Job: [[Job 15:21|The sound of dread is always in his ears: and when there is peace, he always suspecteth treason|Sonitus terroris semper in auribus impii; et quum pax sit, ille insidias suspicatur]] [Denis has "in the ears of the wicked" for "in his ears"]. And again: [[Job 15:24|distress shall surround him, as a king that is prepared for the battle|Angustia vallabit impium, sicut regem qui paratur ad prælium]]. For what the wicked man has brought upon another, he suspects may be brought upon himself. On the other hand, nothing is more at rest than an innocent and sincere mind, which, as it has not harmed its neighbours, so does not suppose that it will be harmed by them. Hence innocence, justice and true wisdom give a good trust and confidence, and make the mind undaunted. Wherefore the Scripture says: [[Prov 28:1|The wicked man fleeth, when no man pursueth: but the just, bold as a lion, shall be without dread|Fugit impius nemine persequente; justus autem quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit]]. And again Wisdom says: [[Prov 1:33|he that shall hear me, shall rest without terror, and shall enjoy abundance, without fear of evils|Qui me audierit, absque terrore quiescet, et abundantia perfruetur, malorum timore sublato]]. Hence it is said of Juda, who with his brethren was falsely accused of theft: [[Gen 44:18|Then Juda coming nearer, said boldly|Accedens autem propius, confidenter ait]]. Aristotle too admits that those who stand better in divine things are of better confidence.

paras.t: Sequitur de Ægyptiorum punitione. Illi autem qui in potentem venere noctem, id est Ægyptii, qui inciderunt in tempus illud tenebrosum palpabilium tenebrarum, et ab infimis et ab altissimis supervenientem : id est, quæ nox causabatur partim ex terra et aqua, id est ex vaporibus et exhalationibus ascendentibus de terra et aqua, et ingrossantibus aerem; partim vero ex causa altissima, scilicet divino imperio, angelicoque ministerio, atque ex spissitudine nubium, illuminationem aeris impedientium, ut aliqui dicunt : verius tamen putatur, quod ex supernaturali subtractione radiorum solarium; eumdem somnum dormientes, id est somnum gravem et tædiosum, nocti illi consimilem;
paras.en: There follows the punishment of the Egyptians. [[17:13|But they that during that night|Illi autem qui in potentem venere noctem]] [Denis reads "qui in potentem venere noctem", "who came into the mighty night", where the Vulgate has "impotentem vere noctem", "a night truly powerless", which the Douay-Rheims renders "that night, in which nothing could be done"], that is, the Egyptians, who fell into that dark time of the palpable darkness, [[17:13|which came upon them from the lowest and deepest|et ab infimis et ab altissimis supervenientem]] [Denis's text lacks "inferis", "hell", and he takes "ab altissimis" as "from the highest"]: that is, that night was caused partly by earth and water, that is, by vapours and exhalations rising from the earth and the water and thickening the air; and partly by the highest cause, namely the divine command and the ministry of angels, and by the thickness of clouds hindering the lighting of the air, as some say: but it is more truly thought to have come from a supernatural withdrawing of the sun's rays; [[17:13|slept the same sleep|eumdem somnum dormientes]], that is, a heavy and wearisome sleep, like that night;

paras.t: aliquando monstrorum eis in somno terribiliter apparentium, ut dictum est, exagitabantur timore; aliquando animæ deficiebant traductione, id est separatione a corpore. Nam intra triduum illud multi Ægyptiorum præ timore et angustia obierunt; et, ut narrant Hebræi, multi quoque ex filiis Israel, qui nolebant exire Ægyptum, tunc obierunt. Ideoque Deus tam diu protraxit tenebras illas, ne Ægyptii mortem perciperent Hebræorum. Vel, Animæ Ægyptiorum deficiebant traductione, id est, nimia terribilium rerum imaginatione, quasi extra se ducebantur, debilesque fiebant. Subitaneus enim illis Ægyptiis, et insperatus, id est improvisus, timor supervenerat ex plagis eis inflictis. Talis autem timor plus torquet, quoniam jacula prævisa minus feriunt. Nam in Exodo, ubi de plaga tenebrarum illarum tractatur, non legitur Deus præadvisasse Ægyptios de hac plaga : sicque improvise creditur eis supervenisse.
paras.en: [[17:14|Were sometimes molested with the fear of monsters|aliquando monstrorum]] appearing terribly to them in sleep, as has been said; [[17:14|sometimes fainted away, their soul failing them|aliquando animæ deficiebant traductione]], that is, by separation from the body ["traductio", literally a leading across or away]. For within those three days many of the Egyptians died of fear and anguish; and, as the Hebrews relate, many also of the children of Israel who would not go out of Egypt died at that time. And therefore God drew out that darkness so long, that the Egyptians might not see the death of the Hebrews. Or: The souls of the Egyptians fainted by "traductio", that is, through too much imagining of terrible things they were as it were led out of themselves and grew weak. [[17:14|for a sudden|Subitaneus enim]] (to them, the Egyptians) [[17:14|and unlooked for|et insperatus]], that is, unforeseen, [[17:14|fear was come upon them|timor supervenerat]] from the plagues inflicted on them. And such fear torments the more, since darts foreseen strike less hard. For in Exodus, where that plague of darkness is treated, we do not read that God forewarned the Egyptians of this plague: and so it is believed to have come upon them unforeseen.

paras.t: Præterea nox illa vocatur potens : primo, quia tam diu duravit; secundo, quia tenebrosissima fuit; tertio, ratione suorum effectuum prædictorum, per quos ita afflixit Ægyptios.
paras.en: Further, that night is called mighty: first, because it lasted so long; secondly, because it was most dark; thirdly, by reason of its effects mentioned above, by which it so afflicted the Egyptians.

paras.t: Deinde si quisquam ex illis decidisset ex timore in terram, custodiebatur in carcere sine ferro reclusus : id est, in loco quo cecidit, mansit absque vinculis ita detentus, ac si fuisset incarceratus. Nam tribus diebus nullus illorum se movit de loco suo, nec vidit proximum suum. Et sumitur hic si, pro quia, quemadmodum in verbis sequentibus.
paras.en: [[17:15|Moreover, if any of them had fallen down|Deinde si quisquam ex illis decidisset]] from fear to the ground, [[17:15|he was kept shut up in prison without irons|custodiebatur in carcere sine ferro reclusus]]: that is, in the place where he fell he stayed, held without chains as if he had been put in prison. For for three days none of them moved from his place, nor saw his neighbour. And "if" here is taken for "since" [Latin "si" for "quia"; so: since any of them had fallen down], as in the words that follow.

paras.t: Si enim rusticus quis erat, aut pastor pecorum, aut agri laborum operarius, id est cultor agrorum, quales utique multa millia fuerant in Ægypto, præoccupatus, id est improvise præventus, esset tenebris illis, et lapsus in eas in agro, aut alibi ubicumque, ineffugibilem sustinebat necessitatem : id est, inevitabiliter cogebatur manere in loco illo, evadere nequiens, nec cernere valens quo ire. Una enim catena, id est conclusione et detentione, tenebrarum illarum, omnes Ægyptii erant colligati, non valentes locum mutare : et ita erant attoniti ac formidolosi, quod quidquid audierunt, intulit eis timorem : quemadmodum homo vehementer formidans, terretur ex sonitu folii, aut strepitu muris. Hinc subditur :
